The image shows a six-membered cyclohexenolate ring with an O⁻ substituent and an R substituent on the two carbons of the ring double bond, together with a separate methyl vinyl ketone fragment (CH₂=CH–C(=O)–CH₃). The image shows an N-protonated fused bicyclic substrate (an indoline/indolium skeleton) with an S‑methyl substituent and an R substituent, plus triethylamine (Et₃N) as the base. The transition-state drawing contains a tetrahedral silicon atom singly bonded to four oxygen atoms; one of these oxygens is also singly bonded to a carbonyl carbon that is double-bonded to oxygen and single-bonded to an aryl group (Ar), another silicon-bound oxygen is singly bonded to the carbon of an R–CH(R1)–O group, and the remaining two silicon-bound oxygens each terminate in a short dash, interpreted as a substituent bond. The image shows a six-membered pyridinium ring with a positively charged nitrogen at the bottom bearing a benzyl (Bn) substituent; the ring carries three aryl-containing substituents—a –CH₂–Ar group on the carbon adjacent to nitrogen and two directly attached –Ar groups on the upper ring carbons—and curved arrows indicating electron flow that are to be ignored. The image shows tributylphosphine (Bu₃P) and an o‑nitrophenyl selenocyanide (a benzene ring substituted with NO₂ and Se–CN); the curved arrows indicate electron flow and are ignored for counting bonds. The structure is a bicyclo[2.2.1]hept-2-ene skeleton bearing two carbonyl substituents: one carbonyl is attached to a negatively charged nitrogen that bears an –OSO₂Ph group, and the other is attached to an –NHAr group. Adding these gives 9 + 6 + 18 + 11 = 44. Final answer: 44.

The drawing shows an amine fragment R-NH2 and a protonated carbonyl fragment [CH2=O-H]+; ignoring the curved arrows, the only bonds that do not involve hydrogen are the R-N single bond in the amine and the C=O double bond in the protonated carbonyl, while the C-H, N-H, and O-H bonds are excluded because they involve hydrogen and the incipient C-N interaction is only an arrow, not a drawn bond. The image shows a central silicon atom bonded to two fluorine atoms and two R groups, with a separate fluoride ion (F⁻) whose curved arrow points toward a Si–R bond; interpreting that arrow as nucleophilic attack at silicon, the transition state is a pentacoordinate silicon species in which the incoming fluoride is attached to silicon while the Si–R bond is still intact, giving the complex an overall −1 charge. Because silicon now forms five single bonds, its formal charge is 4 − 5 = −1, so the SMILES places the negative charge on silicon: [R][Si-](F)(F)([R])F. Final answer: [R][Si-](F)(F)([R])F.

The structure shown is R–N(H)–C(=O)–O–H, with a base :B and curved arrows indicating proton transfer; ignoring the arrows and all bonds to hydrogen, the remaining bonds are the R–N bond, the N–C bond, the C=O bond, and the C–O bond. Counting each depicted bond once gives a total of four non-hydrogen bonds. Final answer: 4

The image shows an N-methyl-8-azabicyclo[3.2.1]octane-derived transition state bearing two carboxylic acid substituents and curved proton-transfer arrows that are ignored. The bicyclic tropane core contributes 9 non-hydrogen bonds, the N-methyl group adds 1 bond, and each carboxylic acid group contributes 1 C–C bond, 1 C–O bond, and 1 C=O double bond counted as 2 bonds, giving 4 bonds per acid; summing these gives 9 + 1 + 2(4) = 18, with all C–H, O–H, and N–H bonds excluded. Final answer: 18

The image shows two species: dimethyl acetylenedicarboxylate, MeO₂C–C≡C–C(=O)OCH₃, and the methyl thioglycolate thiolate anion, ⁻S–CH₂–C(=O)OMe, with curved arrows indicating electron movement; no S–C bond is actually drawn. The image shows a 9,10-dihydroanthracene-like transition state in which two benzene rings are fused to a central saturated six-membered ring; the upper bridge carbon is a CH2 group (one H is shown), the lower bridge carbon bears an R substituent and a protonated hydroxyl group (OH2+), and the curved arrows indicating hydride migration and C–O bond cleavage are ignored for counting. Adding the single C–R bond and the single C–O bond of the OH2+ group gives 22 + 1 + 1 = 24 bonds, with all C–H and O–H bonds excluded. Final answer: 24

The image shows a benzene ring attached to a carbon that is also bonded to a positively charged nitrogen; that nitrogen is bonded to two methyl groups, and a negative charge is indicated elsewhere. Adding these gives 6 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 10 bonds. Final answer: 10.

The transition-state structure shows two benzene rings, a central C=C bond that bears a CO₂H substituent and a phenyl substituent, and an N–N–O fragment attached to the left benzene ring. Counting every line drawn between non-hydrogen atoms as one bond and ignoring all C–H, N–H, and O–H bonds as well as the curved arrows, the two benzene rings contribute 6 + 6 = 12 C–C bonds; the central alkene contributes 1 C=C bond; the left phenyl is connected to the alkene carbon by 1 C–C bond; the alkene carbon is connected to the carboxyl carbon by 1 C–C bond and to the right phenyl by 1 C–C bond; the CO₂H group contributes 1 C=O and 1 C–O bond; and the N–N–O fragment contributes 1 ring–N, 1 N–N, and 1 N–O bond. The transition-state drawing shows a benzene ring fused to a six-membered heterocycle containing an ether oxygen and a carbonyl group, with substituents R, OH, and a methyl group on the saturated ring carbons; the curved arrows are ignored. Counting each non-hydrogen bond once, the benzene ring contributes 6 bonds, the heterocyclic ring adds 5 new bonds beyond the shared benzene edge, the C=O double bond contributes one additional bond, and the substituent bonds C–R, C–OH, and C–CH3 contribute 3 more bonds; C–H and O–H bonds are excluded. The image shows triphenylphosphine attacking the S–S bond of 2,2′-dipyridyl disulfide: the phosphorus lone pair forms a bond to one sulfur while the S–S bonding electrons move to the other sulfur, which is then protonated by H⁺. This produces a phosphonium cation, (2-pyridylthio)triphenylphosphonium, and neutral 2-pyridinethiol. In SMILES the product mixture is c1ccccc1[P+](c2ccccc2)(c3ccccc3)Sc4ccccn4.Sc1ccccn1. Final answer: c1ccccc1[P+](c2ccccc2)(c3ccccc3)Sc4ccccn4.Sc1ccccn1.

The image shows a benzene ring fused to a six-membered saturated ring that bears an exocyclic C=NH₂⁺ iminium group and an –OSO₂NH₄ substituent; the curved arrows are ignored. The transition-state structure shows a sulfur atom bonded to hydrogen (S–H) positioned to attack a carbonyl carbon, which is double-bonded to oxygen and single-bonded to a second sulfur atom that is bonded to an unspecified substituent (S–R). The image shows a six-membered ring bearing a carbonyl group (C=O), a hydroxyl substituent (C–O), and an exocyclic carbon attached to the ring that is double-bonded to NH and single-bonded to R; the curved arrows and H⁺ are ignored, and all bonds to hydrogen (C–H, O–H, N–H) are excluded. Counting each line between non-hydrogen atoms as one bond gives six ring C–C bonds, one C=O bond, one C–O bond, one C–C bond linking the exocyclic carbon to the ring, one C=N bond, and one C–R bond, so 6 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 11. Final answer: 11.

The image depicts propene (CH3CH=CH2) reacting with Br2/H2O to give the halohydrin CH3CH(OH)CH2Br, the same type of product formed when N-bromosuccinimide is used in aqueous dimethyl sulfoxide; the bromine is on the terminal, less substituted carbon and the hydroxyl group is on the internal, more substituted carbon. Markovnikov addition of an unsymmetrical reagent to an unsymmetrical alkene places the electronegative substituent, here bromine, on the more substituted carbon, so finding bromine on the less substituted carbon corresponds to non-Markovnikov orientation. Final answer: non-Markovnikov.

The image shows 2,3-dimethyl-2-butene, which has a central C=C double bond with four methyl groups attached to the two central carbons, and a separate I₂ molecule; the curved arrows indicate electron flow and are disregarded. The image shows a fused bicyclic transition state in which a six-membered heterocyclic ring containing nitrogen, a ring carbonyl, and an ethyl ester substituent is fused to a benzene-like ring; a C–H bond on the bridgehead carbon is visible but is excluded because it involves hydrogen, and the curved arrows are ignored. The image shows three separate species: a morpholine-substituted enamine at the top, a bis(morpholino) disulfide on the left, and a terminal polysulfide with SH groups on the right. The drawing shows a cyclohexene ring bearing a trimethylsilyloxy group on one alkene carbon and a methyl group on the allylic carbon adjacent to the other alkene carbon, with a Pd(II) center ligated by two acetate groups and interacting with the β-vinylic carbon; ignoring the curved arrows and representing that Pd–alkene interaction as a single Pd–C bond gives the SMILES CC(=O)O[Pd](OC(C)=O)C1=C(O[Si](C)(C)C)CCCC1C. The image shows a protonated carbonyl structure containing a benzene ring attached to an NH group, which is connected by a two-carbon chain to a carbonyl carbon double-bonded to a protonated oxygen; hydrogen atoms and curved arrows are ignored. The image depicts the α-diketone Ar–CO–CO–Ar with hydroxide attacking a carbonyl carbon and a curved arrow indicating that the C=O π electrons of the attacked carbonyl are relocated onto oxygen, giving the tetrahedral alkoxide Ar–CO–C(OH)(O⁻)–Ar; taking Ar as phenyl, this corresponds to the SMILES O=C(c1ccccc1)C(O)([O-])c2ccccc2. The image shows a five-membered cyclopentene ring substituted with an O–TiCl₃ group and a –CH₂–CH(SiMe₃) side chain, plus a separate chloride ion; ignoring the curved arrows, the ring contains one C=C and four C–C single bonds, the O–TiCl₃ group contributes one C–O, one O–Ti, and three Ti–Cl bonds, and the side chain contributes two C–C bonds, one C–Si bond, and three Si–C bonds in SiMe₃, while the chloride ion contributes no bonds. The image shows a benzene ring fused to a six-membered heterocyclic ring that contains one nitrogen, a ring carbonyl group, and an ethoxycarbonyl substituent, with one benzene C–H hydrogen drawn explicitly; ignoring the curved arrows, the skeleton is a 4-quinolone core with the CO2Et group on the carbon adjacent to the ring carbonyl, corresponding to ethyl 4-oxo-1,4-dihydroquinoline-3-carboxylate. The image shows a cyclohexadiene (upper six-membered ring with two C=C bonds and a C–H on a saturated carbon) and a phenyl radical (lower benzene ring with a radical dot); the curved arrow from the C–H bond to the radical center represents a hydrogen-atom transfer. The transition-state drawing shows a hypervalent iodine(V) periodane species in which iodine is bonded to the aryl carbon of a benzene ring, to the carbonyl oxygen of an ortho-carboxylate group forming a five-membered ring, and to three acetate ligands (one labeled AcO with a curved arrow and two labeled OAc), while an alcohol substrate R1R2CH–OH is shown attacking iodine via a curved arrow from its oxygen lone pair. The image shows an enolate nucleophile in its oxyanion form, R-CH=C(O⁻)-R¹, and a second carbonyl compound R³-C(=O)-R². The transition-state structure drawn is R–C(=O)–NH–NH–SO₂Ar with a base B: shown approaching a hydrogen, and the curved arrows should be ignored. Final answer: 11.

The image shows an R group attached by a single bond to a carbon, that carbon joined by a triple bond to a second carbon, and the second carbon attached by a single bond to bromine; a butyl anion (Bu⁻) is depicted with a curved arrow toward bromine, and another curved arrow is drawn from the triple-bond region toward bromine, but these arrows are mechanistic arrows and are disregarded. The image shows a cyclohexane-1,2-diol transition state in which one ring oxygen is deprotonated and bound to lead, the adjacent ring carbon bears an OH, an acetate anion (AcO⁻) is positioned to abstract that OH proton, and the lead center bears two acetate-derived ligands—the explicitly drawn one is protonated on its carbonyl oxygen and the Pb(OAc)₂ label supplies a second acetate ligand. The image shows a neutral molecule in which a central carbon is bonded to two generic substituents R1 and R2, to a nitrile group, and to the nitrogen of a carbamic acid fragment (-NH-C(=O)OH); the curved arrows are ignored. The image shows a transition-state assembly containing a 2-furoic acid fragment (furan ring plus carboxylic acid group), tributylamine (NBu3), an N-ethyl-2-bromopyridinium cation, and a tetrafluoroborate (BF4−) counterion; the curved arrows indicate proton transfer and nucleophilic attack but are ignored for counting. The image depicts a six-membered cyclic ketone: a cyclohexanone ring with a chlorine substituent on one α-carbon and an alkoxide base (OR⁻) approaching the hydrogen on the other α-carbon, with curved arrows indicating deprotonation/enolate formation. The figure shows three classes of hexane isomers (all C6H14): Class I contains the most branched isomers (2,2-dimethylbutane and 2,3-dimethylbutane), Class II contains moderately branched isomers (2-methylpentane and 3-methylpentane), and Class III contains the unbranched n-hexane. For constitutional isomers of an alkane, boiling point is governed by the strength of London dispersion forces, which depend on the molecular surface area available for intermolecular contact; increased branching reduces surface area and makes the molecule more compact, thereby weakening these forces and lowering the boiling point. Thus, the straight-chain n-hexane in Class III has the highest boiling point, the singly branched isomers in Class II have intermediate boiling points, and the most highly branched isomers in Class I have the lowest boiling point. Final answer: III > II > I

The image shows four aromatic carboxylic acids: I is 2,6-dihydroxybenzoic acid with hydroxyl groups on both ortho positions relative to the carboxylic acid, II is salicylic acid (2-hydroxybenzoic acid) with one ortho hydroxyl, III is 3-hydroxybenzoic acid (meta), and IV is 4-hydroxybenzoic acid (para). Acidity depends on stabilization of the carboxylate anion after deprotonation: an ortho hydroxyl can form an intramolecular hydrogen bond with the carboxylate, stabilizing the conjugate base, so II is more acidic than the meta and para isomers; I has two ortho hydroxyl groups that can both hydrogen-bond to the carboxylate, giving even greater stabilization and making it the strongest acid. For the meta and para isomers, the hydroxyl group is net electron-donating by resonance, which destabilizes the carboxylate anion and reduces acidity, and this resonance donation is stronger at the para position than at the meta position, so III is more acidic than IV. Therefore the decreasing order of acidity is I > II > III > IV. Final answer: I > II > III > IV

The image shows a five-membered cyclopentanone ring (a pentagon with the carbonyl carbon at one vertex); the ring carbon next to the carbonyl bears an H, an O- substituent, and an N-sulfonyl triazene group (N=N-N-SO2Me). The image shows a Corey–Winter olefination fragmentation intermediate: a 1,3-dioxolane ring bearing R and R1 substituents, one ring oxygen carrying a negative charge, and the acetal carbon attached to sulfur, which is bonded to a trimethyl phosphite unit with a positive charge on phosphorus; a curved arrow runs from sulfur toward phosphorus. The image shows a symmetrical 1,2-diaryl-α-diketone, which is benzil when each Ar represents a phenyl group: the two carbonyl carbons are directly bonded to each other, and each carbonyl carbon also bears an aryl substituent; the hydroxide ion and the curved arrows are mechanistic notation and are ignored for the connectivity. The image shows the enol form of ethyl acetoacetate, CH₃C(OH)=CHC(=O)OCH₂CH₃, and a protonated aryl aldehyde, ArCH=O⁺H, with curved arrows indicating nucleophilic attack of the C=C bond on the carbonyl carbon and electron movement onto the protonated oxygen; disregarding the arrows and excluding every bond to hydrogen, each bond order is counted separately. The image shows a Criegee-like transition-state structure containing a cyclohexyl group attached to a tetrahedral carbon that also bears a methyl substituent, an OH group, and an O–O linkage; the O–O links to a carbonyl carbon that is double bonded to oxygen and single bonded to a chlorinated benzene ring. The image shows an ortho-disubstituted benzene ring: one substituent is a styryl carboxylic acid fragment, –CH=C(CO₂H)(Ph), and the other is a diazonium–water group, –N=N⁺(OH₂), attached to adjacent ring carbons. The image shows a dicobalt hexacarbonyl fragment, (CO)₃Co–Co(CO)₃, in which the two cobalt atoms are bonded to each other and each cobalt carries three terminal carbonyl ligands; a bridging alkyne ligand lies between the cobalt atoms, forming a four-membered Co–C=C–Co ring. The structure contains a cyclohexane ring, a hydroxyl group, and a –CH₂–N=N–OH₂⁺ substituent. Adding these gives 4 + 3 + 3 + 6 + 6 = 22. Final answer: 22.

The image shows a positively charged 1,4-dihydroquinoline-like ring fused to benzene, with an OH and R2 on one alkene carbon, R1 on the adjacent carbon, an N–H group, and a saturated benzylic C–H; the curved arrows indicate that the benzylic C–H σ electrons form a new C=C bond within the ring and the N–H σ electrons form a new N=C bond, which requires the original alkene C=C bond to break and the C–OH bond to cleave, expelling OH− and the two protons and thereby aromatizing the system to a neutral 2-R1-3-R2-quinoline. Final answer: [R1]c1c([R2])cc2ccccc2n1

The image shows a palladium center bonded to bromine and to an ortho-substituted phenyl ring; that phenyl ring also bears a CH2O– linker to a second phenyl ring, which is substituted with a –C≡C–CH2–CH2–OH chain and a –CH2–CO2CH3 group. Treating the Pd–phenyl and Pd–Br bonds as ordinary single bonds, the left phenyl as [Pd]c1ccccc1CO–, the ether oxygen as the bridge to the right ring, and the right ring as Oc2c(C#CCCO)ccc2CC(=O)OC gives the SMILES [Pd](Br)(c1ccccc1COc2c(C#CCCO)ccc2CC(=O)OC). Final answer: [Pd](Br)(c1ccccc1COc2c(C#CCCO)ccc2CC(=O)OC).

The image shows a transition-state structure consisting of a benzene ring fused to a cyclopropane ring, with the bridge carbon of the cyclopropane attached to a methyl ester group, CO2CH3; the curved arrows are disregarded as instructed, and C–H bonds are excluded. The benzene ring contains six C–C bonds, the cyclopropane bridge contributes two additional C–C bonds beyond the shared benzene edge, the carbonyl carbon is attached to the bridge carbon by one C–C bond, and the ester group contains one C=O, one C–O, and one O–CH3 bond. Summing these gives 6 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 12 bonds. Final answer: 12

The image shows a phosphorus center labeled Ph₃P⁺ bonded to three phenyl rings and to the left nitrogen of a di(ethoxycarbonyl)hydrazine fragment, while the oxygen of a secondary alcohol R₁R₂CH–O⁻ attacks that phosphorus; the proton has been transferred to the right-hand nitrogen, giving an N–H there. Ignoring the curved arrows and treating the forming P–O and breaking P–N interactions as ordinary bonds, with the phosphorus retaining its positive charge and the alkoxy oxygen as [O⁻], gives the SMILES [R1]C([R2])[O-][P+](c1ccccc1)(c1ccccc1)(c1ccccc1)N(C(=O)OCC)N(C(=O)OCC). Final answer: [R1]C([R2])[O-][P+](c1ccccc1)(c1ccccc1)(c1ccccc1)N(C(=O)OCC)N(C(=O)OCC)

The structure contains a benzene ring, a pyrrole ring, an amide linkage, and two methyl ester groups, and the curved arrows are ignored. Treating the phenyl ring as benzene gives three C=C double bonds and three C–C single bonds; the pyrrole ring contributes two C=C double bonds and three C–C/N single bonds. The connecting single bonds are phenyl–N, phenyl–C(=O), amide N–C(=O), pyrrole carbonyl C–ring, pyrrole N–CH2, and CH2–C(=O), and each methyl ester contributes one C=O double bond, one C–O single bond, and one O–CH3 single bond. That gives 16 single bonds and 8 double bonds between non-hydrogen atoms, so counting each bond according to its multiplicity yields 16 + 8×2 = 32. Final answer: 32.

The image shows 3,4-dihydro-2H-pyran (DHP), a six-membered cyclic enol ether, reacting with a primary alcohol RCH2OH under anhydrous acidic conditions. This is the standard acid-catalyzed protection of an alcohol as a tetrahydropyranyl (THP) ether: protonation of the enol ether double bond generates a resonance-stabilized oxocarbenium ion at the carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen, the alcohol oxygen attacks this electrophilic carbon, and deprotonation yields the ether. Final answer: the tetrahydropyranyl ether RCH2-O-(tetrahydropyran-2-yl).

The image shows a transition-state diagram with two components: a cyclohexanone-derived species on the left and an N-methylsulfonyl azide (N≡N–N–S(=O)₂–Me) on the right; the curved arrows indicate electron movement and are ignored. Counting only non-hydrogen bonds and treating multiple bonds by their order, the left component contains six C–C single bonds in the ring plus two C=O double bonds, giving 6 + 2 + 2 = 10 bonds. The right component contains an N≡N triple bond (3), an N–N single bond (1), an N–S single bond (1), two S=O double bonds (4), and an S–C single bond to the methyl group (1), giving 3 + 1 + 1 + 4 + 1 = 10 bonds. Adding both components yields 10 + 10 = 20 bonds. Final answer: 20.

The image shows a concerted hetero-Diels–Alder transition state in which a 1-methoxy-1,3-butadiene reacts with ethyl glyoxylate: the carbonyl carbon forms a bond to the methoxy-bearing diene terminus, the carbonyl oxygen forms a bond to the unsubstituted diene terminus, and the diene π system shifts to place a C=C bond between the two internal diene carbons. Ignoring the curved arrows, the resulting six-membered dihydropyran ring contains an oxygen atom, a ring carbon bearing the ethoxycarbonyl group, an adjacent ring carbon bearing the methoxy group, and a C=C bond between the remaining ring carbons, which is represented by the SMILES O1C(C(=O)OCC)C(OC)C=CC1. Final answer: O1C(C(=O)OCC)C(OC)C=CC1

The image shows a phenyl ring attached to a benzylic carbon that bears an R group and a potassium alkoxide group (-O⁻ K⁺). The curved arrows inside the six-membered ring are the standard benzene-resonance arrows that shift the π bonds to the alternative Kekulé form; no atoms are added, removed, or rearranged, and the potassium counterion remains associated with the alkoxide oxygen. Therefore the connectivity after electron relocation is unchanged, giving the same potassium benzylic alkoxide. Final answer: [K+].[R]C([O-])c1ccccc1

The image shows an anionic molecule consisting of an ortho-substituted benzene ring bearing a methyl ester (C(=O)OMe) and a deprotonated amide group (N(−)−C(=O)−), where the amide carbonyl is attached at the 2-position of an N-(methoxycarbonylmethyl)pyrrole ring. Ignoring the curved arrows, the atoms and bonds are: a pyrrole ring with a CH₂CO₂Me substituent on nitrogen and a C(=O)N(−)−phenyl substituent at the adjacent carbon, and the phenyl ring is ortho-substituted with a methyl ester. Encoding this connectivity in SMILES gives COC(=O)Cn1c(C(=O)[N-]c2ccccc2C(=O)OC)ccc1. Final answer: COC(=O)Cn1c(C(=O)[N-]c2ccccc2C(=O)OC)ccc1

The image shows a six-membered carbon ring drawn with alternating single and double bonds, where one ring carbon is bonded to an –OK substituent and an R group; the curved arrows are ignored. Counting each bond by its order, the ring has six C–C bonds: three single and three double, giving 3(1) + 3(2) = 9 bonds. The substituents add three more single bonds: C–O, O–K, and C–R, giving 3 additional bonds. No bonds involving hydrogen are included. Therefore, the total number of bonds is 9 + 3 = 12. Final answer: 12.

The transition-state drawing shows a five-membered S–O–C–C–N ring bearing a sulfonyl group (S double-bonded to two oxygens and single-bonded to the ring oxygen and to N), an N–CO₂Me substituent, and two phenyl groups on the two ring carbons; D is deuterium, an isotope of hydrogen, so any C–D or N–D interaction is excluded, and the curved arrows are ignored. Counting each bond (single, double, or triple) as one connection and omitting all bonds to H/D, the heavy-atom bonds are two S=O, one S–O, one S–N, one O–C, one C–C, one C–N, two C–Ph, one N–C(=O), one C=O, one C–O, one O–Me, and six C–C bonds in each phenyl ring, giving 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 12 = 25. Final answer: 25.

The image shows a benzopyran-like ring in which the carbon bearing the phenyl substituent also carries an exocyclic O⁻ group; a curved arrow starts from that O⁻ and points to the same carbon, while a second curved arrow shows the adjacent C–O ring bond breaking with the electron pair moving onto the ring oxygen. This arrow pushing corresponds to collapse of a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate: the exocyclic O⁻ forms a C=O double bond at that carbon, the C–O ring bond cleaves, and the ring oxygen becomes a phenoxide anion, leaving a β-diketone side chain attached to the aromatic ring. The resulting structure is therefore a phenolate with an ortho –C(=O)–CH₂–C(=O)–Ph substituent. Final answer: [O-]c1ccccc1C(=O)CC(=O)c2ccccc2

The transition-state drawing shows a cyanide (NC) group, two aryl substituents labeled Ar, a negatively charged oxygen, and a carbon bearing Ar, H, and OH; the curved arrows are mechanistic notation and are ignored. Because the aryl groups are represented only as Ar, only their C–Ar attachment bonds are counted and no internal aryl bonds are included. Counting every non-hydrogen bond and treating a triple bond as three bonds, the bonds are: C≡N (3), the forming C–C bond from the cyanide carbon to the central carbon (1), central C–Ar (1), central C–O (1), central C–C to the CH(Ar)OH carbon (1), C–Ar on that carbon (1), and C–O of the hydroxyl group (1); C–H and O–H bonds are excluded. The sum is 3 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 9. Final answer: 9.

The image shows an alcohol R-OH attacking a carbonyl carbon that is bonded to an amide nitrogen; that nitrogen is bonded to a carbon bearing R1, R2, and a C(=O)NH2 group. Interpreting the transition state as the tetrahedral intermediate in which the C=O π bond has broken to give an alkoxide, the attacked carbon is four-coordinate, bonded to the amide nitrogen, to the oxygen of the R-OH nucleophile, to an [O-], and to an implicit hydrogen; the amide nitrogen retains its implicit N-H and the terminal group is C(=O)NH2. Final answer: [R]OC([O-])(N(C(R1)(R2)C(=O)N))

The image shows a tetrahedral transition-state-like structure built on a 3,4-dihydroisoquinolin-1-one core: a benzene ring fused to a six-membered lactam, where the carbon next to nitrogen carries a C(=O)R acyl substituent and the carbon next to the aromatic ring bears both a methoxy group and a negatively charged oxygen. Encoding this connectivity in SMILES, with the negative charge on the alkoxide and the acyl substituent represented as C(=O)R, gives the string O=C1NC(C(=O)R)C([O-])(OC)c2ccccc21. Final answer: O=C1NC(C(=O)R)C([O-])(OC)c2ccccc21

The image shows an ozone molecule in a polar resonance form (one O–O single bond and one O=O double bond, with formal charges on oxygen) positioned above a tetrasubstituted alkene (a C=C double bond with four carbon substituents), and the curved arrows indicating electron movement should be ignored. Counting all drawn covalent bonds while excluding any bonds to hydrogen: ozone contributes 2 bonds, and the alkene contributes 1 C=C double bond plus 4 C–C single bonds for a total of 5 bonds, so 2 + 5 = 7 bonds overall. Final answer: 7

The transition-state drawing shows the heavy-atom framework Ar¹–N=N–CH(Ar²)–C(C(=O)OR²)(C(=N–N⁺(X)H₂)R¹); ignoring the curved arrows and all bonds to hydrogen, the non-H bonds are Ar¹–N, N=N, N–C, C–Ar², C–C to the central carbon, C–C(=O), C=O, C–O, O–R², C–C(=N), C–R¹, C=N, N–N, and N–X. Counting each single, double, or triple bond as one bond gives 14 bonds in total. Final answer: 14

The image shows an N-acyloxy amide skeleton in which a carbonyl carbon attached to R1 is bonded to a nitrogen that also bears a hydrogen, and that nitrogen is bonded to an oxygen that is part of a second carbonyl group attached to R2; the curved arrows indicate base-induced proton abstraction and electron redistribution, but they are to be ignored for the molecular connectivity. Reading the atoms in the order R1–C(=O)–N(H)–O–C(=O)–R2 and using standard SMILES conventions, where the nitrogen has one implicit hydrogen, gives the expression R1C(=O)NOC(=O)R2. Final answer: R1C(=O)NOC(=O)R2

The structure contains a cyclohexenone ring with a carbonyl C=O and an enolic C=C–OH group, plus a methanesulfonyl azide fragment N≡N⁺–N⁻–S(=O)₂Me. Excluding all C–H and O–H bonds and ignoring the curved arrows, the ring and its oxygen substituents contribute one C=O double bond (2), one C=C double bond (2), one C–O single bond (1), and five C–C single bonds (5), giving 10 bonds. The azide/sulfonyl portion contributes one N≡N triple bond (3), one N–N single bond (1), one N–S single bond (1), two S=O double bonds (4), and one S–C single bond (1), giving another 10 bonds. Adding these gives 10 + 10 = 20 bonds. Final answer: 20.

The image shows a five-membered ring in which one ring carbon is bonded to both an ethoxy group and a negatively charged oxygen, while the adjacent ring carbon carries a CO2Et group; the curved arrow from O− to that substituted ring carbon and the arrow showing the C–OEt bond breaking toward oxygen represent collapse of a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate, in which the O− lone pair forms a C=O double bond and ethoxide is expelled. Therefore the carbon bearing the O−/OEt substituents becomes a ring carbonyl, yielding ethyl 2-oxocyclopentanecarboxylate. Final answer: CCOC(=O)C1CCCC1=O.

The image shows a cyclohexane ring bearing an ethoxycarbonyl substituent and an adjacent ethyl ester; an ethoxide ion abstracts the α-hydrogen on the carbon attached to the ethyl ester, the C–H bond electrons form a new C=C bond between that α-carbon and the ester carbonyl carbon, and the C=O π electrons move onto the carbonyl oxygen, producing an ester enolate (and ethanol as the conjugate acid). Assuming the drawn ring is six-membered, the resulting enolate is CCOC(=C1CCCCC1C(=O)OCC)[O-]. Final answer: CCOC(=C1CCCCC1C(=O)OCC)[O-]

Ignoring the curved arrows, the image shows a tetrahedral carbon center bonded to a chlorine atom, a carbonyl carbon that is double-bonded to oxygen and single-bonded to chlorine, a negatively charged oxygen, and an oxygen attached to a sulfonium sulfur; the sulfonium sulfur is drawn with one methyl substituent, but in the DMSO-derived dimethylsulfonio group it carries two methyl groups and a +1 formal charge, while the alkoxide oxygen carries a -1 formal charge, so the neutral connectivity is C[S+](C)OC(Cl)(C(=O)Cl)[O-]. Final answer: C[S+](C)OC(Cl)(C(=O)Cl)[O-]

The image shows an amine labeled R–NH₂ and a benzene ring bearing a fluorine at the carbon under attack, a nitro group ortho to that carbon, and another nitro group para to that carbon, which is 1‑fluoro‑2,4‑dinitrobenzene; the curved arrows only indicate electron flow in the SNAr transition state, and ignoring them leaves the two unconnected species. The amine is written as [R]N and the aromatic substrate as O=[N+]([O-])c1ccc(F)c([N+](=O)[O-])c1, so the transition-state structure, treated as a non-bonded complex, is [R]N.O=[N+]([O-])c1ccc(F)c([N+](=O)[O-])c1. Final answer: [R]N.O=[N+]([O-])c1ccc(F)c([N+](=O)[O-])c1

The image shows a benzene ring bearing a negatively charged oxygen substituent and, on the adjacent ortho carbon, a carbon group labeled CHCl; a second chlorine atom is shown with a curved arrow pointing toward that carbon, indicating formation of a second C–Cl bond. Ignoring the curved arrows, the CHCl carbon plus the additional chlorine gives an ortho-dichloromethyl substituent (–CHCl₂) on a phenoxide ring, so the structure is 2-(dichloromethyl)phenoxide. The SMILES is written by attaching [O-] to one aromatic ring carbon and the C(Cl)Cl group to the ortho ring carbon. Final answer: [O-]c1ccccc1C(Cl)Cl.

The image depicts a protonated ketone in which a phenyl group is directly attached to a carbonyl carbon, that carbonyl oxygen bears a proton and a positive charge, and the carbonyl carbon is connected by a two-carbon chain to a second phenyl group, corresponding to protonated 1,3-diphenylpropan-1-one. Representing the protonated carbonyl as C(=[OH+]), the two phenyl rings as c1ccccc1 and c2ccccc2, and the two methylene carbons as CC gives the SMILES c1ccccc1C(=[OH+])CCc2ccccc2. Final answer: c1ccccc1C(=[OH+])CCc2ccccc2

The image shows an ortho-disubstituted benzene bearing a carboxylic acid group and an amide group (–C(=O)NHR), with two hydroxide ions present: one hydroxide attacks the amide carbonyl carbon and the other removes the carboxylic acid proton. Counting each bond once (so a double bond counts as one bond) and excluding all bonds involving hydrogen, the benzene ring contributes 6 C–C bonds, the two ring-to-substituent C–C bonds contribute 2, the carboxylic acid group contributes its C=O, C–O, and ring C–C bonds for 3, the amide group contributes its C=O, C–N, N–R, and ring C–C bonds for 4, and the attacking hydroxide contributes the forming C–O bond to the carbonyl carbon for 1; the other hydroxide forms only an O–H bond, which is excluded. Adding these gives 6 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 1 = 14. Final answer: 14.

The image shows a sulfonium species—sulfur bears a formal positive charge with an associated negative counterion—linked through oxygen to a secondary carbon fragment R1R2CH–O–. The curved arrows indicate that the O–S sigma bond breaks with its electrons moving onto sulfur while the α C–H bond is cleaved, converting the C–O single bond into a C=O double bond; this is the final elimination step of a Swern-type oxidation of an alcohol to a carbonyl. Consequently, the alcohol carbon is oxidized to a ketone/aldehyde and the sulfonium reagent is reduced to dimethyl sulfide. Final answer: R1C(=O)R2.CSC

The image shows two separate species: a neutral nitrous acid molecule, H–O–N=O, and a cationic species, [H₂O–N=O]⁺, in which an oxonium oxygen is bonded to a nitroso nitrogen; no covalent bond connects the two fragments once the curved mechanistic arrows are removed. Nitrous acid is represented by the SMILES ON=O, and the cationic fragment is represented by [OH2+]N=O, so the overall non-covalent assembly is written as the dot-separated combination of these two SMILES strings. Final answer: ON=O.[OH2+]N=O

The image shows a 2-phenyl-1,2,3,4-tetrahydroquinoline skeleton with a CO2H group at C4; the curved arrow from the C3–H bond to C4 represents a 1,2-hydride shift that moves the positive charge to C3, and the water arrow represents nucleophilic capture of that C3 carbocation to give a protonated alcohol (oxonium) at C3. Final answer: c1ccc2c(c1)NC(c3ccccc3)C([OH2+])C2

The image depicts an molecule in which an acetate group is linked through its ester oxygen to a carbon bearing both an R¹ substituent and a negatively charged oxygen; that same carbon is attached to a second carbon bearing an R group and an SO₂Ar sulfone group, giving the connectivity CH₃C(=O)–O–C(R¹)([O⁻])–C(R)(H)–SO₂Ar. Ignoring the curved arrows, the corresponding SMILES represents the generic substituents as [R], [R1], and [Ar] and the sulfone as S(=O)(=O). Final answer: CC(=O)OC([O-])([R1])C([R])S(=O)(=O)[Ar]

The image shows a tetrahedral carbon attached to R, an alkoxide oxygen bearing a negative charge, an azide group (N3), and a chlorine atom, with a curved arrow from the alkoxide lone pair toward the carbon and a curved arrow from the C–Cl bond toward chlorine; this indicates concerted C=O double-bond formation and C–Cl bond cleavage, converting the alkoxy/halo/azide species into an acyl azide and a chloride ion. The azide substituent is represented in SMILES as N=[N+]=[N-], and the leaving group is [Cl-]. Final answer: [R]C(=O)N=[N+]=[N-].[Cl-]

The structure contains a positively charged nitrogen bonded to two aryl groups (Ar¹ and Ar), to an oxygen, and to a carbon; the oxygen and carbon are also bonded to each other, forming a three-membered N–O–C ring, and the carbon is bonded to a benzene ring that carries a negative charge. Disregarding the curved arrows and excluding any C–H bonds, the bonds are counted as follows: N–Ar¹ (1), N–Ar (1), N–O (1), N–C (1), O–C (1), C–phenyl (1), and the benzene ring contributes three single and three double C–C bonds (6). Adding these gives 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 6 = 12. Final answer: 12.

The image depicts a transition-state assembly composed of a cyclohexene ring that carries a trialkylsilyloxy substituent on one carbon of its C=C bond and an aryl carboxylic acid (ArCOOH) whose hydroxyl group is oriented toward the alkene. Ignoring the curved arrows, the underlying connectivity is that of a (cyclohex-1-en-1-yloxy)trialkylsilane fragment and an ArCOOH fragment held together as a single associated complex; the silyl enol ether portion is written as [R3Si]OC1=CCCCC1 and the carboxylic acid portion as [Ar]C(=O)O, with the two fragments separated by a dot because they are not covalently bonded to each other. Final answer: [R3Si]OC1=CCCCC1.[Ar]C(=O)O

The image shows a tetrahedral carbon atom bonded to R1, R2, an OH group, and a SiR3 group; a separate R species carries a negative charge and is depicted by a curved arrow pointing toward the hydroxyl hydrogen, while a second curved arrow points from the O–H bond toward oxygen. Because these curved arrows are only electron-flow notation and the question says to ignore them, the R− species remains unbound and the O–H bond remains intact, so the underlying structure is the alcohol R1R2C(OH)SiR3 together with the R− anion as a separate component, with the central carbon connected to R1, R2, O, and Si, the silicon atom bonded to three R groups, and the oxygen retaining its hydrogen. In SMILES notation this is written as [R-].[R1]C([R2])(O)[Si]([R])([R])[R]. Final answer: [R-].[R1]C([R2])(O)[Si]([R])([R])[R].

The image shows a bicyclic oxazaborolidine–borane transition state in which a five-membered pyrrolidine ring is fused to an oxazaborolidine ring (N–B(R)–O–C(Ph)₂–C(H)–N), with the nitrogen also coordinated to a BH₃ unit and with two phenyl groups attached to the same carbon. Counting every non-hydrogen bond once, the fused ring system contributes 9 unique bonds (5 in the pyrrolidine ring plus 4 additional oxazaborolidine ring bonds, because the shared N–C bond is counted only once), the B–R substituent adds 1, the N→BH₃ coordinate bond adds 1 (arrow ignored), the two C–Ph ipso bonds add 2, and the two phenyl rings add 12 C–C bonds (6 each), while all B–H, C–H, and N–H bonds are excluded; because R is unspecified, only the B–R bond is counted. Thus 9 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 12 = 25. Final answer: 25

The image shows an anionic aluminum center bearing a negative charge, two R substituents, one hydrogen, and a bond to a carbonyl oxygen; that oxygen is attached to a carbonyl carbon that also bears R1 and is connected to an R–C≡C– fragment. Ignoring the curved electron-pushing arrows, the structure is an aluminate–ynone adduct, and the coordinate O→Al bond is represented in SMILES by the formal-charge pair [O+][Al-] to preserve valence. Therefore the connectivity is encoded as [R]C#CC(=[O+][Al-]([R])([R])[H])[R1]. Final answer: [R]C#CC(=[O+][Al-]([R])([R])[H])[R1]

The image shows a benzene ring attached to an oxygen, that oxygen is coordinated to an AlCl₃ unit, and an acylium-like fragment R–C≡O⁺ is also present; the curved arrows are ignored. Counting all non-hydrogen bonds by bond order: the benzene ring has three single and three double C–C bonds, giving 3 + 3(2) = 9 bonds; the ring-to-oxygen bond is one single bond; the oxygen-to-aluminum coordinate bond is one single bond; AlCl₃ contributes three Al–Cl single bonds; the R substituent is attached by one single C–R bond; and the carbon–oxygen bond in the acylium fragment is a triple bond, counting as three bonds. Adding these gives 9 + 1 + 1 + 3 + 1 + 3 = 18. Final answer: 18.

The image depicts a base (B:) abstracting the alpha hydrogen of a carbonyl compound, with curved arrows showing the C–H bond electrons forming a C=C double bond between the alpha carbon and the carbonyl carbon and the C=O pi electrons moving onto the oxygen to give an enolate. This transformation produces an enolate anion containing a C=C double bond and an alkoxide oxygen, which can be represented generically as [R]C=C([O-])[R1]. Final answer: [R]C=C([O-])[R1]

The structure is a central carbon bonded to three methyl groups and to an –OH₂ group, with an overall +1 charge on the oxygen, corresponding to protonated tert-butanol (tert-butyl oxonium). In SMILES, the tert-butyl skeleton is written as CC(C)(C), and the protonated water ligand is [OH2+], giving the full expression CC(C)(C)[OH2+]. Final answer: CC(C)(C)[OH2+]

The image depicts the carbonyl oxygen of the N‑phenethyl amide R–C(=O)NHCH₂CH₂Ph attacking the phosphorus atom of POCl₃, while a P–Cl bond breaks and chloride departs. This step gives an O‑phosphorylated amide ion pair in which the carbonyl oxygen is now bonded to a P(=O)Cl₂ group, written as [R–C(=[O⁺]–P(=O)Cl₂)–NHCH₂CH₂Ph] Cl⁻. Final answer: the immediate product is the oxophosphonium chloride salt [R–C(=[O⁺]–P(=O)Cl₂)–NHCH₂CH₂Ph] Cl⁻.

The image shows an ion-pair transition state made up of an N-acyliminium cation and a separate acetate anion. The cation contains a positively charged nitrogen bonded to R1 and an acyl group C(=O)R, and it must be double-bonded to the carbon bearing R2 so that nitrogen carries a +1 charge; that carbon also bears an acetoxy substituent, –OC(=O)CH3. The counterion is the acetate ion, CH3CO2−. Therefore the SMILES, using generic R labels, is [R]C(=O)[N+]([R1])=C([R2])OC(C)=O.CC(=O)[O-]. Final answer: [R]C(=O)[N+]([R1])=C([R2])OC(C)=O.CC(=O)[O-]

The image shows a benzene ring fused to a six-membered lactone, giving a dihydrocoumarin (chroman-2-one) skeleton; the lactone ring contains a carbonyl carbon, a ring oxygen, a CH(R) carbon, and a C(OH)(CH3) carbon, where the unlabeled terminal bond on the hydroxyl-bearing carbon is assumed to be a methyl group as is standard in skeletal structures, and the curved arrows indicate base-induced deprotonation and carbonyl polarization and are ignored for the structural SMILES. Starting from the dihydrocoumarin parent O=C1CCc2ccccc2O1, the hydrogen at the 3-position is replaced by the generic R substituent and the two hydrogens at the 4-position are replaced by OH and CH3, yielding the substituted structure O=C1C([R])C(C)(O)c2ccccc2O1. Final answer: O=C1C([R])C(C)(O)c2ccccc2O1

The image shows a protonated ketone transition-state structure with two phenyl rings connected by a three-carbon chain that contains a C=O group, an O–H bond, and a positive charge on oxygen; ignoring the curved arrows and excluding all bonds to hydrogen, each phenyl ring has six C–C single bonds and three C=C double bonds, giving 9 bonds per ring, and each ring is attached to the chain by one C–C single bond, so each aromatic side contributes 10 non-hydrogen bonds; the remaining chain contributes the C=O double bond (2), the C(=O)–CH2 single bond (1), and the CH2–CH2 single bond (1). Adding these gives 10 + 10 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 24. Final answer: 24

The image shows a benzene ring with two adjacent substituents: a neutral amino group (NH2) and a side chain of the form –C(R1)=C(R2)[NH2+], where the side-chain nitrogen is protonated and positively charged. The image shows a transition-state structure consisting of a phenyl group attached to an NH, which is attached to another NH, which is attached to a naphthalen-1-yl group, forming N-phenyl-N'-(naphthalen-1-yl)hydrazine (ignoring the curved arrows). The image shows a protonated indolinium ring connected through a CH2 group to an N-benzoyl imine (C=N–C(=O)Ph); a curved arrow starts from an O⁻ and points to the benzoyl carbonyl carbon, while an H⁺ arrow points to the imine nitrogen. The image shows an N-substituted carbamic acid with the covalent connectivity R–N(H)–C(=O)–O–H; the curved arrows indicate electron movement and the base B is not part of the covalent framework, so both are ignored. The image shows a five-membered cyclic transition-state structure containing, in ring order, a carbon bearing substituents R1 and R2, an NH group, a carbonyl C=O, an oxygen, and a C=NH group, with the C=NH carbon bonded back to the R1/R2 carbon. The image shows an aniline fragment (Ph–NH₂) on the left and a protonated benzaldehyde fragment (Ph–CH=O⁺–H) on the right, with curved arrows indicating electron movement that must be ignored. The image shows the Dess–Martin periodane-derived transition state for oxidation of a secondary alcohol: a hypervalent iodine(V) center in a benziodoxolone ring (benzene fused to a five-membered I–O–C(=O) ring), bearing three acetoxy ligands, with the oxygen of R1R2CHOH coordinated to iodine. The image shows a phenethyl-substituted secondary amide, R–C(=O)–NH–CH2–CH2–Ph, whose carbonyl oxygen is forming a bond to the phosphorus of phosphoryl chloride; the phosphorus is drawn double-bonded to one oxygen and single-bonded to three chlorine atoms, with one P–Cl bond indicated as breaking. The image shows a transition-state arrangement for a Michael addition between a 2-R-cyclohexanone enolate and methyl vinyl ketone (CH2=CHCOCH3); the curved arrows indicate electron movement but are not part of the structural connectivity. The image shows triethyl phosphonoacetate, (EtO)₂P(=O)CH₂CO₂Et, with its α-hydrogen being approached by the bicyclic amidine base DBU (1,8-diazabicyclo[5.4.0]undec-7-ene); ignoring the curved arrows leaves the two neutral molecules. The drawing shows a generic carboxylic acid R–COOH and phosphorus tribromide PBr3; a curved arrow from the carbonyl oxygen to phosphorus indicates an O–P bond is forming, and a curved arrow from a P–Br bond to bromine indicates that P–Br bond is breaking. The structure contains a methoxy-substituted benzene ring attached to a C(H)=N⁺(CH₃)₂Cl group; ignoring the curved arrows and the formal positive charge, the bonds not involving hydrogen are one O–C(aryl) bond, one O–C(methyl) bond, six C–C bonds in the aromatic ring, one C(aryl)–C(iminium) bond, one C–Cl bond, one C=N bond, and two N–C(methyl) bonds, giving 1 + 1 + 6 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 13 when each drawn bond line is counted as one bond. The image shows a six-membered piperidine ring containing a positively charged nitrogen double-bonded to oxygen—an oxoammonium cation—with gem-dimethyl groups on the two ring carbons adjacent to nitrogen, plus a separate alcohol molecule HO-R positioned so its oxygen lone pair is directed toward the nitrogen. The image shows a 2,4-dinitrobenzyl-derived sigma complex: a benzylic carbon is bonded to a carboxymethylthio group (-SCH2CO2H), a sulfonamide group (-SO2NR1R2), and the aromatic ring; the ring carries nitro substituents ortho and para to the benzylic carbon, the anionic charge is placed on the remaining ortho ring carbon (the one near the departing H+), and the separate H+ represents the proton leaving that carbon. The drawing shows a carbon atom bonded to the substituent R², triple-bonded to a positively charged nitrogen, and that nitrogen is also bonded to R¹, which is a nitrilium ion. The image shows a six-membered carbon ring with a protonated carbonyl group (C=OH) at one position and an acyl group (–C(=O)R) at the opposite position; the curved arrows are ignored and any bond involving hydrogen is excluded. The image depicts an O-phosphorylated ketoxime, R¹R²C=N–O–PCl₄, with curved arrows indicating a Beckmann rearrangement step: the N–O bond breaks with its electron pair moving to oxygen, the anti substituent migrates from carbon to nitrogen, and the C=N π bond reorganizes into a C≡N triple bond, giving a nitrilium cation and the [O–PCl₄]⁻ leaving group. The image depicts an N-phenethylamide fragment, PhCH₂CH₂NH–C(=O)–R, and a phosphorus oxychloride molecule, POCl₃, with curved arrows indicating interaction between the carbonyl oxygen and phosphorus and departure of chloride; these arrows are ignored for bond counting. The image depicts the transition state for deprotonation of methyl 2-(di(2,2,2-trifluoroethoxy)phosphoryl)acetate, (CF3CH2O)2P(=O)CH2C(=O)OMe, by the bis(trimethylsilyl)amide anion, N(SiMe3)2−; the curved arrows indicating electron movement are disregarded, and all C–H bonds are excluded from the count. The drawing shows an ortho-aminophenyl α,β-unsaturated carbonyl compound: a benzene ring bearing an –NH2 group and a –CH=C(R)C(=O)R1 side chain on adjacent ring carbons, with curved arrows indicating nucleophilic attack by the nitrogen lone pair on the carbonyl carbon and movement of the C=O π electrons onto oxygen. The image shows the tetrachloroaluminate anion, [AlCl4]−, with one chloride indicated as the basic site, and an acyl-substituted benzenonium (σ-complex) cation in which the ring carbon attached to C(=O)R also bears the proton being removed. The image shows a molecule with a central N=N double bond, where each nitrogen is attached to a quaternary carbon bearing two methyl groups and one cyano group, corresponding to 2,2′-azobis(2-methylpropionitrile). The transition state shows a metal fragment LnM connected by a dashed M–O bond to an oxygen that also bears a hydrogen and is bonded to a carbon chain; that oxygen is attached to a CH2, which is attached to a CH group that is part of a five-membered oxonium ring. The structure is a six-membered heterocycle fused to a benzene ring (a chroman-4-one core), with the ring sequence O–C(Ph)([O⁻])–CH₂–C(=O)–C(aromatic)–C(aromatic); the carbon bearing the phenyl group also carries the negatively charged oxygen, and the carbonyl and ring oxygen are attached to adjacent aromatic carbons. The transition-state drawing contains a fused bicyclic decalin carbon skeleton (two cyclohexane rings sharing one C–C bond), one C=C double bond, an anionic oxygen bonded to a bridgehead carbon, and an N=N–SO₂Ar substituent. The image shows two molecular components connected by curved arrows: the upper component is H–O–N=O and the lower component is [H₂O–N=O]⁺, with a positive charge on the lower species. The image shows a phthalimide framework (a benzene ring fused to a five-membered imide ring containing one nitrogen and two carbonyl groups), an N-CH2-CO-R substituent attached to the imide nitrogen, and a separate methoxide anion (OMe⁻); the curved arrow is ignored as instructed. The image shows a 2-phenyl-1,2,3,4-tetrahydroquinoline core: a neutral ring nitrogen, a phenyl group on the carbon next to nitrogen, a CH₂ at the next ring position (one H is shown), and the carbon adjacent to the fused benzene bearing both a carboxylic acid and a protonated water ligand, [OH2+], which carries the +1 charge. The transition-state structure contains two phenyl rings, a phenolic OH on the left ring, a central C=C bond, an O⁻ substituent on the left central carbon, and a terminal O–OH group on the right central carbon; arrows are ignored and all O–H and C–H bonds are excluded. The image shows a carbonyl transition-state fragment with an R group attached to a carbonyl carbon, a C=O double bond, and a hydrogen attached to that same carbon; the curved arrows indicate electron movement and are ignored. The image shows a cyclohexanone ring with the carbonyl carbon incorporated into the ring, an adjacent alpha carbon bearing a methyl ester substituent (CO2CH3), and a radical dot on that alpha carbon; the curved arrows indicating electron movement are ignored. The drawing shows a phenoxide benzene ring with an O⁻ substituent and an ortho carbon attached to a carbon that bears one hydrogen and one chlorine, while a second chlorine is shown leaving via a curved arrow indicating C–Cl bond cleavage; the curved arrows are ignored for counting. The transition-state drawing contains a fused bicyclic ketone (cyclohexane fused to a cyclopentanone), an exocyclic iminium linkage to a proline-like pyrrolidinium ring bearing a carboxylate group, a water molecule, and curved arrows that are ignored for counting. The image shows a steroid skeleton bearing a C3 ketone, an alcohol (HO), a C17 side chain ending in an acetate (OAc) group, and a separate nitrosyl chloride (O=N–Cl) molecule with curved arrows indicating nucleophilic attack by the alcohol; the arrows are ignored and no bonds to hydrogen are counted. The image shows four conductance-versus-volume plots labeled P, Q, R, and S; plot S displays a nearly flat line before the equivalence volume and then a rising line after it. In the reaction AgNO₃(aq) + KCl(aq) → AgCl(s) + KNO₃(aq), Ag⁺ precipitates Cl⁻ as AgCl, replacing Cl⁻ in solution with NO₃⁻. Because the molar ionic conductivities of Cl⁻ and NO₃⁻ are similar, the conductance changes only slightly before the equivalence point, while after equivalence the added Ag⁺ and NO₃⁻ increase the total ion concentration and thus the conductance rises. Plot S matches this behavior, so the correct choice is D. Final answer: (D) (S)

The image shows that XeF6 undergoes complete hydrolysis to give P plus another product, P reacts with OH⁻/H2O to give Q, and Q then undergoes slow disproportionation in OH⁻/H2O to give final products. Complete hydrolysis of XeF6 produces xenon trioxide, P = XeO3, and HF. XeO3 dissolves in aqueous base to form hydrogen xenate, Q = HXeO4⁻. The slow disproportionation of hydrogen xenate in basic solution is represented by the equation 2 HXeO4⁻ + 2 OH⁻ → XeO6⁴⁻ + Xe + O2 + 2 H2O, in which the gaseous species formed are xenon and oxygen. Therefore, two gaseous products are released in the final step. Final answer: 2.
