Final answer: Y-bus = [ [-j15, j5, 0]; [j5, j7.5, -j12.5]; [0, -j12.5, j2.5] ].

The image depicts a four-pin optocoupler: the right side contains a light-emitting diode connected to pins 1 and 2 (input side), and the left side contains a phototransistor connected to pins 3 and 4 (output side), with arrows showing light coupling from the LED to the transistor. In an optocoupler, the output end is the light-sensitive transistor that responds to the LED’s emission, so it is connected across the phototransistor terminals. Final answer: pins 3 and 4.

The spectrum in the figure shows M(ω) as a rectangular pulse that is nonzero only for |ω| ≤ ω₁, while H₁(ω) is a triangular transfer function nonzero for |ω| ≤ 2ω₁. After filtering, the spectrum of the signal is M′(ω)=M(ω)H₁(ω), so M′(ω) is still zero for |ω| > ω₁ because M(ω)=0 there; the triangular filter does not introduce any new frequency components outside the original band. Therefore the highest angular frequency present in the filtered signal is ω_max = ω₁. By the Nyquist sampling theorem, the sampling angular frequency must satisfy ω_s ≥ 2ω_max = 2ω₁, which corresponds to a sampling rate f_s ≥ ω_s/(2π) = ω₁/π Hz. Final answer: The sampling rate should be at least 2ω₁ rad/s, i.e., f_s ≥ ω₁/π Hz.

The figure shows an inverting op-amp configuration: the input signal \(u_i\) is applied through resistor \(R_1\) to the inverting terminal, feedback resistor \(R_f\) connects the output back to the inverting terminal, and the non-inverting terminal is shown connected through \(R_2\) to ground; in this problem it is instead connected to a 5 V source. For an ideal op-amp with negative feedback, the voltages at the inverting and non-inverting inputs are equal, so the inverting input is at 5 V. Applying Kirchhoff’s current law at the inverting node gives \(\frac{u_i - 5}{R_1} = \frac{5 - u_o}{R_f}\). Substituting \(R_1 = 10\,\text{k}\Omega\), \(R_f = 20\,\text{k}\Omega\), and \(u_i = 10\,\text{V}\) yields \(\frac{10 - 5}{10\,\text{k}} = \frac{5 - u_o}{20\,\text{k}}\), so \(0.5\,\text{mA} = \frac{5 - u_o}{20\,\text{k}}\), giving \(5 - u_o = 10\) and \(u_o = -5\,\text{V}\). Final answer: \(-5\,\text{V}\).

The image shows a three-phase transformer with the left winding connected in star (terminals A, B, C with neutral N) and the right winding connected in delta (terminals a, b, c). For a star-delta transformer, the delta-side line voltage is related to the star-side phase voltage, producing a 30° phase shift between corresponding line-to-line voltages. With negative-sequence excitation on the star side, the star-side phase voltages rotate in the reverse order; taking \(V_{AN}\) as the reference at \(0^\circ\), then \(V_{BN}\) is at \(+120^\circ\). The star line-to-line voltage is \(V_{AB}=V_{AN}-V_{BN}=V(1-e^{j120^\circ})=\sqrt{3}V\angle{-30^\circ}\), while the corresponding delta-side line voltage \(V_{ab}\) is in phase with the star-side phase voltage \(V_{AN}\), hence at \(0^\circ\). Therefore, \(V_{AB}\) lags \(V_{ab}\) by \(30^\circ\). Final answer: \(V_{AB}\) lags \(V_{ab}\) by \(30^\circ\) (equivalently, \(V_{ab}\) leads \(V_{AB}\) by \(30^\circ\)).

The block diagram shows input \(R(s)\), output \(C(s)\), block \(G(s)\), and two summing junctions: the first subtracts \(C(s)\) from \(R(s)\), giving \(R(s)-C(s)\); the second subtracts this signal and adds \(C(s)\), giving \(-[R(s)-C(s)]+C(s)=-R(s)+2C(s)\). Since this is the input to \(G(s)\), we have \(C(s)=G(s)[-R(s)+2C(s)]\). Rearranging yields \(C(s)-2G(s)C(s)=-G(s)R(s)\), so \(C(s)[1-2G(s)]=-G(s)R(s)\), and therefore \(\frac{C(s)}{R(s)}=\frac{-G(s)}{1-2G(s)}=\frac{G(s)}{2G(s)-1}\). Final answer: \(\frac{G(s)}{2G(s)-1}\)

The inductor-current waveform is a triangular steady-state waveform with a minimum of 12 A, a maximum of 16 A, a rising interval of 20 µs, and a falling interval of 30 µs, so the switching period is 50 µs and the duty ratio is D = 20/50 = 0.4. The average inductor current is (12 + 16)/2 = 14 A, and for a buck-boost converter in CCM the average output current is I_o = (1 − D)I_L = 0.6 × 14 = 8.4 A. The output-voltage ripple is given by ΔV_o = I_o D T_s / C, so solving for the capacitor gives C = I_o D T_s / ΔV_o = (8.4)(0.4)(50 × 10⁻⁶)/1 = 168 × 10⁻⁶ F = 168 µF. Final answer: 168

The circuit contains a 12.7 V DC source, a 9900 Ω resistor, and a stack of four series forward-biased diodes, with the small-signal input \(v_i = 100\text{ mV}\cos(\omega t)\) in series with the DC source. Each diode drops 0.7 V, so the total DC diode voltage is \(4(0.7\text{ V}) = 2.8\text{ V}\) and the DC current is \(I_{DC} = (12.7\text{ V} - 2.8\text{ V})/9900\,\Omega = 9.9\text{ V}/9900\,\Omega = 1.0\text{ mA}\). The small-signal resistance of one diode is \(r_d = V_t/I_D = 25\text{ mV}/1.0\text{ mA} = 25\,\Omega\), giving \(4 \times 25\,\Omega = 100\,\Omega\) for the series stack. The AC voltage divides between the 9900 Ω resistor and the 100 Ω diode resistance, so \(V_{ac} = v_i \times 100/(9900+100) = 100\text{ mV} \times 100/10000 = 1.0\text{ mV}\). Final answer: \(V_{ac}(t) \approx 1.0\cos(\omega t)\text{ mV}\), i.e. about 1 mV peak.

For \(x_1(t)=2-2\cos\!\big(\frac{2\pi}{3}t\big)\) the fundamental period is \(T=3\), so \(\omega_0=2\pi/3\). Using Euler’s formula, \(-2\cos(\2\pi/3 t)=-(e^{j\omega_0 t}+e^{-j\omega_0 t})\), giving exponential Fourier series coefficients \(a_0=2\), \(a_1=a_{-1}=-1\), and all other \(a_k=0\). This finite three-point spectrum—nonzero only at \(k=0,\pm1\)—is the coefficient set labeled \(a_k\) in the figure. Final answer: \(a_k\)

The image shows a single-phase full-bridge voltage-source inverter with IGBTs Q1–Q4, antiparallel diodes D1–D4, a dc source Vdc, and an R-L load. For a 50 Hz square-wave output the load time constant is τ = L/R = 55.9 mH / 3 Ω ≈ 18.6 ms, which is larger than the 10 ms half-period, so the load current is continuous and not zero at the voltage transitions. Therefore the IGBTs must be switched in diagonal pairs—Q1 and Q2 for v_o ≈ +Vdc, Q3 and Q4 for v_o ≈ −Vdc—with a short dead time between turning off an outgoing switch and turning on the complementary incoming switch in each leg. During the dead time the inductive load current freewheels through the antiparallel diodes, preventing shoot-through of the dc bus and interruption of the load current. Final answer: Switch the IGBTs in diagonal pairs with a small dead time—turn off the active pair, allow the load current to freewheel through the antiparallel diodes, then turn on the opposite pair.

The dashed box has two inputs: the external T line and a feedback line from the D flip-flop’s Q output, and its output drives the D input. For a T flip-flop, the next state is Q* = T ⊕ Q, meaning Q* = Q when T = 0 and Q* = Q̄ when T = 1. Since a D flip-flop simply copies D to Q on the clock edge, setting D = T ⊕ Q gives the required T flip-flop behavior. The logic function T ⊕ Q is produced by a two-input XOR gate. Final answer: an XOR gate.

The square wave in the figure repeats every three horizontal grid units, with the signal at the high level for one grid unit and at the low level for two grid units in each cycle. The duty cycle of a periodic pulse waveform is defined as the ratio of the pulse width (high-level duration) to the total period, expressed as a percentage: duty cycle = (pulse width / period) × 100%. Substituting the measured values gives (1 grid unit / 3 grid units) × 100% = 33.333...%. Final answer: 33.3%

The oscilloscope display shows a periodic pulse waveform with a timebase setting of 0.2 ms/div. One complete cycle of the waveform spans 5 horizontal grid divisions, with the signal in the high state for 3 divisions and in the low state for 2 divisions. The duty cycle is calculated as the ratio of the on-time (high time) to the total period, multiplied by 100%: D = (t_on / T) × 100% = (3 div / 5 div) × 100% = 60%. Final answer: 60%

The circuit contains two 2-input NAND gates whose outputs drive a 2-input NOR gate: the upper NAND has inputs W and X, the lower NAND has inputs Y and Z, and the NOR gate produces F. The NAND outputs are (W·X)' and (Y·Z)', so the NOR output is F = ((W·X)' + (Y·Z)')'. Applying De Morgan's theorem, F = ((W·X)')' · ((Y·Z)')' = (W·X)·(Y·Z) = W·X·Y·Z. Final answer: F = WXYZ (or F = W·X·Y·Z).

The polar plot shows the open-loop frequency response from ω=0 to ω=∞ crossing the negative real axis at −1.42, which lies to the left of the critical point −1, and the arrow shows the curve moving from below to above the real axis as ω increases. The complete Nyquist plot also includes the negative-frequency branch, the mirror image of the shown curve about the real axis, so the full plot crosses the negative real axis at −1.42 twice and therefore encircles the −1 point twice, giving N=2. By the Nyquist stability criterion N=Z−P, where P is the number of open-loop right-half-plane poles and Z is the number of closed-loop right-half-plane poles; the system is open-loop stable, so P=0, and hence Z=N=2. Final answer: The closed-loop system is unstable and has two poles in the right-half s-plane.

The circuit has a 3 V source with its positive terminal at the bottom and negative terminal at the top, a 3 kΩ resistor in series with that source, and a diode in the right branch. As drawn, the diode symbol’s arrow points downward, the same direction as the labeled current arrow I, so the diode’s anode is the upper terminal and its cathode is the lower terminal. Because the cathode is connected to the higher-potential side of the source while the anode is on the lower-potential side, the diode is reverse-biased. An ideal diode conducts only when forward-biased and acts as an open circuit under reverse bias, so no current flows in the loop. Final answer: 0 A.

The figure shows a 10 A source current splitting at a node into a 2 A branch containing the 1 Ω resistor and \(X_{C1}\) and a branch through \(X_{C2}\); these two branches recombine to feed the series \(R\text{–}X_L\) load, so by KCL the load current is 10 A, and the voltmeter across the load reads 200 V. Since only resistances dissipate real power, the total 1 kW equals the power in the 1 Ω resistor plus the power in the load resistance \(R\): \(P_{1\Omega}=(2\text{ A})^2(1\ \Omega)=4\text{ W}\), giving \(P_R=1000\text{ W}-4\text{ W}=996\text{ W}\). Using \(P_R=I_{\text{load}}^2R\) yields \(R=996/(10)^2=9.96\ \Omega\). The load impedance magnitude is \(|Z|=V/I=200/10=20\ \Omega\), and for a series \(R\text{–}L\) load \(|Z|^2=R^2+X_L^2\), so \(X_L=\sqrt{20^2-9.96^2}\ \Omega\approx17.34\ \Omega\). Final answer: 17.34 Ω.

In the regulator circuit, transistor VT1 has its emitter held at the Zener voltage VZ = 5.3 V above ground by Zener diode VZ, and its base-emitter junction is forward biased with UBE = 0.7 V, so the base voltage is UB1 = UE1 + UBE = VZ + UBE = 5.3 V + 0.7 V = 6.0 V; the transformer secondary voltage and the divider resistances affect the required output voltage but not this base voltage. Final answer: 6 V

The circuit contains a 1 mA current source feeding an NMOS current mirror with W/L = 1 and W/L = 3, so the tail current for the differential pair is \(1\text{ mA} \times \frac{3}{1} = 3\text{ mA}\). With \(V_1 = 0\) and \(V_2 = V_{dd}\), the left input NMOS is off and the right input NMOS carries the full 3 mA. This 3 mA flows through the conducting PMOS branch with W/L = 10, and the PMOS current mirror with output W/L = 40 gives a current gain of \(\frac{40}{10} = 4\). Therefore \(I_{out} = 3\text{ mA} \times 4 = 12\text{ mA}\). Final answer: 12.0

The image shows an N-channel JFET with a channel thickness of \(2a\), where the depletion region extends from the \(p^+\) gate into the N-type channel; pinch-off occurs when the depletion width reaches \(a\). For a one-sided abrupt \(p^+n\) junction, the depletion width is \(W=\sqrt{\frac{2\varepsilon_s(V_{bi}-V_G)}{qN_d}}\), and setting \(W=a\) gives the pinch-off voltage magnitude \(V_p=\frac{qN_da^2}{2\varepsilon_s}-V_{bi}\). Using \(\varepsilon_s=k\varepsilon_0=11.8(8.85\times10^{-12})\,\text{F/m}=1.0443\times10^{-10}\,\text{F/m}\), \(a=2\,\mu\text{m}=2\times10^{-6}\,\text{m}\), and \(N_d=10^{15}\,\text{cm}^{-3}=10^{21}\,\text{m}^{-3}\), the first term is \(\frac{(1.6\times10^{-19})(10^{21})(2\times10^{-6})^2}{2(1.0443\times10^{-10})}=3.064\,\text{V}\). The built-in potential at 300 K is \(V_{bi}=\frac{kT}{q}\ln\left(\frac{N_aN_d}{n_i^2}\right)=0.0259\ln\left[\frac{(10^{18})(10^{15})}{(1.5\times10^{10})^2}\right]=0.0259(29.12)=0.754\,\text{V}\). Therefore \(V_p=3.064-0.754=2.31\,\text{V}\), meaning the gate must be biased to about \(-2.31\,\text{V}\). Final answer: 2.31 V.

The circuit is powered by a 12 V source connected across the right-hand 6 Ω resistor, and the ammeter A1 is in series with a branch made up of the upper 6 Ω resistor, the 3 Ω resistor, and the lower 4 Ω resistor; this entire branch is therefore connected directly across the 12 V source, while the ideal voltmeter draws no current and does not affect the circuit. The total resistance of A1’s branch is 6 Ω + 3 Ω + 4 Ω = 13 Ω, so by Ohm’s law the current through that branch, which is the reading of A1, is I = V/R = 12 V / 13 Ω = 12/13 A ≈ 0.923 A. Final answer: 12/13 A.

The image shows a uniform photo-generation rate \(G = 10^{20}\,\text{cm}^{-3}\text{s}^{-1}\) for \(|x|<l_n\), zero outside that interval, a recombination rate \(R = 10^{20}\exp(-|x|/l_n)\,\text{cm}^{-3}\text{s}^{-1}\), and zero excess minority-carrier density at \(x=\pm 2l_n\) with \(l_n=10^{-4}\,\text{cm}\). In steady state with zero electric field, the electron current density satisfies \(dJ_n/dx = q(G-R)\); by symmetry \(J_n(0)=0\), so integrating to the right boundary gives \(J_n(2l_n)=q\int_0^{2l_n}[G(x)-R(x)]\,dx\). For \(0<x<l_n\), \(G-R=10^{20}(1-e^{-x/l_n})\), and for \(l_n<x<2l_n\), \(G-R=-10^{20}e^{-x/l_n}\), so the integral becomes \(10^{20}l_n e^{-2}\). The magnitude is therefore \(|J_n|=|q|10^{20}l_n e^{-2}=(1.6\times10^{-19})(10^{20})(10^{-4})e^{-2}\,\text{A/cm}^2=2.165\times10^{-4}\,\text{A/cm}^2=0.2165\,\text{mA/cm}^2\approx0.22\,\text{mA/cm}^2\). Final answer: 0.22 mA/cm²

The transformer secondary voltage \(u_2\) is fed to a four-diode bridge rectifier and smoothed by capacitor \(C\), with points \(a\) and \(c\) being the positive and negative terminals of the filtered DC output. Since \(u_2 = 10\sqrt{2}\sin(314t)\ \text{V}\), its RMS value is \(U_2 = \frac{10\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}} = 10\ \text{V}\). For a single-phase bridge rectifier with a capacitor filter, the average DC output voltage is approximately \(U_{ac} \approx 1.2U_2\), so \(U_{ac} \approx 1.2 \times 10\ \text{V} = 12\ \text{V}\). Final answer: 12 V.

The resistor R is connected between the +12 V supply and the common cathode node of the three ideal diodes D1, D2, and D3, whose anodes are connected to 0 V, 6 V, and 0.3 V (or 3 V) respectively. An ideal diode conducts when its anode is more positive than its cathode, and in conduction it clamps the cathode to the anode voltage. Since 6 V is the highest anode voltage, D2 turns on and clamps the common node to 6 V, while D1 and D3 are reverse biased and remain off. The voltage across R is therefore V_R = 12 V − 6 V = 6 V. Final answer: 6 V.

The image shows an normalized impedance Smith chart with point \(P\) located at the intersection of the constant-resistance circle \(r=0.5\) and the constant-reactance arc \(x=-1\), so \(P\) represents the normalized impedance \(z_P=0.5-j1\). On an impedance Smith chart, motion along a constant-resistance circle leaves the resistance unchanged and changes only the reactance, which means a reactive element has been added in series with \(Z\). For a constant-\(r\) circle, clockwise rotation increases the normalized reactance \(x\); starting from \(x=-1\) and moving clockwise by \(45^\circ\) raises \(x\) toward less negative values, i.e., it adds positive reactance. Positive reactance corresponds to an inductor. Final answer: an inductor connected in series with \(Z\).

The figure shows two currents enclosed by the closed loop \(L_4\): a current \(2I\) directed out of the page on the left and a current \(I\) directed into the page on the right, with \(L_4\) being the outermost dashed loop whose arrow points leftward along the bottom side, indicating a clockwise traversal of the loop. By Ampère’s law, \(\displaystyle \oint_{L_4} \vec H\cdot \mathrm d\vec l = I_{\text{enclosed}}\), where the sign of each enclosed current is determined by the right-hand rule relative to the direction of integration. For a clockwise loop, the right-hand thumb points into the page, so currents into the page are taken as positive and currents out of the page as negative. Therefore the net enclosed current is \(I_{\text{enclosed}} = I - 2I = -I\). Final answer: \(-I\)

The figure shows a common-collector power output stage: VT1 is the emitter-follower output transistor, its emitter node E is AC-coupled through C2 to the load RL, and VT2 acts as an active current-sink load; the diodes provide bias. Because the stage has approximately unity voltage gain, Uo ≈ Ui. The quiescent emitter voltage is VE = 11 V, so the maximum undistorted peak swing is limited by the smaller of Vcc − UCES − VE = 20 − 1 − 11 = 8 V upward and VE − UCES = 11 − 1 = 10 V downward, i.e. 8 V peak. Taking the given Ui = 4 V as the RMS value, the output peak is 4√2 ≈ 5.66 V, which is less than 8 V, so no clipping occurs. Therefore the load power is P = Uo²/RL = 4²/4 = 4 W. Final answer: 4 W.

In the circuit the 4-to-1 multiplexer has data inputs \(I_0=x\), \(I_1=x\), \(I_2=y\), and \(I_3=y'\) (the inverted \(y\)), select lines \(A_1=y\) and \(A_0=z\), and an active-low enable \(EN\) driven by \(z\) through an inverter, so the effective enable is \((z')'=z\). The multiplexer selects \(I_0\) for \(A_1A_0=00\), \(I_1\) for \(01\), \(I_2\) for \(10\), and \(I_3\) for \(11\); with \(A_1=y\) and \(A_0=z\) the selected data is \(x\) when \(y=0\), \(y\) when \(y=1,z=0\), and \(y'\) when \(y=1,z=1\), which simplifies to \(x y' + y z'\). Multiplying by the effective enable \(z\) gives \(f = z(x y' + y z') = x y' z + y z' z = x y' z\). Final answer: \(f(x,y,z)=x y' z\).

The circuit is a voltage-divider biased common-emitter amplifier with NPN transistor T, base bias resistors Rb1 to ground and Rb2 to +VCC, collector resistor Rc to +VCC, emitter resistor Re to ground, and capacitors C1, C2, and Ce; for DC analysis the capacitors and load RL are open. The base voltage is VB = VCC·Rb1/(Rb1+Rb2) = 12 V·5 kΩ/(5 kΩ+15 kΩ) = 3 V, so VE = VB−UBEQ = 3 V−0.7 V = 2.3 V and IEQ = VE/Re = 2.3 V/2.3 kΩ = 1 mA. With β = 50, ICQ ≈ IEQ = 1 mA, therefore UCEQ = VCC − ICQ·Rc − IEQ·Re = 12 V − 1 mA·5.1 kΩ − 1 mA·2.3 kΩ = 4.6 V. Final answer: 4.6

The image shows two parallel buck converters fed from a common 100 V DC source, each with an switch (S1/S2), inductor, freewheeling diode, and a common output capacitor and 1 Ω load. The switching frequency is 1 kHz (period 1 ms), and the gate signals show S1 and S2 each conducting for 0.5 ms, so each has a duty ratio D = 0.5. For a buck converter, the output voltage is V_o = D V_in = 0.5 × 100 = 50 V. The total load current is I_o = V_o / R = 50 / 1 = 50 A. Since the two converters share the load equally, each supplies 25 A average inductor current. The average switch current in a buck converter is the product of duty ratio and inductor current, so I_{S1,avg} = D × I_{L1} = 0.5 × 25 = 12.5 A. Final answer: 12.50 A.

The pdf is symmetric, equal to 1/3 on \([-1,-0.5)\cup[0.5,1]\) and 2/3 on \([-0.5,0.5]\). For 4-level uniform quantization over \([-1,1]\), the step size is \(\Delta=(1-(-1))/4=0.5\), with reconstruction levels at the interval midpoints \(-0.75,-0.25,0.25,0.75\). Because the pdf is constant within each quantization interval, the quantization noise power is \(E[(X-Q(X))^2]=\Delta^2/12=0.25/12=1/48\). The signal power is \(E[X^2]=\int_{-1}^{1}x^2p(x)\,dx=2\big[\int_{0.5}^{1}x^2/3\,dx+\int_{0}^{0.5}2x^2/3\,dx\big]=1/4\). Therefore \(\text{SNR}=E[X^2]/E[(X-Q(X))^2]=(1/4)/(1/48)=12\), which is \(10\log_{10}(12)\approx 10.8\) dB. Final answer: 12 (about 10.8 dB).

Figure C is a D flip-flop with its D input connected to the \(\overline{Q}\) output, and figure D is a JK flip-flop with both J and K tied to logic 1 as the input labels show; figure A is a JK flip-flop with J=1 and K=0, while figure B is a D flip-flop with D connected to Q. For a D flip-flop \(Q^{n+1}=D\), so in C \(Q^{n+1}=\overline{Q^n}\); for a JK flip-flop \(Q^{n+1}=J\overline{Q^n}+\overline{K}Q^n\), so in D with J=K=1, \(Q^{n+1}=1\cdot\overline{Q^n}+0\cdot Q^n=\overline{Q^n}\). Figures A and B do not satisfy the relation because A gives \(Q^{n+1}=1\) and B gives \(Q^{n+1}=Q^n\). Final answer: C and D.

The image shows three negative-edge-triggered JK flip-flops labeled FF2, FF1, and FF0 with outputs Q2, Q1, and Q0; the top AND gate has inputs Q2, Q1, and Q0 and its output drives J0; the bottom AND gate has inputs Q2-bar and Q1-bar and its output drives both K2 and K1; additionally J2 is driven by Q1, J1 by Q0, and K0 by Q1. Using the JK characteristic Q^{n+1}=J·Q-bar + K-bar·Q, the next-state equations become Q2^{n+1}=Q2+Q1, Q1^{n+1}=Q1+Q0, and Q0^{n+1}=Q1-bar·Q0. Starting from 000 gives Q2^{n+1}=0, Q1^{n+1}=0, Q0^{n+1}=0, so the circuit remains locked at 000 and does not advance. Final answer: not a valid modulo counter (as drawn it locks at 000).

In the diagram the control circuit is supplied through fuse FU2 and stop contact SB3, with two contactor branches: the KM1 branch uses start button SB1 and the KM1 self-locking contact in parallel, followed by the KM2 normally-closed interlock, while the KM2 branch uses SB2 and the KM2 self-locking contact in parallel, followed by the KM1 normally-closed interlock; the thermal-relay contact FR is a normally-closed contact placed in the common return path for both the KM1 and KM2 coils and their indicator lamps HL1 and HL2. When FR operates it opens, breaking the common return path so the KM1 coil current falls to zero regardless of the SB1 or KM1 self-locking contact, which causes the KM1 main contacts to open, the KM1 self-locking normally-open contact to open, and the KM1 normally-closed interlock contact to close. Therefore the incorrect analysis is the one claiming that FR operation has no effect on KM1, or that it causes the KM1 normally-closed interlock contact to open; the correct effect is that FR tripping de-energizes KM1 and its NC interlock contact closes. Final answer: the incorrect analysis is that FR operation does not affect KM1 or causes KM1’s normally-closed interlock contact to open; in fact FR opening de-energizes KM1 and that contact closes.

The figure shows a causal periodic square wave with period \(T\) that equals \(1\) on the first half of each period, i.e., \(f(t)=1\) for \(0\le t<T/2\), and \(f(t)=0\) for \(T/2\le t<T\), repeating for \(t\ge 0\). For a causal periodic function with period \(T\), the Laplace transform is \(F(s)=\frac{1}{1-e^{-sT}}\int_0^T e^{-st}f(t)\,dt\). Substituting the one-period waveform gives \(\int_0^T e^{-st}f(t)\,dt=\int_0^{T/2}e^{-st}\,dt=\frac{1-e^{-sT/2}}{s}\), so \(F(s)=\frac{1-e^{-sT/2}}{s(1-e^{-sT})}\). Since \(1-e^{-sT}=(1-e^{-sT/2})(1+e^{-sT/2})\), this simplifies to \(F(s)=\frac{1}{s(1+e^{-sT/2})}\). Final answer: \(F(s)=\frac{1}{s(1+e^{-sT/2})}\) (equivalently \(F(s)=\frac{1-e^{-sT/2}}{s(1-e^{-sT})}\)).

The circuit shows two ideal voltage sources, \(120\angle -90^\circ\text{ V}\) and \(120\angle -30^\circ\text{ V}\), each in parallel with an impedance \(Z\), and a third impedance \(Z=(80-j35)\,\Omega\) between the top and bottom rails; since all three impedances are labeled \(Z\), the top and bottom impedances are also taken as \((80-j35)\,\Omega\). The current \(I\) is the line current into the common node of the three impedances, so by KCL it is the negative of the sum of the currents in the two left-hand impedances: \(I=-\dfrac{120\angle -90^\circ+120\angle -30^\circ}{80-j35}\). Adding the source voltages gives \(120\angle -90^\circ+120\angle -30^\circ=60\sqrt3-j180\approx207.85\angle -60^\circ\text{ V}\), and dividing by \(80-j35\approx87.32\angle -23.63^\circ\,\Omega\) gives \(2.381\angle -36.37^\circ\text{ A}\); applying the negative sign yields \(I=2.381\angle 143.63^\circ\text{ A}\). Final answer: \(I\approx 2.38\angle 143.6^\circ\text{ A}\) (approximately \(-1.92+j1.41\text{ A}\)).

The image shows a pi-equivalent line with series impedance 2+j4 ohm and shunt admittances j5.5e-4 S at each end; the receiving-end terminal voltage is labeled 10.2 kV. Because the given ΔU and δU are the longitudinal and transverse components of the voltage drop across the series impedance branch, the terminal complex power S=P+jQ is found from the short-line relations ΔU=(PR+QX)/U₂ and δU=(PX−QR)/U₂, where R=2 ohm, X=4 ohm, and U₂=10.2 kV. Substituting ΔU=−0.39 kV and δU=2.16 kV gives 2P+4Q=10.2(−0.39)=−3.978 and 4P−2Q=10.2(2.16)=22.032; solving, P=[(−3.978)(−2)−4(22.032)]/(−20)≈4.01 MW and Q=[2(22.032)−(−3.978)(4)]/(−20)≈−3.00 Mvar. Thus the terminal complex power is about 4.01−j3.00 MVA. Final answer: S≈4.01−j3.00 MVA.

The circuit contains three clocked D flip-flops whose outputs are labeled P, Q, and R; the top flip-flop’s D input is driven by R, the middle flip-flop’s D input is driven by a NOR gate with inputs P and R, and the bottom flip-flop’s D input is driven by an AND gate with inputs Q and the complement of R, giving the next-state equations P+ = R, Q+ = (P + R)′ = P′R′, and R+ = Q·R′. Starting from the reset state PQR = 000, the state sequence is 000 → 010 → 011 → 100 → 000, which contains four distinct states. Final answer: 4.

In the figure the 74LS161—a 4-bit binary (mod-16) counter—has its parallel data inputs D0–D3 tied to ground, so the synchronous load loads the value 0000; the active-low load input LD is driven by an AND gate whose inputs are the Q1 and Q2 outputs, so LD goes low only when Q2Q1 = 11. Counting upward from 0000, the first state that satisfies Q2 = 1 and Q1 = 1 is 0110 (decimal 6), and because the load is synchronous the next clock edge reloads 0000, giving 6 + 1 = 7 distinct states. Final answer: 7

The spectrum \(M(f)\) consists of two triangular lobes, one from \(-A\) to \(-B\) and one from \(B\) to \(A\), so the message \(m(t)\) has positive-frequency components only between \(B\) and \(A\). After multiplying by \(v(t)=\cos(2\pi f_c t)\), the spectrum is shifted by \(\pm f_c\), giving positive-frequency bands around \([f_c-A,\,f_c-B]\) and \([f_c+B,\,f_c+A]\). The high-pass filter with cutoff \(f_c\) removes the lower band and keeps the upper sideband \([f_c+B,\,f_c+A]\). Multiplying this by \(w(t)=\cos(2\pi (f_c+A)t)\) shifts it by \(\pm (f_c+A)\); the difference-frequency component lands in baseband as \([-(A-B),\,A-B]\), and the low-pass filter with cutoff \(f_c\) passes it. Thus the output signal occupies the frequency range \(-(A-B)\) to \(A-B\), so its bandwidth is \(A-B = 100-40 = 60\) Hz. Final answer: 60 Hz.

The circuit has \(b\) as the 0 V reference, and the \(10\text{ V}\) source \(E_1\) makes the node to its right \(10\text{ V}\). Point \(a\) is connected only to the two parallel branches leading to \(c\), so by KCL the currents in those two branches are equal and opposite; therefore no current can flow in the external \(R_1\) branch, giving \(V_c=10\text{ V}\). With \(V_a=6\text{ V}\), the current in the \(2\,\Omega\) resistor is \(I=(V_a-V_c)/2=(6-10)/2=-2\text{ A}\), so the right branch carries \(2\text{ A}\) from \(a\) to \(c\). This current flows through the \(8\text{ V}\) source \(E_2\) from positive to negative, so its output power is \(P=E_2I=8\times2=16\text{ W}\), which is the only source power output. Final answer: 16.

The circuit shows three negative-edge-triggered JK flip-flops (FF0, FF1, FF2) clocked by the same CP, so it is synchronous; input I is applied to both J and K of FF0 and also to the AND-chain that feeds FF1 and FF2, with the first AND giving I·Q0 and the second giving I·Q0·Q1, so the JK inputs are J0=K0=I, J1=K1=I·Q0, and J2=K2=I·Q0·Q1. For a JK flip-flop, Q* = J·Q' + K'·Q, which reduces to Q* = C⊕Q when J=K=C; therefore Q0* = I⊕Q0, Q1* = (I·Q0)⊕Q1, and Q2* = (I·Q0·Q1)⊕Q2. With I=1 these are the standard binary up-counter recurrences, producing the sequence 000, 001, …, 111 and then returning to 000, which is eight distinct states; with I=0 the flip-flops hold their current state. Final answer: 8

The figure shows a balanced three-phase supply with phase voltages \(200\angle 0^\circ\text{ V}\), \(200\angle -120^\circ\text{ V}\), and \(200\angle 120^\circ\text{ V}\) feeding a delta-connected load where each branch has impedance \(Z = 8 + j6\,\Omega\); the ammeter is in the line from the \(200\angle 0^\circ\text{ V}\) source and therefore reads the line current. Taking the 200 V values as line-to-neutral phase voltages, the line-to-line voltage magnitude is \(V_L = \sqrt{3}\times 200\text{ V}\). The magnitude of the delta branch current is \(I_{\phi}=V_L/|Z|=(\sqrt{3}\times 200)/|8+j6|=(\sqrt{3}\times 200)/10=20\sqrt{3}\text{ A}\). For a balanced delta connection, the line current is \(\sqrt{3}\) times the branch current, so \(I_L=\sqrt{3}\times 20\sqrt{3}=60\text{ A}\). Final answer: 60 A.

The device is a PROM with a fixed 2-input decoder (AND array) whose four horizontal minterm lines are, from top to bottom, A'B', A'B, AB', and AB, as shown by the crosspoint connections to the A, A', B, and B' lines; the programmable OR array is the vertical line feeding the ≥1 gate, and intact crosspoints (dots) appear only at the top and bottom minterm lines, so the output is the OR of A'B' and AB, which is the equivalence (XNOR) function. Final answer: F = A'B' + AB = A ⊙ B.

The op-amp A1 has its non-inverting input at the collector node and its inverting input tied to +4 V, so negative feedback forces the collector voltage to 4 V; with the 3 kΩ resistor between +10 V and the collector, the collector current is I_C = (10 V − 4 V)/3 kΩ = 2 mA. Op-amp A2 is wired as a current-to-voltage converter with the 10 kΩ feedback resistor R2 carrying the base current I_B, so its output voltage is u_o = I_B R2; since the voltmeter reads u_o = 200 mV, I_B = 200 mV/10 kΩ = 20 µA. Therefore the current gain is β = I_C/I_B = 2 mA/20 µA = 100. Final answer: 100.

In the circuit, point A is coupled to point B through a 47 µF capacitor, and point B is the junction of an 81 kΩ resistor to VCC and a 10 kΩ resistor to ground, so the AC equivalent resistance at B is 81 kΩ || 10 kΩ ≈ 8.9 kΩ. The circuit has two positive-edge-triggered T flip-flops, T1 with output Q1 and T0 with output Q0, both clocked by the common CK line. The feedback element is resistor \(R_f\), which in this two-stage amplifier returns a signal from the output stage to the emitter of the input transistor \(VT1\), while the input signal \(u_i\) is coupled to the base of \(VT1\) through \(C_5\). The figure shows two ideal capacitors \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) connected in a loop with an ideal switch \(S\) across the top, and the reference current \(i(t)\) is taken clockwise. The charge that must flow onto \(C_2\) is \(Q=C_2V_f=12C_1C_2/(C_1+C_2)\). Because the circuit has no resistance or inductance, this redistribution occurs instantaneously, so the current is an impulse at \(t=0\) whose strength equals the transferred charge, and it is zero for all other times. Final answer: \(i(t)=\dfrac{12C_1C_2}{C_1+C_2}\,\delta(t)\), with the positive direction as the clockwise arrow shown, and \(i(t)=0\) for \(t\neq0\), assuming \(C_2\) was initially uncharged.

The figure shows a 1 cm × 1 cm Germanium layer of thickness T capped by a 100 nm Silicon dioxide layer, illuminated by a 20 mW, 600 nm laser. The SiO₂ layer reflects one-fourth of the incident power, leaving three-fourths. Of this remaining light, one-third is reflected at the SiO₂–Ge interface, one-third is absorbed in Ge, and one-third is transmitted through the back, so the absorbed and transmitted powers are equal. The light that actually enters the Germanium is the sum of the absorbed and transmitted portions, and the Beer–Lambert law gives absorbed fraction = 1 − e^(−αT). Since absorbed equals transmitted, the absorbed fraction is one-half, so 1 − e^(−αT) = 0.5, hence e^(−αT) = 0.5 and T = ln 2 / α. With α = 3 × 10⁴ cm⁻¹, T = 0.693147 / (3 × 10⁴) cm = 2.31049 × 10⁻⁵ cm = 0.231049 μm, which rounds to 0.231 μm. Final answer: 0.231

The circuit shows an ideal op-amp with its non-inverting input grounded, an input current source \(I_{in}\) feeding the inverting input, a feedback capacitor \(C_f\) connected between the output and the inverting input, and a series output capacitor \(C_c\) through which the output current \(I_{out}\) flows to ground. The nonlinear block is an ideal relay, so with \(a=0.5\) its output is \(u=0.5\,\operatorname{sgn}(f)\) (zero at \(f=0\), \(+0.5\) for \(f>0\), and \(-0.5\) for \(f<0\)). The circuit is a grounded-emitter amplifier: the emitter is at AC and DC ground, the collector connects through \(R_C\) to \(+V_{CC}\), and the output is taken at the collector through coupling capacitor \(C_2\) to \(R_L\), so the AC load resistance is \(R_L' = R_C \parallel R_L\). The image shows a unity negative-feedback discrete-time system whose forward path has system function \(K/(z^2+z-2)\). The closed-loop system function is \(\displaystyle T(z)=\frac{K}{z^2+z-2+K}\), so the closed-loop characteristic polynomial is \(D(z)=z^2+z+(K-2)\). For a causal second-order DT system to be stable, all roots of \(D(z)\) must lie inside the unit circle, which requires \(D(1)>0\), \(D(-1)>0\), and \(|K-2|<1\). These give \(K>0\), \(K-2>0\), and \(1<K<3\), whose intersection is \(2<K<3\). Therefore \(a=2\) and \(b=3\), so \(a+b=5\). Final answer: 5

The figure shows drain current \(i_D\) versus drain-source voltage \(u_{DS}\), with gate-source voltage \(U_{GS}\) as a parameter. For \(U_{GS}=-1\text{ V}\) the drain current is highest, for \(U_{GS}=0\text{ V}\) it is lower, and for \(U_{GS}=1\text{ V}\) it is lowest, so \(i_D\) decreases as \(U_{GS}\) becomes more positive. Because there is significant drain current at \(U_{GS}=0\text{ V}\), the device operates in depletion mode, and because conduction is strongest at negative \(U_{GS}\) and weakest at positive \(U_{GS}\), it must be a P-channel device. A P-channel depletion MOSFET conducts at \(U_{GS}=0\), has its drain current reduced by positive gate voltages, and increased by negative gate voltages, matching the curves. Final answer: P-channel depletion MOSFET.

The figure shows a two-wire transmission line with characteristic impedance \(Z_0=50\,\Omega\); the input section is a \(\lambda/4\) line, at the end of which two parallel branches, each also \(\lambda/4\) long and having \(Z_0=50\,\Omega\), are connected, with one branch terminated in \(100\,\Omega\) and the other in \(200\,\Omega\). For a lossless quarter-wave line the input impedance is \(Z_{\text{in}}=Z_0^2/Z_L\), so the \(100\,\Omega\) branch presents \(50^2/100=25\,\Omega\) and the \(200\,\Omega\) branch presents \(50^2/200=12.5\,\Omega\) at the junction. These two impedances are in parallel, giving \(Z_{\parallel}=25\cdot12.5/(25+12.5)=25/3\,\Omega\). The main \(\lambda/4\) section transforms this to the input as \(Z_{\text{in}}=50^2/(25/3)=300\,\Omega\). The voltage reflection coefficient is therefore \(\Gamma=(Z_{\text{in}}-Z_0)/(Z_{\text{in}}+Z_0)=(300-50)/(300+50)=5/7\approx0.714\). Final answer: \(5/7\) (approximately \(0.714\)).

The CW7812 is a fixed 12 V regulator, so the voltage between its output terminal (point A) and its common terminal (point C) is held at 12 V, giving V_A − V_C = 12 V. The op-amp is connected with negative feedback: its non-inverting input is at ground potential and its inverting input is at point C, so the ideal op-amp virtual-short condition forces V_C to equal the grounded non-inverting input, namely 0 V. (The current through R1 is therefore (12 V − 0 V)/10 kΩ = 1.2 mA, which is supplied through R2 by the op-amp output, but this does not change the potential at C.) Thus the potential at point C is 0 V. Final answer: 0

The image shows a periodic rectangular-pulse signal \(x_1(t)\) with amplitude \(1\); over one period of length \(T=10\) (for example from \(-5\) to \(5\)), it is equal to \(1\) on the two intervals \((-3,-1)\) and \((1,3)\), giving a total nonzero width of \(4\). The DC coefficient is the average value over one period: \(a_0=\frac{1}{T}\int_{T}x_1(t)\,dt\). Thus \(a_0=\frac{1}{10}(1\cdot 4)=\frac{4}{10}=\frac{2}{5}\). Final answer: \(\frac{2}{5}\) (or \(0.4\)).

The figure shows three transistor terminals at +8 V, +5 V, and +4.3 V. For a bipolar junction transistor in the active region, an NPN transistor has terminal voltages in the order collector > base > emitter, while a PNP transistor has emitter > base > collector. The difference between the +5 V terminal and the +4.3 V terminal is 0.7 V, which is the typical forward-biased base-emitter voltage for a silicon BJT. Since the remaining terminal at +8 V is the highest, the voltage order is +8 V > +5 V > +4.3 V, matching the NPN ordering with the collector at +8 V, base at +5 V, and emitter at +4.3 V. Final answer: NPN transistor.

The graph plots gate capacitance C versus gate voltage V_G for two MOS transistors; both curves rise to the same high-capacitance plateau on the accumulation and inversion sides, while Curve2 dips to a lower capacitance in the depletion region than Curve1. For an MOS capacitor the accumulation/inversion capacitance approaches the oxide capacitance C_ox = ε_ox/t_ox, so the plateau height determines the oxide thickness. Because the two high-capacitance plateaus are at essentially the same level, the oxide capacitances—and therefore the oxide thicknesses—of MOS1 and MOS2 are about equal; the deeper minimum of Curve2 indicates a difference in substrate doping rather than oxide thickness. Final answer: the oxide layer thickness of MOS1 is approximately equal to that of MOS2.

The circuit shows an ideal op-amp with its non-inverting input connected to a 10 V source, a 1 kΩ resistor from the inverting input to ground, and a 1 µF capacitor (with its plus terminal on the output side) connected between the inverting input and the output through switch S. For an ideal op-amp with negative feedback, the virtual-short condition gives v = v₊ = 10 V, so the current through the 1 kΩ resistor is I_R = 10 V / 1 kΩ = 10 mA. Because the op-amp input draws no current, this same 10 mA must flow through the capacitor branch from the output toward the inverting input. With the capacitor voltage defined as V_C = v_o − v₋ (positive at the output terminal), this current leaves the positive terminal, so the capacitor current is i_C = −10 mA. Using i_C = C dV_C/dt gives dV_C/dt = (−10 mA)/(1 µF) = −10000 V/s. Since the capacitor is initially uncharged, V_C(0) = 0, integration yields V_C(t) = −10000 t V. At t = 1 ms = 0.001 s, V_C = −10000 × 0.001 V = −10 V. Final answer: −10 V.

The figure shows a unijunction transistor with intrinsic standoff ratio η = 0.8 powered by a 15 V DC source V_BB, with base B1 grounded and base B2 connected to V_BB. The emitter trigger voltage V_p is the UJT peak-point voltage, given by V_p = η V_BB + V_D, where V_D is the emitter-base diode forward voltage (assumed to be the typical silicon value of 0.7 V since it is not specified in the figure). Substituting values: V_p = (0.8)(15 V) + 0.7 V = 12 V + 0.7 V = 12.7 V. Final answer: 12.7

The diagram shows a unity negative-feedback loop whose summing junction produces the error signal \(E(s)=R(s)-Y(s)\), with the plant output \(Y(s)=G(s)E(s)\). Solving for the error gives \(E(s)=\frac{R(s)}{1+G(s)}\). For a unit step input, \(R(s)=\frac{1}{s}\), so applying the final-value theorem yields \(e_{ss}=\lim_{s\to 0}sE(s)=\lim_{s\to 0}\frac{1}{1+G(s)}\). Since \(G(s)=\frac{6}{s(s+1)(s+2)}\) has a pole at the origin, \(\lim_{s\to 0}G(s)=\infty\), and therefore \(e_{ss}=0\). Final answer: \(e(t)\to 0\) as \(t\to\infty\).

The figure shows an ideal three-winding transformer with windings 1, 2 and 3 on a common core; the polarity marks indicate the dotted terminals, so the dotted-to-undotted voltages of all three windings is in phase. With turns ratio N1:N2:N3 = 4:2:1 and V1 = 400∠0° V, the ideal-transformer voltage relation gives V2 = (N2/N1)V1 = (2/4)(400∠0°) = 200∠0° V and V3 = (N3/N1)V1 = (1/4)(400∠0°) = 100∠0° V. The load currents leaving the dotted terminals are therefore IR = V2/R = 200/10 = 20 A and IC = V3/(-jXc) = 100/(-j2.5) = j40 A. Ampere-turn balance for the ideal transformer gives I1 = (N2/N1)IR + (N3/N1)IC = (2/4)(20) + (1/4)(j40) = 10 + j10 A = 10√2 ∠45° A. Final answer: 10 + j10 A (≈14.14∠45° A).

In the circuit, the NPN transistor’s base is connected through a 10 kΩ resistor to +12 V, the emitter is connected to two series 1 kΩ resistors to ground, U1 is the DC base voltage, and U2 is the DC voltage at the node between the two 1 kΩ emitter resistors. For DC analysis the capacitors are open, so the total emitter resistance to ground is 2 kΩ. Using the base-emitter loop, I_B = (12 V − U_BEQ) / [R_B + (1+β)R_E] = (12 − 0.6) / [10 kΩ + 101×2 kΩ] = 11.4 / 212 kΩ 53.8 μA. The emitter current is I_E = (1+β)I_B = 101×53.8 μA ≈ 5.43 mA. The voltage U2 across the lower 1 kΩ resistor is I_E×1 kΩ 5.43 V, and the voltage across the upper 1 kΩ resistor is also I_E×1 kΩ ≈ 5.43 V. Therefore U1 − U2 = U_BEQ + I_E×1 kΩ = 0.6 V + 5.43 V ≈ 6.03 V. Final answer: 6.03 V.

The circuit contains a 10 V independent source, a left 1 Ω resistor in parallel with it, a top 1 Ω resistor in parallel with a current-controlled voltage source 3i₀ (polarity – on the left/top-left node and + on terminal P), a right 1 Ω resistor carrying current i₀ downward from P toward Q, and a bottom 1 Ω resistor from the source’s negative terminal to Q. To find the Thevenin resistance across P–Q, compute the open-circuit voltage and short-circuit current. With the bottom-left node at 0 V and the top-left node at 10 V, KCL at the open terminal Q gives the current through the bottom 1 Ω resistor equal to i₀, so V_Q = V_P/2; the dependent source gives V_P – 10 = 3i₀, and since i₀ = V_P – V_Q = V_P/2, solving yields V_P = –20 V, V_Q = –10 V, and V_oc = V_P – V_Q = –10 V. Shorting P and Q makes i₀ = 0, so the dependent source becomes 0 V and V_P = V_Q = 10 V; the bottom 1 Ω resistor then carries 10 A from the shorted terminals to ground, giving I_sc = 10 A from P to Q. Therefore R_th = V_oc/I_sc = –10/10 = –1 Ω. Final answer: -1

The circuit is a clocked D latch: the two cross-coupled gates on the right form the storage latch, and the two left-hand gates are controlled by CLK so that D can affect the latch only while CLK is high (the CLK input has no inversion bubble, indicating active-high enabling). For such a latch, Q follows D when CLK = 1 and holds the last value when CLK = 0. Just before the transition, CLK = 1 and D = 0, so Q = 0. When CLK falls to 0, the latch closes and captures the present D value, which is still 0; afterward D changes to 1, but because CLK is now 0 the input path is disabled and the new D cannot propagate to the storage node. Therefore, at the CLK transition and afterward Q remains unchanged. Final answer: Q stays at 0 (low).

The 10 V source has its positive terminal at the top rail and its negative terminal at the bottom-left rail, so the top rail is 10 V above the bottom-left rail; the 2 V source has its positive terminal on the bottom-left rail and its negative terminal on the bottom-right rail, so the bottom-left rail is 2 V above the bottom-right rail. Taking the bottom-right rail as the reference node, the top rail voltage is therefore 10 V + 2 V = 12 V. The 3 Ω resistor is connected directly between the top rail and the bottom-right rail, so by Ohm’s law the current through it is I = V/R = 12 V / 3 Ω = 4 A. Final answer: 4

The state diagram shows two states, 0 and 1, with transitions labeled by two input variables. From state 0, the self-loop is labeled 0X (input J=0, K don't care) and the transition to state 1 is labeled 1X (input J=1, K don't care). From state 1, the self-loop is labeled X0 (input K=0, J don't care) and the transition back to state 0 is labeled X1 (input K=1, J don't care). These transition rules match the behavior of a JK flip-flop, where J controls the set-to-1 transition when Q=0 and K controls the reset-to-0 transition when Q=1. Final answer: JK flip-flop.

The circuit is a single loop containing a 4 V independent voltage source with its positive terminal at the top, a 1 Ω resistor on the top branch, and a 2 A independent current source on the right branch with its arrow pointing upward. Because the current source is in series with the other elements, it fixes the loop current at 2 A in the direction of its arrow, so 2 A flows through the resistor from right to left and enters the positive terminal of the voltage source. The power absorbed by the resistor is P_R = I²R = (2 A)²(1 Ω) = 4 W. Applying Kirchhoff’s voltage law around the loop in the direction of the current gives a 4 V rise across the voltage source, a 2 V drop across the resistor, and therefore a 6 V rise across the current source, so the current source delivers P = (6 V)(2 A) = 12 W. Since current enters the positive terminal of the voltage source, that source absorbs P = (4 V)(2 A) = 8 W, leaving the current source as the net supplier of the resistor’s power. Final answer: the 2 A current source.

The Nyquist plot of \(G(s)\) is a closed curve traversed clockwise, consisting of a large elliptical loop and a small double loop on the negative real axis; the indicated real-axis distances place the small-loop region roughly between \(-0.8\) and \(-0.4\), so for \(K=2\) the critical point is \(-1/K=-0.5\), which lies inside the right-hand small loop. For unity negative feedback the characteristic equation is \(1+KG(s)=0\), and with the clockwise Nyquist contour the Nyquist criterion is \(N=Z-P\), where \(N\) is the number of clockwise encirclements of \(-1/K\), \(Z\) is the number of closed-loop poles in the closed right-half plane, and \(P\) is the number of open-loop right-half-plane poles. Since \(G(s)\) has no closed right-half-plane poles, \(P=0\). The large ellipse encircles \(-0.5\) once clockwise, and the right-hand small loop also encircles \(-0.5\) once clockwise, while the left-hand small loop does not enclose \(-0.5\), giving \(N=2\). Therefore \(Z=N+P=2+0=2\). Final answer: 2

The block diagram shows a unity-feedback loop with error \(e=r-c\), a gain of 5 giving \(x=5e\), a dead-zone relay that produces \(u=0\) whenever \(|x|\le 0.5\) and \(u=\pm M\) outside that range, and a plant \(k/[s(Ts+1)]\) that contains an integrator. For a unit-step input \(r(t)=1\), the system can reach a steady state only when the relay output is zero, because a nonzero constant \(u\) would keep the integrator changing \(c\). Setting \(u=0\) requires the operating point to lie inside the dead zone: \(|x|\le 0.5\). Since \(x=5e\), this gives \(|5e_{ss}|\le 0.5\), so \(|e_{ss}|\le 0.5/5=0.1\). Therefore the steady-state error is not a single value but can be any value in the interval \([-0.1,\,0.1]\), and its largest possible value is \(0.1\). Final answer: 0.1

From the figure, \(i_1\) is the left waveform with peak value \(10\ \text{mA}\), zero at \(t=0\), and period \(T=4\ \text{ms}\), so \(\omega=2\pi/T=500\pi\ \text{rad/s}\) and \(i_1=10\sin(500\pi t)\ \text{mA}\); \(i_2\) has the same period, passes through zero at \(t=1.5\ \text{ms}\) with positive slope, and has peak amplitude \(5\sqrt2\ \text{mA}\), giving \(i_2=5\sqrt2\sin[500\pi(t-1.5\times10^{-3})]=5\sqrt2\sin(500\pi t-3\pi/4)\ \text{mA}\). Adding the two currents: \(i=10\sin(500\pi t)+5\sqrt2\sin(500\pi t-3\pi/4)=10\sin\theta+5\sqrt2[\sin\theta\cos(3\pi/4)-\cos\theta\sin(3\pi/4)]=10\sin\theta-5\sin\theta-5\cos\theta=5\sin\theta-5\cos\theta=5\sqrt2\sin(500\pi t-\pi/4)\ \text{mA}\). Final answer: \(i=5\sqrt2\sin(500\pi t-\pi/4)\ \text{mA}\) with \(t\) in seconds.

The circuit is a common-emitter NPN amplifier with base bias provided by the \(R_{B1}\)–\(R_{B2}\) voltage divider, an emitter resistor \(R_E\), and a collector resistor \(R_C\). For the DC operating point the base voltage is taken as set by the divider, so \(V_{BQ}\approx V_{CC}\frac{R_{B2}}{R_{B1}+R_{B2}}=12\text{ V}\cdot\frac{10\text{ k}\Omega}{20\text{ k}\Omega+10\text{ k}\Omega}=4\text{ V}\). The emitter current is then \(I_{EQ}=\frac{V_{BQ}-U_{BEQ}}{R_E}=\frac{4\text{ V}-0.6\text{ V}}{2\text{ k}\Omega}=1.7\text{ mA}\), and because \(I_{EQ}=(1+\beta)I_{BQ}\), the quiescent base current is \(I_{BQ}=\frac{I_{EQ}}{1+\beta}=\frac{1.7\text{ mA}}{51}\approx 33.3\ \mu\text{A}\). Final answer: 33.3 μA.

The image shows a two-stage amplifier using op-amps A1 and A2: A1 has its non-inverting input grounded and its inverting input receives the input signal ui through resistor R1, A1's output drives the non-inverting input of A2, and A2 has its inverting input grounded with its output uo returned through resistor R2 to the inverting input of A1. Because R2 is connected directly to the output voltage node uo, the feedback signal is proportional to the output voltage, so the output sampling is voltage feedback. At the input, both the signal current through R1 and the feedback current through R2 converge at the inverting input node of A1 and combine according to Kirchhoff's current law, so the input mixing is parallel (shunt) feedback. The feedback opposes the input change, making it negative. Final answer: voltage-parallel negative feedback (also called voltage-shunt negative feedback).

The figure shows a three-phase source with each line having a line-to-ground capacitance \(C_0\); during a single-phase ground fault the capacitances of the healthy phases produce the given capacitive current of 35 A. An arc-suppression coil connected at the neutral must supply an inductive current opposite to this capacitive current, and during the fault the voltage across the coil is the phase voltage \(U/\sqrt{3}\), where \(U = 10\,\text{kV}\) is the line voltage. To reduce the residual grounding current to 20 A, the coil current must be \(I_L = 35\,\text{A} - 20\,\text{A} = 15\,\text{A}\). Using \(I_L = U_{\text{ph}}/(\omega L)\) with \(U_{\text{ph}} = 10\,000/\sqrt{3}\,\text{V}\) and \(\omega = 2\pi \times 50 \approx 314\,\text{rad/s}\), the inductance is \(L = \dfrac{10\,000/\sqrt{3}}{314 \times 15} \approx 1.23\,\text{H}\). Final answer: 1.23 H

The circuit has b as the reference point, with E1 = 10 V, R1 = 10 Ω, E2 = 8 V, R2 = 4 Ω, R = 2 Ω, and R3 = 2 Ω, and the potential at point a is given as 6 V. Since node a is connected only to the 2 Ω resistor R and to the branch containing E2, R2, E3, and R3, the current through R must be equal and opposite to the current through that branch; therefore no current can flow through the E1–R1 branch, the voltage drop across R1 is zero, and Vc = E1 = 10 V. The current in resistor R is I = (Va - Vc)/R = (6 - 10)/2 = -2 A, so the actual current is 2 A from c toward a in R and hence 2 A from a toward c in the right-hand branch. Applying Kirchhoff’s voltage law from a to c along that branch gives Va - Vc = E2 + I R2 - E3 + I R3, so -4 = 8 + 8 - E3 + 4, which yields E3 = 24 V. Final answer: 24 V.

The image shows a 1 kΩ resistor in series with a parallel combination of a 100 kΩ resistor and a 1 kΩ resistor, with terminals a and b across the entire network. For the parallel branch, the equivalent resistance is given by R_parallel = (R1 × R2)/(R1 + R2) = (100 kΩ × 1 kΩ)/(100 kΩ + 1 kΩ) ≈ 0.99 kΩ, which by engineering approximation is about 1 kΩ because the 100 kΩ resistor is much larger than the 1 kΩ resistor and therefore has little effect. Adding the series 1 kΩ resistor gives R_ab ≈ 1 kΩ + 1 kΩ = 2 kΩ. Final answer: 2 kΩ.

The circuit contains two tri-state TTL gates whose outputs are wired together to form F. The upper gate is a tri-state NAND gate with data inputs A and B and active-high enable C (no bubble on EN), so it drives the line low when C=1 and AB=1. The lower gate is a tri-state inverter with data input C and active-low enable B (bubble on EN), so it drives the line low when B=0 and C=1. Therefore the line is low exactly when F' = C·AB + B'·C = C(AB + B') = C(A + B') = AC + B'C, and hence F = (AC + B'C)' = (AC)'(B'C)' = (A' + C')(B + C') = A'B + C'. Final answer: F = A'B + C'.

In the circuit, terminal A is open, so no current flows through R1 and the potential at A equals the potential of the node between R2 and R3. The left loop contains the 16 V source, R2, R3, and the 7 V source with its positive terminal at the top, so the net driving voltage is 16 V − 7 V = 9 V across R2+R3 = 10 Ω, giving loop current I = 9/10 = 0.9 A. The junction voltage is V_A = 16 V − I R2 = 16 − 0.9×4 = 12.4 V (also 7 V + 0.9×6 = 12.4 V). The 12 V source is connected with its positive terminal at B, so V_B = 12 V relative to the common rail. Therefore U_AB = V_A − V_B = 12.4 V − 12 V = 0.4 V. Final answer: 0.4 V.

The image shows a lossless 100 Ω TEM line driven by a Thevenin step source \(A u(t)\) with source resistance \(R_{\text{Th}}\), and the input voltage \(v(t)\) is a pulse of amplitude 1 for \(0<t<\tau\) followed by an exponential recovery. The smooth exponential rise after the first reflected wave returns indicates that the source end is matched to the line, because any mismatch would produce additional reflected steps rather than a simple exponential. For a matched source, \(R_{\text{Th}} = Z_0\). Since \(Z_0 = 100\ \Omega\), it follows that \(R_{\text{Th}} = 100\ \Omega\), which is also consistent with the initial incident voltage being one-half of the final source level. Final answer: 100

The image shows a single-loop circuit with a voltage source E on the left (positive terminal at the top) and a current source I_K on the right whose arrow points upward. Because the current source determines the loop current, a current of magnitude I_K flows upward through the current source, leftward along the top wire, downward through E from its positive terminal to its negative terminal, and rightward along the bottom wire back to the current source. For the voltage source E, current enters its positive terminal, so E absorbs power P_E = E I_K. For the current source I_K, the voltage across it equals E with its top terminal positive, while the current I_K flows from the lower-potential terminal to the higher-potential terminal; a source whose current is driven from lower to higher potential delivers power, so the current source outputs power P_I = E I_K. Final answer: the current source I_K.

Figure I shows that D1 enters reverse breakdown at about −80 V and D2 at about −70 V, while Figure II shows the two diodes in series with a 0–100 V supply whose positive terminal is at the top. In the circuit, D1 is oriented with its cathode toward the positive supply and D2 with its anode toward the positive supply, so D1 is reverse biased and D2 is forward biased. The reverse voltage across D1 therefore increases with the supply and reaches D1’s zener breakdown voltage of 80 V before the supply reaches 100 V, causing D1 to conduct in breakdown; D2 never sees a large reverse voltage because it is forward biased. Final answer: D1.

The image shows a ring network formed by a 220 kV bus, a 110 kV line, and a 35 kV bus, interconnected by three transformers rated 220/38.5 kV, 220/121 kV, and 110/38.5 kV. Circulating power in a closed transformer loop exists when the product of the voltage ratios around the loop is not equal to unity. Traversing the loop in the direction 220 kV → 220/121 kV transformer → 110 kV line → 110/38.5 kV transformer → 35 kV bus → 220/38.5 kV transformer → back to 220 kV gives the voltage-ratio product (121/220) × (38.5/110) × (220/38.5) = 121/110 ≈ 1.1, which is not equal to 1, so circulating power does exist. Because this product exceeds 1, the net voltage rises in this clockwise direction, driving the circulating power in the same clockwise direction around the ring. Final answer: Yes, circulating power exists; it circulates clockwise as 220 kV bus → 220/121 kV transformer → 110 kV line → 110/38.5 kV transformer → 35 kV bus → 220/38.5 kV transformer → 220 kV bus.

Figure 1 shows a permanent magnet moving along a drift tube through a coil, and Figure 2 shows the open-circuit coil voltage, which is zero when the magnet is at the coil center and antisymmetric about that point. The induced emf is \(v=-d\lambda/dt\), so for the measured voltage at \(u=5\ \mathrm{m/s}\), \(v(t)=A t e^{-a t}\) with \(t=x/u\) gives \(d\lambda/dx=-v/u\) and, after integrating, \(\lambda(x)=(A/a^2)(1+a x/u)e^{-a x/u}\) for \(x>0\). At the starting position \(x_0=1\ \mathrm{cm}=0.01\ \mathrm{m}\), \(a x_0/u=500(0.01)/5=1\), so \(\lambda(x_0)=(1000e/500^2)(2/e)=0.008\ \mathrm{Wb}\). With a constant coil current \(I_0\), the force on the magnet is \(F=I_0\,d\lambda/dx\), and the work done from \(x_0\) to far outside the coil is \(W=I_0[\lambda(\infty)-\lambda(x_0)]=-I_0\lambda(x_0)\). To raise the \(0.050\ \mathrm{kg}\) magnet through \(h=1\ \mathrm{m}\) requires \(W=mgh=(0.050)(9.8)(1)=0.49\ \mathrm{J}\), so \(I_0=-0.49/0.008\approx -61\ \mathrm{A}\); the negative sign means the current must be opposite the defined positive direction so the magnetic force pushes the magnet in the launch direction. Final answer: -61 A

The image shows the overall transfer function \(X(f)\) as a triangle centered at \(0\ \text{Hz}\), nonzero from \(-2000\ \text{Hz}\) to \(2000\ \text{Hz}\). For zero intersymbol interference, the folded spectrum must be constant, i.e. \(\sum_k X(f - k/T_s) = \text{constant}\). For a triangular frequency response with one-sided bandwidth \(B = 2000\ \text{Hz}\), the maximum symbol rate is \(R_s = B\), because shifting the triangular spectrum by its one-sided bandwidth \(2000\ \text{Hz}\) makes the overlapping copies sum to a constant. Thus \(R_s = 2000\ \text{Baud} = 2\ \text{kBaud}\). Final answer: 2.

The circuit shows that \(f\) is the OR of the AND of \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) with \(f_3\), so \(f = f_1 f_2 + f_3\). Given \(f_1 = \sum 8,9,10\) and \(f_2 = \sum 7,8,12,13,14,15\), their intersection is \(f_1 f_2 = \sum 8\). Since \(f = \sum 8,9\), the minterm \(8\) is already produced by \(f_1 f_2\), so \(f_3\) must supply the remaining minterm \(9\). Final answer: \(f_3(w,x,y,z)=\sum 9\).

The image shows a right-circularly-polarized wave in air with εr1=1 incident at 60° to the normal on a dielectric of relative permittivity εr2, and the reflected wave is stated to be linearly polarized. For a nonmagnetic dielectric interface the Fresnel reflection coefficients are real, so an incident circularly polarized wave would normally remain elliptically or circularly polarized upon reflection unless one of its orthogonal polarization components is eliminated. The p-polarized reflection coefficient vanishes at Brewster’s angle, leaving only the s-polarized component and thus a linearly polarized reflected wave. Therefore the 60° incidence angle is Brewster’s angle, satisfying tan θ_B = √(εr2/εr1). With θ_B = 60° and εr1 = 1, tan 60° = √3 = √εr2, giving εr2 = 3. Final answer: 3.

The image shows a 4:1 multiplexer with data inputs P, Q, R, S connected to positions 0, 1, 2, 3, select lines S1 = X (MSB) and S0 = Y (LSB), and output F(X,Y). The general 4:1 MUX output is F = ¬S1¬S0·P + ¬S1S0·Q + S1¬S0·R + S1S0·S, so substituting S1 = X and S0 = Y gives F = ¬X¬Y·P + ¬XY·Q + X¬Y·R + XY·S. The desired function F = X¬Y + ¬X can be expanded as F = X¬Y + ¬X(Y + ¬Y) = ¬X¬Y + ¬XY + X¬Y, meaning the minterms for (X,Y) = (0,0), (0,1), and (1,0) must be 1, while the minterm for (1,1) must be 0. Matching these coefficients yields P = 1, Q = 1, R = 1, and S = 0. Final answer: P=1, Q=1, R=1, S=0.

The image shows a Schmitt-trigger inverter with its output connected back to its input through a 10 kΩ resistor, and a 47 nF capacitor connected from the input node to ground, forming an astable relaxation oscillator. For this circuit, the capacitor alternately charges toward the high output level V_OH = 5 V and discharges toward the low output level V_OL = 0 V, bounded by the upper threshold V_T+ = 2.4 V and lower threshold V_T- = 1.6 V. The period is T = RC [ln((V_OH - V_T-)/(V_OH - V_T+)) + ln((V_T+ - V_OL)/(V_T- - V_OL))], so with R = 10 kΩ and C = 47 nF we have RC = 10×10^3 × 47×10^(-9) = 4.7×10^(-4) s. Substituting the thresholds gives T = 4.7×10^(-4) [ln((5-1.6)/(5-2.4)) + ln((2.4-0)/(1.6-0))] = 4.7×10^(-4) [ln(3.4/2.6) + ln(2.4/1.6)] = 4.7×10^(-4) [0.26824 + 0.40547] = 4.7×10^(-4) × 0.67371 3.1664×10^(-4) s. The frequency is therefore f = 1/T ≈ 3158.37 Hz. Final answer: 3158.37 Hz.

The figure shows a transmission gate (TG) symbol with input A, output Y, a top control line marked "0" with a bubble indicating active-low/PMOS control, and a bottom control line marked "1" indicating active-high/NMOS control. A transmission gate is a CMOS bidirectional analog switch consisting of an NMOS and a PMOS transistor connected in parallel, where the NMOS turns on when its gate is high and the PMOS turns on when its gate is low, so with the top control at 0 and the bottom control at 1 both devices conduct and create a low-resistance path between A and Y. Because the symbol is labeled TG and uses complementary control signals to enable a conducting path between input and output, the circuit is a CMOS transmission gate. Final answer: CMOS transmission gate.

The image shows a JK flip-flop with both J and K inputs tied to logic 0, with an active-low clock input (indicated by the bubble), and active-low asynchronous set (S_D) and reset (R_D) inputs. For a JK flip-flop, the characteristic equation is Q_{n+1} = J\bar{Q}_n + \bar{K}Q_n; substituting J=0 and K=0 gives Q_{n+1} = 0\cdot\bar{Q}_n + \bar{0}\cdot Q_n = 0 + 1\cdot Q_n = Q_n, meaning the next state equals the present state. Therefore, the circuit performs the hold (memory) function, retaining the previous output state on each active clock edge. Final answer: The circuit performs a hold (memory) function, where the output Q retains its previous state.

The block diagram shows a unity-feedback system whose open-loop transfer function is \(L(s)=\dfrac{K+0.366s}{s(s+1)}\). A phase margin of \(60^\circ\) at the gain-crossover frequency \(\omega=1\) rad/s means \(|L(j1)|=1\) and \(\angle L(j1)=-120^\circ\). At \(\omega=1\), \(L(j1)=\dfrac{K+j0.366}{j(1+j)}=\dfrac{K+j0.366}{-1+j}\), so the denominator contributes a phase of \(135^\circ\). Thus \(\angle L(j1)=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{0.366}{K}\right)-135^\circ=-120^\circ\), giving \(\tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{0.366}{K}\right)=15^\circ\). Therefore \(K=\dfrac{0.366}{\tan 15^\circ}\approx\dfrac{0.366}{0.2679}\approx1.366\), which also satisfies the magnitude condition \(\sqrt{K^2+0.366^2}/\sqrt{2}=1\). Final answer: 1.366.

The solenoid’s winding current is upward on the front side at the right end, so the right-hand grip rule gives a magnetic field inside the solenoid pointing to the right, toward the coaxial loop on the right. The induced current \(i\) is drawn clockwise when the loop is viewed from the left (solenoid side), and the right-hand rule for a current loop shows that such a clockwise current produces an induced magnetic field to the right through the loop. By Lenz’s law, an induced field in the same direction as the solenoid’s field opposes a decrease in magnetic flux, which occurs when the solenoid is moved away from the loop. Final answer: Move the solenoid away from the loop, i.e., to the left along the axis.

The circuit contains two D flip-flops sharing CLK; the left flip-flop has D=A and Q=C, the right flip-flop has D=C and Q=D, a NOR gate produces B with A as one input, and an XOR gate produces D from B and C. For a D flip-flop, the next state equals its D input, so C+=A and D+=C; a state that does not change with the clock requires C+=C and D+=D, giving A=C and C=D, hence A=C=D. The XOR relation D=B⊕C then becomes C=B⊕C, which forces B=0. With B=0 the NOR gate output is 0 only when at least one input is 1, so A must be 1 (the second NOR input is either A or the feedback B, and in either case the stable condition forces A=1). Therefore [A,B,C,D]=[1,0,1,1], whose decimal equivalent is 11. Final answer: 11

The circuit is a series RLC circuit with R = 1 Ω, L = 1 H, and C = 1 F, with current i(t) defined entering the positive terminal. For t ≥ 0 the input is v(t) = u(t), so V(s) = 1/s. In the Laplace domain the resistor contributes I(s), the inductor contributes sI(s) − i_L(0−) = sI(s) − 1, and the capacitor contributes I(s)/s + v_C(0−)/s = I(s)/s − 1/s. Applying KVL gives 1/s = (1 + s + 1/s)I(s) − 1 − 1/s, so (1 + s + 1/s)I(s) = 1 + 2/s. Multiplying numerator and denominator by s yields I(s) = (s + 2)/(s^2 + s + 1). Final answer: I(s) = (s + 2)/(s^2 + s + 1).

The CD4060 is driven by a 32768 Hz crystal and its Q14 output (pin 3) is fed to the clock input C1 of a 74LS74 D flip-flop, whose D input is connected to its own Q complement so it toggles on every clock edge. CD4060 divides the oscillator by 2^14, giving 32768 Hz / 16384 = 2 Hz at Q14. The 74LS74 then divides this by another factor of 2, so the final Q output is 2 Hz / 2 = 1 Hz. Final answer: 1 Hz.

The figure shows two impedances \(Z_1\) and \(Z_2\) connected in series, with the voltmeter connected across the entire series combination, so the voltage it reads is the phasor sum of the two branch voltages \(u_1\) and \(u_2\). The given voltages have RMS values \(U_1 = 80\ \text{V}\) at phase \(45^\circ\) and \(U_2 = 60\ \text{V}\) at phase \(-45^\circ\). In rectangular form, \(U_1 = 80(\cos45^\circ + j\sin45^\circ) = 40\sqrt2 + j40\sqrt2\) and \(U_2 = 60(\cos(-45^\circ) + j\sin(-45^\circ)) = 30\sqrt2 - j30\sqrt2\). Adding them gives \(U = U_1 + U_2 = 70\sqrt2 + j10\sqrt2\), whose magnitude is \(\sqrt{(70\sqrt2)^2 + (10\sqrt2)^2} = \sqrt{9800 + 200} = \sqrt{10000} = 100\ \text{V}\). Final answer: 100 V.

The circuit has a 100 V independent source fixing the left node at 100 V relative to the bottom reference, a middle branch of two series 4 Ω resistors with the controlled voltage \(V_x\) defined across the left 4 Ω resistor (positive on the right), a top branch containing a dependent voltage source \(V_x\) (positive on the right) in series with a 4 Ω resistor, and the load \(R_L\) connected between the right-hand node and the bottom reference. Let \(V\) be the voltage at the right-hand node; the middle-branch current is \(I_m=(100-V)/8\), so \(V_x=-4I_m=(V-100)/2\). The top-branch current is \(I_t=(100+V_x-V)/4=(100-V)/8\). Applying KCL at the right-hand node gives \(I_m+I_t=V/R_L\), which simplifies to \((100-V)/4=V/R_L\) and yields \(V=100R_L/(R_L+4)\). This relationship is equivalent to a 100 V Thevenin source in series with a 4 Ω resistance, so the Thevenin resistance seen by \(R_L\) is \(R_{th}=4\ \Omega\). By the maximum power transfer theorem, maximum power is delivered to \(R_L\) when \(R_L=R_{th}\). Final answer: \(4\ \Omega\).

The figure shows a balanced three-phase network in which three inductors L are connected in a delta and three capacitors C are connected in a star to the same three terminals. For balanced 50 Hz excitation, the delta of inductors is equivalent to a wye with inductance L/3 per phase, so the inductor branch contributes a line current 3V/(jωL); the star capacitors have their neutral at the system neutral, contributing jωC V. Setting the total line current to zero gives 3/(jωL) + jωC = 0, hence C = 3/(ω²L). With f = 50 Hz, ω = 2πf ≈ 314.16 rad/s, and L = 10 mH = 0.01 H, C = 3/((314.16)² × 0.01) ≈ 3.04 × 10⁻³ F = 3.04 mF. Final answer: 3.04 mF.

The image shows a resistor \(R\) and an inductor \(L\) connected in series, so the same current flows through both elements and the total voltage \(u\) is the phasor sum of \(u_R\) and \(u_L\); in a series \(RL\) circuit the inductor voltage leads the resistor voltage by \(90^\circ\). The given voltages have rms phasors \(U_R = 5\angle 10^\circ\) V and \(U_L = 5\angle 100^\circ\) V, so \(U = 5\angle 10^\circ + 5\angle 100^\circ = 5(\cos10^\circ + j\sin10^\circ) + 5(\cos100^\circ + j\sin100^\circ) = 5\sqrt{2}\angle 55^\circ\) V rms. Converting back to a sinusoid, the peak value is \(\sqrt{2}\times 5\sqrt{2}=10\) V, giving \(u = 10\sin(\omega t + 55^\circ)\) V. Final answer: \(u = 10\sin(\omega t + 55^\circ)\) V.

The graph shows current i (A) versus time t (s): from 0 to 2 s the current rises linearly from 0 to 4 A, from 2 to 4 s it stays constant at 4 A, from 4 to 6 s it rises linearly from 4 to 6 A, and from 6 to 8 s it falls linearly from 6 A to 0 A. For an inductive coil, the self-induced electromotive force has magnitude |e| = L |di/dt|, so it is proportional to the absolute value of the slope of the i–t graph. The slopes are: 0–2 s, (4−0)/(2−0) = 2 A/s; 2–4 s, 0 A/s; 4–6 s, (6−4)/(6−4) = 1 A/s; 6–8 s, (0−6)/(8−6) = −3 A/s, with magnitude 3 A/s. Since 3 A/s is the largest magnitude of the slope, the self-induced emf is greatest during 6 s to 8 s. Final answer: 6 s to 8 s.

The figure shows two capacitors, \(C_1\) and \(C_2\), connected in series in the upper branch, with a switch \(S\) in the lower branch that completes a single closed loop when closed. Initially \(C_1\) carries charge \(Q_0=C_1U\) while \(C_2\) has no charge. After the switch is closed, charge is conserved at the isolated node between the capacitors and the loop rule requires the two capacitors to have equal voltage magnitudes but opposite polarities. Let that common voltage magnitude be \(V\). Conservation of charge at the internal node gives \(-C_1V-C_2V=-C_1U\), so \(V=\dfrac{C_1U}{C_1+C_2}\). Since \(C_1=2C_2\), we get \(V=\dfrac{2C_2U}{2C_2+C_2}=\dfrac{2}{3}U\). Final answer: \(\dfrac{2}{3}U\).

The given speed–torque graph shows the motor runs at 1500 rpm when torque is zero and at 1400 rpm when torque is 5 Nm. With rotational losses neglected, the no-load armature current is zero, so the back EMF equals the 200 V supply at 1500 rpm. For a separately excited DC motor with constant field, E = kφω and T = kφI_a. Taking ω0 = 1500 rpm = 1500·2π/60 rad/s, kφ = 200/ω0 = 200/(1500·2π/60) ≈ 1.273 Nm/A. At 5 Nm, I_a = T/kφ ≈ 5/1.273 ≈ 3.927 A. At 1400 rpm the back EMF is E = 200·(1400/1500) ≈ 186.67 V, so the armature resistance is R_a = (V − E)/I_a ≈ (200 − 186.67)/3.927 ≈ 3.395 Ω. Final answer: 3.395 Ω (approximately 3.4 Ω).

The image shows an NPN transistor with terminals C (collector), B (base), and E (emitter), with base current I_B entering the base and collector current I_C flowing out of the collector, and a note indicating β_dc is the dc current gain. For a BJT operating in saturation, the collector current is limited by the external circuit rather than by the base current, so the transistor is fully turned on and cannot sustain the active-mode relationship I_C = β_dc I_B; instead, the base current is larger than the minimum required for the actual collector current, giving I_C < β_dc I_B. Final answer: I_C < β_dc I_B.

The circuit is a 555 timer configured as an astable multivibrator: pins 6 (TH) and 2 (TR) are tied together, a 0.1 µF timing capacitor is connected from that junction to ground, the discharge pin 7 is at the node between the 5.1 kΩ and 1 kΩ resistors, and diode D is in parallel with the 1 kΩ resistor. Assuming the diode is oriented to conduct during the charging phase, the capacitor charges through the 5.1 kΩ resistor (with the diode bypassing the 1 kΩ resistor) and discharges through the 1 kΩ resistor, so the period is T ≈ 0.693(R_A + R_B)C and the frequency is f ≈ 1.44/[(R_A + R_B)C]. Substituting R_A = 5.1 kΩ, R_B = 1 kΩ, and C = 0.1 µF gives f 1.44/[(5.1 kΩ + 1 kΩ)(0.1 µF)] = 1.44/(6.1 kΩ × 0.1 µF) ≈ 2.36 × 10³ Hz. Final answer: approximately 2.4 kHz.

The image shows an op-amp powered from ±10 V, with the inverting input connected to a 100 µF capacitor and a 10 kΩ resistor to −10 V, and the noninverting input connected to a 1 kΩ/4 kΩ divider from Vo; Vo is clamped by Z1 and Z2 to ±5 V. Interpreting the switch/capacitor branch so that closing the switch holds V− at +10 V and opening it leaves the capacitor in series with the 10 kΩ resistor to −10 V, the noninverting threshold is Vo·1k/(1k+4k)=Vo/5=±1 V. Initially Vo=−5 V because V−=+10 V > −1 V, so the switching threshold is −1 V. The inverting node decays as V−(t)=−10+20e^(−t/RC) with τ=RC=(10 kΩ)(100 µF)=1 s. Setting V−(t1)=−1 V gives −1=−10+20e^(−t1), so e^(−t1)=0.45 and t1=−ln(0.45)≈0.80 s. Final answer: approximately 0.80 s.

The circuit consists of a 9 Ω resistor in series with the input and a shunt branch of 1 Ω in series with a 1 F capacitor from the output node to ground, so the transfer function is H(s)=V_o/V_in=(1+1/s)/(9+1+1/s)=(1−j/ω)/(10−j/ω) with s=jω. The phase is φ(ω)=∠H(jω)=arctan(1/(10ω))−arctan(1/ω), which is negative for all ω>0. To find the maximum phase lag, set dφ/dω=0: d/dω[arctan(1/(10ω))−arctan(1/ω)] = −10/(100ω^2+1)+1/(ω^2+1)=0, giving 1/(ω^2+1)=10/(100ω^2+1). Solving yields 100ω^2+1=10ω^2+10, so 90ω^2=9 and ω=1/√10 rad/s. Final answer: 1/√10 rad/s.

The figure shows four labeled components: A is a two-terminal cylindrical diode with a polarity band; B is a three-leaded device in a TO-92-style package, which is a bipolar junction transistor (transistor/triode); C is a three-terminal thyristor/SCR with terminals labeled K (cathode), G (gate), and A (anode); and D is a surface-mount resistor marked “R100.” A triode (transistor) is a three-terminal active semiconductor device, and among the choices, only component B is a transistor, whereas A is a diode, C is a thyristor, and D is a resistor. Final answer: B.

The image shows a D flip-flop with its D input driven by a dashed-box gate whose inputs are T and the flip-flop's Q output, so the next state is determined by Q(next) = D. To make the circuit behave as a T flip-flop, the characteristic equation must be Q(next) = T ⊕ Q, which gives T = 0 → no change (Q(next) = Q) and T = 1 → toggle (Q(next) = Q̄). Since a D flip-flop satisfies Q(next) = D, we need D = T ⊕ Q, which is exactly the function of a two-input XOR gate. Final answer: XOR gate.

The circuit shows resistor R1 in series with a parallel branch containing resistor R2 (controlled by switch S) and light bulb L. With the total circuit voltage held constant, closing S connects R2 in parallel with L, which reduces the equivalent resistance of that branch because a parallel combination has lower resistance than either individual branch. The total circuit resistance therefore decreases, so the total current from the source increases. Because R1 is in series, the voltage drop across R1 increases (V = IR1), leaving less voltage across the parallel branch and thus less voltage across bulb L. Since the power dissipated by L is P = V_L² / R_L, a smaller voltage across L means less power and reduced brightness. Final answer: The brightness of light bulb L decreases (it becomes dimmer) when switch S is closed.

The circuit contains a 5 V independent source, a 2 kΩ resistor in series with it, a 2 kΩ resistor from that node to terminal B, a dependent voltage source labeled 3V_AB with its positive terminal on the left and negative terminal on the right, and a 1 kΩ resistor from terminal A to terminal B. To find the Thevenin resistance across A and B, the independent 5 V source is deactivated (replaced by a short), leaving the two 2 kΩ resistors in parallel, which combine to 1 kΩ. Let V be the voltage across A and B (so V_AB = V), and let the node to the left of the dependent source be C; because the dependent source has value 3V_AB with the shown polarity, V_C − V_A = 3V, giving V_C = 4V. The current drawn from a test source connected across A and B is the sum of the current through the 1 kΩ resistor from A to B, which is V/1 kΩ, and the current that flows from A through the dependent source and then through the equivalent 1 kΩ resistor from C to B, which is V_C/1 kΩ = 4V/1 kΩ. Thus I = V/1 kΩ + 4V/1 kΩ = 5V/1 kΩ, and R_th = V/I = 1 kΩ/5 = 200 Ω. Final answer: 200 Ω.

The circuit shows two capacitors \(C_1=3\text{F}\) and \(C_2=1\text{F}\) connected in series with a \(10\,\Omega\) resistor and a switch; initially \(V_{C_1}=1\text{V}\) and \(V_{C_2}=3\text{V}\), with both positive terminals oriented the same way. Since there is no external source, the total charge on the two top plates is conserved, and at steady state the current is zero so KVL requires the two capacitor voltages to be equal. Initial charges are \(Q_{1i}=C_1V_{1i}=3\times1=3\text{C}\) and \(Q_{2i}=C_2V_{2i}=1\times3=3\text{C}\), giving a total conserved charge of \(6\text{C}\). With final common voltage \(V_f\), \(C_1V_f+C_2V_f=4V_f=6\), so \(V_f=1.5\text{V}\). Initial stored energy is \(\frac12(3)(1)^2+\frac12(1)(3)^2=6\text{J}\), final stored energy is \(\frac12(4)(1.5)^2=4.5\text{J}\), and the energy dissipated in the resistor is the difference \(6-4.5=1.5\text{J}\). Final answer: \(1.5\text{ J}\)

The signal-flow graph has one forward path from \(R(s)\) to \(C(s)\) with gain \(P_1=1\), because \(C(s)\) is taken from the node reached directly from \(R(s)\) through the gain-1 branch. The three individual loops are \(L_1=(1/s)(-2)=-2/s\) around the first integrator, \(L_2=(1/s)(-3)=-3/s\) around the second integrator, and \(L_3=(6)(-4)=-24\) between the node after the gain \(6\) and the node before it. Only \(L_1\) and \(L_2\) are nontouching, so the determinant is \(\Delta=1-(L_1+L_2+L_3)+L_1L_2=1+2/s+3/s+24+6/s^2=25+5/s+6/s^2\). The forward path touches \(L_1\) but not \(L_2\) or \(L_3\), giving \(\Delta_1=1-(L_2+L_3)=25+3/s\). Applying Mason’s gain formula gives \(C(s)/R(s)=P_1\Delta_1/\Delta=(25+3/s)/(25+5/s+6/s^2)=s(25s+3)/(25s^2+5s+6)\). Final answer: \(s(25s+3)/(25s^2+5s+6)\).

The figure shows the input \(m(t)\) multiplied by \(s(t)\), then added to \(n(t)\), then multiplied again by \(s(t)\), and finally passed through an ideal lowpass filter with cutoff \(1\) Hz and passband gain \(1\), so the signal before filtering is \([m(t)s(t)+n(t)]s(t)=m(t)s^2(t)+n(t)s(t)\). Since \(s^2(t)=\cos^2(200\pi t)=\frac12[1+\cos(400\pi t)]\), we have \(m(t)s^2(t)=\frac{m(t)}2+\frac{m(t)}2\cos(400\pi t)\); the cosine term is centered at \(\pm200\) Hz and is removed by the \(1\) Hz LPF, while \(\frac{m(t)}2=\frac{\sin(2\pi t)}{t}\) lies entirely in the passband. For the interference term, \(n(t)s(t)=\frac{\sin(199\pi t)}{t}\cos(200\pi t)=\frac{\sin(399\pi t)-\sin(\pi t)}{2t}\); the \(-\frac{\sin(\pi t)}{2t}\) part has support below \(0.5\) Hz and passes unchanged, and the \(\frac{\sin(399\pi t)}{2t}\) part has a rectangular spectrum of height \(\pi/2\) over \(|f|<199.5\) Hz, of which the ideal \(1\) Hz LPF keeps only \(|f|<1\), giving \(\frac{\sin(2\pi t)}{2t}\). Adding the surviving contributions yields \(y(t)=\frac{\sin(2\pi t)}{t}+\frac{\sin(2\pi t)-\sin(\pi t)}{2t}=\frac{3\sin(2\pi t)-\sin(\pi t)}{2t}\). Final answer: \(y(t)=\dfrac{3\sin(2\pi t)-\sin(\pi t)}{2t}\).

The image shows a two-terminal component A with voltage U across it, where the positive terminal is at the top, and current I is defined to enter the positive terminal; this is the associated reference direction. Under the associated reference direction, the power absorbed or consumed by the component is P = U I. Substituting U = 220 V and I = -1 A gives P = 220 × (-1) W = -220 W. The negative sign indicates that the component is actually delivering power to the external circuit rather than consuming power. Final answer: -220 W

The image shows a series circuit containing an inductor L and a resistor R, with the voltage across L indicated as 80 V and the voltage across R indicated as 60 V; a voltmeter is connected across the entire series combination.
