The image shows right triangle ABC with the right angle at A, where vertical side AB = 2 and horizontal side AC = 4, so the triangular tail has area (1/2)(2)(4) = 4. The star body attached along AB is bounded by four quarter-circle arcs; since AB = 2, these arcs are quarter-circles of radius 1, forming a square of side 2 with the four corner quarter-circles removed, so the star-body area is 2^2 - π·1^2 = 4 - π. Thus the total area is X = (4 - π) + 4 = 8 - π, giving 6X = 48 - 6π. Therefore a = 48 and b = 6, so a + b = 54. Final answer: 54

The image shows a bug on the bottom edge of a conical frustum lampshade and a drop of honey on the top edge at the point farthest around from the bug. For a frustum with height \(3\sqrt3\), top radius \(3\), and bottom radius \(6\), the slant height is \(\sqrt{(3\sqrt3)^2+(6-3)^2}=6\). Completing the cone, the full slant height from the apex to the bottom is \(12\), so the lateral surface unfolds into an annular sector with outer radius \(12\), inner radius \(6\), and sector angle \(\frac{2\pi\cdot6}{12}=\pi\). The bug and honey are half a circumference apart on the frustum, which corresponds to an angular separation of half the sector angle, or \(\frac{\pi}{2}\), in the development. The straight-line distance in the sector is therefore \(\sqrt{12^2+6^2-2\cdot12\cdot6\cos(\pi/2)}=\sqrt{144+36}=6\sqrt5\). Final answer: \(6\sqrt5\) inches.

The picture shows that the removed squares are exactly the cells in both an even-numbered row and an even-numbered column, and that an \(L\)-triomino occupies three cells of a \(2\times2\) block. In the \(101\times101\) board, after the removals the remaining parity classes are \((\text{odd},\text{odd})\), \((\text{odd},\text{even})\), and \((\text{even},\text{odd})\), with counts \(51^2=2601\), \(51\cdot50=2550\), and \(50\cdot51=2550\), respectively. Since every \(L\)-triomino uses one cell of each of these three classes, at most \(2550\) triominoes can be placed. This bound is attainable by induction on odd side length \(2k+1\): for \(k=1\) a \(3\times3\) board holds \(2\) triominoes; assuming a \((2k-1)\times(2k-1)\) board can be tiled leaving \(k\) unused \((\text{odd},\text{odd})\) squares, add a two-square-wide border to obtain a \((2k+1)\times(2k+1)\) board. Tile the new bottom two rows with \(k\) triominoes in the \(2\times2\) blocks whose top-left corners are \((2k,1),(2k,3),\dots,(2k,2k-1)\), and tile the new right two columns with another \(k\) triominoes in the blocks whose top-left corners are \((1,2k),(3,2k),\dots,(2k-1,2k)\), leaving only the new corner \((2k+1,2k+1)\) uncovered. Thus the \((2k+1)\times(2k+1)\) board is tiled by \(k(k+1)\) triominoes, and for \(k=50\) this gives \(50\cdot51=2550\). Final answer: 2550.

The T-shaped outlined region consists of the four unlettered squares: three in a vertical column with one square attached to the right of the middle square; the eight lettered squares A–H are placed around it, each adjacent to the T. Adding one lettered square produces a five-square figure, and a five-square figure can fold into a topless cube only if it is a net of five faces of a cube, which means its squares must form a tree and must not contain a 2×2 block of four squares, since four squares surrounding a single point cannot all be faces of a cube. Checking the eight possibilities: A and H attach the missing top face to the front/back side, B and F attach the missing left face to the front/back side, D attaches the missing left face to the bottom, and E attaches the missing top face to the right side, giving six valid tree-shaped nets; C and G each complete a 2×2 block with existing squares and therefore cannot fold into a cube. Final answer: 6

The image shows a \(3\times3\times3\) cube made of 27 unit cubes with the central cube and the six face-center cubes removed, leaving six square face holes and three orthogonal square tunnels. The ant walks on the resulting polyhedral surface. Every interior wall of a tunnel is parallel to one of the original outer faces, and flattening such a wall onto that outer face is a translation that preserves length. Therefore any path on the modified surface corresponds to a path of the same length on the surface of the original solid cube from A to B. The shortest path on a cube between opposite corners unfolds two adjacent faces into a \(3\times6\) rectangle, giving \(\sqrt{3^2+6^2}=3\sqrt5\). This exterior geodesic only touches the corners of the removed face cubes, so it remains valid on the modified surface. Final answer: 3√5

The figure shows a rectangle divided into four smaller rectangles arranged in a \(2\times2\) grid, so the four sections form a 4-cycle of adjacencies. Label the crops corn, wheat, soybeans, potatoes and let \(M\) be the \(4\times4\) matrix whose rows and columns are indexed by these crops, with \(M_{ij}=1\) if the two crops may be adjacent and \(0\) otherwise. The only forbidden adjacent pairs are corn–wheat and soybeans–potatoes, so \[ M=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1&1\\0&1&1&1\\1&1&1&0\\1&1&0&1\end{pmatrix}. \] The number of valid plantings equals the number of closed walks of length \(4\) on this adjacency relation, which is \(\operatorname{tr}(M^4)\). Since \(M=J-B\) where \(J\) is the all-ones matrix and \(B\) is the adjacency matrix of the two forbidden disjoint edges, we have \(B^2=I\), \(JB=BJ=J\), and \(J^2=4J\). Thus \(M^2=(J-B)^2=2J+I\), and \[ M^4=(2J+I)^2=4J^2+4J+I=20J+I. \] Therefore \(\operatorname{tr}(M^4)=\operatorname{tr}(20J+I)=20\cdot 4+4=84\). Final answer: 84.

The diagram is the well-known order-9 simple perfect rectangle, whose nine square side lengths are 1, 4, 7, 8, 9, 10, 14, 15, and 18. Arranging the 18×18 square in the lower-left corner, the 15×15 in the lower-right, the 14×14 above the 18, the 10×10 and 9×9 across the top, the 8×8 on the right edge between the 15 and 9, and the 7×7, 4×4, and 1×1 in the remaining central region produces a rectangle of width 33 and height 32. Since 33 and 32 are relatively prime, the perimeter is 2(33+32)=130. Final answer: 130.

The image shows two congruent squares joined along a common segment, with a circle removed from that shared region. Each square has side length 4, so the area of one square is $4^2=16$ and the combined area of the two squares is $2\cdot 16=32$. Because the squares intersect at right angles and their intersecting sides are bisected, the common segment has length equal to half a side, which is $4/2=2$. This segment is the diameter of the circle, so the circle has radius $2/2=1$ and area $\pi\cdot 1^2=\pi$. The shaded area is therefore the total area of the two squares minus the area of the circle, giving $32-\pi$. Final answer: $32-\pi$

The image shows a square containing four semicircles of radius 1, each placed in a corner with its diameter lying on one side of the square; the gray shaded regions are the small corner regions outside the semicircles, and the hatched region is the central region bounded by the four semicircular arcs, which are tangent to one another. Let the square have side length \(s\). By symmetry, adjacent semicircles are tangent, so the distance between the centers of two adjacent semicircles equals 2; for example, the bottom-left semicircle has center \((1,0)\) and the bottom-right has center \((s,1)\), giving \(\sqrt{(s-1)^2+1}=2\), hence \((s-1)^2=3\) and \(s=1+\sqrt{3}\). The square's area is \(s^2=(1+\sqrt{3})^2=4+2\sqrt{3}\). Each gray corner region is a \(1\times 1\) square minus a quarter circle of radius 1, so the total shaded area is \(4\left(1-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=4-\pi\). The four semicircles have total area \(4\cdot \frac{\pi}{2}=2\pi\). Thus the hatched area is \((4+2\sqrt{3})-2\pi-(4-\pi)=2\sqrt{3}-\pi\). The absolute difference is \(|(4-\pi)-(2\sqrt{3}-\pi)|=4-2\sqrt{3}\). Final answer: \(4-2\sqrt{3}\).

The figure is a trefoil made by drawing three congruent 60° circular sectors of radius 2 outward from the sides of a central equilateral triangle of side 2, with the horizontal base as one side. Each sector has area (60/360)π(2)² = 2π/3, so the three sectors have combined area 2π. The central equilateral triangle has area (√3/4)(2)² = √3 and, being the overlap of the three sectors, is counted three times in the sector sum, so two copies must be subtracted: 2π − 2√3. Final answer: 2π − 2√3.

The path for \(r\) is made only of horizontal and vertical grid segments, so its length is the sum of those segment lengths: \(2+2+1+3+2+1+2=11\). The path for \(s\) has two straight horizontal parts totaling \(2+2=4\) plus two semicircular arcs, each of radius one grid unit; each semicircle has length \(\pi\), so \(s=4+2\pi\approx 10.28\). The path for \(t\) has two horizontal segments of length \(2\) each, two diagonal segments each spanning a \(2\times2\) right triangle so each has length \(\sqrt{2^2+2^2}=2\sqrt2\), and one vertical segment of length \(4\), giving \(t=2+2\sqrt2+4+2\sqrt2+2=8+4\sqrt2\approx 13.66\). Since \(4+2\pi<11<8+4\sqrt2\), the order from shortest to longest is \(s\), \(r\), \(t\). Final answer: \(s<r<t\) (or \(s,r,t\)).

The figure is made of 14 unit cubes: the bottom layer is a 4-by-3 L-shape with the two back-right cubes missing, and four cubes are stacked on top at the front-left, middle-left, third-front, and right-front positions. Since the entire surface including the bottom is painted, a cube has a red face for each of its six faces that is not glued to another cube; therefore a cube has exactly four red faces exactly when it shares faces with exactly two other cubes. Counting face-sharing neighbors, the back-right base cube and the two cubes in the back-left extension each touch only two other cubes, while every other cube touches one, three, or four others. Thus three individual cubes have exactly four red faces. Final answer: 3

The image shows a cube with three visible faces labeled 11, 14, and 15, which are adjacent to one another and thus not opposite faces. Since the six face numbers are consecutive whole numbers and must include 11, 14, and 15, the only possible set is 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16. The condition that each pair of opposite faces has the same sum requires pairing the smallest with the largest, the second smallest with the second largest, and the middle two: (11, 16), (12, 15), and (13, 14), each pair summing to 27. Therefore the total sum of the six numbers is 3 × 27 = 81. Final answer: 81

The grid is a 3×3 cross-number with two shaded (blocked) cells at top-right and bottom-left; the white cells form the entries 1 across (one digit), 1 down (two digits), 2 down (three digits), 3 across (three digits), 4 down (two digits), and 5 across (two digits). Let 4 down be the two-digit number x. Then 1 down = x − 11, and the HCF condition gives gcd(x − 11, x) = gcd(x, 11) > 1, so x must be a multiple of 11; since 1 down is two-digit, x ≥ 22, hence x ∈ {22, 33, …, 99}. 5 across is a two-digit square and shares its last digit with x, while 2 down is a three-digit number one less than a cube, so 2 down ∈ {124, 215, 342, 511, 728, 999} and its last digit equals the first digit of 5 across. Matching the last digit of 5 across with the last digit of x and the first digit of 5 across with the last digit of 2 down leaves only x = 55, 5 across = 25, and 2 down = 342. Then 1 down = 44, so 1 across = 4, and the crossing digits give 3 across = 445. Final answer: 445.

The three centers form an equilateral triangle with side length 2, with A at the top and B and C below on the left and right. Place A at (0, sqrt(3)), B at (1,0), and C at (-1,0). The intersections of circle A and circle B have y-coordinates (sqrt(3) ± sqrt(r^2 - 1))/2; the one outside circle C is the right-hand point C', and by symmetry B' is the left-hand intersection of circles A and C. Thus B' and C' have the same y-coordinate, and their x-coordinates differ by 1 + sqrt(3) sqrt(r^2 - 1), so the length B'C' is 1 + sqrt(3) sqrt(r^2 - 1). Final answer: 1 + sqrt(3)*sqrt(r^2 - 1).

The image shows eight eyelets arranged four on each long side of a rectangle, with the lace running along one width side and then forming three crisscross levels before reaching the opposite width side, where each end extends outward. The rectangle has width 50 mm and length 80 mm, so the equal spacing between adjacent eyelets on a side is 80/3 mm. Each crisscross segment is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 50 mm and 80/3 mm, giving length sqrt(50^2 + (80/3)^2) = sqrt(2500 + 6400/9) = sqrt(28900/9) = 170/3 mm. There are six such diagonal segments, one width segment of 50 mm, and two end extensions of at least 200 mm each, so the minimum lace length is 50 + 6(170/3) + 2(200) = 50 + 340 + 400 = 790 mm. Final answer: 790 mm.

The L-shaped region consists of three unit squares: the bottom-left, top-left, and bottom-right squares of a 2×2 square, with the top-right unit square missing. For two independent uniform points, the midpoint can lie outside the region only when the two points are in the two nonadjacent squares, the top-left and bottom-right ones. Condition on \(A\) in the top-left square and \(B\) in the bottom-right square, writing \(A=(X_A,1+Y_A)\) and \(B=(1+X_B,Y_B)\) with all variables uniform on \([0,1]\). The midpoint is \(\left(\frac{1+X_A+X_B}{2},\frac{1+Y_A+Y_B}{2}\right)\), which lands in the missing top-right square exactly when \(X_A+X_B\ge 1\) and \(Y_A+Y_B\ge 1\). For independent \(U,V\sim\text{Uniform}[0,1]\), \(\Pr(U+V\ge 1)=\frac12\), so the conditional probability the midpoint is outside is \(\left(\frac12\right)^2=\frac14\). There are \(3\cdot3=9\) equally likely ordered square choices, and the two cross cases are the only bad ones, so the overall probability is \(1-\frac{2}{9}\cdot\frac14=\frac{17}{18}\). Thus \(m=17\), \(n=18\), and \(m+n=35\). Final answer: 35.

The image shows a \(120^\circ\) angle with vertex \(O\) and a point \(P\) on its angle bisector. Place \(O\) at the origin, the bisector on the positive \(x\)-axis, and let \(P=(d,0)\). The upper ray is \(\{(t/2,t\sqrt3/2):t\ge0\}\) and the lower ray is \(\{(s/2,-s\sqrt3/2):s\ge0\}\). For any \(t\) with \(0\le t\le d\), take \(Q=(t/2,t\sqrt3/2)\) on the upper ray and rotate \(Q\) by \(60^\circ\) about \(P\); the image is \(R=((d-t)/2,-(d-t)\sqrt3/2)\), which lies on the lower ray. Since a \(60^\circ\) rotation about \(P\) preserves the distance \(PQ\) and makes \(\angle QPR=60^\circ\), each such choice gives an equilateral \(\triangle PQR\), and different values of \(t\) produce distinct triangles. Hence there is a continuous family of equilateral triangles satisfying the conditions. Final answer: infinitely many.

In each figure we have a congruent regular hexagon. For X, the unshaded region is an equilateral triangle whose vertices are three alternating vertices of the hexagon, so the three shaded corner regions are congruent equilateral triangles each with side length equal to the hexagon side; together they occupy three of the six equilateral triangles that make up the hexagon, which is one-half of its area. For Y, the hexagon is divided into six congruent equilateral triangles from the center and exactly three are shaded, so the shaded area is one-half of the hexagon. For Z, the shaded region is the same alternating-vertex equilateral triangle as the unshaded region in X, and its area is also one-half of the hexagon. Since the hexagons are congruent, all three shaded areas are equal. Final answer: X = Y = Z

The image shows four \(5\times5\) arrays of lattice points, one in each quadrant, so \(G\) is the set of integer points with \(3\le |x|\le 7\) and \(3\le |y|\le 7\). Two points in the same block are at most \(\sqrt{32}\) apart, so a square of side at least \(6\) cannot have two vertices in one block; hence each such square has exactly one vertex in each block. Write the upper-left vertex as \((-a,b)\) and the lower-right vertex as \((c,-d)\), where \(a,b,c,d\in\{3,4,5,6,7\}\). The other two vertices are then forced, and requiring them to lie in the upper-right and lower-left blocks gives \(6\le S-2t\le 14\) for each \(t\in\{a,b,c,d\}\), where \(S=a+b+c+d\). Since the remaining vertices are lattice points, \(S\) must be even. Set \(t=5+e_t\), so \(e_t\in\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}\) and \(S=20+E\). The inequalities become \(-4\le E-2e_t\le 4\), i.e. each \(e_t\) lies in \([\max(-2,\lceil (E-4)/2\rceil),\min(2,\lfloor (E+4)/2\rfloor)]\). Counting 4-tuples with even total \(E\) gives, for \(E=-8,-6,-4,-2,0,2,4,6,8\), the counts \(1,6,19,44,85,44,19,6,1\), whose sum is \(225\). Final answer: 225.

In the equilateral triangle \(ABC\), points \(E_1,E_2\) lie on \(AB\), \(F_1,F_2\) lie on \(BC\), and \(G_1,G_2\) lie on \(AC\), with \(AE_1=BE_2=BF_1=CF_2=CG_1=AG_2=m\); the three corner triangles are \(\triangle AE_1G_2\), \(\triangle BF_1E_2\), and \(\triangle CG_1F_2\), and the central polygon \(E_1E_2F_1F_2G_1G_2\) is the remaining hexagon. Each corner triangle has two sides of length \(m\) meeting at a \(60^\circ\) angle, so its area is \(\frac12 m^2\sin 60^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}{4}m^2\), giving the three corner triangles a combined area of \(3\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{4}m^2\). The area of \(\triangle ABC\) is \(\frac{\sqrt3}{4}M^2\). Since the hexagon’s area equals the combined area of the three corner triangles, the whole triangle’s area is twice that combined area: \(\frac{\sqrt3}{4}M^2=2\cdot3\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{4}m^2=6\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{4}m^2\), so \(M^2=6m^2\) and therefore \(\frac{m}{M}=\frac1{\sqrt6}\). Final answer: \(1/\sqrt6\)

The image shows a silo composed of a right circular cylinder with a right circular cone on top, and the total height of the entire silo is labeled as 27 meters. Since the diameter of the base is 10 meters, the common radius of the cylinder and cone is 5 meters. Letting the height of the cylinder be h, the height of the cone is h/2, so h + h/2 = 27, giving 3h/2 = 27 and h = 18 meters; thus the cone height is 9 meters. The volume of the cylinder is πr²h = π(5²)(18) = 450π cubic meters, and the volume of the cone is (1/3)πr²(9) = (1/3)π(25)(9) = 75π cubic meters. Adding these gives 450π + 75π = 525π cubic meters. Final answer: 525π

The image shows a 4 by 4 grid numbered 1 through 16 in reading order, with rows 1–4 from top to bottom and columns 1–4 from left to right. Folding the top half over the bottom half places row 2 on row 3 and row 1 on row 4, so after this fold each column’s stack from bottom to top is row 3 face up, row 2 face down, row 1 face up, row 4 face down. Folding the bottom half over the top half stacks the row-4 portion onto the row-3 portion, reversing and flipping those layers, leaving a single row in which every remaining column has, from bottom to top, the original row-3 square, the row-2 square face down, the row-1 square, and the row-4 square face down. Folding the right half over the left half places columns 3–4 onto columns 2–1, and the final left-over-right fold places the left column onto the right column; tracking these layer reversals shows the top physical layer is the original square in row 3, column 1, whose number is 9 (with its printed side facing down). Final answer: 9

The network has 16 vertices, its outer face is a pentagon with 5 edges, and every interior face is a triangle, so for this triangulated pentagon \(E=3V-3-5=3\cdot16-3-5=40\); hence the sum of all degrees is \(2E=80\). The center circle has 6 neighbors, so its degree is 6. Let \(a_v\) be the initial coins at vertex \(v\). Since each student gives \(a_v/\deg(v)\) to each neighbor and ends with the same amount, \(a_u=\sum_{v\sim u}a_v/\deg(v)\) for every vertex \(u\). Setting \(g_v=a_v/\deg(v)\) gives \(\deg(u)g_u=\sum_{v\sim u}g_v\), so \(g_u\) equals the average of its neighbors’ values; on a connected graph this forces all \(g_v\) to be equal. Thus \(a_v=c\cdot\deg(v)\) for some constant \(c\). Then \(3360=\sum a_v=c\sum\deg=c\cdot80\), so \(c=42\), and the center student originally had \(6c=6\cdot42=252\) coins. Final answer: 252.

The image shows two intersecting planes \(\mathcal P\) and \(\mathcal Q\) meeting along line \(\ell\), with three spheres wedged between them; each sphere is tangent to both planes and to the other two spheres. Let the dihedral angle between the planes be \(2\theta\). For a sphere of radius \(r\) tangent to both planes, its center lies in the angle-bisecting plane through \(\ell\) at distance \(r/\sin\theta\) from \(\ell\), and the foot of the perpendicular to plane \(\mathcal P\) is at distance \(r\cot\theta\) from \(\ell\). The two radius-36 spheres have equal distances from \(\ell\), so their centers are \(72\) apart along a line parallel to \(\ell\); place them at \(x=\pm 36\) in the bisecting plane, with the radius-13 sphere centered midway at \(x=0\). Tangency between the small and a large sphere gives \(36^2+\left(\frac{36-13}{\sin\theta}\right)^2=(36+13)^2\), so \(\left(\frac{23}{\sin\theta}\right)^2=49^2-36^2=1105\). Thus \(\cot^2\theta=\frac{1-\sin^2\theta}{\sin^2\theta}=\frac{1105-529}{529}=\frac{576}{529}\), giving \(\cot\theta=\frac{24}{23}\). The required distance for the radius-13 sphere is \(13\cot\theta=13\cdot\frac{24}{23}=\frac{312}{23}\). Therefore \(m=312\), \(n=23\), and \(m+n=335\). Final answer: 335.

In the three views, the red face is adjacent to the brown face (on top in the first two views), the green face (on the right in the first view), the white face (on the front in the second view), and the purple face (on the front in the third view). Since each face of a cube is adjacent to exactly four other faces, those four colors are all the neighbors of red; the only remaining color, aqua, must therefore be on the face opposite red. Final answer: red.

The diagram shows four regions meeting at a common point: a 4 mm square, a 5 mm square, a triangle, and a parallelogram. The two squares are built outward on adjacent sides of the parallelogram, so those sides have lengths 4 mm and 5 mm and include an angle θ. The triangle is formed by the other two sides of those squares meeting at the common point, so its two sides are also 4 mm and 5 mm, and the angle between them is 180° − θ. The area of a triangle with two sides a and b and included angle φ is ½ab sin φ, and the area of a parallelogram with adjacent sides a and b and included angle θ is ab sin θ. Since sin(180° − θ) = sin θ, the triangle area is ½·4·5·sin θ = 10 sin θ = 8 mm², giving sin θ = 0.8. Therefore the parallelogram area is 4·5·sin θ = 20·0.8 = 16 mm². Final answer: 16.

In the rectangle, place \(K\) at the origin, \(L=(KL,0)\), \(M=(KL,KJ)\), and \(J=(0,KJ)\). The distance from \(N\) to side \(LM\) is \(8\) cm, so the horizontal distance from \(N\) to \(M\) is \(8\), and the distance from \(N\) to side \(KL\) is \(1\) cm, so the vertical coordinate of \(N\) is \(1\). Thus \(N=(KL-8,1)\). Since \(N\) lies on diagonal \(KM\), the slope from \(K\) to \(N\) equals the slope from \(K\) to \(M\), giving \(\frac{1}{KL-8}=\frac{KJ}{KL}\), or \(KJ(KL-8)=KL\). The angle bisector of \(\angle KJM\) makes a \(45^\circ\) angle with the sides through \(J\), so its equation is \(x+y=KJ\); substituting \(N\) gives \((KL-8)+1=KJ\), hence \(KJ=KL-7\). Letting \(KL=x\), we have \(KJ=x-7\) and \((x-7)(x-8)=x\), which simplifies to \(x^2-16x+56=0\). Solving yields \(x=8+2\sqrt2=8+\sqrt8\), so \(a=8\) and \(b=8\). Final answer: 16.

The diagram shows two identical $3\text{ cm}\times 9\text{ cm}$ rectangles overlapping so that the shaded region is a parallelogram whose two opposite vertices are opposite corners of the horizontal rectangle and whose other two vertices lie on the horizontal rectangle's top and bottom sides. Place the horizontal rectangle with vertices $(0,0)$, $(9,0)$, $(9,3)$, $(0,3)$; then the shaded parallelogram has vertices $(0,0)$, $(a,0)$, $(9,3)$, $(9-a,3)$. Its slanted sides lie on sides of the tilted rectangle, so the distance between those parallel lines must equal the tilted rectangle's short side, $3\text{ cm}$. That distance is $\frac{3a}{\sqrt{(9-a)^2+9}}$, and setting it equal to $3$ gives $a=5$. Thus the parallelogram has base $5\text{ cm}$ and height $3\text{ cm}$, so its area is $5\cdot 3=15\text{ cm}^2$. Final answer: $15\text{ cm}^2$

In the diagram the three circles intersect pairwise at six squares, so label the left–right pair as top and bottom, the left–bottom pair as 6 and the blank next to it, and the right–bottom pair as x and the remaining blank. Each circle contains four numbers, and since every number lies on two circles the total of the three circle sums is \(2(1+2+3+4+5+6)=42\), making each circle sum \(14\). Writing the three circle equations \(a+b+6+c=14\), \(a+b+d+x=14\), and \(6+c+d+x=14\) gives \(6+c=d+x\) and \(a+b=6+c\); adding the first and third equations and using \(a+b+d+x=14\) yields \(14+2(6+c)=28\), so the blank next to 6 must be \(1\). Then \(d+x=7\) and \(a+b=7\); with 1 and 6 used, the remaining numbers \(\{2,3,4,5\}\) form two pairs each summing to 7, so x can be any of those four values. Final answer: 2, 3, 4, or 5.

The rectangle in image1 has corners J (top left), M (top right), K (bottom left), and L (bottom right), and Tess runs counterclockwise J → M → L → K → J. Her straight-line distance from J starts at 0, increases linearly along JM, then continues to increase along ML because it is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with one leg JM and the other leg her progress from M toward L, reaching its maximum at L (the corner diagonally opposite J); it then decreases along LK and decreases linearly back to 0 along KJ. Therefore the graph must be a single-humped curve that starts at 0, rises to one peak at L, and falls back to 0. Among the choices, only image5 has this single-peak shape; image4 has an extra dip, and the other graphs are linear or step-like, so they do not fit. Final answer: image5

The image shows a 2 by 1 rectangle divided into two unit squares, so the figure has seven unit edges. A chosen set of edges can be traced without lifting a pencil exactly when the resulting graph is connected and has 0 or 2 vertices of odd degree, i.e., an Eulerian circuit or trail. Counting by the number of chosen edges: one edge gives 7 choices; two edges must share a vertex, giving 10 adjacent pairs; three edges give 14 three-edge paths (the two three-edge stars have too many odd vertices); four edges give 10 four-edge paths on five vertices plus the 2 unit-square cycles; five edges form a spanning tree, and only the 6 Hamiltonian paths have at most two odd vertices; six edges correspond to deleting one edge from the full graph, and 5 of the 7 deletions leave 0 or 2 odd vertices; all seven edges give two odd vertices, so they work. Adding these gives 7+10+14+12+6+5+1=55. Final answer: 55

The image shows the cube partially inserted in the right circular cylinder with a space diagonal of the cube vertical and aligned with the cylinder’s axis, so the lower vertex lies inside the barrel and the circular rim cuts the cube. Place the lower vertex at the origin with the three incident edges along the coordinate axes; the body diagonal is the line \(x=y=z\). At distance \(t\) along this diagonal from the vertex, the perpendicular cross-section is an equilateral triangle whose vertices are at distance \(s=t\sqrt3\) along the three edges, and its circumradius (the distance from the diagonal to each vertex) is \(R=t\sqrt2\). Since the cylinder has radius \(4\), the cube is stopped when \(t\sqrt2=4\), giving \(t=2\sqrt2\); this is less than the barrel height \(10\), and since \(2\sqrt2<8/\sqrt3\), the cutting plane meets only those three edges. The submerged part is therefore a tetrahedron bounded by the three face planes and the plane \(x+y+z=s\) with \(s=t\sqrt3=2\sqrt6\), so its volume is \(v=s^3/6=(2\sqrt6)^3/6=8\sqrt6\). Thus \(v^2=(8\sqrt6)^2=384\). Final answer: 384

The diagram shows five triangles meeting at the common vertex \(O\), with angles at \(O\) of \(24^\circ\), \(48^\circ\), \(72^\circ\), \(96^\circ\), and \(120^\circ\). Since the smallest angle is \(m^\circ\) and the other four are \(2m^\circ\), \(3m^\circ\), \(4m^\circ\), and \(5m^\circ\), the five angles around \(O\) must sum to \(m+2m+3m+4m+5m=15m\) degrees. For the triangles to fit around \(O\) without gaps or overlaps, this total must be \(360^\circ\), so \(15m=360\), giving \(m=24\). If \(m\) were smaller, the angles would sum to less than \(360^\circ\) and the chain of triangles could not close; if \(m\) were larger, they would overlap. Each triangle can be made isosceles by taking the two sides from \(O\) to be equal. Final answer: 24.

The image shows rhombus $ABCD$ with point $P$ on side $\overline{AD}$ and segment $\overline{BP}$ perpendicular to $\overline{AD}$, forming a right angle at $P$, where $AP = 3$ and $PD = 2$. Since $P$ lies on $\overline{AD}$, the base length is $AD = AP + PD = 3 + 2 = 5$, and because $ABCD$ is a rhombus all sides equal $5$, so $AB = 5$. In right triangle $ABP$, the Pythagorean theorem gives $BP = \sqrt{AB^2 - AP^2} = \sqrt{5^2 - 3^2} = \sqrt{25 - 9} = \sqrt{16} = 4$. The area of a rhombus equals base times height, so the area is $AD \cdot BP = 5 \cdot 4 = 20$. Final answer: 20

In the given circle, \(AB\) and \(CD\) are perpendicular diameters intersecting at center \(O\), and chord \(AM\) meets diameter \(CD\) at \(P\). Let \(\angle BAM=\alpha\). Since \(AB\) is a diameter, \(\angle AMB=90^\circ\), so in right triangle \(AMB\) we have \(AM=AB\cos\alpha\). Because \(CD\perp AB\) and \(P\) lies on \(CD\), the horizontal projection of \(AP\) onto \(AB\) equals \(AO\), giving \(AP\cos\alpha=AO\). Therefore \(AP\cdot AM=AP\cdot(AB\cos\alpha)=AB\cdot(AP\cos\alpha)=AB\cdot AO\). Final answer: \(AP\cdot AM=AO\cdot AB\).

The two white regions are right-angled triangles, and in each triangle the side of the central square is the hypotenuse, so by the Pythagorean theorem the area of the central square equals the sum of the areas of the squares on the two legs. On the left, the central square therefore has area \(22 + 3 = 25\) m\(^2\). On the right, the same central square has area \(7 + {?}\), so \({?}=25-7=18\). Final answer: 18.

The four small circles each have radius \(1\text{ cm}\) and are tangent to their neighbours, so their centres are \(2\text{ cm}\) apart. Each large circle is tangent to two adjacent small circles; because those two small circles touch each other at the large circle’s centre, the large circle’s centre is their point of tangency and the large radius is \(1+1=2\text{ cm}\). Each shaded region is bounded by a semicircle of a large circle and two semicircles of small circles, so its area is \(\tfrac12\pi(2)^2-2\cdot\tfrac12\pi(1)^2=2\pi-\pi=\pi\text{ cm}^2\). Since there are three congruent shaded regions, the total shaded area is \(3\pi\text{ cm}^2\). Final answer: \(3\pi\text{ cm}^2\).

The diagram shows concentric semicircles whose common centre is the middle black dot; since adjacent black dots are 1 cm apart, the semicircles have radii 1 cm, 2 cm, 3 cm, 4 cm, and 5 cm. The shaded grey regions are the central semicircle of radius 1 cm and the annular semicircles between radii 2 and 3 cm and between radii 4 and 5 cm, so the grey area is \(\frac12\pi(1^2)+\frac12\pi(3^2-2^2)+\frac12\pi(5^2-4^2)=\frac12\pi(1+5+9)=\frac{15}{2}\pi\) cm\(^2\). Setting \(\frac{15}{2}\pi=\frac18 k\pi\) gives \(k=60\). Final answer: 60.

The image shows a regular hexagonal point grid with 19 points arranged in five rows of 3, 4, 5, 4, and 3 points. A line through two of these points contains more than two points only along the three main lattice directions or along the three “long-diagonal” directions; in each main direction there are five lines containing 3, 4, 5, 4, and 3 points, giving 6 lines of length 3, 6 lines of length 4, and 3 lines of length 5, while each of the three long-diagonal directions contains three lines of exactly three points, for 9 more lines of length 3. The total number of pairs of points is C(19,2)=171, and the pairs lying on lines with three or more points are 6·C(3,2)+6·C(4,2)+3·C(5,2)+9·C(3,2)=6·3+6·6+3·10+9·3=18+36+30+27=111. Subtracting these from all point pairs leaves 171−111=60 pairs, each defining a distinct line that passes through exactly two grid points. Final answer: 60.

Counting the triangles in each box gives: box A has 1 triangle, box B has 4 triangles, box C has 2 triangles, box D has 3 triangles, and box E has 1 triangle. Since 4 is greater than 1, 2, and 3, box B contains the most triangles. Final answer: B.

The image shows five labeled figures, each built from 4 equally sized cubes: (A) a straight row of 4 cubes, (B) a 2×2 stacked square, (C) and (D) L-shaped arrangements, and (E) a T-shaped arrangement with one cube on top of a middle cube. The amount of colour needed equals the total exposed surface area. Each cube has 6 faces, so 4 cubes have 24 faces in total; every pair of touching faces hides 2 faces from being coloured. Therefore exposed faces = 24 − 2 × (number of touching face pairs). Figure (A) has 3 touching pairs, (B) has 4 touching pairs, (C) and (D) each have 3, and (E) has 3. Thus (B) has the fewest exposed faces: 24 − 2×4 = 16, compared with 18 for the others. Final answer: B.

The image shows segment \(AE\) divided into four equal parts by points \(B\), \(C\), and \(D\), so let each part be length \(x\). Then \(AE=4x\), \(AD=3x\), and \(DE=x\). The upper path is a semicircle with diameter \(AE\), so its length is \(\frac{\pi(4x)}{2}=2\pi x\). The lower path consists of semicircles with diameters \(AD\) and \(DE\), so its length is \(\frac{\pi(3x)}{2}+\frac{\pi(x)}{2}=2\pi x\). Therefore the ratio of the upper path to the lower path is \(2\pi x:2\pi x=1:1\). Final answer: \(1:1\).

The rectangle has vertical side AB = 4 cm and horizontal side BC = 16 cm. Folding C onto A means the crease MN is the perpendicular bisector of diagonal AC, so the folded quadrilateral ANMD' is congruent to the original quadrilateral CNMD. Let BN = x; then AN = CN = 16 - x. In right triangle ABN, x^2 + 4^2 = (16 - x)^2, which gives 32x = 240 and x = 7.5, so CN = 8.5 cm. Let AM = y; since M also lies on the perpendicular bisector of AC, AM = CM, so y^2 = (16 - y)^2 + 4^2, giving 32y = 272 and y = 8.5, hence MD = 16 - 8.5 = 7.5 cm. Therefore CNMD is a trapezoid with parallel sides 8.5 cm and 7.5 cm and height 4 cm, so its area is ((8.5 + 7.5)/2) * 4 = 32 cm^2, and the same area applies to ANMD'. Final answer: 32 cm^2.

In the diagram, each labeled strip is formed by bolting two equally long original metal strips together; the greater the overlap of the two original strips, the shorter the resulting combined strip, because combined length equals twice the length of one original strip minus the overlap length. Strips C, D, and E each use only one bolt, so their overlap is just one hole and they are relatively long. Strip A uses two bolts that are next to each other, giving an overlap of about two holes. Strip B uses two bolts that are farther apart, so the two original strips overlap across more holes than in A, making B the shortest combined strip. Final answer: B

The image shows a square billiard table with side length \(2\,\text{m}\); points \(A\) and \(B\) are the two bottom corners, and the arrowed path leaves \(A\), strikes the right side, then the top side, then the left side, and ends at \(B\), with the law of reflection (incident angle equals emergent angle) illustrated. Using the unfolding method, reflect the endpoint \(B\) across the three bounce sides in reverse order: reflecting across the left side gives \((-2,0)\), across the top side gives \((-2,4)\), and across the right side gives \((6,4)\). Thus the actual path length equals the straight-line distance from \(A=(0,0)\) to \((6,4)\), which is \(\sqrt{6^2+4^2}=\sqrt{52}=2\sqrt{13}\) meters. Final answer: \(2\sqrt{13}\,\text{m}\).

The diagram shows a flower bed made of a large square at the bottom, a right-angled triangle on top of it, and two equal squares attached to the two legs of the triangle. Because the two upper squares are the same size, the right triangle is isosceles; let each leg be \(a\). Then the hypotenuse is \(a\sqrt2\), so the large square has side \(a\sqrt2\). The overall width and height of the bed are both \(16\text{ m}\); in this symmetric figure the width equals twice the large square’s side, because the small squares extend half that side beyond each side of the large square, so \(2(a\sqrt2)=16\), giving \(a\sqrt2=8\) and \(a^2=32\). The total area is the large square plus the two small squares plus the triangle: \((a\sqrt2)^2+2a^2+\frac12a^2=2a^2+2a^2+\frac12a^2=\frac92a^2=\frac92\cdot32=144\text{ m}^2\). Final answer: \(144\text{ m}^2\).

The figure shows a quarter circle of radius 6 with a smaller inscribed circle \(K\) tangent to both straight radii and to the curved arc. Place the quarter circle with its center at the origin and the two straight sides along the positive \(x\)- and \(y\)-axes; then the center of the inscribed circle is \((r,r)\), since it is \(r\) units from each radius. Because the small circle is internally tangent to the arc of the quarter circle, the distance from the origin to \((r,r)\) equals \(6-r\). Thus \(\sqrt{r^2+r^2}=6-r\), so \(r\sqrt2=6-r\), giving \(r(\sqrt2+1)=6\). Solving yields \(r=\frac{6}{\sqrt2+1}=6(\sqrt2-1)\). Final answer: \(6(\sqrt2-1)\).

In the diagram there are ten islands and fifteen bridges; island A is joined by exactly three bridges, and these three neighbors lead to B by three visibly separate routes—an upper route through the top-left and top-middle islands, a middle route through the central island to B, and a lower route through the bottom-left, bottom-middle, and bottom-right islands. By Menger’s theorem, the minimum number of bridges whose removal disconnects A from B equals the maximum number of edge-disjoint A–B paths; the three routes described above share no bridges, so at least three bridges must be closed. Conversely, closing the three bridges incident to A is sufficient to block every path from A to B. Final answer: 3

The image shows right triangle \(ABC\) with \(\angle BCA=90^\circ\), \(\angle CAB=60^\circ\), and \(M\) as the midpoint of the hypotenuse \(AB\). In any right triangle, the median drawn from the right angle to the hypotenuse equals half the hypotenuse, so \(CM=AM=BM\). Thus \(\triangle AMC\) is isosceles with \(AM=CM\), and since \(\angle CAM=60^\circ\), \(\triangle AMC\) is actually equilateral, giving \(\angle AMC=60^\circ\). Because \(A\), \(M\), and \(B\) lie on a straight line, \(\angle AMC\) and \(\angle BMC\) are supplementary, so \(\angle BMC=180^\circ-60^\circ=120^\circ\). Final answer: \(120^\circ\).

In the rectangle, place \(A=(0,0)\), \(B=(w,0)\), \(C=(w,h)\), and \(D=(0,h)\), so \(DC\) is the top side. Then \(M_1\), the midpoint of \(DC\), is \((\frac{w}{2},h)\); \(M_2\), the midpoint of \(AM_1\), is \((\frac{w}{4},\frac{h}{2})\); \(M_3\), the midpoint of \(BM_2\), is \((\frac{5w}{8},\frac{h}{4})\); and \(M_4\), the midpoint of \(CM_3\), is \((\frac{13w}{16},\frac{5h}{8})\). Applying the shoelace formula to quadrilateral \(M_1M_2M_3M_4\) gives area \(\frac12\big[\frac{w}{2}\cdot\frac{h}{2}+\frac{w}{4}\cdot\frac{h}{4}+\frac{5w}{8}\cdot\frac{5h}{8}+\frac{13w}{16}\cdot h - h\cdot\frac{w}{4}-\frac{h}{2}\cdot\frac{5w}{8}-\frac{h}{4}\cdot\frac{13w}{16}-\frac{5h}{8}\cdot\frac{w}{2}\big] = \frac12\big(\frac{97}{64}wh-\frac{69}{64}wh\big)=\frac{7}{32}wh\). Since the rectangle has area \(wh\), the ratio is \(\frac{7}{32}\). Final answer: 7/32.

The image shows a mother kangaroo with a smaller joey, representing Max, in her pouch, which corresponds to the two animals whose combined mass is given. To find Max’s mass, subtract the mother’s mass from their total mass: \(60 \mathrm{~kg} - 52 \mathrm{~kg} = 8 \mathrm{~kg}\). Final answer: 8 kg.

In the figure, points \(B\), \(C\), and \(D\) are collinear, with equilateral \(\triangle ABC\) of side \(2\) and equilateral \(\triangle ECD\) of side \(1\). The quadrilateral \(ABCE\) is divided by diagonal \(AC\) into \(\triangle ABC\) and \(\triangle ACE\). The area of \(\triangle ABC\) is \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\cdot 2^2=\sqrt{3}\). Place \(B=(0,0)\), \(C=(2,0)\), and \(D=(3,0)\); then \(A=(1,\sqrt{3})\) and \(E=(\frac{5}{2},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})\). Using the shoelace formula for \(\triangle ACE\), the area is \(\frac{1}{2}\left|1\cdot0+2\cdot\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}+\frac{5}{2}\cdot\sqrt{3}-\left(\sqrt{3}\cdot2+0\cdot\frac{5}{2}+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot1\right)\right|=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\). Adding the two areas gives \(\sqrt{3}+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\). Final answer: \(\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\).

The image shows a standard Cartesian plane with the quadrants labeled I in the upper right, II in the upper left, III in the lower left, and IV in the lower right. The graph of the linear function \(f(x)=-3.5x+7\) is the line \(y=-3.5x+7\), which has a positive \(y\)-intercept at \((0,7)\) and an positive \(x\)-intercept found by solving \(-3.5x+7=0\), giving \(x=2\). For \(x<0\), \(y=-3.5x+7\) is greater than \(7\), so those points lie in Quadrant II; for \(0<x<2\), \(y>0\), so those points lie in Quadrant I; and for \(x>2\), \(y<0\), so those points lie in Quadrant IV. Because \(x\) and \(y\) are never both negative on this line, no point of the graph lies in Quadrant III. Final answer: III.

The image shows the river starting at A and splitting into two branches, with the upper branch carrying \(\frac{2}{3}\) of the water and the lower branch carrying the remaining \(1-\frac{2}{3}=\frac{1}{3}\). The upper \(\frac{2}{3}\) branch then splits into three parts labeled \(\frac{1}{8}\), \(\frac{5}{8}\), and an unlabeled remainder; the unlabeled remainder is \(1-\frac{1}{8}-\frac{5}{8}=\frac{1}{4}\) of that branch, and this is the part that flows down to meet the lower branch at B. Therefore the fraction of the original water at B is the lower branch plus the remainder of the upper branch: \(\frac{1}{3}+\frac{2}{3}\times\frac{1}{4}=\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{6}=\frac{1}{2}\). Final answer: \(\frac{1}{2}\)

The image shows bananas, apples, and round citrus fruits (oranges/mandarins), illustrating the three kinds of fruit involved in the exchanges. The square has side length 1 with \(M\) the midpoint of base \(AB\), and the shaded region is the quadrilateral bounded by segments \(DM\), \(CM\), \(AC\), and \(BD\), whose vertices are \(M\), the intersection of \(DM\) and \(AC\), the center \(O=AC\cap BD\), and the intersection of \(CM\) and \(BD\). Place coordinates \(A(0,0)\), \(B(1,0)\), \(C(1,1)\), \(D(0,1)\), so \(M(\tfrac12,0)\); then \(DM\) has equation \(y=1-2x\), \(CM\) has \(y=2x-1\), \(AC\) has \(y=x\), and \(BD\) has \(y=1-x\). Solving, \(DM\cap AC=(\tfrac13,\tfrac13)\), \(CM\cap BD=(\tfrac23,\tfrac13)\), and \(O=(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)\). The quadrilateral is a kite with perpendicular diagonals of lengths \(\tfrac12\) (from \(M\) to \(O\)) and \(\tfrac13\) (from \((\tfrac13,\tfrac13)\) to \((\tfrac23,\tfrac13)\)), so its area is \(\frac12\cdot \frac12\cdot \frac13=\frac1{12}\). Final answer: \(\frac{1}{12}\).

The image shows three semicircles whose diameters are the three sides of a right-angled triangle, with the right angle between the sides corresponding to the semicircles of areas \(X\) and \(Y\), and the semicircle of area \(Z\) constructed on the hypotenuse. The area of a semicircle with diameter \(d\) is \(\frac12\pi(d/2)^2=\frac{\pi d^2}{8}\), so if the diameters are \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\) with \(c\) the hypotenuse, then \(X=\frac{\pi a^2}{8}\), \(Y=\frac{\pi b^2}{8}\), and \(Z=\frac{\pi c^2}{8}\). By Pythagoras, \(a^2+b^2=c^2\), and multiplying by \(\frac{\pi}{8}\) gives \(\frac{\pi a^2}{8}+\frac{\pi b^2}{8}=\frac{\pi c^2}{8}\), so \(X+Y=Z\). Final answer: \(X+Y=Z\).

In the figure, \(ABCD\) is a convex quadrilateral of area \(1\); triangle \(ADB\) is isosceles with base \(AB\), and triangle \(BCD\) is isosceles with base \(BD\), so the marked angles give \(AD=BD\), \(BC=CD\), \(\angle ADB=20^\circ\), and \(\angle BCD=100^\circ\). Place \(D=(0,0)\) and \(B=(x,0)\), so \(BD=x\); then \(A=(x\cos20^\circ,x\sin20^\circ)\) and, since the apex angle at \(C\) is \(100^\circ\), \(C=(x/2,-x/(2\tan50^\circ))\). The area is the sum of the areas of \(\triangle ABD\) and \(\triangle BCD\), namely \(1=\frac12x^2\sin20^\circ+\frac{x^2}{4\tan50^\circ}\), so \(x^2=1/\bigl(\frac12\sin20^\circ+\frac14\cot50^\circ\bigr)\). The distance \(AC\) equals \(x\) times \(\sqrt{(\cos20^\circ-\frac12)^2+(\sin20^\circ+\frac12\cot50^\circ)^2}\), and using \(\cot50^\circ=\tan40^\circ\) and the identity \(\tan40^\circ+2\sin20^\circ=\sqrt3\,(2\cos20^\circ-1)\), this simplifies to \(AC=\frac{4}{\sqrt3}\,x\bigl(\frac12\sin20^\circ+\frac14\cot50^\circ\bigr)\). Therefore \(AC\cdot BD=AC\cdot x=\frac{4}{\sqrt3}\,x^2\bigl(\frac12\sin20^\circ+\frac14\cot50^\circ\bigr)=\frac{4}{\sqrt3}\). Final answer: \(4/\sqrt3\)

In the figure, triangle \(ABC\) has points \(M\) and \(N\) on side \(AB\) in the order \(A\!-\!M\!-\!N\!-\!B\), with \(AN=AC\) and \(BM=BC\), and \(\angle MCN=43^\circ\). Because \(AN=AC\), triangle \(ACN\) is isosceles with base \(CN\), so \(\angle ACN=(180^\circ-\angle A)/2=90^\circ-\angle A/2\). Because \(BM=BC\), triangle \(BCM\) is isosceles with base \(CM\), so \(\angle BCM=(180^\circ-\angle B)/2=90^\circ-\angle B/2\). These two angles overlap inside \(\angle ACB\), with their overlap being \(\angle MCN\), so \(\angle ACN+\angle BCM=\angle ACB+\angle MCN\). Let \(\angle ACB=\gamma\); then \(\angle A+\angle B=180^\circ-\gamma\), and substituting gives \((90^\circ-\angle A/2)+(90^\circ-\angle B/2)=\gamma+43^\circ\), which simplifies to \(180^\circ-(\angle A+\angle B)/2=\gamma+43^\circ\), then \(180^\circ-(180^\circ-\gamma)/2=\gamma+43^\circ\), so \(90^\circ+\gamma/2=\gamma+43^\circ\). Solving yields \(\gamma/2=47^\circ\), hence \(\gamma=94^\circ\). Final answer: 94°.

The image shows a regular five-pointed star, and the angle \(\alpha\) is marked at one of the five identical outer points of the star. A regular five-pointed star can be drawn by connecting every second vertex of a regular pentagon inscribed in a circle; the central angle between adjacent pentagon vertices is \(360^\circ/5 = 72^\circ\). At a given star point, the two lines forming the angle connect to the two vertices that are separated from it by one pentagon vertex each, so the angle \(\alpha\) is an inscribed angle that intercepts an arc of \(72^\circ\). An inscribed angle equals half its intercepted arc, so \(\alpha = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 72^\circ = 36^\circ\). Final answer: \(36^\circ\).

The diagram shows a rectangle divided into a left flower strip of width 2 m, a lower-right strawberry strip of height 3 m, and an upper-right vegetable strip. Since the flower section is a rectangle with area 10 m² and one side 2 m, its other side—the total height of the garden—is 10 ÷ 2 = 5 m. The garden’s total area is 30 m², so its total width is 30 ÷ 5 = 6 m. The width of the right-hand sections is therefore 6 − 2 = 4 m. The strawberry section has height 3 m, so its area is 4 × 3 = 12 m². Subtracting the flower and strawberry areas from the total gives the vegetable area: 30 − 10 − 12 = 8 m². Final answer: 8 m².

The image shows a 27 cm paper ribbon divided by three vertical lines into four adjacent rectangles of different widths, with two horizontal segments drawn: one connecting the center of the first rectangle to the center of the second, and another connecting the center of the third rectangle to the center of the fourth. Let the widths of the four rectangles be w1, w2, w3, and w4, so w1 + w2 + w3 + w4 = 27. The distance between the centers of the first and second rectangles is w1/2 + w2/2 = (w1 + w2)/2, and the distance between the centers of the third and fourth rectangles is w3/2 + w4/2 = (w3 + w4)/2; therefore the sum of the two segment lengths is (w1 + w2)/2 + (w3 + w4)/2 = (w1 + w2 + w3 + w4)/2 = 27/2 = 13.5 cm. Final answer: 13.5 cm

The image shows rectangle \(ABCD\) with three additional rectangles centered at corners \(A\), \(B\), and \(D\), their sides parallel to \(ABCD\), and each overlapping its corner. For one such added rectangle, if its half-sides along the two directions from the corner are \(x\) and \(y\), its perimeter is \(4(x+y)\). The part of the original perimeter it covers is \(x+y\), and the part of its own boundary that remains on the outside is \(4(x+y)-(x+y)=3(x+y)\), so the border length increases by \(3(x+y)-(x+y)=2(x+y)\), which is exactly half the added rectangle’s perimeter. Therefore the total border length equals the perimeter of \(ABCD\) plus half the sum of the perimeters of the three added rectangles: \(30+\frac{20}{2}=40\) cm. Final answer: 40 cm.

The rectangle is tiled by squares with the smallest side being 20 cm. The two top-left squares and the three squares in the middle horizontal band are the smallest squares; the left column contains three equal squares whose side equals the combined width of the two top-left squares, and the two large right-hand squares have side equal to the width of the three smallest squares in the band. Let a smallest square have side s. Then the left-column squares have side 2s and the right-hand large squares have side 3s. The left-hand height is s + 3(2s) = 7s, and the right-hand height is 3s + s + 3s = 7s, confirming the figure closes and giving s = 20 cm. Thus the outer rectangle measures 5s by 7s, that is 100 cm by 140 cm. The total length of the black line includes the outer border and all internal edges. The five smallest squares have total perimeter 5(4s) = 20s, the three 2s-squares have total perimeter 3(8s) = 24s, and the two 3s-squares have total perimeter 2(12s) = 24s, so the sum of all square perimeters is 68s. Since this sum counts each internal edge twice and the outer border once, the total black line length is (sum of perimeters + outer perimeter)/2 = (68s + 24s)/2 = 46s = 46(20 cm) = 920 cm. Final answer: 920 cm.

The image shows a right triangle with the right angle marked at the bottom-right vertex; the two gray marked angles are exterior angles adjacent to the two acute interior angles of the triangle. In any right triangle, the two acute interior angles sum to 90°. Each marked exterior angle forms a linear pair with its adjacent acute interior angle, so the two marked angles together with the two acute interior angles sum to 2 × 180° = 360°. Therefore, the sum of the two marked angles is 360° − 90° = 270°. Final answer: 270°

In the figure the circle is tangent to the bottom side of the rectangle and passes through the two top vertices, and the top side of the rectangle appears to be a diameter of the circle; the square of area \(20\ \mathrm{cm}^2\) rests on this top side with its upper two vertices on the circle. Let the square have side \(s\), so \(s^2=20\). Place the center of the circle at the origin with the top side of the rectangle along the \(x\)-axis, making the circle’s radius \(R\). The upper vertices of the square are at \(\left(\pm \frac{s}{2},s\right)\), and since they lie on the circle \(x^2+y^2=R^2\), we have \(\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)^2+s^2=R^2\). Thus \(R^2=\frac{5}{4}s^2=\frac{5}{4}\cdot20=25\), so \(R=5\ \mathrm{cm}\). The rectangle has width \(2R=10\ \mathrm{cm}\) and height \(R=5\ \mathrm{cm}\), giving an area of \(10\cdot5=50\ \mathrm{cm}^2\). Final answer: \(50\ \mathrm{cm}^2\).

The visible part of the calendar shows the German weekday headings Mo, Di, Mi, Do, Fr, Sa, So and the dates 2 under Do (Thursday), 3 under Fr (Friday), and 7 under Di (Tuesday). Since 2 is Thursday, the 1st of the month is Wednesday, making 3 Friday and 7 Tuesday, which matches the visible numbers. Counting forward from the 1st as Wednesday, the 22nd is also Wednesday, so the 25th is three days later: Wednesday + 3 days = Saturday. Final answer: Saturday.

The image shows a circle of radius 3 cm with a white square inscribed in it (the square’s vertices lie on the circle), and two outer squares of the same size are also drawn; the shaded region is the part of the circle outside the inscribed square. The area of the circle is π(3)² = 9π cm². For the inscribed square, its diagonal equals the circle’s diameter 6 cm, so if the side length is s then s√2 = 6, giving s = 3√2 cm and area s² = 18 cm². Hence the shaded area is 9π − 18 cm². Final answer: 9π − 18 cm².

The image shows two vertical stacks of identical glasses, one containing eight glasses and the other containing two glasses. Since each additional glass adds the same amount of height, the height of a stack with \(n\) glasses follows the linear form \(H(n)=H(1)+(n-1)d\), where \(H(1)\) is the height of one glass and \(d\) is the height added by each extra glass. From the given data, \(H(8)=42\) and \(H(2)=18\), so the difference is \(42-18=24\) cm over \(8-2=6\) additional glasses, giving \(d=24/6=4\) cm. Then \(H(1)=H(2)-d=18-4=14\) cm. For six glasses, \(H(6)=14+(6-1)\cdot4=14+20=34\) cm. Final answer: 34 cm.

The diagram shows a five-pointed star with vertices A, B, C, D, E, where the angle at B is 58°, and two interior intersection angles are 100° and 93°; the angle at A is unknown. In the small triangle at vertex B, the angle adjacent to the marked 100° angle forms a linear pair with it, so that interior angle equals 180° − 100° = 80°; since the angles in a triangle sum to 180°, the remaining angle in that triangle is 180° − 58° − 80° = 42°. This 42° angle is vertically opposite to one base angle of the small triangle at vertex A. In the small triangle at A, the angle adjacent to the marked 93° angle is 180° − 93° = 87°. Therefore, angle A = 180° − 42° − 87° = 51°. Final answer: 51°

The diagram shows a square at the bottom with a labeled side of 9 cm, a rectangle on top whose width matches the base of the equilateral triangle above it, and the rectangle’s vertical side is marked with a question mark. Since all three shapes have the same perimeter, the square’s perimeter is 4 × 9 = 36 cm, so the equilateral triangle’s side is 36 ÷ 3 = 12 cm. The rectangle’s width equals that triangle side, 12 cm, and its perimeter is also 36 cm; using P = 2(l + w), we get 36 = 2(12 + h), so 12 + h = 18 and h = 6 cm. Final answer: 6 cm.

The diagram shows five congruent rectangles arranged in a staircase pattern from the bottom-left corner to the top-right corner of the square, alternating horizontal and vertical orientations, with the first rectangle flush against the left and bottom sides and the last flush against the top and right sides. Let each rectangle have length \(l\) and width \(w\). The total horizontal span of the arrangement is \(3l+2w\) and the total vertical span is \(2l+3w\), and because the enclosing square has side length 24, both spans equal 24. Solving \(3l+2w=24\) and \(2l+3w=24\) gives \(l=w\), so \(5l=24\) and \(l=w=\frac{24}{5}\). Therefore the area of one rectangle is \(\left(\frac{24}{5}\right)^2=\frac{576}{25}\). Final answer: \(\frac{576}{25}\)

The diagram shows five identical circles, with the central circle fully shaded and the square connecting the centres of the four outer circles; because the square’s corners are right angles, the shaded portion of each outer circle is exactly a quarter of that circle. Let each circle have radius \(r\). The shaded area is the area of the central circle plus four quarter-circles, which equals \(\pi r^2 + 4\left(\frac14\pi r^2\right)=2\pi r^2\). The total area of the five circles is \(5\pi r^2\), so the unshaded area is \(5\pi r^2-2\pi r^2=3\pi r^2\). Therefore the ratio of shaded area to unshaded area is \(2\pi r^2:3\pi r^2=2:3\). Final answer: 2:3

The figure shows nine 100 m paths forming a triangular grid with side length two small triangles; A and B are two outer corners connected by two paths meeting at the midpoint of side AB. Treating the paths as edges of a graph, every vertex has even degree, so a single trail that uses every edge exactly once must be a closed Eulerian circuit, not a trail from A to B. For an open trail from A to B, A and B must have odd degree and all other vertices even, which requires deleting a set of edges whose endpoints include A and B with odd multiplicity; the smallest such set is a shortest A–B path, namely the two edges on side AB. Removing those two edges leaves 9 − 2 = 7 edges, with A and B odd and all other vertices even, and the remaining graph is connected, so an Eulerian trail from A to B using all seven edges exists. Therefore the longest possible walk is 7 × 100 m = 700 m. Final answer: 700 m.

The diagram shows a regular hexagon of side length 1, so the distance from the centre to any vertex is 1, and the grey flower consists of six identical lens-shaped petals, each running from one vertex of the hexagon to the centre and bounded by two circular arcs of radius 1 centred at the two vertices adjacent to that outer vertex. For one petal, the two arc-centres are vertices separated by two edges of the hexagon, so their distance is √3, and the two unit circles intersect at the outer vertex and the centre, which are 1 unit apart; thus each bounding arc subtends an angle of 60° at its centre. The area of one petal is the sum of the two 60° sectors minus the area of the kite whose diagonals are 1 and √3, namely 2·(π/6) − (1/2)·1·√3 = π/3 − √3/2. Since the six petals only meet at the centre and have no overlapping interior, the total grey area is 6(π/3 − √3/2) = 2π − 3√3. Final answer: 2π − 3√3.

The image shows a rectangular blackboard with total length 6 m, divided into three sections where the middle section measures 3 m and the two outer sections appear equal in width. Since the total length is 6 m and the middle section is 3 m, the combined length of the two outer sections is 6 - 3 = 3 m. Because the two outer sections are equal in width, each section is 3 ÷ 2 = 1.5 m long. Final answer: 1.5 m.

The figure is a cross-shaped polyomino made of eight equally sized squares arranged as two squares in the top row, four in the middle row, and two in the bottom row, equivalent to a 4-unit-by-3-unit rectangle with its four corner unit squares removed. Since removing each corner square replaces two outer edges with two inner edges and leaves the perimeter unchanged, the perimeter equals 2(4s + 3s) = 14s, where s is the side length of one square; setting 14s = 42 cm gives s = 3 cm. The area of one square is s² = 9 cm², so the total area of the eight squares is 8 × 9 = 72 cm². Final answer: 72 cm²

The image shows a square garden divided into four rectangular regions, with the pool \(P\) at the top left, the flowerbed \(F\) at the top right, the lawn \(L\) at the bottom left, and the sandpit \(S\) at the bottom right; \(L\) and \(F\) are squares. Since the perimeter of square \(L\) is \(20\,\text{m}\), its side length is \(20\div4=5\,\text{m}\); since the perimeter of square \(F\) is \(12\,\text{m}\), its side length is \(12\div4=3\,\text{m}\). The right column consists of \(F\) above \(S\), so \(S\) has the same width as \(F\), namely \(3\,\text{m}\), and the bottom row consists of \(L\) beside \(S\), so \(S\) has the same height as \(L\), namely \(5\,\text{m}\). Therefore the whole garden has side length \(5+3=8\,\text{m}\). The pool \(P\) has width \(8-3=5\,\text{m}\) and height \(8-5=3\,\text{m}\), so its perimeter is \(2(5+3)=16\,\text{m}\). Final answer: \(16\,\text{m}\).

The image shows the same cuboid-shaped container resting on three different faces, with the water depth equal to \(2\ \text{m}\), \(3\ \text{m}\), and \(5\ \text{m}\) respectively, and the volume of water is \(120\ \text{m}^3\) in each case. Let the edge lengths of the cuboid be \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\). When the container stands so that the edge of length \(a\) is vertical, the water volume is \((b \cdot c) \cdot 2 = 120\), giving \(bc = 60\). Similarly, the other two orientations give \(ac = \frac{120}{3} = 40\) and \(ab = \frac{120}{5} = 24\). Multiplying these three equations yields \((bc)(ac)(ab) = a^2b^2c^2 = (abc)^2 = 60 \cdot 40 \cdot 24 = 57600\), so the total volume is \(abc = \sqrt{57600} = 240\ \text{m}^3\). Final answer: \(240\ \text{m}^3\)

The image shows a cube of side length 1, which has 12 edges and therefore requires a total wire length of 12. Viewing the cube’s frame as a graph, all 8 vertices have degree 3, an odd number; each wire piece is a trail with two endpoints, and each odd-degree vertex must be an endpoint of some piece, so at least 4 pieces are needed. This bound can be achieved using pieces of lengths 1 cm, 2 cm, 3 cm, and 6 cm, whose total length is 12: label the bottom face A-B-C-D and top face E-F-G-H with vertical edges AE, BF, CG, DH; then use the 6 cm piece along A-B-C-D-H-G-F, the 3 cm piece along H-E-A-D, the 2 cm piece along E-F-B, and the 1 cm piece along C-G. These four paths cover all 12 edges exactly once with no overlap. Final answer: 4.

The image shows a plant that winds exactly 5 times around a vertical post while rising a total height of \(1 \mathrm{~m}=100 \mathrm{~cm}\), and the post has a circumference of \(15 \mathrm{~cm}\). If the helical path is unrolled onto a flat surface, it becomes the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose vertical leg is the total rise \(100 \mathrm{~cm}\) and whose horizontal leg is the total distance traveled around the post, \(5 \times 15 \mathrm{~cm}=75 \mathrm{~cm}\). Using the Pythagorean theorem, the length of the plant is \(\sqrt{100^2+75^2}\mathrm{~cm}=\sqrt{10000+5625}\mathrm{~cm}=\sqrt{15625}\mathrm{~cm}=125 \mathrm{~cm}\). Final answer: 125 cm (1.25 m).

The rectangle \(PRSV\) has width \(PR = 20\text{ cm}\) and height \(PV = 12\text{ cm}\). The unshaded regions are triangles \(PQU\) and \(QTR\), each with a base on \(PR\) and its opposite vertex on \(VS\), so each triangle has height \(12\text{ cm}\). Their bases add to \(PQ + QR = PR = 20\text{ cm}\), so the total unshaded area is \(\frac12 \times 20 \times 12 = 120\text{ cm}^2\). The area of the rectangle is \(20 \times 12 = 240\text{ cm}^2\), and therefore the shaded area is \(240 - 120 = 120\text{ cm}^2\). Final answer: \(120\text{ cm}^2\).

The two pictures show the maximum packings for a \(5\times5\) board with \(9\) chips and for a \(6\times6\) board with \(9\) chips, where every pair of occupied cells is separated by at least one empty row and one empty column so that no two occupied cells share even a corner. This is the non-attacking kings problem, and the maximum number of chips on an \(n\times n\) board is \(\left\lceil \frac{n}{2}\right\rceil^2\). For \(n=2020\), we get \(\left\lceil \frac{2020}{2}\right\rceil^2 = 1010^2 = 1{,}020{,}100\). Final answer: \(1010^2 = 1{,}020{,}100\) chips.

From the diagram the diameters \(AB\) and \(CD\) are each divided into two segments of length \(1\), so \(AB=CD=2\); the semicircles therefore have radius \(1\), and because the line of each diameter is tangent to the other semicircle, the two parallel lines are exactly one radius apart. Place \(A=(0,0)\) and \(B=(2,0)\), so the left semicircle has center \((1,0)\) and the upper line is \(y=1\). Let the right semicircle have center \((x,1)\); since the semicircles touch externally, the distance between their centers equals \(2\), giving \((x-1)^2+(1-0)^2=2^2\), so \((x-1)^2=3\) and \(x=1+\sqrt3\). Then \(D\) is one radius to the right of this center, so \(D=(2+\sqrt3,1)\). Hence \(AD^2=(2+\sqrt3-0)^2+(1-0)^2=(4+4\sqrt3+3)+1=8+4\sqrt3\). Final answer: \(8+4\sqrt3\)

The diagram shows two lower semicircular arcs with centres \(E\) and \(F\) on the base line, and a shaded upper semicircular arc with endpoints \(A\) and \(B\); the points \(A, B, E, F\) form a rectangle, so \(A\) is directly above \(E\), \(B\) is directly above \(F\), and each side \(AE\) and \(BF\) equals the radius \(2\mathrm{~cm}\), while \(EF=AB=4\mathrm{~cm}\). The upper semicircle therefore has radius \(2\), and the shaded region is the area under that upper arc from \(A\) to \(B\) minus the area under the two lower arcs. The area under the upper arc equals the rectangle of base \(4\) and height \(2\) plus a half-disk of radius \(2\): \(4\cdot2+\frac12\pi(2^2)=8+2\pi\). The area under the two lower arcs consists of two quarter-disks of radius \(2\): \(2\cdot\frac14\pi(2^2)=2\pi\). Hence the shaded area is \((8+2\pi)-2\pi=8\mathrm{~cm}^2\). Final answer: \(8\mathrm{~cm}^2\).

The left image shows a single isosceles trapezium with parallel sides \(a\) and \(b\), where \(a\) is the longer base and \(b\) is the shorter base; the right image shows three congruent copies of this trapezium assembled so that each longer base \(a\) forms a side of the large equilateral triangle and each shorter base \(b\) forms a side of the central equilateral triangular hole. Since the hole is an equilateral triangle with side length \(b\), its perimeter is \(b+b+b=3b\). Final answer: 3b

The diagram shows a right triangle with one 90-degree angle indicated by a square symbol and two other angles marked with arcs. The sum of the interior angles in any triangle is 180 degrees, so the sum of the two non-right angles is 180° − 90° = 90°. Final answer: 90°

The diagram shows a square with a triangle attached along one full side of the square, so that shared side becomes an internal line and is not part of the pentagon’s perimeter. Let the side length of the square be \(s\). The perimeter of the square is \(4s\), and since the triangle has the same perimeter, the triangle’s perimeter is also \(4s\). The triangle’s base equals the side of the square, \(s\), so the sum of its other two sides is \(4s - s = 3s\). The pentagon’s perimeter consists of the three remaining sides of the square plus the two non-base sides of the triangle, giving \(3s + 3s = 6s\). Therefore the ratio of the pentagon’s perimeter to the square’s perimeter is \(\frac{6s}{4s} = \frac{3}{2}\). Final answer: 3:2.

The diagram shows a cube with side length 18 cm, where the ant travels from point X on the left front vertical edge to point Y on the right back vertical edge along a path marked by thick arrows. The route consists of five straight segments, each equal in length to one edge of the cube: first down the left front vertical edge, then right along the bottom front edge, then up the vertical edge between the front and right faces, then right/back along the top of the right face, and finally down the right back vertical edge to Y. Since each edge of the cube is 18 cm, the total distance is 5 × 18 cm = 90 cm. Final answer: 90 cm

The image shows a trapezium containing a grey rectangle whose top side is the segment XY, with X and Y being the midpoints of the trapezium's non-parallel sides (legs) and the rectangle's base lying on the trapezium's base. Since the segment joining the midpoints of the legs of a trapezium is its median, XY equals the average of the two parallel bases, and because X and Y are midpoints, the rectangle's height is exactly half the trapezium's height. Letting the bases be a and b and the trapezium's height be h, the rectangle's area is XY × h/2 = (a+b)/2 × h/2 = (a+b)h/4, while the trapezium's area is (a+b)h/2, so the trapezium's area is twice the rectangle's area. Final answer: 26 cm².

The image shows a circle of radius 3 cm with two identical squares whose edges are parallel; their intersection is the central white square, and the shaded regions are the four parts of the circle outside this central square. The vertices of the central square lie on the circle, so the square is inscribed in the circle and its diagonal equals the circle's diameter, which is \(2 \times 3 = 6\) cm. A square with diagonal 6 cm has area \(\frac{6^2}{2} = 18\) cm\(^2\), and the circle has area \(\pi \times 3^2 = 9\pi\) cm\(^2\). Thus the total shaded area is the circle's area minus the central square's area, giving \(9\pi - 18\) cm\(^2\). Final answer: \(9\pi - 18\).

The image shows four unit squares arranged edge to edge in a staircase pattern, with point P at the bottom-left corner of the leftmost square and point Q at the top-right corner of the rightmost square, so the horizontal distance from P to Q spans three unit lengths and the vertical distance spans two unit lengths. The segment PQ is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 3 and 2, so by the Pythagorean theorem its length is sqrt(3^2 + 2^2) = sqrt(9 + 4) = sqrt(13). Final answer: sqrt(13).

The square has side length \(s\); the two large circles are centered at opposite corners of the square and the two small circles are centered at the other two opposite corners. Because the two large circles touch each other, the distance between their centers equals the diagonal of the square, so \(2R = s\sqrt{2}\), which gives \(R = s/\sqrt{2}\). Each large circle also touches each small circle, and the distance between adjacent centers is a side of the square, so \(s = R + r\). Substituting \(R = s/\sqrt{2}\) gives \(r = s - s/\sqrt{2} = s(1 - 1/\sqrt{2})\). Therefore the required factor is \(R/r = (s/\sqrt{2}) / [s(1 - 1/\sqrt{2})] = 1/(\sqrt{2} - 1) = \sqrt{2} + 1\). Final answer: 1 + sqrt(2).

The diagram shows unit square \(KLMN\) with \(K\) on the right, \(L\) on top, \(M\) on the left, and \(N\) on the bottom; four unit-radius arcs are centered at the vertices, and \(Q\) and \(P\) are the interior intersections of the arcs centered at \(K,L\) and \(M,N\), respectively. Place the square with \(K=(1,0)\), \(L=(1,1)\), \(M=(0,1)\), \(N=(0,0)\). The arcs centered at \(K\) and \(L\) satisfy \((x-1)^2+y^2=1\) and \((x-1)^2+(y-1)^2=1\); subtracting gives \(y=\frac12\), and substituting yields \((x-1)^2=\frac34\), so the interior intersection is \(Q=\left(1-\frac{\sqrt3}{2},\frac12\right)\). The arcs centered at \(M\) and \(N\) satisfy \(x^2+(y-1)^2=1\) and \(x^2+y^2=1\); subtracting gives \(y=\frac12\), and substituting yields \(x^2=\frac34\), so the interior intersection is \(P=\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2},\frac12\right)\). Therefore \(PQ=\left|\frac{\sqrt3}{2}-\left(1-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)\right|=\sqrt3-1\). Final answer: \(\sqrt3-1\).

The square has side length \(1\text{ cm}\); the larger circle is tangent to the left and bottom sides with its center on the diagonal from the bottom-left to the top-right corner, and the smaller circle is tangent to the top and right sides with its center on the same diagonal. Let the radii be \(r\) and \(s\). Then the centers are \((r,r)\) and \((1-s,1-s)\), so the distance between them is \(\sqrt{2}\,(1-r-s)\). Since the circles touch each other, this distance also equals \(r+s\). Thus \(r+s=\sqrt{2}\,(1-(r+s))\), which gives \((r+s)(1+\sqrt{2})=\sqrt{2}\) and hence \(r+s=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{1+\sqrt{2}}=2-\sqrt{2}\). Final answer: \(2-\sqrt{2}\) cm.

The diagram shows square \(PQRS\) with side length \(10\) rolling to the right along a line, with the first rotation about \(Q\); point \(P\) starts on the line and first returns to the line after three \(90^\circ\) rolls. In the first roll about \(Q\), \(P\) is adjacent to the pivot, so it traces a quarter circle of radius \(PQ=10\). In the second roll the pivot is \(R\), and since \(P\) is opposite \(R\), it traces a quarter circle of radius \(RP=10\sqrt2\), the diagonal of the square, which is the arc labeled \(RP\). In the third roll about \(S\), \(P\) is again adjacent to the pivot, tracing a quarter circle of radius \(SP=10\). A \(90^\circ\) arc has length \(\frac14\cdot 2\pi r=\frac{\pi r}{2}\), so the total distance is \(\frac{\pi}{2}(10+10\sqrt2+10)=5\pi(2+\sqrt2)\). Final answer: \(5\pi(2+\sqrt2)\).

The shaded square in the upper-left corner has area \(9\text{ cm}^2\), so its side length is \(\sqrt{9}=3\text{ cm}\). Let the width and height of rectangle \(ABCD\) be \(w\) and \(h\); then the entire large rectangle has dimensions \((w+3)\) by \((h+3)\). Since the large rectangle’s perimeter is \(30\text{ cm}\), we have \(2[(w+3)+(h+3)]=30\), which simplifies to \(w+h+6=15\), so \(w+h=9\). Therefore, the perimeter of rectangle \(ABCD\) is \(2(w+h)=2(9)=18\text{ cm}\). Final answer: \(18\text{ cm}\).

The image shows a large equilateral triangle with side length \(6\mathrm{~cm}\) with three congruent small equilateral triangles cut from its corners, leaving a gray hexagon in the middle. Let the side length of each small triangle be \(x\). The total perimeter of the three small triangles is \(3(3x)=9x\). The remaining hexagon has six sides: three outer segments, each of length \(6-2x\), and three inner cut edges, each of length \(x\), so its perimeter is \(3(6-2x)+3x=18-3x\). Setting the two perimeters equal gives \(9x=18-3x\), so \(12x=18\) and \(x=1.5\). Final answer: \(1.5\mathrm{~cm}\).

In the isosceles triangle \(ABC\), the vertex angle at \(B\) is \(40^\circ\), so the base angles satisfy \(\angle BAC=\angle ACB=70^\circ\). Points \(D\) on \(AB\) and \(E\) on \(BC\) determine cevians \(AE\) and \(CD\) intersecting at \(F\), and the marked angles satisfy \(\angle EAB=\angle DCA=x\). Then in \(\triangle AFC\), the angle at \(A\) is \(\angle CAF=\angle BAC-\angle EAB=70^\circ-x\), and the angle at \(C\) is \(\angle ACF=\angle DCA=x\). Therefore \(\angle AFC=180^\circ-(70^\circ-x)-x=110^\circ\). Since \(A\), \(F\), \(E\) are collinear, \(\angle CFE\) is supplementary to \(\angle AFC\), giving \(\angle CFE=180^\circ-110^\circ=70^\circ\). Final answer: \(70^\circ\).

The plan is an orthogonal polygon whose horizontal segments along the top are \(a\), \(a\), and \(a\), so the total width of the room is \(a+a+a=3a\), and its vertical segments on the right are \(b\), \(2b\), and \(b\), so the total height is \(b+2b+b=4b\). In the diagram, triangle \(ABC\) has \(\angle C = 60^\circ\) and the angle at \(A\) between \(CA\) and the dashed line \(AB\) is \(75^\circ\), so \(\angle B = 180^\circ - 75^\circ - 60^\circ = 45^\circ\). The descending stairs follow the line \(AB\), so the total stair length equals the sum of the horizontal and vertical projections of \(AB\); since \(AB\) makes a \(45^\circ\) angle with the horizontal base, this length is \(AB(\cos 45^\circ + \sin 45^\circ) = AB\sqrt{2}\). Therefore the ratio of the ascending path \(CA\) to the descending stair path is \((AB\sqrt{2}/\sqrt{3})/(AB\sqrt{2}) = 1/\sqrt{3}\), or \(1:\sqrt{3}\). Final answer: 1:sqrt(3).

The square flowerbed has side length 12 m, and the two crossing straight lines meet each side 4 m from a corner, intersecting at the square’s center; the sunflowers are planted in the upper-right and lower-left regions. The figure is a \(3\times3\) grid of squares. From the lower-left corner, the lower ray passes through the grid point \(3\) units right and \(2\) units up, so \(\tan\alpha=\frac{2}{3}\). The diagram shows an equilateral triangle with the ant’s speeds marked on the three sides as 5 cm/min, 15 cm/min, and 20 cm/min, with arrows indicating motion around the triangle. In the figure, the square contains two circles that are tangent to each other at \(O\); the upper-left circle is tangent to the top and left sides of the square, with \(A\) its point of tangency on the top side, and the lower-right circle is tangent to the right and bottom sides, with \(B\) its point of tangency on the right side. Place the square with side length \(1\), top-left corner at \((0,0)\), \(x\) rightward and \(y\) downward; let the radii be \(r\) and \(R\). The centers are \((r,r)\) and \((1-R,1-R)\), and because the circles are tangent, the distance between centers equals \(r+R\), giving \(\sqrt{2}\bigl(1-r-R\bigr)=r+R\), so \(r+R=2-\sqrt2\). The tangency point \(O\) lies on the diagonal line of centers, so \(A=(r,0)\), \(B=(1,1-R)\), and \(O=\bigl(r(1+\tfrac1{\sqrt2}),r(1+\tfrac1{\sqrt2})\bigr)\). Thus \(\overrightarrow{OA}=\bigl(-\tfrac{r}{\sqrt2},-r(1+\tfrac1{\sqrt2})\bigr)\) and \(\overrightarrow{OB}=\bigl(R(1+\tfrac1{\sqrt2}),\tfrac{R}{\sqrt2}\bigr)\); computing the dot product gives \(\cos\angle AOB=-\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\), hence the angle is \(135^\circ\). Final answer: \(135^\circ\).

The square has side 10 cm, so its area is 100 cm². On the top side, S, N, M, R are in order and MN = 6 cm, leaving 10 − 6 = 4 cm to be shared equally by the two top corner squares; thus each small square has side 2 cm and area 4 cm², giving a total of 4 × 4 = 16 cm² for the four corner squares. The four unshaded isosceles triangles each have base 6 cm. Because the figure has fourfold rotational symmetry, the two arms of the shaded X are perpendicular, so each unshaded triangle is a right isosceles triangle with the right angle at its apex; in such a triangle the altitude to the hypotenuse equals half the hypotenuse, so each triangle has height 6/2 = 3 cm and area ½ × 6 × 3 = 9 cm². The four triangles therefore have total area 4 × 9 = 36 cm². Subtracting the unshaded areas from the whole square gives 100 − 16 − 36 = 48 cm². Final answer: 48 cm².

The diagram shows a triangle and a circle overlapping, so the total diagram is divided into three non-overlapping parts: the region inside both shapes (intersection), the part of the triangle not in the circle, and the part of the circle not in the triangle. Since the intersection is 45% of the total area and the triangle outside the circle is 40% of the total area, the remaining part—the circle outside the triangle—must be 100% − 45% − 40% = 15% of the total area. The whole circle therefore accounts for the intersection plus this remaining part, which is 45% + 15% = 60% of the total area. The percentage of the circle that lies outside the triangle is the circle-outside region divided by the whole circle: 15% / 60% = 0.25 = 25%. Final answer: 25%.

In the diagram, triangles VWX and XYZ are congruent equilateral triangles, so every side has the same length and each interior angle is 60 degrees; the marked angle at X is angle VXY = 80 degrees. In equilateral triangle VWX, angle VXW is 60 degrees, so the angle between rays XW and XY is angle WXY = 60 degrees + 80 degrees = 140 degrees. The image shows a large triangle with vertices \(X\), \(Y\), and an unlabeled bottom-left vertex, divided by its three midpoints into four smaller triangles, giving nine distinct paths each \(100\ \text{m}\) long. To obtain an trail from \(X\) to \(Y\), the unused edges must leave exactly \(X\) and \(Y\) with odd degree, which requires deleting at least the two edges of a shortest \(X\)-to-\(Y\) path; the shortest such path has length \(2\), leaving \(9-2=7\) edges. Seven edges each \(100\ \text{m}\) long give a total length of \(700\ \text{m}\), and an example route is \(X\to M\to N\to C\to M\to B\to C\to Y\). Final answer: \(700\ \text{m}\).

The diagram shows five congruent right-angled isosceles triangles placed side by side along a 30 cm horizontal line, with their hypotenuses lying on that line, so the total 30 cm length is divided equally among the five hypotenuses, giving each hypotenuse a length of 30 ÷ 5 = 6 cm. The image shows a circular cake divided into slices, with one separated slice labeled “15%” and an angle inside that slice marked with a question mark. In the diagram, \(O\) is the center, \(A\) and \(P\) lie on a straight line through \(O\) with \(A\) on the circle and \(P\) outside, \(PT\) is tangent to the circle at \(T\), and the angle bisector \(PB\) meets chord \(AT\) at \(B\). Triangle \(AOT\) is isosceles with \(OA=OT\), so \(\angle OAT=\frac{180^\circ-(90^\circ+2\alpha)}{2}=45^\circ-\alpha\), which equals \(\angle PAT\). Final answer: \(45^\circ\).

The image shows Tank X filled to a depth of 5 cm and Tank Y with a height of 7 cm, while the problem gives Tank X a base area of 200 cm² and Tank Y a base area of 100 cm². Therefore, for a final common water level \(h\), the water volume is \(200h\). Setting \(200h = 1000\) gives \(h = 5\) cm, which is less than Tank Y’s 7 cm height, so no water is lost over the top.
