The image shows 12 empty circles arranged in a ring, with no adjacent pair singled out. Treating the numbers 1 to 12 as vertices with edges between any two numbers differing by 1 or 2, a valid placement is a Hamiltonian cycle in this graph. Vertices 1 and 12 each have only two neighbors, so 1 must be adjacent to 2 and 3, and 12 must be adjacent to 10 and 11. Vertex 2 cannot be adjacent to 3, otherwise the triangle 1-2-3 would isolate the remaining vertices, so 2 is adjacent to 4; similarly 11 is adjacent to 9. Considering the cut {1,2,3,4,5}, only 4 and 5 have neighbors outside, and a Hamiltonian cycle must cross this cut twice; since 4's only outside neighbor is 6, the crossing edges must be 4-6 and 5-7. This forces the path 4-2-1-3-5 inside the cut, and because 12 must lie between 10 and 11, the only path covering {6,...,12} from 6 to 7 is 6-8-10-12-11-9-7. Hence the only Hamiltonian cycle is 1-2-4-6-8-10-12-11-9-7-5-3-1, up to reversal and rotation. Because the diagram provides no marked adjacent pair, a rotation of this cycle can put any of its adjacent pairs in any given adjacent circles, so the unmarked image does not determine a unique pair. Final answer: The pair cannot be determined from the unmarked diagram; the unique valid placement up to rotation/reflection is 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 11, 9, 7, 5, 3 around the ring, giving adjacent pairs {1,2}, {1,3}, {2,4}, {3,5}, {4,6}, {5,7}, {6,8}, {7,9}, {8,10}, {9,11}, {10,12}, {11,12}.

The flag has three horizontal stripes of equal height, so each stripe has the same area. The top stripe is divided into 4 equal parts with the 1st and 3rd shaded, so 2/4 = 1/2 of it is shaded; the middle stripe is divided into 3 equal parts with the 1st and 3rd shaded, so 2/3 of it is shaded; the bottom stripe is divided into 2 equal parts with the 1st shaded, so 1/2 of it is shaded. In the diagram, point \(F\) lies on the diagonal \(AC\) of pentagon \(ABCDE\), so the pentagon is split into equilateral triangle \(ABC\) and three congruent isosceles triangles \(AEF\), \(DFE\), and \(CDF\); the segments \(EF\) and \(DF\) are common sides, so in triangle \(DFE\) the two equal sides are \(EF\) and \(DF\). Let each congruent isosceles triangle have equal legs of length \(x\) and base \(y\); then \(DE=y\), \(EF=DF=x\), and by congruence the sides along \(AC\) must be the bases, giving \(AF=CF=y\) and \(AE=CD=x\) (the alternative \(AF=CF=x\) would force \(y=4x\) from the equal-perimeter condition, contradicting the triangle inequality). Thus \(AC=AF+CF=2y\), and since \(\triangle ABC\) is equilateral its perimeter is \(3(AC)=6y\). The equal-perimeter condition gives \(x+x+y=6y\), so \(x=\frac{5}{2}y\). The pentagon perimeter is \(AB+BC+CD+DE+EA=2y+2y+x+y+x=5y+2x=5y+5y=10y\). Therefore the ratio of the perimeter of pentagon \(ABCDE\) to the perimeter of triangle \(ABC\) is \(\frac{10y}{6y}=\frac{5}{3}\). Final answer: 5/3

The diagram shows Kengu starting at 0, making two big jumps of length 3 each (0→3→6), then three small jumps of length 1 each (6→7→8→9), and this 5-jump pattern repeats, so each complete cycle covers 9 units on the number line. The image shows a large triangle divided by three internal segments, each joining a vertex to the opposite side and crossing the other two, forming four small triangles and three quadrilaterals. The four unit squares are arranged in a staircase shape, with point \(A\) at the lower-left corner of the bottom-left square and point \(B\) at the upper-right corner of the top-right square. The points \(A_1, B_1, D_1, C_1\) are the feet of the perpendiculars from \(A, B, D, C\) to the same straight line, so \(AA_1, BB_1, DD_1, CC_1\) are the perpendicular distances from the vertices of parallelogram \(ABCD\) to that line. Substituting into \(-4+7=BB_1-5\) yields \(3=BB_1-5\), so \(BB_1=8\) cm. Final answer: 8 cm.

The diagram shows a rectangular pool with one side labeled 50 m and the unknown width marked with a question mark. Let the width be \(w\) meters. Sarah swims six lengths of the pool, so she swims \(6 \times 50 = 300\) m. Ruth runs around the perimeter five times; the perimeter is \(2(50 + w)\), so five times around is \(5 \times 2(50 + w) = 10(50 + w) = 500 + 10w\) m. Since Ruth runs three times as fast as Sarah swims and the times are equal, we have \(\frac{300}{v} = \frac{500 + 10w}{3v}\), where \(v\) is Sarah’s speed. Canceling \(v\) and multiplying by 3 gives \(900 = 500 + 10w\), so \(10w = 400\) and \(w = 40\). Final answer: 40 m.

In the left picture, the top of the sitting cat on the table is higher than the top of the sleeping cat on the floor by 150 cm, and in the right picture, the top of the sleeping cat on the table is higher than the top of the sitting cat on the floor by 110 cm. The flag has three horizontal stripes of equal width, so each stripe has the same area. The top stripe is divided into 4 equal parts with 2 grey, giving a grey fraction of 2/4 = 1/2. The image shows a regular hexagon with center \(O\) and three alternating vertices marked; the three unmarked vertices are also alternating. Folding each marked vertex to \(O\) reflects the three outer triangular flaps across these creases onto the central equilateral triangle, with the three marked vertices meeting at \(O\), so the outline of the folded paper is that equilateral triangle. Final answer: an equilateral triangle.

The diagram shows a rectangle with horizontal midline \(MN\) connecting the midpoints of the left and right sides, so \(MN\) lies at half the rectangle’s height. A zigzag line runs from the bottom-left corner to the bottom-right corner with vertices alternating on the top and bottom sides, producing five shaded triangles each having one side on \(MN\) and the opposite vertex on the top or bottom of the rectangle. Place the rectangle with width \(W\) and height \(H\), so its area is \(WH\), and let the zigzag vertices be \((0,0)\), \((a,H)\), \((b,0)\), \((c,H)\), \((W,0)\). The five shaded triangles therefore have areas \(aH/8\), \(bH/8\), \((c-a)H/8\), \((W-b)H/8\), and \((W-c)H/8\), and their sum is \(\frac{H}{8}[a+b+(c-a)+(W-b)+(W-c)] = \frac{H}{8}\cdot 2W = \frac{WH}{4}\). Thus the shaded area equals one quarter of the rectangle’s area. Final answer: 1/4

The triangle is divided by lines parallel to its base into 10 horizontal strips of equal height, since the two non-base sides are each separated into 10 equal parts; the top strip is a small grey triangle, and the strips alternate grey and white, with the bottom strip being white, so the grey strips are the 1st, 3rd, 5th, 7th, and 9th from the top. For a strip bounded by the lines at distances corresponding to \(k-1\) and \(k\) tenths of the way from the apex, its area fraction equals the difference of the areas of the similar triangles: \(\frac{k^2-(k-1)^2}{10^2}=\frac{2k-1}{100}\). Summing this for the grey strips \(k=1,3,5,7,9\) gives \(\frac{1+5+9+13+17}{100}=\frac{45}{100}\). Final answer: 45%.

The image shows square \(PQRS\) with side \(10\text{ cm}\), where \(P\) is the top-left vertex, \(Q\) the bottom-left, \(R\) the bottom-right, and \(S\) the top-right. Place \(Q=(0,0)\), \(P=(0,10)\), \(S=(10,10)\), and \(R=(10,0)\). Since \(\angle SPT=75^\circ\) and \(PS\) is horizontal, the ray \(PT\) makes a \(75^\circ\) angle below the horizontal, so \(T=(t\cos75^\circ,\,10-t\sin75^\circ)\) for some length \(PT=t\). Since \(\angle TSP=30^\circ\) and \(SP\) points left, the ray \(ST\) makes a \(30^\circ\) angle below the leftward horizontal, so \(T=(10-s\cos30^\circ,\,10-\tfrac{s}{2})\) for some length \(ST=s\). Equating \(y\)-coordinates gives \(s=2t\sin75^\circ\); substituting into the \(x\)-coordinate equation yields \(t(\cos75^\circ+\sqrt3\sin75^\circ)=10\), hence \(t=\frac{5}{\sin75^\circ}\). Therefore \(T=(5\cot75^\circ,\,5)=(10-5\sqrt3,\,5)\). Finally, \(TR=\sqrt{(10-(10-5\sqrt3))^2+(0-5)^2}=\sqrt{(5\sqrt3)^2+25}=\sqrt{100}=10\text{ cm}\). Final answer: \(10\text{ cm}\).

The image shows a long horizontal pole with an ant and a beetle on it, indicating that Adam and Benny are crawling along the same straight pole. Let the pole length be \(1\). The distance between them is the difference of their positions: \(\frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{4}=\frac{8}{12}-\frac{3}{12}=\frac{5}{12}\). Final answer: \(\frac{5}{12}\)

The diagram shows the square divided by one full vertical cut and two full horizontal cuts, forming six rectangles arranged in two columns and three rows. Each internal cut is counted twice when adding the perimeters of the individual rectangles, while the outer boundary is counted once. Setting this equal to \(120\ \text{cm}\) gives \(10s = 120\), so \(s = 12\ \text{cm}\). Therefore the area of the square is \(s^2 = 12^2 = 144\ \text{cm}^2\). Final answer: \(144\ \text{cm}^2\)

The image shows two rectangles: a 16:9 rectangle fully shaded and a 4:3 rectangle with a shaded horizontal band in the middle and white bands above and below, indicating the picture fills the width of the 4:3 screen but not its full height. The covered fraction is (9/16)W² ÷ (3/4)W² = (9/16) × (4/3) = 3/4, so the uncovered fraction is 1 − 3/4 = 1/4. Final answer: 1/4

The image shows three wheels, A, B, and C, connected by a single belt; wheel B appears as a double wheel, so both belt runs rotate with the same number of B rotations. Because the belt does not slip, the length of belt passing over a wheel equals the number of rotations multiplied by the wheel’s circumference. For wheels A and B, 5 rotations of A and 4 rotations of B mean 5C_A = 4C_B, so C_A = (4/5)C_B. For wheels B and C, 6 rotations of B and 7 rotations of C mean 6C_B = 7C_C; with C_C = 30 cm, this gives C_B = (7/6)(30 cm) = 35 cm. Substituting into the first relation, C_A = (4/5)(35 cm) = 28 cm. Final answer: 28 cm.

In square \(ABCE\), the vertices are arranged with \(A\) and \(B\) on the top side, \(C\) on the bottom right, and \(E\) on the bottom left, so \(D\) lies on side \(CE\) and \(F\) lies on side \(AE\). Let the side length of the square be \(s\). Since \(AF=2FE\) and \(AF+FE=s\), we get \(FE=\frac{s}{3}\), so \(F\) is \(\frac{s}{3}\) above \(E\). Similarly, \(CD=2DE\) and \(CD+DE=s\) give \(DE=\frac{s}{3}\), so \(D\) is \(\frac{s}{3}\) to the right of \(E\). Using coordinates \(E=(0,0)\), \(C=(s,0)\), \(B=(s,s)\), \(A=(0,s)\), we have \(F=(0,\frac{s}{3})\) and \(D=(\frac{s}{3},0)\). The area of \(\triangle BFD\) can be found by subtracting the areas of the three surrounding right triangles from the square: \(\text{Area}(ABF)=\frac12\cdot s\cdot \frac{2s}{3}=\frac{s^2}{3}\), \(\text{Area}(BCD)=\frac12\cdot \frac{2s}{3}\cdot s=\frac{s^2}{3}\), and \(\text{Area}(EFD)=\frac12\cdot \frac{s}{3}\cdot \frac{s}{3}=\frac{s^2}{18}\). Their total is \(\frac{s^2}{3}+\frac{s^2}{3}+\frac{s^2}{18}=\frac{13s^2}{18}\), leaving \(\text{Area}(\triangle BFD)=s^2-\frac{13s^2}{18}=\frac{5s^2}{18}\). Therefore the ratio of the area of \(\triangle BFD\) to the area of square \(ABCE\) is \(\frac{5}{18}\). Final answer: 5/18.

In the right triangle \(ABC\), \(\angle C=90^\circ\), \(AC=6\), and \(BC=8\), so \(AB=\sqrt{6^2+8^2}=10\). Points \(D\) on \(\overline{AB}\) and \(E\) on \(\overline{BC}\) satisfy \(\angle BED=90^\circ\), which means \(\overline{DE}\perp\overline{BC}\); since \(\overline{AC}\perp\overline{BC}\), we have \(\overline{DE}\parallel\overline{AC}\). Therefore \(\triangle BED\sim\triangle BCA\) by the shared angle at \(B\) and the right angles at \(E\) and \(C\). The similarity ratio is \(\dfrac{DE}{AC}=\dfrac{4}{6}=\dfrac{2}{3}\), so \(\dfrac{BD}{BA}=\dfrac{2}{3}\). Thus \(BD=\dfrac{2}{3}\cdot 10=\dfrac{20}{3}\). Final answer: \(\dfrac{20}{3}\).

The graph is a dot plot in which each X stands for the same number of employees, so the percent can be found from the ratio of X’s. Counting the X’s in each column for years 1 through 10 gives column counts of 5, 5, 8, 3, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1, and 1, for a total of 5+5+8+3+2+2+1+1+1+1=29 employees. The image shows two arrangements: in one, a bottle stands on the table and a can sits on the floor, with the distance from the top of the can to the top of the bottle being 150 cm; in the other, a can stands on the table and a bottle sits on the floor, with the distance from the top of the bottle to the top of the can being 110 cm. Adding these two equations eliminates \(b\) and \(c\): \(2h = 150 + 110 = 260\), so \(h = 130\). Final answer: 130 cm.

The image shows right triangle \(ABC\) with the right angle at \(B\), vertical leg \(AB=1\), horizontal leg \(BC=2\), and point \(D\) on \(\overline{BC}\) where the angle bisector of \(\angle BAC\) meets \(\overline{BC}\). By the Pythagorean theorem, \(AC=\sqrt{AB^2+BC^2}=\sqrt{1^2+2^2}=\sqrt{5}\). The Angle Bisector Theorem gives \(\frac{BD}{DC}=\frac{AB}{AC}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\), and since \(BD+DC=BC=2\), we have \(BD=\frac{2}{1+\sqrt{5}}\). Rationalizing yields \(BD=\frac{2(\sqrt{5}-1)}{(\sqrt{5}+1)(\sqrt{5}-1)}=\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}\). Final answer: \((\sqrt{5}-1)/2\).

In the figure, $\triangle ABC$ is isosceles with $AB=BC$, so altitude $BD$ is also a median and $D$ is the midpoint of $AC$; the points $A,D,C,E$ lie on a line with $C$ between $D$ and $E$. Let $\angle DBC=x$ and $\angle CBE=y$. The arithmetic progression $\cot(x+y),\cot y,\cot x$ gives $2\cot y=\cot(x+y)+\cot x$, which simplifies to $\cot^2x-2\cot^2y=1$. The geometric progression $\tan y,\tan(x+y),\tan(2x+y)$ makes $\cot y,\cot(x+y),\cot(2x+y)$ also geometric; using $\cot(2x+y)=\dfrac{\cot x\cot(x+y)-1}{\cot x+\cot(x+y)}$ and the arithmetic relation yields $\cot x\cot(x+y)=2\cot^2(x+y)+1$. Combining these with the cotangent addition formula forces $\cot^4(x+y)=1$; since $x+y$ is acute, $\cot(x+y)=1$, hence $\cot x=3$ and $\cot y=2$. Thus $\tan x=\tfrac13$ and $\tan(x+y)=1$. In right $\triangle BDE$, $\tan\angle DBE=\tan(x+y)=\dfrac{DE}{BD}=1$, so $DE=BD$; with $BE=10$, $BD^2+DE^2=2BD^2=100$, giving $BD=5\sqrt2$. Then $DC=BD\tan x=5\sqrt2/3$, and the area of $\triangle ABC$ is $\tfrac12(2DC)(BD)=DC\cdot BD=(5\sqrt2/3)(5\sqrt2)=50/3$. Final answer: 50/3.

The image shows a $3\text{ cm}\times 3\text{ cm}\times 3\text{ cm}$ cube made up of $1\text{ cm}\times 1\text{ cm}\times 1\text{ cm}$ unit cubes, so the large cube has $3$ unit cubes along each edge. The original surface area of the large cube is $6(3^2)=54\text{ cm}^2$. A cube has $8$ corners, and each corner unit cube has three faces on the exterior of the large cube; removing a corner cube removes those three exterior faces but exposes three new interior faces of equal area, so the net change in surface area from removing each corner cube is zero. Therefore, the surface area of the remaining figure is $54\text{ cm}^2$. Final answer: $54\text{ cm}^2$

The image shows an isosceles triangle containing two stacked, centered squares: a lower square of side length 3 with its base on the triangle's base, and an upper square of side length 2 resting on the lower square with its bottom two vertices on the lower square and its top two vertices on the sides of the triangle. Place the triangle with base on the x-axis and apex on the y-axis; let the base half-width be \(b\) and the height be \(h\). The lower square's top side is at height 3, so its top right corner \((1.5, 3)\) lies on the right side of the triangle, giving \(3 = h(1 - 1.5/b)\), or \(3b = h(b - 1.5)\). The upper square has side 2 and rests on the lower square, so its top side is at height 5; its top right corner \((1, 5)\) lies on the right side, giving \(5 = h(1 - 1/b)\), or \(5b = h(b - 1)\). Equating the two expressions for \(h\) yields \(\frac{3b}{b - 1.5} = \frac{5b}{b - 1}\), so \(3(b - 1) = 5(b - 1.5)\), which simplifies to \(2b = 4.5\), hence \(b = \frac{9}{4}\). Substituting gives \(h = \frac{5(9/4)}{9/4 - 1} = \frac{45/4}{5/4} = 9\). The base is \(2b = \frac{9}{2}\), so the area is \(\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{9}{2} \cdot 9 = \frac{81}{4}\). Final answer: \(\frac{81}{4}\)

The polygon is an L-shaped figure with a top horizontal side of length 8 and a left vertical side of length 6, and all interior angles are right angles. The cube in the diagram has six faces, each divided into four squares, so there are \(6\times4=24\) squares in total. At each of the eight corners of the cube, the three squares meeting there lie on the three faces that meet at that corner and share edges with one another pairwise, so those three squares must all be different shapes—one cross, one triangle, and one circle. Thus the 24 squares are split into eight disjoint triples, each containing exactly one of each shape, which means every valid coloring must have eight crosses, eight triangles, and eight circles. Since the listed combinations 6 crosses and 8 triangles, 7 crosses and 8 triangles, 5 crosses and 8 triangles, and 7 crosses and 7 triangles all have either the number of crosses or the number of triangles different from eight, none of them can occur. Final answer: none of the listed combinations are possible; the only possible counts are 8 crosses, 8 triangles, and 8 circles.

The table shows a 5×5 contingency table with Test 1 grades A, B, C, D, F as rows and Test 2 grades A, B, C, D, F as columns, where each cell gives the number of students with the corresponding pair of grades. The lattice points form a 4-by-7 array with unit spacing. The flag is a square containing a central red square, several congruent small white squares arranged around it, and congruent blue right isosceles triangles filling the gaps; each white square can be divided by a diagonal into two right triangles that are congruent to the blue triangles, and the blue triangles are twice as numerous as the white squares, so the total area of the blue triangles equals the total area of the white squares. The square is made of five equal-width nested L-shaped layers ending in a small central square, with black on the outermost, third, and center layers. In the large triangle the top angle is 40° and the left base angle is 70°, so the right base angle is 180° − 40° − 70° = 70°. The square \(ABCD\) has area \(16\), so each side has length \(4\). In the figure, equilateral triangles \(AKB\), \(BLC\), \(CMD\), and \(DNA\) are built outward on sides \(AB\), \(BC\), \(CD\), and \(DA\), respectively. Place \(A=(0,4)\), \(B=(4,4)\), \(C=(4,0)\), and \(D=(0,0)\); then the apexes are \(K=(2,4+2\sqrt3)\), \(L=(4+2\sqrt3,2)\), \(M=(2,-2\sqrt3)\), and \(N=(-2\sqrt3,2)\). These four points form a square whose diagonals \(KM\) and \(LN\) are vertical and horizontal, each of length \(4+4\sqrt3\). The area of a square with diagonal length \(d\) is \(\frac12d^2\), so the area of \(KLMN\) is \(\frac12(4+4\sqrt3)^2=\frac12\cdot16(1+\sqrt3)^2=8(4+2\sqrt3)=32+16\sqrt3\). Final answer: \(32+16\sqrt3\).

The image shows a shaded sector of a circle with radius 1 cm, where the missing (unshaded) mouth has central angle 60°, so the shaded monster has central angle 360° − 60° = 300°. The perimeter of the monster equals the length of its outer arc plus the two straight radii that form the sides of the mouth. Using the arc length formula (θ/360°) · 2πr with θ = 300° and r = 1, the arc length is (300/360) · 2π(1) = 5π/3 cm. Adding the two radii gives 5π/3 + 1 + 1 = 5π/3 + 2 cm. Final answer: 2 + 5π/3.

The clock face has radius \(R=20\) cm and the rolling disk has radius \(r=10\) cm, so the disk’s center travels around a circle of radius \(R+r=30\) cm. For a disk rolling externally without slipping, if its center sweeps an angle \(\phi\) around the clock center, the disk rotates through \(\frac{R+r}{r}\phi\) relative to a fixed direction. Setting this equal to \(2\pi\) for the arrow to first return to the upward vertical direction gives \(\frac{30}{10}\phi=2\pi\), so \(\phi=\frac{2\pi}{3}=120^\circ\). Since the disk rolls clockwise from the 12 o’clock position, a \(120^\circ\) clockwise movement corresponds to \(120^\circ/30^\circ=4\) hours on the clock face. Final answer: 4 o’clock.

The cube has side length 2, so the centers of two adjacent faces are separated by moving half the side length in two perpendicular directions, giving a distance of \(\sqrt{1^2+1^2}=\sqrt{2}\). Each hemispherical is part of a sphere centered at a face center, and two neighboring holes touch when the distance between their centers equals the sum of their radii. Since the holes are identical, \(2r=\sqrt{2}\), so the diameter is \(2r=\sqrt{2}\). The point of contact lies inside the cube, confirming the hemispherical halves meet. Final answer: \(\sqrt{2}\) units.

The image shows a machine that takes an input \(N\) and outputs \(\frac{N}{2}\) when \(N\) is even and \(3N+1\) when \(N\) is odd. To find all starting values that give a final output of \(1\) after six applications, work backwards: a value \(y\) can be reached from the even input \(2y\), and it can also be reached from the odd input \(\frac{y-1}{3}\) whenever that quotient is a positive odd integer, which occurs exactly when \(y\equiv 4\pmod 6\). Applying these inverse rules for six steps starting from \(1\) produces the preimage sets \(\{2\}\), \(\{4\}\), \(\{8,1\}\), \(\{16,2\}\), \(\{32,5,4\}\), and \(\{64,10,8,1\}\), so the possible starting integers are \(1,8,10,64\). Their sum is \(1+8+10+64=83\). Final answer: 83

The rectangular solid measures 1 ft by 3 ft by 9 ft, and a 1 ft cube is cut from its top in such a way that the cube had three faces on the original surface and three faces hidden inside the solid. The image shows a \(3\times3\times3\) cube with three \(1\times1\) square tunnels drilled through its center, one along each of the three orthogonal directions; each tunnel is a \(1\times1\times3\) rectangular parallelepiped, and all three tunnels meet in the central \(1\times1\times1\) cube. The original volume is \(3^3=27\). Each tunnel has volume \(1\cdot1\cdot3=3\), so the three tunnels have total volume \(3\cdot3=9\), but this overcounts the overlapping regions. Each pair of tunnels intersects in the central \(1\times1\times1\) cube, giving three pairwise intersections of volume \(1\) each, and all three tunnels also intersect in that same central cube, so by inclusion–exclusion the removed volume is \(9-3\cdot1+1=7\). The remaining volume is \(27-7=20\). Since weight is proportional to volume, the remaining weight is \(810\cdot\frac{20}{27}=600\) grams. Final answer: 600 grams.

The image shows a \(3\times3\) table with the four given entries: top middle \(2\), middle left \(1\), middle right \(3\), and bottom middle \(4\); the other five cells are empty. Label the empty cells as \(a,c,e,g,i\) with \(e\) in the center, so the four \(2\times2\) square-sum conditions give \(a+e=7\), \(c+e=5\), \(e+g=5\), and \(e+i=3\). Thus \(a=7-e\), \(c=5-e\), \(g=5-e\), \(i=3-e\), and the sum of the five remaining numbers is \(S=(7-e)+(5-e)+e+(5-e)+(3-e)=20-3e\). Since all entries must be whole numbers, \(e\) must satisfy \(0\le e\le 3\), so \(S\) can only be \(20,17,14,\) or \(11\). Final answer: none of \(9,10,12,\) or \(13\) is possible.

The square has perimeter 4, so each side has length 1. In the figure the square is inscribed in the equilateral triangle with its base on the triangle’s base and its upper two vertices on the triangle’s other two sides, so the small triangle above the square is similar to the whole triangle and therefore equilateral with side length 1. The height of an equilateral triangle with side 1 is √3/2, so the large triangle’s height is 1 + √3/2. Since the height of an equilateral triangle with side s is (s√3)/2, we have (s√3)/2 = 1 + √3/2, giving s = (2/√3)(1 + √3/2) = 1 + 2/√3. Thus the perimeter is 3s = 3 + 2√3. Final answer: 3 + 2√3.

The diagram shows two concentric circles, with the distance from the common center to the outer circle labeled \(6 \text{ cm}\) and the distance from the center to the inner circle labeled \(4 \text{ cm}\), so the annulus has outer radius \(R = 6 \text{ cm}\) and inner radius \(r = 4 \text{ cm}\). Since the pendants are made of the same material, have the same thickness, and weigh the same, their areas must be equal. The area of the annulus is \(\pi R^2 - \pi r^2 = \pi(6^2 - 4^2) = \pi(36 - 16) = 20\pi \text{ cm}^2\). Let the radius of the solid circular pendant be \(x\); then \(\pi x^2 = 20\pi\), so \(x^2 = 20\) and \(x = \sqrt{20} = 2\sqrt{5}\). Final answer: \(2\sqrt{5}\text{ cm}\) (approximately \(4.47\text{ cm}\)).

The image shows the rod \(OA\) of length \(r\) from the centre \(O\) to the joint \(A\), and the wiper blade \(AB\) of length \(w=r\) from \(A\) to the tip \(B\) of the outer arc; the marked angle \(\alpha\) is between the extension of \(OA\) beyond \(A\) and the blade \(AB\), so in \(\triangle OAB\) the interior angle \(\angle OAB = 180^\circ-\alpha\). Because \(OA=AB=r\), \(\triangle OAB\) is isosceles with base \(OB\), hence the base angles are equal and \(\angle OBA=\frac{180^\circ-(180^\circ-\alpha)}{2}=\frac{\alpha}{2}\). The outer arc is part of a circle centred at \(O\), so the tangent at \(B\) is perpendicular to the radius \(OB\); therefore the angle \(\beta\) between the blade \(AB\) and the tangent is \(90^\circ-\angle OBA=90^\circ-\frac{\alpha}{2}\). Final answer: \(\beta = 90^\circ-\frac{\alpha}{2}\).

The image shows quadrilateral \(ABCD\) with diagonal \(BD\), \(\angle BDC=80^{\circ}\), and \(\angle ACB=20^{\circ}\); it is given that \(BD\) bisects \(\angle ABC\) and \(AC=BC\). Let \(\angle ABD=\angle DBC=x\). Since \(AC=BC\), \(\triangle ABC\) is isosceles, so \(\angle CAB=\angle CBA=2x\); then \(\angle ACB=180^{\circ}-4x=20^{\circ}\), giving \(x=40^{\circ}\). Thus \(\angle ABC=80^{\circ}\) and \(\angle BAC=80^{\circ}\). In \(\triangle BCD\), \(\angle BCD=180^{\circ}-40^{\circ}-80^{\circ}=60^{\circ}\), so \(\angle ACD=\angle BCD-\angle ACB=60^{\circ}-20^{\circ}=40^{\circ}\). By the Law of Sines in \(\triangle BCD\), \(BC/\sin80^{\circ}=CD/\sin40^{\circ}\), hence \(AC=BC=CD\cdot\sin80^{\circ}/\sin40^{\circ}=2CD\cos40^{\circ}\). Let \(\angle CAD=\theta\); then \(\angle ADC=180^{\circ}-40^{\circ}-\theta=140^{\circ}-\theta\). Applying the Law of Sines in \(\triangle ACD\) gives \(AC/CD=\sin(140^{\circ}-\theta)/\sin\theta=2\cos40^{\circ}\). Since \(\sin(140^{\circ}-\theta)=\sin(40^{\circ}+\theta)\), this becomes \(\sin(40^{\circ}+\theta)/\sin\theta=2\cos40^{\circ}\), which simplifies to \(\sin40^{\circ}\cot\theta+\cos40^{\circ}=2\cos40^{\circ}\), so \(\cot\theta=\cot40^{\circ}\) and \(\theta=40^{\circ}\). Therefore \(\angle BAD=\angle BAC+\angle CAD=80^{\circ}+40^{\circ}=120^{\circ}\). Final answer: \(120^{\circ}\)

In the rectangle, P, Q, R, S are the bottom-left, bottom-right, top-right, and top-left vertices, respectively, with T the midpoint of the top side RS; the diagonal PR slopes upward to the right and QT meets it at a right angle. Place P at (0,0), Q at (a,0), R at (a,b), and S at (0,b), so T = (a/2,b); then vector PR = (a,b) and vector QT = (-a/2,b). Because QT is perpendicular to PR, their dot product is zero: a(-a/2) + b(b) = 0, giving b² = a²/2, so b = a/√2. Therefore PQ:QR = a:b = a:(a/√2) = √2:1. Final answer: √2:1.

The board uses columns A–D and rows 1–4, so each code letter is found at the intersection of the given column and row: column B, row 3 is M; column B, row 2 is A; column C, row 4 is T; column D, row 2 is H. Final answer: MATH.

The 3×3 magic square has the letter \(a\) in the top-left cell, the number \(47\) in the middle-right cell (row 2, column 3), and the number \(63\) in the bottom-middle cell (row 3, column 2). Let the magic sum be \(S\), let the center be \(e\), and let the bottom-right corner be \(i\). From the middle column, the top-middle entry is \(S-63-e\); from the right column, the top-right entry is \(S-47-i\). Using the top row gives \(a = 110 + e + i - S\), and using the main diagonal gives \(a = S - e - i\). Adding these two expressions for \(a\) eliminates \(S\), \(e\), and \(i\), yielding \(2a = 110\), so \(a = 55\). Final answer: 55.

The square has side length 1, the large circle is centered at the lower-left corner of the square with radius 1, and the small circle lies in the upper-right corner tangent to the top side, right side, and the large circle. Place the square with corners at (0,0) and (1,1), so the large circle has equation x^2 + y^2 = 1 and the small circle has center (1-r, 1-r) and radius r. Since the small circle is externally tangent to the large circle, the distance between centers equals 1 + r, giving sqrt((1-r)^2 + (1-r)^2) = 1 + r, or sqrt(2)(1-r) = 1 + r. Solving gives r = (sqrt(2)-1)/(sqrt(2)+1) = 3 - 2*sqrt(2). Final answer: 3 - 2*sqrt(2).

The image shows rectangle $S_1$ with width $x$ and height $5-y$, since its left side lies on the $y$-axis, its right side is at $x$-coordinate $x$, its bottom is at $y$-coordinate $y$, and its top is at $y$-coordinate $5$; rectangle $S_2$ has width $8-x$ and height $y$, since its left side is at $x$-coordinate $x$, its right side is at $x$-coordinate $8$, its bottom lies on the $x$-axis, and its top is at $y$-coordinate $y$. Final answer: $8:5$

Image1 and Image2 show the two possible over/under choices at a single crossing, and Image3 shows the three-crossing projection of the string with its two free ends. Each of the three coins independently chooses one of the two crossing types, giving \(2^3=8\) equally likely configurations. Therefore the number of knotted configurations is 2, and the probability is \(2/8=1/4\). Final answer: 1/4

The first box contains P, K, T, H, M; the second contains T, M; the third contains T, K, M, P; the fourth contains K, T; and the fifth contains only M. The diagram shows a stepped pyramid made of cubes with side length 10 cm: the base is a 3×3 square of cubes, the next layer is a 2×2 square, and the top is a single cube. The dividing lines are parallel to the sides of equilateral triangle \(ABC\) and trisect each side, so the whole triangle is split into \(3\times 3=9\) congruent small equilateral triangles. The figure consists of seven fields: the central field with the question mark, five fields that each share an edge or a corner with it, and the single bottom-most field that does not touch the central field. Because two consecutive numbers cannot be adjacent, a number placed in the central field must not have either of its consecutive numbers among its adjacent fields. Final answer: 1 and 7.

The map shows four triangular tours: the A–Zoo–Port tour is 10 km, the Zoo–B–Park tour is 12 km, the Port–C–Park tour is 13 km, and the Zoo–Park–Port tour is 15 km. Let the lengths of the inner roads Zoo–Port, Zoo–Park, and Park–Port be x, y, and z, so x+y+z=15. A tour from A to B to C and back to A must follow the outer boundary A–Zoo–B–Park–C–Port–A, so its length is (10−x)+(12−y)+(13−z)=35−(x+y+z)=35−15=20 km. Final answer: 20 km.

In the diagram, the nine points are equally spaced around the circle and image1 shows the first two steps: 1 joined to 3 and 3 joined to 5. Joining “the next but one” point each time means moving two positions around the circle, i.e. adding 2 modulo 9. Because gcd(2,9)=1, the path visits every point before returning to the start: 1→3→5→7→9→2→4→6→8→1. This is the regular star polygon {9/2}, with chords 1-3, 3-5, 5-7, 7-9, 9-2, 2-4, 4-6, 6-8, and 8-1. The figure shows a large square of side length \(9\) cm made of four identical rectangles surrounding a small central square, and the red square has side length equal to the diagonal of each rectangle. Let the rectangle have side lengths \(a\) and \(b\). Then \(a+b=9\) and the diagonal satisfies \(a^{2}+b^{2}=64\). Squaring the first equation gives \((a+b)^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}+2ab=81\), so \(64+2ab=81\) and \(2ab=17\). The side of the central square is \(a-b\), and \((a-b)^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}-2ab=64-17=47\). Final answer: \(47\) cm\(^2\).

The image shows a river starting at A and splitting first into two branches, where the lower branch carries 1/3 of the water and the upper branch carries the remaining 2/3; this upper branch then splits again, with the lower branch labeled 3/4 and the upper branch labeled B. The picture shows a parallelogram split into two regions, \(P_1\) and \(P_2\), by a single zigzag line that serves as a common boundary for both regions; the remaining part of each perimeter consists of two adjacent sides of the parallelogram. In any parallelogram, opposite sides are equal in length, so the sum of the two adjacent sides forming the outer boundary of \(P_1\) equals the sum of the two adjacent sides forming the outer boundary of \(P_2\). Adding the same common boundary length to each of these equal sums gives equal perimeters. Final answer: The perimeters of \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) are equal.

The wall forms a checkerboard of grey and striped tiles that is 8 tiles wide and 5 tiles high, with the top-left tile grey, so every tile where the row and column numbers have the same parity is grey. Counting the remaining grey tiles gives 4 in the top row, 3 in the second row, 2 in the third row, 1 in the fourth row, and 4 in the bottom row, for a total of 14 grey tiles still on the wall. Since each of the 5 rows contains 4 grey tiles, the original wall had 5 × 4 = 20 grey tiles, so the number of grey tiles that fell off is 20 − 14 = 6. Final answer: 6.

The grey region is a unit circle overlapped by three other unit circles, so its boundary is made of the remaining arcs of the grey circle together with the arcs of the three white circles that lie inside the grey circle. For any two intersecting equal circles, the arc of one circle inside the other has the same length as the corresponding arc of the other circle inside the first, because the circles have the same radius and the same central angle. Therefore the total length of the white arcs equals the total length of the grey-circle arcs they replace, so the perimeter of the grey area equals the full circumference of a unit circle, \(2\pi\cdot1=2\pi\). Final answer: \(2\pi\) units.

The image shows a large triangle divided by three cevians, each joining a vertex to the opposite side; these cevians intersect inside, creating one central triangle, three corner triangles, and three quadrilaterals. Let \(L\) be the total length of the three dissecting lines. The combined perimeters of all seven regions are \(20 + 25 = 45\ \text{cm}\). In this total, the three sides of the big triangle are each counted exactly once, contributing the big triangle’s perimeter \(19\ \text{cm}\), while every internal segment of the three cevians is shared by two adjacent regions and therefore counted twice, contributing \(2L\). Thus \(45 = 19 + 2L\), so \(2L = 26\) and \(L = 13\ \text{cm}\). Final answer: 13 cm.

The image shows the subtraction KAN − GAR = OO, where different letters represent different digits. Since the tens digit A appears in both the minuend and subtrahend, it cancels, giving the equation 100(K−G) + (N−R) = 11O. The result OO is a two-digit multiple of 11, so K−G must be 1; thus 100 + (N−R) = 11O. Because −9 ≤ N−R ≤ 9, the left side lies between 91 and 109, and the only multiple of 11 in that range is 99, so O = 9 and R = N+1. To maximize KAN, choose the largest possible K not equal to O=9; with K = G+1, this gives K = 8 and G = 7. The largest available tens digit A is then 6, and the largest units digit N for which R = N+1 is also unused is N = 4 (since N = 5 would make R = 6 = A). Therefore KAN = 864, and indeed 864 − 765 = 99. Final answer: 864.

The diagram shows the left pan holding three black pearls and one white pearl, while the right pan holds one black pearl and a 30 g iron weight, with the beam balanced. Let the mass of one black pearl be \(b\) and the mass of one white pearl be \(w\). Since the pans balance, \(3b + w = b + 30\), which simplifies to \(2b + w = 30\). The required total mass of 6 black pearls and 3 white pearls is \(6b + 3w = 3(2b + w) = 3 \times 30 = 90\) g. Final answer: 90 g.

The grid has six columns with the fold line between the third and fourth columns, so a square in column 3 folds onto column 4, column 2 onto column 5, and column 1 onto column 6. The pie chart shows five sectors with percentages 47%, 24%, 12%, 11%, and 6%, which sum to 100%. Since the central zone equals the sum of the north, west, and east zones, the central zone must be the largest single sector, so central = 47%. The total of all zones is 100%, so central + north + west + east + south = 100%; substituting central = north + west + east gives 2 × central + south = 100%, hence south = 100% − 2 × 47% = 6%. Since south is half of west, west = 2 × 6% = 12%. Then north + east = central − west = 47% − 12% = 35%, and the two remaining sectors are 24% and 11%, which sum to 35%. The percentage difference between north and east is therefore 24% − 11% = 13%. Final answer: 13%

Both clocks show 10:20. The first reading is right-side up at night, so Elisa left at 10:20 PM. The second reading is seen while she is hanging upside down; a digital display rotated 180° reverses the order of its symmetric digits, so the upside-down image 10:20 corresponds to the actual time 02:01. Because she returned in the morning, that is 2:01 AM. The elapsed time from 10:20 PM to 2:01 AM is 3 hours and 41 minutes. Final answer: 3 hours 41 minutes.

In square \(ABCD\), with \(P\), \(Q\), \(R\) the midpoints of \(DA\), \(BC\), \(CD\) respectively, the shaded region is the part of \(\triangle RAB\) that lies above the two crossing segments \(QA\) and \(PB\); equivalently, it is \(\triangle RAB\) minus the unshaded bottom triangle formed by \(A\), \(B\), and the intersection \(I\) of \(QA\) and \(PB\). Take the square to have side length \(2\), so \(A(0,0)\), \(B(2,0)\), \(R(1,2)\), \(Q(2,1)\), \(P(0,1)\); then line \(QA\) is \(y=\frac{x}{2}\) and line \(PB\) is \(y=1-\frac{x}{2}\), which intersect at \(I(1,\frac12)\). The area of \(\triangle RAB\) is \(\frac12\cdot 2\cdot 2=2\), and the area of \(\triangle AIB\) is \(\frac12\cdot 2\cdot \frac12=\frac12\), so the shaded area is \(2-\frac12=\frac32\). Since the square has area \(4\), the required fraction is \(\frac{3/2}{4}=\frac38\). Final answer: \(\frac38\).

The diagram shows a rectangular garden divided into a grid of equal square lots, specifically 2 lots high and 7 lots wide, with starting point S at the bottom-left corner and labeled points A, B, C, D placed left-to-right along the top edge (and E along the bottom). The two snails start together at S and travel around the perimeter in opposite directions at 1 m/h and 2 m/h, so their closing speed is 3 m/h and they first meet when the total distance they have covered equals the perimeter. Taking each square lot to be 1 m by 1 m, the garden is 7 m wide and 2 m high, giving a perimeter of 2(7 + 2) = 18 m; thus the meeting time is 18/3 = 6 hours. The slower snail travels 1 × 6 = 6 m: 2 m up the left side and then 4 m along the top edge, which places it at point A. The faster snail travels 2 × 6 = 12 m: 7 m along the bottom, 2 m up the right side, and 3 m back along the top, also arriving at the point 4 m from the top-left corner. Final answer: A

The image shows a cube with side length $12 \mathrm{~cm}$, where point $M$ is at the top of the left-front vertical edge and point $N$ is at the bottom of the shaded right face; the ant's route follows five consecutive edges of the cube, with each segment equal to one full edge length. Since all edges of a cube have equal length, the total path length is $5 \times 12 \mathrm{~cm} = 60 \mathrm{~cm}$. Final answer: $60 \mathrm{~cm}$

The figure shows an upward-opening parabola with y-intercept above the origin, and a line with positive slope that passes through the parabola's y-intercept. Since the parabola is $y = ax^2 + bx + c$, its y-intercept is $(0, c)$, so the line has y-intercept $c$. A line using the same coefficients with y-intercept $c$ has the form $y = mx + c$ where $m$ is $a$ or $b$. The line $y = bx + c$ intersects the parabola where $ax^2 + bx + c = bx + c$, giving $ax^2 = 0$, which has a double root at $x = 0$ and is therefore tangent at the y-intercept; this contradicts the figure, which shows a secant line crossing the parabola at two distinct points. The line $y = ax + c$ intersects the parabola where $ax^2 + bx + c = ax + c$, giving $x(ax + b - a) = 0$, which has the two distinct solutions $x = 0$ and $x = (a-b)/a$ because $a \neq b$; this matches the secant line in the figure. Final answer: $y = ax + c$.

The image shows the upper-left corner of a 10 by 10 grid, with the top-left little square coloured red and subsequent diagonals coloured in the repeating order red, white, blue, green, purple; squares with the same value of i + j share the same colour, where i is the row number and j is the column number counted from the upper-left corner. Using the pattern, the colour index is (i + j − 2) mod 5, with 0 = red, 1 = white, 2 = blue, 3 = green, 4 = purple. For the lower-right corner, i = 10 and j = 10, so (10 + 10 − 2) mod 5 = 18 mod 5 = 3, which corresponds to green. Final answer: green.

The diagram shows a regular nonagon with two of its sides extended until they meet at the external point X, forming a triangle with the single side of the nonagon that lies between the two extended sides. For any regular n-gon, the exterior angle is 360°/n, so for a nonagon (n = 9) each exterior angle is 360°/9 = 40°. Each base angle of the small triangle at X equals this exterior angle, 40°, because each is formed by a side of the nonagon and the extension of the adjacent side. Therefore angle X = 180° − 40° − 40° = 100°. Final answer: 100°.

The figure is a 10 cm by 6 cm stepped stack of congruent rectangles arranged in rows of 5, 4, 3, 2, and 1 rectangles from bottom to top. Since the bottom row of five rectangles spans the full 10 cm width, each rectangle is 10 ÷ 5 = 2 cm wide, and with five rows over the 6 cm height, each rectangle is 6 ÷ 5 = 1.2 cm high. The total area of all rectangles is therefore (5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1) × (2 × 1.2) = 15 × 2.4 = 36 cm². The large white triangle has base 10 cm and height 6 cm, giving an area of ½ × 10 × 6 = 30 cm², and because the triangle lies entirely within the rectangle stack, the grey area equals the total rectangle area minus the triangle area: 36 − 30 = 6 cm². Final answer: 6 cm²

The square garden is 5 m by 5 m, so its perimeter is \(5+5+5+5=20\) m, and the rectangular garden is 10 m by 5 m, so its perimeter is \(10+5+10+5=30\) m. Since Ahmed and Sara start together at point A and walk at the same speed, they will both be back at A at the same time after a distance equal to the least common multiple of their perimeters, which is \(\operatorname{lcm}(20,30)=60\) m. The number of complete rounds Ahmed walks is therefore \(60 \div 20 = 3\). Final answer: 3.

The image shows a square with one equilateral triangle attached to each of its four sides, where each triangle shares one side with the square. Since the perimeter of the square is 36 cm, each side of the square is 36 cm ÷ 4 = 9 cm. Because all sides of each triangle are equally long, each triangle side also equals 9 cm, so the part of each triangle that contributes to the star’s outer perimeter is its two non-shared sides, totaling 2 × 9 cm = 18 cm per triangle. With four triangles, the total outer perimeter is 4 × 18 cm = 72 cm. Final answer: 72 cm.

The diagram shows three squares placed edge to edge, with PQRS and TUVR sharing point R, and T lying on side QR; since the area of PQRS is 36, its side length is 6, and since the area of TUVR is 16, its side length is 4. Place S at (0,0), so P=(0,6), R=(6,0), T=(6,4), U=(10,4), and V=(10,0). Let the side length of square UWXY be s; from the diagram U is its top-left vertex and X its bottom-right vertex, so X=(10+s,4-s). Because P, T, and X are collinear, the line through P and T has slope (4-6)/(6-0) = -1/3 and equation y = 6 - x/3; substituting X gives 4 - s = 6 - (10+s)/3, which simplifies to s = 2, so X=(12,2). The area of triangle PXV is then 1/2 |(x_X-x_P)(y_V-y_P) - (x_V-x_P)(y_X-y_P)| = 1/2 |12(-6) - 10(-4)| = 1/2 * 32 = 16. Final answer: 16.

The table contains rows 9,1,5; 3,7,6; 4,7,4 and columns 9,3,4; 1,7,7; 5,6,4. The diagram shows four identical circles of radius \(5 \mathrm{~cm}\) arranged in a \(2 \times 2\) array inside a square, with each circle touching two sides of the square and its neighboring circles, and an equilateral triangle is drawn outward on each side of the square to form the star. Each equilateral triangle therefore has side length \(20 \mathrm{~cm}\), and the perimeter of the star consists of the two exposed sides of each of the four triangles, giving \(4 \times 2 \times 20 = 160 \mathrm{~cm}\). Final answer: \(160 \mathrm{~cm}\).

The diagram shows two arrangements of four adjacent vertical ribbons, each 10 cm wide, so each shape has a total width of 40 cm. In the first shape the ribbons are arranged in increasing order of length; in the second they are arranged as third-longest, second-shortest, longest, shortest. Let the ribbon lengths be \(a\), \(a+25\), \(a+50\), and \(a+75\). For a row of adjacent rectangles, the perimeter equals twice the total width plus the two end heights plus the sum of the absolute differences of adjacent heights. For the first shape this is \(80 + a + (a+75) + 25 + 25 + 25 = 2a + 230\). For the second shape this is \(80 + (a+50) + a + 25 + 50 + 75 = 2a + 280\). The difference is \(50\) cm. Final answer: 50 cm.

The diagram shows a triangle with three identical circles centered at its three vertices, and the shaded region is the portion of the triangle remaining after removing the three circular sectors that lie inside the triangle. Because the interior angles of any triangle sum to 180°, the three sectors, each with radius 2 cm, together form exactly one half of a full circle of radius 2 cm. The area of this combined semicircle is (1/2)π(2)² = 2π cm². Subtracting this from the triangle's area of 80 cm² gives the shaded area. Final answer: 80 - 2π

The graph plots distance covered (Strecke) vertically against time taken (Zeit) horizontally, so each student’s average speed is the ratio distance/time, which is the slope of the line from the origin to that student’s point. The diagram shows four nested heart shapes with alternating shaded and unshaded regions, where the outermost ring and the third ring from the outside are shaded while the second ring and the center are unshaded. Since the hearts are arranged largest to smallest from outside to inside, their areas in order are \(16 \mathrm{~cm}^{2}\), \(9 \mathrm{~cm}^{2}\), \(4 \mathrm{~cm}^{2}\), and \(1 \mathrm{~cm}^{2}\). The total shaded area is the sum of the outer shaded ring and the inner shaded ring, calculated as \((16-9)+(4-1)=7+3=10 \mathrm{~cm}^{2}\). Final answer: \(10 \mathrm{~cm}^{2}\)

The diagram shows a regular octagon whose eight vertices are joined by the eight sides and the eight long diagonals (the star), so each vertex is adjacent to the four vertices one or three steps away; the top vertex is labeled 1, the right-middle vertex is labeled 2, and the bottom vertex is labeled 3. Each of the four remaining vertices—upper-right, lower-right, lower-left, and upper-left—is adjacent to the labeled vertices 1, 2, and 3, so none of these four can be 1, 2, or 3 and therefore each must be 4. The only unlabeled vertex, left-middle, is adjacent only to those four 4’s, so it can be 1, 2, or 3 and is never a 4. Hence the integer 4 appears exactly four times. Final answer: 4

The diagram shows a central region, a middle ring divided into three regions, and an outer ring divided into three regions, with the divisions staggered so each middle-ring region borders two outer-ring regions; the given numbers are 2 in one middle-ring region and -4 in one outer-ring region. Let the common value of the three middle-ring regions be \(a\) and the common value of the three outer-ring regions be \(b\); the rotational symmetry of the adjacency forces these triples to be constant. The central region borders only the three middle-ring regions, so its value is \(C=3a\). A middle-ring region borders the centre, the two other middle-ring regions, and two outer-ring regions, giving \(a=C+2a+2b\). An outer-ring region borders the two other outer-ring regions and two middle-ring regions, giving \(b=2b+2a\). The outer equation simplifies to \(b=-2a\), which the given numbers satisfy because \(-4=-2\cdot 2\). Hence \(a=2\) and \(C=3a=6\). Final answer: 6

The image shows a rectangle with one side 12 cm and a diagonal of 20 cm, so the other side is \(\sqrt{20^2-12^2}=16\) cm by the Pythagorean theorem; the gray region is the triangular overlap formed when the rectangle is folded along this diagonal. Place the diagonal from \((0,0)\) to \((16,12)\); folding reflects the corner \((0,12)\) across the diagonal to \(\left(\frac{288}{25},-\frac{84}{25}\right)\). The line from this reflected point to the opposite corner \((16,12)\) meets the bottom side \(y=0\) at \(x=\frac{25}{2}\), giving the overlap triangle a base of \(\frac{25}{2}\) cm and height 12 cm. Therefore the overlapping area is \(\frac12\cdot \frac{25}{2}\cdot 12 = 75\) cm\(^2\). Final answer: 75 cm\(^2\).

The reflex angle at \(P\) is \(330^{\circ}\), so the smaller angle \(\angle QPS\) is \(360^{\circ}-330^{\circ}=30^{\circ}\). Since \(Q\), \(R\), \(T\) are collinear, \(\angle PQT=\angle PQR=20^{\circ}\). In \(\triangle PQT\), \(\angle QPT=30^{\circ}\) and \(\angle PQT=20^{\circ}\), so \(\angle PTQ=180^{\circ}-30^{\circ}-20^{\circ}=130^{\circ}\). Because \(S\), \(T\), \(P\) are collinear, the angle between \(QT\) and the line \(SP\) is \(180^{\circ}-130^{\circ}=50^{\circ}\). Since \(SU \perp QT\), the angle between \(SU\) and \(SP\) is \(90^{\circ}-50^{\circ}=40^{\circ}\), and this is \(\angle RSP\). Final answer: \(40^{\circ}\)

In the figure, equilateral triangle \(AZC\) has \(\angle AZC=\angle CAZ=60^\circ\), and because triangle \(RZT\) is obtained by rotating \(AZC\) about \(Z\), the rotation preserves distances so \(AZ=ZR\). Since \(\beta=\angle CZR=70^\circ\), the angle between \(ZA\) and \(ZR\) is \(\angle AZR=\angle AZC+\angle CZR=60^\circ+70^\circ=130^\circ\). Triangle \(AZR\) is therefore isosceles with \(AZ=ZR\), so its base angles are equal: \(\angle ZAR=(180^\circ-130^\circ)/2=25^\circ\). Thus \(\alpha=\angle CAR=\angle CAZ-\angle ZAR=60^\circ-25^\circ=35^\circ\). Final answer: \(35^\circ\).

The image shows a square with side length 8 cm, with a 1 cm segment marked on the top side and a 1 cm segment marked on the bottom side; the ends of these segments are joined by two line segments that intersect at the center of the square, forming two shaded triangles. Because the segments are on opposite sides and the configuration is symmetric, the two joining lines cross at the square's center, so each shaded triangle has a base of 1 cm and a height equal to half the side of the square, which is 8 ÷ 2 = 4 cm. The area of one triangle is (1/2) × base × height = (1/2) × 1 × 4 = 2 cm², and since there are two congruent shaded triangles, the total shaded area is 2 × 2 = 4 cm². Final answer: 4 cm²

The diagram shows a 7 cm square with a 3 cm square inside it and a 5 cm grey square that overlaps the other two; the exact overlap is not specified, but the side lengths determine the areas. The total grey area is the area of the 5 cm square, \(5^2 = 25\) cm². Therefore the difference is \(40 - 25 = 15\) cm². Final answer: 15 cm².

The large square is divided into four equal quadrants; the bottom-right quadrant is completely shaded, the top-right quadrant is split by a diagonal into two equal right triangles with one shaded, and the top-left quadrant is divided into four equal small squares with two of those small squares shaded, while the bottom-left quadrant is unshaded. Taking the area of the large square as 1, the bottom-right shaded region has area 1/4, the shaded triangle in the top-right quadrant has area half of 1/4, which is 1/8, and the two shaded small squares in the top-left quadrant each have area 1/16, giving 2/16 = 1/8. Adding these gives 1/4 + 1/8 + 1/8 = 1/2. Final answer: 1/2.

The reflex angle at the top is labeled 330°, so the interior apex angle of the large triangle is 360° − 330° = 30°; therefore the two base angles of the large triangle sum to 180° − 30° = 150°. The two crossing lines meet at the marked right angle, so in the triangle formed by the two base vertices and that crossing point the two acute angles sum to 90°. Those acute angles are the parts of the base angles left after removing the given 20° angle and the unknown angle, so (sum of base angles) − 20° − ? = 90°, giving 150° − 20° − ? = 90° and hence ? = 40°. The image shows two adjacent squares with side lengths 4 cm and 5 cm, a triangle at the bottom, and a grey parallelogram at the top, where the two sides of the triangle meeting the squares have lengths 4 cm and 5 cm, and the parallelogram has adjacent sides of lengths 4 cm and 5 cm with an angle supplementary to the triangle's included angle (so both angles have the same sine). The area of a triangle with two sides a and b and included angle θ is (1/2)ab sin θ, while the area of a parallelogram with adjacent sides a and b and included angle θ is ab sin θ, which is exactly twice the area of the corresponding triangle. Since the given triangle has area 8 cm², the parallelogram's area is 2 × 8 = 16 cm². Final answer: 16 cm²

The diagram shows five equal circles, with the four outer circles centered at the corners of a square and the central circle shaded entirely; in each outer circle, the part inside the square is a 90° sector, so the shaded portion of each outer circle is one-quarter of its area. Let each circle have radius r, so the area of one circle is πr². The total shaded area is the central circle plus four quarter-circles: πr² + 4(¼πr²) = 2πr². The total area of all five circles is 5πr², leaving an unshaded area of 5πr² − 2πr² = 3πr². Therefore the ratio of shaded area to unshaded area is 2πr² : 3πr² = 2 : 3. Final answer: 2:3.

The five rectangles have side numbers, reading top-right-bottom-left, as A: 5,4,8,7; B: 8,5,0,3; C: 0,7,2,9; D: 2,3,6,1; and E: 1,9,6,4. In the second image the positions are arranged with I, II, III across the top and IV under I, V under II, so the touching pairs are I(right)-II(left), II(right)-III(left), II(bottom)-V(top), I(bottom)-IV(top), and IV(right)-V(left). Since position II has three neighbors, its left, right, and bottom sides must each match a different remaining rectangle; only A satisfies this: A’s left 7 matches C’s right 7, A’s right 4 matches E’s left 4, and A’s bottom 8 matches B’s top 8. The diagram shows a single input pipe at the top that forks once into a left branch leading to container X and a right branch leading to container Y; along each branch the pipe spreads into two outlets, but both outlets on the right side empty into container Y, so all water that enters the right branch reaches Y. Since the first fork splits the water equally, the right branch receives half of the total: 296 ÷ 2 = 148 litres. Final answer: 148.

The figure shows a regular heptagon divided into seven equal sectors, with the heart and arrow starting in two different sectors; counting clockwise, the arrow is three sectors ahead of the heart. In each routine the arrow moves three places clockwise, while the heart moves four places anticlockwise. Since moving four places anticlockwise on a seven-sector wheel is equivalent to moving three places clockwise, both objects move three sectors clockwise every routine. Therefore the clockwise separation between them stays fixed at its initial value of three sectors, so their positions can never coincide. Final answer: No, the heart and the arrow will never land in the same place.

The large rectangle is made of four identical small rectangles: a vertical small rectangle on each end and two small rectangles stacked in the middle. Let the longer side of each small rectangle be \(x\) cm and the shorter side be \(10\) cm. The height of the large rectangle equals the longer side \(x\) of an end small rectangle, and the two middle stacked rectangles together make up that same height, so each middle rectangle has a vertical side of \(\frac{x}{2}\). Since that vertical side is the shorter side of a small rectangle, \(\frac{x}{2}=10\), giving \(x=20\) cm. The horizontal length of the large rectangle is the sum of the left shorter side, the middle longer side, and the right shorter side: \(10+20+10=40\) cm. This is greater than the height of \(20\) cm, so the longer side of the large rectangle is \(40\) cm. Final answer: 40 cm.

The image shows a large equilateral triangle with a circle inscribed in it, and inside that same circle both a regular hexagon and a smaller equilateral triangle are inscribed, all sharing the same center. Let the common circle have radius \(R\). For the large equilateral triangle, which has the circle as its incircle, the side length is \(2\sqrt{3}R\), so its area is \(L=\frac{\sqrt3}{4}(2\sqrt3R)^2=3\sqrt3\,R^2\). For the smaller equilateral triangle inscribed in the circle, the side length is \(\sqrt3R\), so \(S=\frac{\sqrt3}{4}(\sqrt3R)^2=\frac{3\sqrt3}{4}R^2\). A regular hexagon inscribed in a circle of radius \(R\) has area \(H=6\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{4}R^2=\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}R^2\). Thus \(L=2H\) and \(H=2S\), which gives \(H^2=LS\). Final answer: \(H^2=LS\) (equivalently, \(H\) is the geometric mean of \(L\) and \(S\)).

The diagram lists five rounds with one broadcast match each: Round 1 A–B, Round 2 C–D, Round 3 A–E, Round 4 E–F, Round 5 A–C. The image shows the cryptarithm A + AB + ABA = BEBA, where different letters stand for different digits, equal letters stand for equal digits, and B is nonzero. Because A is a single digit and B ≠ 0, B must be 1 and A must be 9, making the sum BEBA = 1019. The sum of the digits of 1019 is 1 + 0 + 1 + 9 = 11. Final answer: 11.

The picture shows two smaller semicircles, each of diameter 4 (radius 2), sitting on a straight line and tangent to each other at point T, while a larger semicircle of diameter 8 (radius 4) rests above them with its straight edge on top and center S at the midpoint of that edge; by symmetry S is directly above T. The image shows three concentric circular regions: a central black circle, a surrounding white ring, and an outermost black ring. Let the radius of the inner black circle be \(r\). The two circles intersect at X and Y, XY is a diameter of the small circle, and S, the centre of the large circle of radius r, lies on the small circle. The image shows a 3 by 3 multiplication magic square with 20 in the top-left cell, 1 in the top-middle cell, and the question mark in the middle-right cell. The product of 1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 20, 25, 50, and 100 is 1,000,000,000 = 10^9, so the center entry is (10^9)^(1/9) = 10 and the magic product is 10^3 = 1000. With center 10 and top-right 50, the main diagonal 20 · 10 · (bottom right) = 1000 gives bottom right = 5, and the anti-diagonal 50 · 10 · (bottom left) = 1000 gives bottom left = 2. Then the first column 20 · (middle left) · 2 = 1000 gives middle left = 25, and the middle row 25 · 10 · (question mark) = 1000 gives the question mark = 4. Final answer: 4.

The diagram shows an equilateral triangle with six perpendiculars drawn from each side’s midpoint to the other two sides; these six lines bound the grey hexagon, and by the triangle’s 120° rotational symmetry they form three pairs of parallel lines equally spaced at 60°, so the hexagon is regular with the three side midpoints as three of its vertices. The dartboard consists of an inner circle of radius 3 and an outer annulus from radius 3 to radius 6, divided into three congruent 120° sectors. For the sum of two independent darts to be odd, one must be odd and the other even, so the probability is \(2 \cdot \frac{7}{12} \cdot \frac{5}{12} = \frac{70}{144} = \frac{35}{72}\). Final answer: 35/72.

The field is a right triangle with legs 3 and 4, so its area is \(\frac12\cdot3\cdot4=6\). The figure shows a regular hexagon with side length 2, with six semicircles of radius 1 drawn inward so that each side is a diameter; the shaded region is the part of the hexagon lying outside all six semicircles. There are six such overlaps and no other overlaps, so the total area covered by the semicircles is 3π − 6(π/3 − √3/2) = π + 3√3. Therefore the shaded area is 6√3 − (π + 3√3) = 3√3 − π. In square \(ABCD\), place \(A\) at the origin, let the side length be \(s\), and give coordinates \(B(0,s)\), \(C(s,s)\), \(D(s,0)\); then midpoint \(M\) of \(BC\) is \((\tfrac{s}{2},s)\) and midpoint \(N\) of \(CD\) is \((s,\tfrac{s}{2})\). In the square, place \(A=(0,1)\), \(B=(1,1)\), \(C=(1,0)\), \(D=(0,0)\), so the center is \(O=(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)\), \(E=(1,\tfrac12)\), \(F=(1-x,1)\), and \(G=(1-x,0)\). The figure shows an equilateral hexagon \(ABCDEF\) with vertices in order, where the three nonadjacent acute interior angles at \(B\), \(D\), and \(F\) each measure \(30^\circ\); therefore the remaining three interior angles each measure \(210^\circ\). Each of the three corner triangles \(ABF\), \(BCD\), and \(DEF\) has area \(\frac12 s^2\sin150^\circ=\frac{s^2}{4}\), and the hexagon is \(\triangle BDF\) minus these three corner triangles. Thus the hexagon’s area is \(\frac{\sqrt3}{4}s^2(2+\sqrt3)-3\cdot\frac{s^2}{4}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}s^2\). Setting this equal to \(6\sqrt3\) gives \(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}s^2=6\sqrt3\), so \(s^2=12\) and \(s=2\sqrt3\). The perimeter is \(6s=6(2\sqrt3)=12\sqrt3\). Final answer: 12√3

The trapezoid has parallel bases 3 and 9 and non-parallel sides 6 and 4, and a line parallel to the bases cuts both legs. Let the line divide the side of length 6 into segments of lengths \(a\) and \(6-a\) and the side of length 4 into segments of lengths \(b\) and \(4-b\), and let the new parallel segment have length \(x\). The perimeters of the two smaller trapezoids are equal, so \(3 + x + a + b = x + 9 + (6-a) + (4-b)\), which simplifies to \(a+b=8\). Spinner A has four equal sectors numbered 1, 2, 3, and 4, so each number has probability 1/4; spinner B has three equal sectors numbered 1, 2, and 3, so each number has probability 1/3. In the figure, \(ABCDE\) is a regular pentagon with all its diagonals drawn; their intersections form the smaller regular pentagon \(FGHIJ\), where \(F\) and \(G\) lie on diagonal \(EB\), \(G\) and \(H\) lie on diagonal \(AC\), and \(JH\) is a diagonal of the inner pentagon. The image shows a regular hexagon of side length 6 with six congruent circular sectors of radius 3 centered at its vertices; the shaded region is the part of the hexagon not covered by these sectors. Final answer: \(54\sqrt{3}-18\pi\)

The diagram shows three adjacent squares of side lengths 3 cm, 5 cm, and 8 cm sharing a common base, with a diagonal drawn from the bottom-left corner of the 3 cm square to the top-right corner of the 8 cm square; the shaded trapezium lies inside the middle 5 cm square, bounded below by the base and above by the diagonal. The outer square has side length sqrt(3) and the inscribed inner square has side length sqrt(2). The figure shows the skeleton of an octagonal prism: two concentric regular octagons with corresponding vertices joined, giving 16 vertices and 24 edges. The inner vertices are opposite to their corresponding outer vertices, so P and S are in the same partite set as Start, while Q is in the opposite partite set. Final answer: Q.

The image shows a cube with a pyramid inside it whose base is one face of the cube and whose apex is at the center of the cube. The volume of a pyramid is \(\frac{1}{3}\times\text{base area}\times\text{height} = \frac{1}{3}\times 4\times 1 = \frac{4}{3}\). Final answer: \(\frac{4}{3}\).

In the figure, square \(ABCD\) has \(A\) at the lower left, \(B\) at the lower right, \(C\) at the upper right, and \(D\) at the upper left; diagonal \(BD\) runs from \(D\) to \(B\), and equilateral triangle \(ABE\) lies inside the square with \(E\) above \(AB\), so \(F\) is the intersection of \(BD\) and \(AE\). The image shows a penny-farthing bicycle with a large front wheel and a small rear wheel. For a valve on a wheel to return to its lowest point, the bicycle must roll forward a distance equal to an integer multiple of that wheel’s perimeter. The large wheel has perimeter 4.2 m and the small wheel 0.9 m, so the required distance is the least common multiple of 4.2 and 0.9. Writing the perimeters as fractions, 4.2 = 21/5 and 0.9 = 9/10, the LCM of two fractions in lowest terms is LCM(21, 9)/GCD(5, 10) = 63/5 = 12.6. Thus both valves are next at their lowest points after the bicycle has rolled 12.6 metres. Final answer: 12.6 metres.

Assuming the two cubes that show "no" on top are displaying the same face, the four side faces around that top "no" face are revealed by the first and third positions: the first shows two "YES" faces and the third shows one "YES" and one "no", so there are three "YES" faces and one "no" face surrounding the top "no". The figure shows a right triangle with the right angle at the bottom left, vertical and horizontal legs, and a hypotenuse sloping down to the right; the shaded equilateral triangle has one vertex on each of the three sides. Thus the minimal equilateral area is (sqrt(3)/4)(300/67) = 75sqrt(3)/67, so m=75, n=67, p=3, and m+n+p=145. Final answer: 145.

In the figure, square \(ABCD\) has side length \(2\), with semicircle on diameter \(AB\) inside the square; the tangent from \(C\) to the semicircle meets side \(AD\) at \(E\). The figure shows a circle with center \(O\) representing the cylindrical cross-section, with the oil surface as a horizontal chord \(AB\) near the bottom of the circle. The figure shows right triangle \(ABC\) with the right angle at \(C\), so angles \(A\) and \(B\) are complementary and \(A+B=90^\circ\). In the figure, points \(A\), \(B\), and \(E\) lie on the same horizontal line with \(E\) to the right of \(B\), and \(BE=15\,\text{cm}\). The image shows a downward-opening parabola passing through $A(0,2)$ on the $y$-axis and $C(4,0)$ on the $x$-axis, with a second $x$-intercept $B$ to the left of the origin, so the leading coefficient must be negative; taking the parabola as $y=-\frac14x^2+bx+c$, substituting $A(0,2)$ gives $c=2$, and substituting $C(4,0)$ gives $0=-\frac14(16)+4b+2=-4+4b+2$, so $b=\frac12$ and $y=-\frac14x^2+\frac12x+2$. For a point $M(x,y)$ on the parabola, the area of $\triangle ACM$ is given by the shoelace formula as $\frac12|4y_M-8+2x|=\frac12|4(-\frac14x^2+\frac12x+2)-8+2x|=\frac12|-x^2+4x|=-\frac12x^2+2x$ for $0<x<4$, which is a downward-opening quadratic attaining its maximum at $x=2$; at $x=2$, $y=-\frac14(4)+\frac12(2)+2=2$ and the maximum area is $-\frac12(4)+4=2$. Final answer: maximum area is $2$, point $M(2,2)$.

The figure shows a semicircular protractor with center \(O\) and diameter \(AB\), whose \(0^\circ\) baseline lies along \(AB\); point \(E\) is on the left side of the semicircular, so the \(50^\circ\) reading means arc \(AE=50^\circ\). From the figure, the decreasing line \(y=-x+a\) meets the \(x\)-axis at \(-1\), and the increasing line \(y=x+b\) meets the \(x\)-axis at \(-3\); the two lines intersect where \(x=-2\). Using the \(x\)-intercepts gives \(0=-(-1)+a\), so \(a=-1\), and \(0=-3+b\), so \(b=3\). The inequality becomes \(-x-1>x+3>0\). The right part \(x+3>0\) gives \(x>-3\), and the left part \(-x-1>x+3\) simplifies to \(-2x>4\), so \(x<-2\). Combining these yields \(-3<x<-2\). Final answer: \(-3<x<-2\).

In the rhombus, diagonals bisect each other, so \(O\) is the midpoint of \(BD\); since \(DH\perp AB\), \(\angle DHB=90^\circ\) and \(\triangle DHB\) is right-angled at \(H\) with hypotenuse \(BD\), making \(OH\) the median to the hypotenuse, so \(OH=OB\) and \(\angle OHB=\angle OBH\). The diagonal \(BD\) bisects \(\angle ABC\), and consecutive angles of a rhombus are supplementary, so \(\angle OBH=\angle ABD=\frac{180^\circ-\angle DAB}{2}=90^\circ-\frac{\angle DAB}{2}\). Because \(\angle DHB=\angle DHO+\angle OHB=90^\circ\), we have \(\alpha=\angle DHO=90^\circ-\left(90^\circ-\frac{\angle DAB}{2}\right)=\frac{\angle DAB}{2}\), hence \(\angle DAB=2\alpha\). Final answer: \(\angle DAB=2\alpha\).

In Figure 2 the parabola meets the x-axis at \(C\) (left) and \(D\), and the line \(y=kx+1\) intersects the parabola at \(A\) and \(B\); the point \(Q\) lies on this line and satisfies \(\angle OQC=90^\circ\). Because \(\angle OQC=90^\circ\), \(Q\) must lie on the circle with diameter \(OC\). Factoring the parabola gives \(y=(x+k)(x-1)\), so \(C=(-k,0)\); hence the circle with diameter \(OC\) has center \((-k/2,0)\) and radius \(k/2\). A unique point \(Q\) on the line \(y=kx+1\) means the line is tangent to this circle, so the distance from the center to the line equals the radius. Writing the line as \(kx-y+1=0\), the distance from \((-k/2,0)\) is \(|k(-k/2)+1|/\sqrt{k^2+1}=|1-k^2/2|/\sqrt{k^2+1}\), and setting this equal to \(k/2\) for \(k>0\) yields \((1-k^2/2)^2=(k^2/4)(k^2+1)\). Simplifying gives \(1=(5/4)k^2\), so \(k^2=4/5\) and \(k=2\sqrt5/5\). Final answer: \(k=2\sqrt5/5\).

The figure shows two linear functions, $y_1=kx+b$ and $y_2=mx+n$, whose graphs intersect at the point $(2,1)$, where the dashed horizontal line at $y=1$ meets the dashed vertical line at $x=2$. Therefore, the inequality $kx+b \geq mx+n$ holds precisely where $y_1$ is above or equal to $y_2$, which corresponds to $x \leq 2$. Final answer: $x \leq 2$

In the figure, \(AB\) is a diameter of \(\odot O\), point \(D\) lies on \(AB\) with \(CD \perp AB\), point \(C\) is on the circle, and \(\angle A = \angle CAD = 26^\circ\). Since \(OA\) and \(OC\) are radii, \(\triangle AOC\) is isosceles, so \(\angle OAC = \angle OCA = 26^\circ\); thus the central angle \(\angle AOC = 180^\circ - 26^\circ - 26^\circ = 128^\circ\). An inscribed angle intercepting minor arc \(AC\) is half the central angle, giving \(\frac{1}{2} \cdot 128^\circ = 64^\circ\), while the inscribed angle on the opposite side intercepting major arc \(AC\) is \(180^\circ - 64^\circ = 116^\circ\). Final answer: \(64^\circ\) or \(116^\circ\).

In the image, \(l_1\) is the line through \(A(1,0)\) and \(B(0,2)\), \(l_2\) is the line obtained by translating \(l_1\) downward 4 units, and \(P\) lies on side \(AB\) of quadrilateral \(ABCD\). The equation of \(l_1\) is \(y=-2x+2\), so translating down 4 units gives \(l_2: y=-2x-2\); thus \(C=(-1,0)\) and \(D=(0,-2)\). Using the shoelace formula on \(A(1,0), B(0,2), C(-1,0), D(0,-2)\), the area of quadrilateral \(ABCD\) is \(\frac12|4-(-4)|=4\). Since \(P\) is on \(AB\), segment \(CP\) splits \(ABCD\) into \(\triangle CBP\) and quadrilateral \(CPAD\). The area of \(\triangle CBA\) is \(\frac12\cdot 2\cdot 2=2\), and \(\text{Area}(\triangle CBP)=\frac{BP}{BA}\cdot \text{Area}(\triangle CBA)\). For a \(1:3\) division, the smaller area must be \(1\), so \(\frac{BP}{BA}\cdot 2=1\), giving \(\frac{BP}{BA}=\frac12\); hence \(P\) is the midpoint of \(AB\). Therefore \(P=\left(\frac{1+0}{2},\frac{0+2}{2}\right)=\left(\frac12,1\right)\). Final answer: \(\left(\frac12,1\right)\).

The image shows the Cartesian coordinate system with the origin O, point A in the first quadrant, and a right triangle formed by O, A, and the foot of the perpendicular from A to the x-axis; the angle α is the angle between the positive x-axis and the segment OA. In the figure, $\triangle ABC$ is isosceles with $AC=BC$, so let $\angle A=\angle B=\alpha$; $O$ is the circumcenter, so $OB=OC$ and the central angle $\angle BOC=2\angle A=2\alpha$. In isosceles $\triangle OBC$, $\angle OBC=(180^\circ-2\alpha)/2=90^\circ-\alpha$, hence $\angle ABD=\angle ABC-\angle OBC=\alpha-(90^\circ-\alpha)=2\alpha-90^\circ$. Since $D$ lies on $AC$, $\triangle ABD$ has angles $\angle BAD=\alpha$, $\angle ABD=2\alpha-90^\circ$, and $\angle ADB=180^\circ-\alpha-(2\alpha-90^\circ)=270^\circ-3\alpha$. For $\triangle ABD$ to be isosceles, the equal-angle cases give: $AB=AD$ when $\angle ADB=\angle ABD$, so $270^\circ-3\alpha=2\alpha-90^\circ$ and $\alpha=72^\circ$; $AB=BD$ when $\angle BAD=\angle ADB$, so $\alpha=270^\circ-3\alpha$ and $\alpha=67.5^\circ$; $AD=BD$ would give $\alpha=2\alpha-90^\circ$, i.e. $\alpha=90^\circ$, which is impossible. Both $72^\circ$ and $67.5^\circ$ are greater than $45^\circ$, so $D$ lies on side $AC$. Final answer: $72^\circ$ or $67.5^\circ$.

In the figure the shaded region is the entire square \(ACMN\) together with the part of square \(AGFB\) that lies outside square \(BCDE\). The figure shows right triangle \(ABC\) with the right angle at \(A\), point \(E$ on $BC\), point \(F$ on $AC\), and the folded image \(C'$ lying on side \(AB\); the stated condition \(CE=BC\) would force \(E$ to coincide with $B\), which conflicts with the drawing, so the intended condition is taken to be \(CE=CF\) (equivalently \(C'E=CF\)). In the figure, \(ABCD\) is a square of side \(4\), and \(P\) lies on diagonal \(AC\). In square \(PAQB\), the diagonal \(PQ\) equals \(\sqrt2\) times a side, so \(PQ=\sqrt2\cdot PA=\sqrt2\cdot 2\sqrt2=4\). Since this is the only point on \(AC\) satisfying the square condition, the minimum value is \(4\). Final answer: 4.

The figure shows triangle \(ABC\) with point \(D\) on side \(BC\) and point \(E\) on side \(AC\); folding \(\triangle ABC\) along line \(AD\) carries point \(B\) to point \(E\), so \(AD\) is the angle bisector of \(\angle BAC\), \(AE=AB=4\), and \(DE=BD\). Since both triangles share \(\angle C\), the Law of Cosines gives \(\frac{9k^2+20}{36k}=\frac{5k^2+4}{12k}\). Solving yields \(k^2=\frac{4}{3}\), so \(k=\frac{2\sqrt3}{3}\) and \(DC=3k=2\sqrt3\). Final answer: \(2\sqrt3\).

In the figure, \(\triangle ABC\) has \(\angle A=65^\circ\); \(D\) on \(AB\) and \(E\) on \(BC\) are the fold line sending \(B\) to \(B'\), while \(F\) on \(AC\) and \(G\) on \(BC\) are the fold line sending \(C\) to \(C'\); the marked angles are \(\angle 1=\angle AFC'\), \(\angle 2=\angle EGC'\), and \(\angle 3=\angle B'EG\), with \(\angle ADB'=35^\circ\). Since \(E,G,C\) are collinear and \(\angle C'GF=\angle CGF\), we get \(\angle 2=\angle EGC'=180^\circ-2\angle CGF=2\angle C-\angle 1\), hence \(\angle 1+\angle 2=2\angle C\). Therefore \(\angle 1+\angle 2+\angle 3=2\angle C+2\angle B-35^\circ=2(\angle B+\angle C)-35^\circ\). With \(\angle B+\angle C=180^\circ-65^\circ=115^\circ\), the sum is \(2\cdot115^\circ-35^\circ=195^\circ\). Final answer: \(195^\circ\).

The image shows the line \(y=2x\) and the line \(y=kx+b\) intersecting at point \(A\), whose \(y\)-coordinate is \(2\); since \(A\) lies on \(y=2x\), its \(x\)-coordinate satisfies \(2=2x\), so \(A=(1,2)\). The line \(y=kx+b\) also passes through \(B(2,0)\), so its slope is \(k=\frac{0-2}{2-1}=-2\), and substituting \(B(2,0)\) gives \(0=-2(2)+b\), hence \(b=4\). The inequality \(0<kx+b<2x\) becomes \(0<-2x+4<2x\). Solving \(-2x+4>0\) gives \(x<2\), and solving \(-2x+4<2x\) gives \(x>1\). Therefore the solution set is \(1<x<2\). Final answer: \(1<x<2\).

The figure shows a regular hexagon \(ABCDEF\) inscribed in circle \(\odot O\) of radius \(2\text{ cm}\), with the shaded region being \(\triangle ABC\) where \(A\), \(B\), and \(C\) are consecutive vertices. In a regular hexagon, each side equals the circumradius, so \(AB=BC=2\text{ cm}\), and each interior angle is \(120^\circ\), so \(\angle ABC=120^\circ\). The area of a triangle is \(\frac12ab\sin C\), giving \(\frac12(2)(2)\sin 120^\circ = 2\cdot \frac{\sqrt3}{2}=\sqrt3\text{ cm}^2\). Final answer: \(\sqrt3\text{ cm}^2\).

From the image, the parabola opens upward and crosses the x-axis at two points A and B, with A to the left of the origin and B to the right, and its vertex is given as \(\left(\frac{3}{2}, -\frac{25}{8}\right)\). Using the vertex form \(y=\frac12(x-h)^2+k\) with \(h=\frac32\) and \(k=-\frac{25}{8}\), we get \(y=\frac12\left(x-\frac32\right)^2-\frac{25}{8}\). Expanding gives \(y=\frac12x^2-\frac32x-2\). Setting \(y=0\) yields \(\frac12x^2-\frac32x-2=0\), or \(x^2-3x-4=0\), which factors as \((x+1)(x-4)=0\). Thus the x-intercepts are \(x=-1\) and \(x=4\), so with A to the left of B, \(A=(-1,0)\) and \(B=(4,0)\). Final answer: \(A(-1,0)\), \(B(4,0)\).

The image shows two parallel lines \(m\) and \(n\) with a \(45^\circ\) right-angled triangle ruler placed across them, where \(\angle \alpha\) is the exterior angle between line \(m\) and one side of the triangle and \(\angle \beta\) is the exterior angle between line \(n\) and another side. The figure shows the straight line passing through \(P(3,2)\) and \(B(0,-2)\), with \(B\) on the \(y\)-axis and \(A\) the \(x\)-intercept. The slope of the line is \(\frac{2-(-2)}{3-0}=\frac{4}{3}\), so its equation is \(y=\frac{4}{3}x-2\); setting \(y=0\) gives \(A\left(\frac{3}{2},0\right)\). Since \(M\) is on the \(y\)-axis, write \(M(0,t)\).
