The endpoints are excluded because \(P=A\) would be required for collinearity, but then \(PB=AB=5\neq3\). Final answer: \(1<PC<7\).

In the figure, right triangle \(ABC\) has its right angle at \(C\), with \(AC=6\) as one leg and \(M\) the midpoint of hypotenuse \(AB\); after a clockwise \(90^\circ\) rotation about \(C\), point \(A\) goes to \(A'\) on \(BC\), and since \(A'\) lies between \(C\) and \(B\), we have \(CA'=CA=6<CB\), so \(AC\) is opposite the \(30^\circ\) angle at \(B\). Therefore the hypotenuse \(AB=2AC=12\). For any right triangle, the midpoint of the hypotenuse is equidistant from \(C\), so \(CM=\frac{1}{2}AB=6\). The rotation carries \(M\) along a quarter-circle of radius \(CM=6\), so the path length is \(\frac{90^\circ}{360^\circ}\cdot 2\pi\cdot 6=\frac{1}{4}\cdot 12\pi=3\pi\). Final answer: \(3\pi\)

In the diagram, \(\triangle ABC\) is right-angled at \(C\) with \(BC=6\) and \(AC=8\); folding \(A\) onto \(B\) means the crease \(DE\) is the perpendicular bisector of \(\overline{AB}\), with \(D\) on \(AB\) and \(E\) on \(AC\), so \(EA=EB\). The figure shows right triangle \(ABC\) with the right angle at \(C\), and three shaded isosceles right triangles constructed externally on sides \(AC\), \(BC\), and \(AB\). In the diagram, \(OABC\) is a rectangle with \(O\) at the origin, \(A\) on the \(y\)-axis, and \(C\) on the \(x\)-axis; the hyperbola \(y=\frac{k}{x}\) meets horizontal side \(AB\) at \(M(1,3)\) and vertical side \(BC\) at \(N\). Since \(M(1,3)\) lies on the hyperbola, \(k=1\cdot 3=3\), so the curve is \(y=\frac{3}{x}\). Thus side \(AB\) is the line \(y=3\), giving \(B=(c,3)\) and \(C=(c,0)\) where \(OC=c\), and \(N=(c,\frac{3}{c})\). The slope of \(MN\) is \(\frac{\frac{3}{c}-3}{c-1}=-\frac{3}{c}\). Because \(B'\) is the reflection of \(B\) across line \(MN\) and lies on the \(x\)-axis, \(MN\) is the perpendicular bisector of \(BB'\). The midpoint of \(BB'\) has \(y\)-coordinate \(\frac{3}{2}\); substituting into the equation \(y-3=-\frac{3}{c}(x-1)\) gives \(\frac{3}{2}-3=-\frac{3}{c}\left(\frac{c+x_{B'}}{2}-1\right)\), which simplifies to \(x_{B'}=2\), so \(B'=(2,0)\). The slope of \(BB'\) is \(\frac{0-3}{2-c}=\frac{3}{c-2}\). Perpendicularity with \(MN\) requires \(\frac{3}{c-2}\cdot\left(-\frac{3}{c}\right)=-1\), so \(c(c-2)=9\). Solving \(c^2-2c-9=0\) with \(c>1\) yields \(c=1+\sqrt{10}\). Final answer: \(1+\sqrt{10}\).

In the figure, \(D\), \(E\), and \(F\) are the midpoints of sides \(AB\), \(BC\), and \(AC\) of \(\triangle ABC\), so segments \(DF\), \(DE\), and \(EF\) are the midlines of the triangle. A midline is parallel to the opposite side and half its length, so \(DF \parallel BC\), \(DE \parallel AC\), and \(EF \parallel AB\), with each side of \(\triangle DEF\) equal to half the corresponding side of \(\triangle ABC\). Therefore \(\triangle DEF \sim \triangle ABC\) with a scale factor of \(\frac12\), and the ratio of their areas is the square of the scale factor: \(\left(\frac12\right)^2 = \frac14\). Since the area of \(\triangle ABC\) is \(1\), the area of \(\triangle DEF\) is \(1 \times \frac14 = \frac14\). Final answer: \(\frac14\)

In the figure, points \(B, F, G, D\) lie on a straight line, and lines \(AC\) and \(AE\) intersect this line at \(F\) and \(G\) respectively, so \(A, F, C\) are collinear and \(A, G, E\) are collinear; therefore \(\angle BFC\) and \(\angle AFG\) are vertical angles, and \(\angle DGE\) and \(\angle AGF\) are vertical angles. Hence \(\angle A + \angle B + \angle C + \angle D + \angle E = \angle A + (180^\circ + \angle A) = 180^\circ + 2\angle A = 180^\circ + 2(31^\circ) = 242^\circ\). Final answer: \(242^\circ\).

The image shows \(\triangle OAB\) in the first quadrant with \(O\) at the origin, \(B\) on the positive \(x\)-axis, and \(A(4,3)\), while the similar figure \(\triangle OCD\) lies in the third quadrant with \(D\) on the negative \(x\)-axis and \(C\) below the \(x\)-axis, so the homothety centered at \(O\) that maps \(\triangle OAB\) to \(\triangle OCD\) must use a negative scale factor. In the figure, \(\triangle ABC\) is an isosceles right triangle with \(\angle BAC=90^\circ\), \(D\) is the midpoint of \(BC\) so \(AD\perp BC\); \(E\) lies on \(AC\), \(EG\perp BC\), \(EH\perp AD\), and the unshaded quadrilateral \(HDGE\) is a rectangle; \(BF\parallel AC\) meets the extension of \(EG\) at \(F\), and the shaded region is the polygon \(A\!-\!B\!-\!F\!-\!E\!-\!C\!-\!A\) with rectangle \(HDGE\) removed. Since \(AD\) has equation \(y=x\) and \(EG\) has slope \(1\), we get \(G=\bigl((a-e)/2,(a+e)/2\bigr)\) and \(H=(e/2,e/2)\); because \(BF\parallel AC\), \(BF\) is the vertical line \(x=a\), giving \(F=(a,a+e)\). The area of \(\triangle ABC\) is \(a^2/2\); the area of \(\triangle BFG\) is \(\frac12(a+e)\bigl[a-(a-e)/2\bigr]=(a+e)^2/4\); the area of rectangle \(HDGE\) is \(\bigl((a-e)/\sqrt2\bigr)\bigl(e/\sqrt2\bigr)=e(a-e)/2\). Thus the shaded area equals \(a^2/2+(a+e)^2/4-e(a-e)/2=3(a^2+e^2)/4\). From \(A(0,0)\) and \(G\bigl((a-e)/2,(a+e)/2\bigr)\), \(AG^2=\bigl((a-e)^2+(a+e)^2\bigr)/4=(a^2+e^2)/2\), and \(AG=3\) gives \(a^2+e^2=18\). Hence the shaded area is \(3\cdot18/4=27/2\). Final answer: 27/2.

In the figure, \(O\) lies on line \(AB\) and rays \(OD\), \(OC\), \(OE\) are drawn on the same side of \(AB\) with \(D\) between \(A\) and \(C\) and \(E\) between \(C\) and \(B\). Let \(\angle COD=x\) and \(\angle BOC=y\). Since \(\angle BOD\) and \(\angle COD\) are complementary, \(\angle BOD+\angle COD=90^\circ\); also \(\angle BOD=\angle BOC+\angle COD=y+x\), so \(y+x+x=90^\circ\), giving \(y=90^\circ-2x\). Because \(\angle BOC=4\angle EOC\), we have \(\angle EOC=y/4\), hence \(\angle DOE=\angle COD+\angle EOC=x+y/4=x+(90^\circ-2x)/4=22.5^\circ+x/2\). Since \(A\), \(O\), \(B\) are collinear, \(\angle AOD+\angle BOD=180^\circ\); with \(\angle AOD=\alpha\) and \(\angle BOD=90^\circ-x\), this yields \(\alpha+90^\circ-x=180^\circ\), so \(x=\alpha-90^\circ\). Substituting gives \(\angle DOE=22.5^\circ+(\alpha-90^\circ)/2=\frac12\alpha-22.5^\circ\). Final answer: \(\angle DOE=\frac12\alpha-22.5^\circ\).

In the figure, point P is the lighthouse with the east direction as the horizontal right ray, north as the upward ray, and south as the downward ray; ship A lies 30° north of east from P, so ray PA makes a 30° angle with the east direction toward north, and ship B lies 70° south of east from P, so ray PB makes a 70° angle with the east direction toward south. The figure shows a downward-opening parabola passing through the x-axis intercepts A(1,0) and B(-3,0), with y-intercept C(0,3), axis of symmetry between B and O, vertex D, and line BC meeting the axis of symmetry at E. In the figure, triangle \(ABC\) has base \(BC=12\text{ m}\) and altitude \(AD=8\text{ m}\); the square has its base on \(BC\) with top side \(PN\parallel BC\), where \(P\) lies on \(AB\), \(N\) lies on \(AC\), and \(E\) is where the altitude \(AD\) meets \(PN\). In the figure, \(P\) is the lighthouse with north, east, and south reference rays; ship \(A\) lies in the upper-right quadrant, ship \(B\) in the lower-right quadrant, and ship \(C\) is on the angle bisector in the upper-right quadrant. The figure shows a downward-opening parabola through the x-axis points A and B, with y-axis intercept C, vertex D, and axis of symmetry x=1. Since B(3,0) lies on the curve, 0=-9+6+c gives c=3, so the equation is y=-x^2+2x+3; hence C(0,3), D(1,4), and E, the reflection of C across x=1, is (2,3). Let M=(1,m). Then DM=|4-m|, MB=√(4+m^2), and DB=√((3-1)^2+(0-4)^2)=2√5; also BC=3√2, CE=2, and BE=√10. For similarity, compare corresponding sides. If △DMB∼△BCE, then DM/BC=MB/CE=DB/BE=√2, so DM=6 and MB=2√2; |4-m|=6 gives m=-2 or 10, and only m=-2 yields MB=2√2, giving M(1,-2). If △DMB∼△BEC, then DM/BE=MB/EC=DB/BC=√10/3, so DM=10/3 and MB=2√10/3; |4-m|=10/3 gives m=2/3 or 22/3, and only m=2/3 yields MB=2√10/3, giving M(1,2/3). In the figure, \(AB\) is a diameter, chord \(CD\perp AB\) at \(E\), and the shaded region is bounded by arc \(CB\) and segments \(CE\) and \(EB\). Since \(\angle CDB\) is an inscribed angle intercepting arc \(CB\), the central angle \(\angle COB=2\cdot30^\circ=60^\circ\). A diameter perpendicular to a chord bisects the chord, so \(CE=\frac12CD=\sqrt3\). In right triangle \(COE\), \(OC=\frac{CE}{\sin60^\circ}=\frac{\sqrt3}{\sqrt3/2}=2\), giving radius \(2\), and \(OE=OC\cos60^\circ=1\). The area of sector \(COB\) is \(\frac{60}{360}\pi\cdot2^2=\frac{2\pi}{3}\), and the area of \(\triangle COE\) is \(\frac12\cdot OE\cdot CE=\frac12\cdot1\cdot\sqrt3=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\). Therefore the shaded area equals the sector minus \(\triangle COE\), which is \(\frac{2\pi}{3}-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\). Final answer: \(\frac{2\pi}{3}-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\).

The figure shows the parabola passing through \(A(-1,0)\), \(C(0,-4)\), and \(B\) on the positive \(x\)-axis, with \(O\) as the origin and \(H\) a point on the parabola. Since \(C(0,-4)\) lies on the parabola, \(c=-4\). Substituting \(A(-1,0)\) gives \(0=\frac{4}{3}-b-4\), so \(b=-\frac{8}{3}\), and the parabola is \(y=\frac{4}{3}x^{2}-\frac{8}{3}x-4\). For \(H(x,y)\) on this parabola, \(\triangle OCH\) has base \(OC=4\) along the \(y\)-axis, so its area is \(\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot |x|=2|x|\). Setting \(2|x|=8\) yields \(|x|=4\), so \(x=4\) or \(x=-4\). When \(x=4\), \(y=\frac{4}{3}(16)-\frac{8}{3}(4)-4=\frac{20}{3}\); when \(x=-4\), \(y=\frac{4}{3}(16)-\frac{8}{3}(-4)-4=28\). Final answer: \((4,\frac{20}{3})\) or \((-4,28)\).

The image shows the line y = x + b crossing the positive y-axis at A and the negative x-axis at B, and intersecting y = -2x at point C in the second quadrant; however, the problem statement says the line meets the x-axis at A and the y-axis at B, so the labeling of A and B is inconsistent. Using the text's order (A is the x-intercept, B is the y-intercept): since C lies on y = -2x and its y-coordinate is 4, C = (-2, 4); substituting into y = x + b gives 4 = -2 + b, so b = 6 and the line is y = x + 6. Thus A = (-6, 0) and B = (0, 6). The area of triangle OBC is (1/2)|0·4 - (-2)·6| = 6, so the area of triangle OAP must be 6/8 = 3/4. Parametrize ray CA as P = C + t(A - C) = (-2 - 4t, 4 - 4t) with t ≥ 0; then the area of triangle OAP is (1/2)|(-6)(4 - 4t) - 0| = 12|t - 1|. Setting this equal to 3/4 gives |t - 1| = 1/16, so t = 15/16 or t = 17/16, yielding P = (-23/4, 1/4) or P = (-25/4, -1/4). If the image's labels are used instead (A = (0, 6), B = (-6, 0)), the same method gives P = (-1/2, 11/2) or P = (1/2, 13/2). Final answer: under the text's A = x-intercept convention the points are (-23/4, 1/4) and (-25/4, -1/4); under the image's A = y-intercept convention the points are (-1/2, 11/2) and (1/2, 13/2).

The figure shows points A, C, D, B on a straight line in that order, with D between C and B. Since D is the midpoint of segment BC and CD = 3 cm, we have BD = CD = 3 cm, so BC = 6 cm. With AB = 16 cm, AC = AB − BC = 16 − 6 = 10 cm, and AD = AC + CD = 10 + 3 = 13 cm. Point E is on line AB and AE = 2 cm. If E lies on segment AB, then DE = AD − AE = 13 − 2 = 11 cm; if E lies on the extension of AB beyond A, then DE = AD + AE = 13 + 2 = 15 cm. Final answer: 11 or 15 cm.

The image shows line \(l_1\) passing through \(A(-3,0)\) on the \(x\)-axis and intersecting the \(y\)-axis at \(B\), while line \(l_2: y=\frac{4}{3}x\) passes through the origin \(O\) and meets \(l_1\) at \(C(a,4)\). Since \(C\) lies on \(l_2\), we have \(4=\frac{4}{3}a\), so \(a=3\) and \(C(3,4)\). The slope of \(l_1\) through \(A(-3,0)\) and \(C(3,4)\) is \(\frac{4-0}{3-(-3)}=\frac{2}{3}\), giving \(l_1: y=\frac{2}{3}(x+3)\); thus \(B\) is \((0,2)\). For quadrilateral \(ODBC\) to be a parallelogram, its diagonals \(OB\) and \(DC\) bisect each other, so the midpoint of \(OB\), which is \((0,1)\), must equal the midpoint of \(DC\). Solving \(\frac{x_D+3}{2}=0\) and \(\frac{y_D+4}{2}=1\) yields \(x_D=-3\) and \(y_D=-2\). Final answer: \((-3,-2)\)

The table for X gives values 0, 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1, and the table for Y gives values 1, 2, 3, 4 with probabilities 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4 (where the Y table’s header P(X=x) should read P(Y=y)). Since X and Y are independent, P(X=x and Y=y)=P(X=x)P(Y=y). For Z=X+Y to be at most 2, the possible pairs are (X=0,Y=1), (X=0,Y=2), and (X=1,Y=1), because the smallest Y is 1. Thus P(Z≤2)=P(X=0)P(Y=1)+P(X=0)P(Y=2)+P(X=1)P(Y=1)=(0.4)(0.1)+(0.4)(0.2)+(0.3)(0.1)=0.04+0.08+0.03=0.15. Final answer: 0.15

The graph shows the curve rising from left to right near the labeled points a, b, and c, while it is falling near d. A positive derivative g'(x) means the function is increasing at that point, and g'(x) decreasing means the slope is becoming smaller as x increases, which geometrically means the curve is concave down there. At point b the curve is clearly rising, so g'(b) > 0, and it is bending downward, so the slope is positive and decreasing. At a the curve is also rising but appears concave up, so the slope is increasing; at c the curve is rising steeply toward the vertical asymptote, so the slope is positive and increasing; at d the curve is falling, so g'(d) < 0. Final answer: b

The image shows a normal distribution with mean 67.0 and standard deviation 5.1, and the vertical line labeled x is located one standard deviation to the right of the mean. To find that data point, add one standard deviation to the mean: 67.0 + 5.1 = 72.1. Final answer: 72.1

The residual plot displays residuals on the y-axis and fitted values on the x-axis, with the response being exports in millions of dollars. The residuals do not appear randomly scattered around zero; instead, they exhibit a pattern where the spread or magnitude of residuals changes across fitted values, with notably large positive residuals at lower and higher fitted values, indicating non-constant variance (heteroscedasticity). When a residual versus fits plot shows increasing or changing spread, a log transformation of the response variable is commonly applied because it compresses larger values and expands smaller ones, thereby stabilizing the variance and producing a more homoscedastic residual pattern. Final answer: A log transformation should be applied to the response variable (exports).

The image shows a vertical cylinder with diameter 2 feet, so radius 1 foot, and total height 4 feet, and it is half-full of oil, giving an oil depth of 2 feet. The oil weighs 50 pounds per cubic foot. To find the work, consider a thin horizontal slice of oil at height y feet above the bottom, where y ranges from 0 to 2. The volume of the slice is π(1)^2 dy = π dy cubic feet, its weight is 50π dy pounds, and it must be lifted (4 − y) feet to the top. Therefore the work is the integral from 0 to 2 of 50π(4 − y) dy, which equals 50π[4y − y^2/2] from 0 to 2 = 50π(8 − 2) = 300π foot-pounds, or about 942 foot-pounds. Final answer: 300π foot-pounds (approximately 942 foot-pounds).

The two-way table shows observed counts for rows w and x and columns y and z: w-y = 5, w-z = 25, x-y = 10, and x-z = 15. The row totals are 30 and 25, the column totals are 15 and 40, and the grand total is 55. For a 2×2 table, the chi-squared statistic can be computed as χ² = N(ad − bc)² / [(a+b)(c+d)(a+c)(b+d)], where a=5, b=25, c=10, d=15, and N=55. Substituting gives χ² = 55(5·15 − 25·10)² / (30·25·15·40) = 55(−175)² / 450000 = .743055… Final answer: 3.743 (approximately).

The table shows that 152 of 254 surveyed males approve and 199 of 301 surveyed females approve. To test whether the female approval proportion exceeds the male approval proportion, use a two-proportion z-test for H0: p_f = p_m versus Ha: p_f > p_m. The sample proportions are p̂_m = 152/254 ≈ 0.598 and p̂_f = 199/301 ≈ 0.661. The pooled proportion is p̂ = (152+199)/(254+301) = 351/555 ≈ 0.632, giving a standard error of sqrt(0.632(1-0.632)(1/254 + 1/301)) ≈ 0.0411 and a test statistic z = (0.661-0.598)/0.0411 ≈ 1.53. For a one-tailed test at the 5% level the critical value is 1.645 and the p-value is about 0.063, so the test statistic does not exceed the critical value and the p-value exceeds 0.05. Final answer: Fail to reject the null hypothesis; at the 5% significance level there is not sufficient evidence to conclude that the proportion of women who approve of the new design plan is higher than the proportion of men who approve.

The image shows a semicircular conducting loop of radius ℓ with resistor R on its straight edge; a uniform conducting rod of length ℓ is pivoted at the center of the semicircle, its free end slides on the arc, and it makes a small angle α with the vertical radius, while the magnetic field B points out of the yz-plane. The enclosed loop area is a sector, A = (1/2)ℓ²α, so dΦ/dα = (1/2)Bℓ² and the induced emf is E = −dΦ/dt = −(1/2)Bℓ²α̇; the current i = E/R produces a magnetic damping torque τ_B = i dΦ/dα = −(B²ℓ⁴/(4R))α̇. The gravitational restoring torque on the uniform rod is −(mgℓ/2)α for small α, and the moment of inertia about the pivot is I = mℓ²/3, giving (mℓ²/3)α̈ = −(mgℓ/2)α − (B²ℓ⁴/(4R))α̇, or α̈ + [3B²ℓ²/(4mR)]α̇ + [3g/(2ℓ)]α = 0. For θ = A(t)cos(ωt+φ), the damped frequency satisfies ω² = 3g/(2ℓ) − [3B²ℓ²/(8mR)]². Substituting ℓ = 0.1 m, m = 0.05 kg, R = 0.2 Ω, B = 2 T yields ω² = 15g − 2.25; with g ≈ 9.8 m/s² this is approximately 144.75 s⁻². Final answer: ω² = 15g − 2.25 ≈ 144.75 s⁻² (using g ≈ 9.8 m/s²).

The image shows a cube of side \(\ell = 10\ \text{cm}\) with a square-based pyramid whose base exactly matches the top face of the cube; the pyramid’s height is not labeled. When the cube slides on the rough floor, the ground friction decelerates the entire cube-plus-pyramid system at \(a=\mu g\), because the ground normal supports both objects. For the pyramid not to tip about the front edge of its base, the inertial torque must not exceed the restoring weight torque. For a solid right square pyramid the center of mass is \(h/4\) above the base, so the no-tip condition is \(\mu mg(h/4) \le mg(\ell/2)\), i.e. \(\mu \le 2\ell/h\). With \(\mu=0.3\) and \(\ell=0.10\ \text{m}\) this gives \(h \le 2\ell/\mu \approx 0.667\ \text{m}\); any ordinary pyramid in the figure is far shorter than this, so the actual deceleration \(\mu g\) is well below the tipping threshold. Since the deceleration is constant and independent of the initial speed, the base stays parallel to the cube top for any value of \(v\). Final answer: there is no finite maximum; the pyramid’s base remains parallel for any initial speed (formally, \(v_{\max}=\infty\ \text{m/s}\)).

The image shows a thin conducting slab of side length s between two infinite parallel conducting plates with surface charge densities +σ on top and −σ on bottom, separated by distance d, with the slab initially at the midpoint and moving with speed v at an angle θ toward the upper plate. The plates create a uniform electric field E = σ/ε0 directed downward, so the charged slab experiences a vertical acceleration a = qE/m = qσ/(mε0) ≈ 5.65 m/s², while the horizontal velocity component v_x = v cosθ remains constant; thus the time to travel L = 15 m horizontally is t = L/(v cosθ). Because a d = 0.028 m²/s² is much smaller than v² sin²θ = 2.25 m²/s², the vertical crossing time is very close to d/(v sinθ), and the exact accelerated motion gives the same integer count. Starting from the center, the first collision occurs after covering the half-gap d/2, and each subsequent collision occurs after a full gap d, so the number of collisions is N = 1 + floor{[t − d/(2v sinθ)]/[d/(v sinθ)]} = floor(L tanθ/d + 1/2). Substituting L = 15 m, d = 0.005 m, and θ = 30° gives N = floor(15 tan30°/0.005 + 0.5) = floor(1732.55) = 1732. Final answer: 1732 collisions.

The image shows the coin edge-on as a tilted line segment of length \(2r\) making a small angle \(\theta\) with the horizontal, pivoting on one rim point on the surface, so the center of mass is a distance \(r\) from the pivot and the opposite rim point strikes the surface when \(\theta=0\). Modeling the coin as a uniform disk, its moment of inertia about a rim point is \(I=\frac12mr^2+mr^2=\frac32mr^2\). For the small tilt, the gravitational torque about the pivot is \(\tau\approx mgr\), giving an approximately constant angular acceleration \(\alpha=\tau/I=2g/(3r)\). The potential energy relative to the flat position is \(U=mgr\sin\theta\approx mgr\theta\), so the energy just before an impact with amplitude \(\theta_n\) is \(mgr\theta_n\) and the next amplitude satisfies \(\theta_{n+1}=k\theta_n\). The half-swing time from amplitude \(\theta_n\) to \(\theta=0\) is \(t_n=\sqrt{2\theta_n/\alpha}=\sqrt{2I\theta_n/(mgr)}=\sqrt{3r\theta_n/g}\). The initial half-swing from \(\theta_0=8^\circ=0.1396\ \text{rad}\) gives \(t_0=\sqrt{3(0.01)(0.1396)/9.8}\approx0.0207\ \text{s}\). After the first collision the coin makes full back-and-forth swings between impacts, each taking \(2t_n\) with \(t_n=t_0k^{n/2}\), so the total time is \(T=t_0+2(t_1+t_2+\dots)=t_0[1+2\sqrt{k}/(1-\sqrt{k})]=t_0(1+\sqrt{k})/(1-\sqrt{k})\). With \(k=0.9\), \(\sqrt{k}\approx0.9487\), and \(T\approx0.0207(1.9487/0.0513)\approx0.785\ \text{s}\). Final answer: approximately \(0.79\ \text{s}\).

The figure shows two particles of equal mass starting together at point A on a circular orbit and moving in opposite tangential directions with speeds v and 2v. Because the particles have equal mass, each elastic collision simply exchanges their velocities, which is equivalent to imagining them passing through each other; thus the number of collisions equals the number of times their positions coincide. Their relative speed is v + 2v = 3v, so successive meetings occur every time interval C/(3v), where C is the circumference. They will both be back at A simultaneously when each has completed an integer number of laps: the slower particle takes time C/v for one lap and the faster takes time C/(2v) for two laps, so the first common return time is T = C/v. During this time the number of meetings is T divided by the meeting interval, (C/v)/(C/(3v)) = 3, which includes the meeting at A at the start/end. Therefore, excluding the collision at A, the particles undergo 2 elastic collisions before again reaching A. Final answer: 2.

The lower segment of the loop carries current to the right along +x and the axle is along the y-axis; a clockwise torque as viewed from the +y side corresponds to a torque vector τ pointing along +y. For a planar current loop the magnetic moment is μ = I A n, and with the indicated current in the x-y plane the right-hand rule gives n = +z, so μ is along +z. The torque on a magnetic dipole is τ = μ × B, so to obtain τ along +y with μ along +z we need B along +x because (+z) × (+x) = +y. Final answer: the magnetic field should be oriented in the +x direction.

The image shows a sphere split into two hemispheres with a thin horizontal water-filled gap between their flat faces, the upper hemisphere being fixed to a support. Modeling the water as a capillary bridge of radius r between the flat faces, the curved meniscus produces a pressure difference Δp = 2γ cosθ / h across the gap, where h is the separation. The upward capillary force on the lower hemisphere is therefore F = Δp πr^2, while the downward weight of the lower gold hemisphere is W = (2/3)πr^3 ρg. Setting F = W gives (2γ cosθ / h)πr^2 = (2/3)πr^3 ρg, so h = 3γ cosθ / (rρg). Substituting r = 0.04 m, ρ = 19300 kg m^-3, g = 9.81 m s^-2, γ = 0.072 N m^-1, and θ = 10° yields h = 3(0.072) cos 10° / (0.04 × 19300 × 9.81) m ≈ 2.8 × 10^-5 m = 0.028 mm. Final answer: 0.028 mm.

The free-body diagram shows a box on a stationary horizontal surface with three force vectors: gravitational force acting downward, normal force acting upward, and friction force acting horizontally to the left. The relevant physical principle is that friction always opposes the relative motion between two surfaces in contact, meaning the kinetic friction force points in the direction opposite to the box's actual motion. Since the friction vector in the diagram points to the left, the box must be moving in the opposite direction. Final answer: to the right

The crane is a light-rod truss made of square panels of side 1 m, with the right vertical tower containing points C and D one panel apart, so rod CD is a vertical 1 m member; the 5 kN load hangs at the left end of the boom, which extends two unit panels from the tower, giving a 2 m horizontal lever arm about B. Taking moments about B for the whole truss gives \(R_A(1\text{ m}) - 5\text{ kN}(2\text{ m}) = 0\), so the roller at A supplies 10 kN upward, and vertical equilibrium then gives the pin at B pushing down with 5 kN. At joint B the only vertical member is BR1, so it carries 5 kN tension; joint L1 has no horizontal force except L1R1, so L1R1 = 0, and then joint R1 horizontal equilibrium makes the diagonal zero, leaving vertical equilibrium requiring member R1D to be 5 kN compression. Joint D is connected only to the vertical members R1D and CD and the horizontal L2D, so vertical force balance gives the 5 kN upward push from R1D balanced by a 5 kN downward push in CD, meaning CD is in compression. Final answer: -5 kN.

The image shows the coin’s edge as a line segment of length \(2r\) resting on the horizontal surface at one rim point and inclined at angle \(\theta\) to the horizontal, so the center of mass is at the midpoint, a distance \(r\) from the pivot. Taking the flat position \(\theta=0\) as the zero of gravitational potential energy gives \(U=mgr\sin\theta\); for the small \(8^\circ\) tilt we use \(\sin\theta\approx\theta\), making the restoring torque approximately constant and producing angular acceleration \(\alpha=mgr/I=2g/(3r)\), where \(I=(3/2)mr^2\) is the moment of inertia of a uniform disk about a rim point. A fall from a small angle \(\theta_n\) to the horizontal takes \(t_n=\sqrt{2\theta_n/\alpha}\). Each collision preserves a fraction \(k=0.9\) of the energy just before impact, so successive amplitudes satisfy \(\theta_{n+1}\approx k\theta_n\). The first fall takes \(t_0=\sqrt{2\theta_0/\alpha}\), and each subsequent round trip between collisions takes \(2t_n\), giving total time \(T=t_0+2\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}t_n=\sqrt{2\theta_0/\alpha}\,(1+\sqrt{k})/(1-\sqrt{k})\). Substituting \(r=0.01\ \text{m}\), \(\theta_0=8^\circ=0.1396\ \text{rad}\), \(k=0.9\), and \(g=9.8\ \text{m/s}^2\) yields \(\alpha\approx 653\ \text{s}^{-2}\), \(t_0\approx0.0207\ \text{s}\), and \(T\approx0.79\ \text{s}\). Final answer: about \(0.79\ \text{s}\).

The image shows a uniform bar hanging vertically from a ceiling by a thread attached to one end. Because the thread is very long, it stays nearly vertical and the bar’s upper end moves essentially along a horizontal line; to leading order there is no horizontal external force, so the centre of mass of the bar remains on the vertical line of the thread. Let φ be the angle the bar makes with the upward vertical. The end displacement is x = −(l/2) sin φ and the centre-of-mass height is y = (l/2) cos φ. Energy conservation gives (1/24) m l² \dotφ² (1 + 3 sin² φ) + (1/2) m g l cos φ = (1/2) m g l, and vertical force balance gives the thread tension T = m g − (m l/2)(\ddotφ sin φ + \dotφ² cos φ) = m g (3 cos² φ − 6 cos φ + 4)/(4 − 3 cos² φ)². Minimizing this over 0 ≤ φ ≤ π gives the minimum at cos φ ≈ 0.4767, where T ≈ 0.165 m g. Final answer: α ≈ 0.165.

The image shows two horizontal conducting plates with surface charge densities +σ and −σ separated by a distance d, with a thin conducting slab of charge q moving with speed v at an angle θ to the horizontal in the gap. Between the plates the electric field is uniform and has magnitude E = σ/ε₀, directed from the positive plate to the negative plate, so the slab experiences a constant vertical acceleration a = qE/m = qσ/(mε₀) = (1.0×10⁻⁷ C)(50×10⁻⁶ C/m²)/[(0.100 kg)(8.85×10⁻¹² C²/N·m²)] ≈ 5.65 m/s². The horizontal motion is uniform, so vₓ = v cosθ = 3 cos30° ≈ 2.60 m/s and the time to travel L = 15 m is t = L/vₓ ≈ 5.77 s. At the midpoint the vertical speed is vᵧ = v sinθ = 1.5 m/s, and for elastic bouncing in a uniform field the collision frequency is f = [√(vᵧ² + ad) + √(vᵧ² − ad)]/(2d), which is very nearly vᵧ/d = 300 s⁻¹ because ad ≪ vᵧ². Using the exact expression gives f ≈ 299.99 s⁻¹, so the number of collisions is N = ft ≈ 1732. Final answer: 1732.

The image shows a small block on a plane inclined at angle α to the horizontal, with the x-axis directed down the line of steepest descent and the magnetic field perpendicular to the slope; the relevant forces are the downhill component of gravity mg sin α, the normal force mg cos α, and therefore kinetic friction μ mg cos α opposing the velocity. In the long-time steady state the velocity is constant, so the vector sum of the downhill gravity component, friction, and the magnetic force Q v B₀ (which is perpendicular to the velocity) is zero; since friction and the magnetic force are perpendicular, the force triangle gives (mg sin α)² = (μ mg cos α)² + (Q B₀ v)², hence v = (mg/(Q B₀)) √(sin² α − μ² cos² α). For α = 40° and μ = 0.3, β = √(sin² 40° − 0.3² cos² 40°) ≈ 0.60. Final answer: β ≈ 0.60.

The side-view diagram shows a horizontal 200 m test section of a long chamber; the cylinder of radius R moves to the right at 10 m/s and spins counterclockwise, with gravity acting downward. In the cylinder’s rest frame the fluid approaches from the right to the left with speed u = v = 10 m/s, so the given potential for rightward flow is used with u replaced by -u. The circulation is Γ = 2πR²ω, and the Magnus lift on a cylinder of span H is L = ρuΓH = 2πρvR²ωH, directed upward for the stated counterclockwise spin when the relative flow is leftward. For no vertical acceleration the upward lift must balance the net downward gravitational force Mg - ρgπR²H, so Mg - ρgπR²H = 2πρvR²ωH. Substituting M = 10 kg, R = 0.08 m, H = 0.20 m, ρ = 700 kg/m³, v = 10 m/s, and g = 9.8 m/s² gives a displaced volume πR²H ≈ 4.021 × 10^-3 m³, a buoyant force ≈ 27.6 N, a net downward force 98 N - 27.6 N ≈ 70.4 N, and a denominator 2π(700)(10)(0.08)²(0.20) ≈ 56.3 N/(rad/s), yielding ω ≈ 70.4 / 56.3 ≈ 1.25 rad/s. The 200 m chamber length does not affect this force balance. Final answer: 1.25 rad/s.

The image shows a dense fan of thin halflenses sharing a common center, with the incoming ray perpendicular to the first lens at radial distance λ/2 and the outgoing ray leaving the last lens at radial distance 2λ. For an ideal thin lens, a ray at distance r from the center is deflected through an angle r/f; with n lenses per radian this gives an accumulated turning n r/f = r/λ per radian. In the dense limit the total deflection is therefore Θ ≈ ∫ (r/λ) dφ. Because the ray crosses the radially arranged lenses at an order-unity angle, the smooth spiral scales as dr ∼ r dφ, so dφ ≈ dr/r and Θ ≈ (1/λ)∫_{λ/2}^{2λ} dr = (2λ − λ/2)/λ = 3/2. Final answer: 3/2 rad.

The image shows a simple pendulum of length L with the bob at the lowest point A, a horizontal velocity V at A, and the top point B on the same vertical line; the angle θ is measured from the vertical radius AB to the radius locating the bob. Because the speed at A is just enough to reach B, the initial kinetic energy equals the gain in gravitational potential energy: 1/2 M V² = M g (2L), so V² = 4 g L. At angle θ the bob has risen a height L(1 + cos θ) above A, so energy conservation gives 1/2 M v² = 1/2 M V² − M g L(1 + cos θ), or v² = V² − 2 g L(1 + cos θ). Setting v = V/2 and using V² = 4 g L yields V²/4 = V² − 2 g L(1 + cos θ), which simplifies to 1 + cos θ = 3/2, hence cos θ = 1/2 and θ = 60°. Final answer: θ = 60° from the vertical line AB.

The graph shows a straight-line plot of maximum kinetic energy versus frequency, and the line intercepts the frequency axis at about \(4\times10^{14}\ \text{Hz}\). In the photoelectric effect, \(E_{km}=hf-\phi\), so at the threshold frequency \(f_0\) where \(E_{km}=0\), the work function is \(\phi=hf_0\). Using \(h\approx4.14\times10^{-15}\ \text{eV}\cdot\text{s}\), we get \(\phi=(4.14\times10^{-15})(4\times10^{14})\approx1.66\ \text{eV}\), which rounds to about \(1.7\ \text{eV}\). Final answer: approximately 1.7 eV.

The photo shows a red cylinder with a black thread wrapped once around it, tied in a knot with a free end pulled parallel to the cylinder axis by the white arrow. When the loop slides without changing shape it forms a single helical turn; unwrapping the cylinder turns this helix into a straight line of horizontal extent \(2\pi R\) and vertical rise \(h\), so the loop length is \(L=\int_0^{2\pi R}\sqrt{1+(dz/dx)^2}\,dx\). For a helix the slope is constant, \(dz/dx=h/(2\pi R)=\tan\alpha\), where \(\alpha\) is the angle between the thread and the circumferential direction, and the arc length is therefore \(L=2\pi R\sqrt{1+\tan^2\alpha}\). The loop is self-locking when the helix is shallower than the friction angle, i.e. when \(\tan\alpha\le \mu\), and it just begins to slide at the critical condition \(\tan\alpha=\mu\). Thus the critical pitch is \(h_0=2\pi R\mu\), giving \(L_0=\sqrt{(2\pi R)^2+(2\pi R\mu)^2}=2\pi R\sqrt{1+\mu^2}\). Final answer: \(L_0=2\pi R\sqrt{1+\mu^2}\).

The image shows four fixed charges on the x-axis: Q1 at (-2a,0), Q2 at (-a,0), Q3 at (+a,0), and Q4 at (+2a,0), with a positive charge q located at (0,b). Because the four charges have equal magnitude, Q1 and Q4 are equidistant from q with distance sqrt((2a)^2 + b^2), and Q2 and Q3 are equidistant with distance sqrt(a^2 + b^2). The positive charge q is repelled by the positive charges Q1 and Q2, giving force components with upward (+y) and rightward (+x) parts, and it is attracted toward the negative charges Q3 and Q4, giving force components with downward (-y) and rightward (+x) parts. The upward y-component from Q1 cancels the downward y-component from Q4 because they have the same magnitude, and the upward y-component from Q2 cancels the downward y-component from Q3 for the same reason. Meanwhile, every individual force on q has a positive x-component, so the horizontal components add. Thus the net force has no y-component and points along the positive x-axis. Final answer: the net force on q points in the positive x-direction (to the right).

The image shows four charges fixed on the x-axis at (-2a,0), (-a,0), (+a,0), and (+2a,0), with Q1 and Q4 positive and Q2 and Q3 negative, and a positive charge q placed at (0,b). Because the arrangement is symmetric about the y-axis, the horizontal components of the Coulomb forces on q cancel, leaving only a y-component. The positive charges repel q, giving upward (+y) force components, while the negative charges attract q, giving downward (-y) force components. For equal charge magnitudes Q, the net vertical force is F_y = 2k q Q b[(4a^2+b^2)^(-3/2) - (a^2+b^2)^(-3/2)]. Since a^2+b^2 < 4a^2+b^2, the downward term dominates and F_y < 0. Final answer: the net force on q is directed downward along the negative y-axis (toward the x-axis).

The image shows four equal-magnitude charges fixed on the x-axis at \((-2a,0)\), \((-a,0)\), \((+a,0)\), and \((+2a,0)\), labeled \(Q_1,Q_2,Q_3,Q_4\), and a positive test charge \(q\) at \((0,b)\) on the positive y-axis. With \(Q_1\) and \(Q_3\) positive and \(Q_2\) and \(Q_4\) negative, the vertical components of the Coulomb forces on \(q\) cancel by mirror symmetry, so the net force is purely horizontal. Using \(\mathbf{F}=k\,q\,Q_i(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_i)/|\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_i|^3\), the x-component of the net force is \(F_x=kqQa\big[4/(4a^2+b^2)^{3/2}-2/(a^2+b^2)^{3/2}\big]\), where \(Q\) is the common magnitude; this is negative for \(b\lesssim 2.0a\) and positive for larger \(b\). Final answer: the net force on \(q\) is horizontal along the x-axis, pointing toward \(-x\) when \(b\) is small and toward \(+x\) when \(b\) is large.

Interpreting the motion as the cube being suddenly given speed \(v\) while the pyramid starts from rest, the image shows a cube of side \(\ell=10\,\text{cm}\) with a symmetrical square-based pyramid on top whose base matches the cube's top face. Since the pyramid's height is not labeled, I take the regular shape in the diagram to be a regular square pyramid with slant edges equal to the base edge \(\ell\), so its height is \(h=\ell/\sqrt2\) and, with equal density, \(m/M=V_{\text{pyramid}}/V_{\text{cube}}=(\ell^2h/3)/\ell^3=h/(3\ell)=1/(3\sqrt2)\). Kinetic friction acts at both contacts: the pyramid accelerates forward at \(a_p=\mu g\), while the cube is retarded by ground friction \(\mu(M+m)g\) plus the pyramid's backward reaction \(\mu mg\), giving \(a_c=\mu g(M+2m)/M\). The relative acceleration of the pyramid with respect to the cube is therefore \(a_{\text{rel}}=a_p+a_c=2\mu g(1+m/M)\). The pyramid stays seated with its base parallel to the cube top as long as the backward relative slide \(v^2/(2a_{\text{rel}})\) does not exceed \(\ell/2\), so \(v_{\max}^2=a_{\text{rel}}\ell\). This regular pyramid also does not tip, because \(\mu=0.3\) is well below the tipping threshold \(2\ell/h=2\sqrt2\). Substituting \(\ell=0.10\,\text{m}\), \(\mu=0.3\), \(g=9.8\,\text{m/s}^2\), and \(m/M=1/(3\sqrt2)\) gives \(v_{\max}=\sqrt{2(0.3)(9.8)(0.10)\left(1+1/(3\sqrt2)\right)}\approx 0.85\,\text{m/s}\). Final answer: approximately \(0.85\,\text{m/s}\).

The image shows fixed charges Q1 at (-2a,0), Q2 at (-a,0), Q3 at (+a,0), Q4 at (+2a,0), and a positive charge q at (0,b). Q1 and Q4 are positive, so they repel q upward and away from the x-axis; Q2 and Q3 are negative, so they attract q downward toward the x-axis. By Coulomb's law, the vertical force component from each charge is k q |Q| b / (x_i^2 + b^2)^{3/2}, with sign positive for repulsion from the positive charges and negative for attraction to the negative charges. The left-right symmetry makes all horizontal components cancel, so only the vertical sum matters: F_y is proportional to 2b/(4a^2 + b^2)^{3/2} - 2b/(a^2 + b^2)^{3/2}. Because a^2 + b^2 is smaller than 4a^2 + b^2, the negative (downward) term dominates, giving a net force along the negative y-axis. Final answer: the net force on q points straight downward toward the x-axis.

The image shows four equal-magnitude charges fixed on the x-axis at (-2a,0), (-a,0), (+a,0), and (+2a,0), with Q1 and Q3 positive and Q2 and Q4 negative, and a positive charge q at (0,b). By Coulomb’s law the force on q from a charge Q_i at (x_i,0) is k q Q_i (-x_i, b)/(x_i^2+b^2)^(3/2). The y-components are k q Q_i b/(x_i^2+b^2)^(3/2); the upward forces from the two positive charges have magnitudes proportional to 1/[(2a)^2+b^2]^(3/2) and 1/[a^2+b^2]^(3/2), while the downward forces from the two negative charges have exactly the same two magnitudes, so the net vertical force is zero. The horizontal component is F_x = 2 k q |Q| a [2/((2a)^2+b^2)^(3/2) - 1/(a^2+b^2)^(3/2)], which is negative when b is small and positive when b is large, passing through zero at b = a sqrt((4 - 2^(2/3))/(2^(2/3) - 1)) ≈ 2.03 a. Final answer: the net force on q is horizontal, parallel to the x-axis; it points in the negative x-direction for b less than that critical value, vanishes at the critical value, and points in the positive x-direction for larger b.

The photo shows a red cylinder with a black thread wrapped once around it; a knot is visible where the free end leaves the contact region, and the white arrow shows the free end being pulled parallel to the cylinder axis. Treat the contacting part of the loop as a curve on the cylinder that makes one full turn. Let φ be the angle between the thread and the circumferential direction on the unwrapped cylinder, so tan φ = dz/(R dθ). The normal reaction per unit length from the cylinder on the thread is N = T cos²φ/R, where T is the local tension. At the limiting sliding condition the axial friction per unit length is μN, and its component perpendicular to the thread within the tangent plane balances the geodesic curvature, giving |dφ/ds| = (μ/R) cos³φ. Since dθ/ds = cos φ/R, this becomes d tan φ/dθ = −μ, so tan φ = C − μθ. For the loop to close after one turn the axial displacement must vanish: 0 = ∫_0^{2π} R tan φ dθ = 2πR(C − πμ), hence C = πμ. The critical length is the length of this limiting curve: L0 = ∫ ds = R∫_0^{2π} sec φ dθ = R∫_0^{2π} sqrt(1+μ²(π−θ)²) dθ = (R/μ)∫_{−πμ}^{πμ} sqrt(1+x²) dx. Using 2∫sqrt(1+x²)dx = x sqrt(1+x²)+arcsinh x gives L0 = (R/μ)[πμ sqrt(1+π²μ²)+arcsinh(πμ)] = R[π sqrt(1+π²μ²)+(1/μ)arcsinh(πμ)]. Final answer: L0 = R[π sqrt(1+π²μ²)+(1/μ)arcsinh(πμ)].

The image shows four charges fixed on the \(x\)-axis at \((-2a,0)\), \((-a,0)\), \((+a,0)\), and \((+2a,0)\), with a positive charge \(q\) at \((0,b)\). Because \(q\) is positive, the positive charges \(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\) repel \(q\), producing forces components directed away from \((-2a,0)\) and \((-a,0)\), both of which have a positive \(x\)-component; the negative charges \(Q_3\) and \(Q_4\) attract \(q\), producing force components directed toward \((+a,0)\) and \((+2a,0)\), which also have positive \(x\)-components. The vertical force components from the symmetric pairs \((Q_1,Q_4)\) and \((Q_2,Q_3)\) cancel each other, leaving no net \(y\)-component. Final answer: the net force on \(q\) is in the positive \(x\)-direction (to the right).

The image shows the ball at the apex of an equilateral triangle: the fixed steel rod and each half of the string all have length L = 1 m, so the stretched total string length is 2L = 2 m while its relaxed length is L = 1 m, giving an extension ΔL = L = 1 m. For an ideal elastic string, the stored potential energy is U = (1/2)k(ΔL)^2 = (1/2)(10 N/m)(1 m)^2 = 5 J. When the ball reaches the midpoint of the rod, the string returns to its relaxed length, the tension becomes zero, and the acceleration stops; by conservation of energy, (1/2)mv^2 = U, so v = sqrt(2U/m) = sqrt(2·5 J / 2 kg) = sqrt(5) m/s ≈ 2.24 m/s. Final answer: sqrt(5) m/s (approximately 2.24 m/s).

The image shows a table of height \(h_1=4\ \text{m}\) above the floor, a frictionless ramp of height \(h_2=0.5\ \text{m}\) on the table, and a spring compressed by \(\Delta x=0.3\ \text{m}\); the box starts on the ramp and, assuming it leaves the table edge horizontally, its speed at the edge is found from conservation of energy: the spring potential energy plus the gravitational potential energy lost descending the ramp becomes kinetic energy, \(\frac12 k\Delta x^2 + mgh_2 = \frac12 mv^2\). With \(m=0.060\ \text{kg}\) and \(k=6.5\ \text{N/m}\), this gives \(v=\sqrt{(6.5)(0.3)^2/(0.060)+2(9.8)(0.5)}\approx 4.42\ \text{m/s}\). The time to fall from height \(h_1\) is \(t=\sqrt{2h_1/g}=\sqrt{2(4)/9.8}\approx 0.904\ \text{s}\), so the horizontal distance is \(\Delta d = vt \approx (4.42)(0.904)\approx 4.0\ \text{m}\). Final answer: 4.0 m

The image shows the ball of mass m attached to the midpoint of the elastic string, with the string’s two ends fixed to the ends of a rigid rod of length L; in the pulled position each side of the string has length L, making the total stretched string length 2L. Since the string’s relaxed length is L, the initial extension is 2L − L = L, so the stored elastic potential energy is U = ½ kL². In zero gravity this potential energy is converted entirely into the ball’s kinetic energy when the string relaxes to length L and the tension drops to zero, which is when the ball stops accelerating, so ½ kL² = ½ m v². Substituting k = 10 N/m, L = 1 m, and m = 2 kg gives v = √(kL²/m) = √(10·1²/2) = √5 ≈ 2.24 m/s. Final answer: √5 m/s (approximately 2.24 m/s).

The graph plots displacement \(x\) (in metres) against time \(t\) (in seconds) and is a straight line passing through the points \((0, -0.2)\) and \((4, 0.2)\), crossing the \(t\)-axis at \(t = 2\ \text{s}\); because the \(x\)-\(t\) graph is a straight line, the slope is constant, so the particle moves with uniform rectilinear motion (constant velocity). The velocity is the slope of the \(x\)-\(t\) graph: \(v = \dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{0.2 - (-0.2)}{4 - 0} = \dfrac{0.4}{4} = 0.1\ \text{m/s}\). Since the slope is positive, the velocity is directed in the positive \(x\)-direction. Final answer: the particle moves with uniform linear motion at \(0.1\ \text{m/s}\) in the positive \(x\)-direction.

The figure shows a cylindrical magnet A with a superconducting ring B placed horizontally above it. While ring B is being moved into the magnetic field of A, the magnetic flux through B changes; by Faraday’s law, \(\mathcal{E}=-\frac{d\Phi}{dt}\), this changing flux induces an electromotive force and therefore an induced current in B. Because B is a superconductor and has zero electrical resistance, the induced current does not decay by Joule heating after the ring becomes stable; it becomes a persistent current that continues to flow, producing a magnetic field that repels the magnet and supports levitation. Final answer: Yes, an induced current is generated while B is being placed into the magnetic field; after stabilization, the induced current still exists as a persistent current.

The image shows a smooth rod inclined downward to the right at \(45^{\circ}\) to the horizontal, with a light spring lying along the rod; the lower end of the spring is fixed and a ball is threaded on the rod. In an inertial frame the ball accelerates horizontally to the right with acceleration \(g\). Let \(\mathbf{e}\) be the unit vector down the rod, so \(\mathbf{e}=(\cos45^{\circ},-\sin45^{\circ})\). The forces on the ball are gravity \((0,-mg)\), the normal force perpendicular to the rod, and the spring force \(T\) along the rod. Taking the dot product of Newton’s second law with \(\mathbf{e}\) eliminates the normal force: \(T+(0,-mg)\cdot\mathbf{e}=m(g,0)\cdot\mathbf{e}\). Since \((0,-mg)\cdot\mathbf{e}=mg\sin45^{\circ}\) and \((g,0)\cdot\mathbf{e}=g\cos45^{\circ}\), this gives \(T+mg\sin45^{\circ}=mg\cos45^{\circ}\), so \(T=mg(\cos45^{\circ}-\sin45^{\circ})=0\). Final answer: 0.

The image shows a horizontal conducting ring and a bar magnet with its S pole downward falling vertically through the ring’s axis. As the magnet approaches the ring from above, the magnetic field through the ring due to the S pole points downward and is increasing, so by Lenz’s law the induced current creates an upward magnetic field; using the right-hand rule this corresponds to a counterclockwise current when viewed from above. After the magnet passes through the ring and moves away below, the downward magnetic flux through the ring decreases, so the induced current now creates a downward magnetic field, corresponding to a clockwise current when viewed from above. Final answer: first counterclockwise, then clockwise (viewed from top to bottom).

The circuit shows two solenoids, a sliding rheostat \(R\), and a power source connected in series, with the closed rectangular coil \(ab\) free to rotate about the axis \(O\) perpendicular to the paper and located between the solenoids. As the slider \(P\) moves from left to right, the portion of the rheostat in the circuit increases, so the series current decreases; therefore the magnetic field produced by the solenoids weakens. By Lenz’s law the induced current in coil \(ab\) opposes this decrease in magnetic flux \(\Phi = \vec B\cdot \vec A\), so it produces an induced magnetic field in the same direction as the solenoid field and gives the coil a magnetic moment aligned with that field. The resulting magnetic torque rotates the coil so that its normal aligns more closely with the field, thereby increasing the flux. In the figure this motion is a counterclockwise rotation about \(O\). Final answer: coil \(ab\) rotates counterclockwise (as viewed in the plane of the figure).

The dart starts at the same height as the top point P and a horizontal distance L away, while the disk rotates about the horizontal axis through O, so P moves on a vertical circle of radius R with angular speed ω. Let t be the flight time and θ = ωt the angle P turns. The dart falls a vertical distance ½gt², and P descends a vertical distance R(1 − cos θ); equating these gives ½gt² = R(1 − cos ωt). If P rotates toward the dart, its horizontal displacement R sin ωt reduces the distance the dart must travel, so v0t = L − R sin ωt; if it rotates the other way, v0t = L + R sin ωt. Eliminating R with the vertical equation gives v0 = L/t − (gt sin ωt)/(2(1 − cos ωt)) for rotation toward the dart, or v0 = L/t + (gt sin ωt)/(2(1 − cos ωt)) for rotation away, where t is any positive solution of ½gt² = R(1 − cos ωt). If the horizontal shift of P is neglected, this reduces to R[1 − cos(ωL/v0)] = ½g(L/v0)². Since R and ω are not specified, no single numerical value can be given. Final answer: v0 = L/t ∓ (gt sin ωt)/(2(1 − cos ωt)) with t satisfying ½gt² = R(1 − cos ωt) (upper sign when P rotates toward the dart, lower sign when away); in the small-displacement approximation, R[1 − cos(ωL/v0)] = ½g(L/v0)².

In the figure the solenoid is connected in series with a switch, a resistor, and a battery whose longer (positive) plate is on the left, so when the switch is closed conventional current enters the left end of the solenoid; the visible front conductors slope downward to the right, indicating a right-handed winding, and the right-hand rule then gives a magnetic field inside the solenoid pointing toward the right. At the instant the circuit is connected this field increases from zero toward the right, so by Lenz’s law the induced current in the copper ring must produce a magnetic field directed to the left to oppose that increase in flux. For a current loop, a clockwise current as viewed from left to right produces a magnetic field pointing to the left, so the induced current in the ring is clockwise when viewed from left to right. Final answer: clockwise (viewed from left to right).

The image shows a rectangular wire loop \(abcd\) with side \(bc\) already inside a uniform magnetic field \(\vec B\) directed into the page, while side \(ad\) is still outside the field region. An induced current is produced whenever the magnetic flux through the loop changes. With the field perpendicular to the loop, the flux is \(\Phi = BA\), where \(A\) is the area of the loop inside the field. If the frame moves to the right, the portion of the loop inside \(\vec B\) increases, so \(\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt}=B\dfrac{dA}{dt}=BLv\neq 0\); by Faraday’s law an induced emf and therefore an induced current are generated. This remains true as long as \(ad\) has not yet entered the field, because the area in the field is still increasing. Final answer: right.

From the v-t graph the passenger car starts braking at 40 m/s and stops at t = 20 s, while the truck starts at 30 m/s and stops at t = 30 s; their speeds are equal at t = 10 s. The displacement of each vehicle equals the area under its v-t graph, so by t = 20 s the passenger car has traveled s_p = ½·40·20 = 400 m and the truck has traveled s_t = ½·(30+10)·20 = 400 m, meaning the original 30 m gap is still present when the passenger car stops. After t = 20 s the passenger car is stationary, while the truck continues moving with an initial speed of 10 m/s and a deceleration of 1 m/s², so it can still travel an additional ½·10·10 = 50 m before stopping, which is greater than the remaining 30 m gap. Solving 10τ − 0.5τ² = 30 gives τ = 10 − 2√10 ≈ 3.68 s, so the collision occurs at t ≈ 23.7 s, after the passenger car has already stopped. Final answer: Yes, the two vehicles will have a rear-end collision, and it occurs after the passenger car stops.

The image shows a uniform magnetic field directed into the page, a U-shaped rail forming loop PQRS, a movable metal rod PQ, and a circular wire frame T located inside the area enclosed by PQRS. When rod PQ suddenly moves to the right, the motional emf drives an induced current in loop PQRS; using the right-hand rule for v × B with v to the right and B into the page, positive charges are pushed upward, so the current in PQRS is counterclockwise. A counterclockwise current loop produces a magnetic field out of the page inside the loop, so at frame T the magnetic field due to the rail current is out of the page and increasing from zero as the current starts to grow. By Lenz’s law, the induced current in T must create a field opposing this increase, namely a field into the page; the right-hand rule shows that a current producing a field into the page through T flows clockwise. Final answer: clockwise.

The figure shows a fixed horizontal conducting ring and a bar magnet whose S pole is downward falling along the vertical axis through the ring. Because magnetic field lines outside the magnet run from N to S, the magnetic flux through the ring is directed upward while the magnet approaches. As the S pole approaches the ring from above, this upward flux increases, so by Lenz’s law the induced current creates a downward magnetic field to oppose the increase; using the right-hand rule, a downward field viewed from above means a clockwise current. After the magnet passes through and its S pole moves below the ring, the upward flux through the ring decreases, so the induced current creates an upward magnetic field to oppose the decrease, which corresponds to a counterclockwise current when viewed from above. Final answer: the induced current is first clockwise and then becomes counterclockwise.

The image shows a smooth incline of angle θ with two equal masses A and B joined by a light spring of stiffness k; block B rests against a fixed stop C, and the system is initially at rest. Initially block A is in equilibrium on the incline, so the spring is compressed by an amount x1 satisfying kx1 = mg sin θ, giving x1 = mg sin θ/k. When block B is just about to leave C, the normal force from C becomes zero, so the spring must exert an upward force along the incline equal to B’s weight component: kx2 = mg sin θ, giving extension x2 = mg sin θ/k. Since B has not moved, the distance A travels equals the increase in the spring’s length from its compressed state to its extended state, s = x1 + x2 = mg sin θ/k + mg sin θ/k = 2mg sin θ/k. Final answer: 2mg sin θ/k.

The graph shows car B’s curve passing through the point (5 s, 20 m) and being tangent to the t-axis at t = 10 s, so at t = 10 s its displacement is 0 and its velocity (the slope of the x–t graph) is 0. For uniformly accelerated straight-line motion, x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at² and v = v₀ + at. From v(10) = 0 we get v₀ = –10a; from x(10) = 0 we get x₀ + (–10a)(10) + ½a(10)² = 0, so x₀ = 50a. Substituting t = 5 s and x = 20 m gives 20 = x₀ + v₀(5) + ½a(5)² = 50a + (–10a)(5) + 12.5a = 12.5a, so a = 20/12.5 = 1.6 m/s². Final answer: 1.6 m/s².

Both paper tapes show counting points \(t_0\) through \(t_4\), with \(t_0\) at the 0 cm mark on each tape and \(t_4\) at the 8.0 cm mark on each tape, and the problem states that the time interval between consecutive counting points is the same for both tapes. Average velocity is defined as total displacement divided by total time, so for particle A the average velocity from \(t_0\) to \(t_4\) is \((8.0\ \text{cm} - 0)/(4T)\), and for particle B it is also \((8.0\ \text{cm} - 0)/(4T)\), where \(T\) is the common time interval between counting points. Since both particles have the same total displacement over the same total time, their average velocities are equal. Final answer: The average velocities of particles A and B are equal, \(\bar v_A = \bar v_B\).

The graph shows two straight-line velocity–time graphs, labeled 甲 (A) and 乙 (B), both starting from the origin, with A’s line steeper than B’s. For velocity–time graphs, displacement equals the area under the graph, so for motion starting from rest with constant acceleration the displacement from 0 to t1 is the triangular area \(x = \frac{1}{2} v t_1\), where \(v\) is the velocity at \(t_1\). At time \(t_1\), A’s velocity is greater than B’s velocity, and both have the same time interval, so the area under A’s graph is larger.
