The image shows the tall twin-tower structure of the “Twin Heroes of Heaven and Earth” ride, which matches the described motion. Since the braking system starts only when the cabin reaches 28 m above the ground, at 40 m the cabin is still in free fall with acceleration \(g\). For the 1 kg bottle, Newton’s second law gives \(mg - N = ma\), where \(a = g\); thus \(N = m(g - a) = 1(9.8 - 9.8) = 0\ \text{N}\). By Newton’s third law, the force the bottle exerts on the hand is equal to this normal force. Final answer: 0 N.

The left-hand block is a magnet whose right half is labeled S, so the right face of the magnet is a south pole and the magnetic field lines outside the magnet point toward the left into that S pole; coil P is wound around this end and is part of a closed circuit with coil Q. When coil P swings to the right, it moves away from the magnet, so the leftward magnetic flux through P decreases. By Lenz’s law, the induced current must produce a magnetic field directed to the left to oppose this decrease in flux. Using the right-hand rule for a solenoid, a leftward magnetic field corresponds to a current that, when viewed from the right side looking toward the left, flows clockwise. Final answer: clockwise.

The image shows a copper disk rotating about a vertical copper axle in a uniform magnetic field \(B\) directed vertically upward, with copper sheet \(P\) contacting the disk’s edge, copper sheet \(Q\) contacting the axle, and resistor \(R\) connected between \(P\) and \(Q\). A rotating conducting disk in a magnetic field generates a motional emf between the axle and the rim; for a disk of radius \(r\) rotating with constant angular velocity \(\omega\), the induced emf is \(\mathcal{E}=\frac{1}{2}B\omega r^{2}\). Since \(B\), \(\omega\), and \(r\) are constant, the emf is constant, and the current through the resistor has magnitude \(I=\frac{\mathcal{E}}{R}=\frac{B\omega r^{2}}{2R}\), which is also constant. Final answer: The magnitude of the current through resistor \(R\) remains constant.

From Figure A the voltage has period \(T=2\times10^{-2}\,\text{s}\); for the first half-cycle \(u=100\,\text{V}\), and for the second half-cycle it is a sinusoidal half-wave with amplitude \(50\,\text{V}\). The ideal AC ammeter reads the rms current, so for the resistor \(R=100\,\Omega\) we first find the rms voltage: \(U_{\text{rms}}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{T}\int_0^T u^2\,dt}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}(100)^2+\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{(50)^2}{2}}=\sqrt{5000+625}=75\,\text{V}\). Then \(I_{\text{rms}}=\frac{U_{\text{rms}}}{R}=\frac{75}{100}=0.75\,\text{A}\). Final answer: 0.75 A.

In the circuit, a DC source and switch feed a series resistor \(R\) followed by the parallel combination of inductor \(L\) and bulb \(A\), while bulb \(B\) and capacitor \(C\) are connected in parallel across the supply lines. After the switch has been closed long enough for steady state, the capacitor is fully charged so no current flows through \(B\), and the inductor behaves as a resistor of resistance \(R_L\). Because \(L\) and \(A\) are in parallel, they share the same voltage \(V\), so the steady currents are \(I_L=V/R_L\) and \(I_A=V/R_A\); since \(R_L<R_A\), it follows that \(I_L>I_A\), meaning the inductor current is larger than the current for which bulb \(A\) is rated. When the switch is opened, the inductor current cannot change instantaneously and the only closed path available is through bulb \(A\), forcing this larger current through \(A\). Therefore the filament of bulb \(A\) overheats and burns out. Final answer: Yes, the filament of bulb A will be burned out.

In Figure A, the square frame has side length \(l\), total resistance \(R\), and is uniform, so each side has resistance \(R/4\); side \(ab\) carries the same current as the rest of the series frame. Figure B shows the magnetic field varying with a constant nonzero rate during each interval, producing a constant induced emf and hence a constant induced current magnitude. The heating power in side \(ab\) is given by \(P=I^{2}R_{ab}\), where \(R_{ab}=R/4\). Solving for the current gives \(I=\sqrt{\dfrac{P}{R/4}}=2\sqrt{\dfrac{P}{R}}\). Final answer: \(2\sqrt{\dfrac{P}{R}}\).

The diagram shows that the helicopter moves horizontally from C to D through the distance L, with the light rope making a constant angle β with the vertical; the other track features are not needed. Since the helicopter starts from rest and undergoes uniform horizontal acceleration a, the displacement relation L = ½ a t² gives a = 2L/t². For the camera there is no vertical acceleration, so vertical equilibrium gives T cos β = mg and the horizontal component of tension is T sin β = mg tan β. The horizontal air force opposes the motion, so the net horizontal force toward D is T sin β − F = ma. Substituting a and the tension component yields F = mg tan β − m(2L/t²) = m(g tan β − 2L/t²). Final answer: m(g tan β − 2L/t²).

The image shows a copper disk of radius \(L\) rotating in a uniform magnetic field \(\mathbf B\) directed perpendicularly downward through the disk, with wire \(a\) contacting the rim of the disk and wire \(b\) contacting the central axis, forming a closed circuit of total resistance \(R\). For a rotating conducting disk, each radial element at distance \(r\) from the center moves with tangential speed \(v=\omega r\), so the induced emf between the center and the rim is obtained by integrating the motional emf along a radius: \(\mathcal E=\int_0^L Bv\,dr=\int_0^L B\omega r\,dr=\frac12B\omega L^2\). By Ohm’s law, the current in the circuit is \(I=\frac{\mathcal E}{R}=\frac{B\omega L^2}{2R}\). Final answer: \(\displaystyle I=\frac{B\omega L^2}{2R}\).

In Figure B the magnetic induction B is positive (upward along the solenoid axis) and increases from t1 to t2, and the curve’s slope also increases, so the induced current in the solenoid–frame circuit grows. By Lenz’s law this induced current produces a magnetic field opposing the increasing upward field, i.e. downward inside the solenoid; using the right-hand rule the current in frame abcd flows d→a→b→c→d, so the magnetic field at ring L points out of the page and is increasing. The increasing outward flux through L induces a clockwise current in L (viewed from the front), and by the left-hand rule a clockwise current in an out-of-page magnetic field experiences a radially inward Ampere force. Therefore the ring tends to reduce its area. Final answer: L has a tendency to contract (shrink).

The figure shows a spring D holding an armature F, with a contact set C and two coils A and B wound on the same iron core; coil A is in series with switch S1 and a battery, while coil B forms a closed circuit through switch S2. When S1 is opened, the current in coil A begins to decrease, causing the magnetic flux through the core to drop; because coil B is short-circuited, this changing flux induces a current in coil B, and by Lenz’s law the induced current creates a magnetic field that opposes the decrease, so the electromagnet remains energized for a short time and delays the release of D. Final answer: coil B.

The image shows “Luojia-1” in a circular orbit of radius \(R\) centered on Earth. For uniform circular motion, the angular speed is the angle swept divided by the elapsed time, so \(\omega=\theta/t\). The orbital period is the time to sweep \(2\pi\) radians, giving \(T=2\pi/\omega\). Substituting \(\omega=\theta/t\) yields \(T=2\pi t/\theta\). The given \(G\) and \(R\) are not needed to find the period from the stated angular displacement. Final answer: \(T=\dfrac{2\pi t}{\theta}\).

The x-t graph shows two curves, labeled 甲 (Car A) and 乙 (Car B), both starting from the origin O, with the two curves intersecting at time t1. In an x-t graph, the vertical coordinate represents the position x of an object relative to the starting point, and an intersection point of two curves means both objects have the same position at that same moment. Therefore, at time t1, Car A and Car B have the same displacement from the starting point and are located at the same position, which means the two cars meet. Final answer: The two cars are at the same position (they meet).

The voltage waveform in Figure A has period \(T=2\times10^{-2}\,\text{s}\); from \(0\) to \(1\times10^{-2}\,\text{s}\) the voltage is constant at \(100\,\text{V}\), and from \(1\times10^{-2}\,\text{s}\) to \(2\times10^{-2}\,\text{s}\) it follows a negative half-sinusoid with amplitude \(50\,\text{V}\). For a resistor, the ammeter reads the rms current \(I_{\text{rms}}=U_{\text{rms}}/R\), where the rms voltage is found from the mean square value over one period: \(U_{\text{rms}}^2=\dfrac{1}{T}\int_0^T u^2\,dt\). The first half-period contributes \(100^2=10000\,\text{V}^2\); the second half-period, being sinusoidal with amplitude \(50\,\text{V}\), has a mean square value of \(\dfrac{50^2}{2}=1250\,\text{V}^2\). Averaging the two equal halves gives \(U_{\text{rms}}^2=\dfrac{10000+1250}{2}=5625\,\text{V}^2\), so \(U_{\text{rms}}=\sqrt{5625}=75\,\text{V}\). Therefore \(I_{\text{rms}}=\dfrac{75}{100}=0.75\,\text{A}\). Final answer: 0.75 A.

The left bar magnet has its S pole on the right, so the magnetic field at coil P, which is just to the right of this magnet, points leftward into the S pole. As coil P swings to the right it moves away from the magnet, so the leftward magnetic flux through the coil decreases. By Lenz’s law the induced current must produce a magnetic field directed to the left in order to oppose that decrease. Using the right-hand rule, a leftward magnetic field inside the coil corresponds to a current that is clockwise when the coil is viewed from the right looking toward the left. Final answer: clockwise.

The image shows a circle with uniformly distributed positive charges and three collinear points M, O, and N, with O at the center and M and N on opposite sides of O. For a uniformly charged insulating sphere, the electric field inside is directed radially outward from the center for positive charge, with magnitude given by \(E = \dfrac{kQ}{R^3}r\), where \(r\) is the distance from the center. Since M and N are at equal distances \(r = \frac{1}{2}R\) from O but on opposite sides, the field at M points away from O along the diameter toward M, while the field at N points away from O along the diameter toward N. Therefore, the electric field intensities at M and N have the same magnitude but opposite directions. Final answer: the electric field directions at M and N are opposite (radially outward from O, away from each other along the diameter).

The image shows workers on high-voltage power lines wearing full-body suits made of conductive metal mesh. A conductive enclosure surrounding an object acts as a Faraday cage: when exposed to a high external electric field, free charges in the conductor redistribute themselves on the outer surface until the electric field inside the enclosed volume is zero, so no electric current passes through the worker’s body. Therefore, the metal-woven shielding clothing uses the principle of electrostatic shielding by a Faraday cage. Final answer: Faraday cage (electrostatic shielding).

The ball is thrown horizontally from A, so its initial vertical velocity is zero, and both above and below MN there are no horizontal forces, meaning the horizontal component of velocity remains unchanged. From A to B the only acceleration is gravity downward, so the velocity change is entirely vertical and equals the downward vertical velocity acquired at B. From B to C the ball’s velocity becomes horizontal at C, meaning its vertical velocity returns to zero; since the horizontal component is still unchanged, the velocity change from B to C is again purely vertical and has the same magnitude as the vertical velocity at B. Therefore the magnitude of the velocity change from A to B equals the magnitude of the velocity change from B to C. Final answer: the two velocity-change magnitudes are equal, |Δv_AB| = |Δv_BC|.

The image shows two fixed charges A and B on a horizontal tabletop and a charge C threaded on a vertical insulating rod located at the midpoint of the line joining A and B, so C moves along the perpendicular bisector of AB. Because A and B carry equal and opposite charges +Q and -Q, the electric potential at any point on the perpendicular bisector is V = k(+Q)/r + k(-Q)/r = 0, where r is the equal distance from the point to A and to B. Therefore the electric potential energy of C is U = qV = 0 at every position along the rod and does not change; equivalently, the electric field on that bisector is horizontal, so the electric force on C is always perpendicular to its vertical displacement and does no work. Final answer: Yes, the electric potential energy remains unchanged.

In the figure, point A is at a fixed height h above the horizontal line through B, C is the foot of the vertical from A, and the two drawn inclines through A have angles θ1 and θ2 with different intersection points on the horizontal, so the total horizontal distance from B to C is unchanged. Let μ be the common coefficient of kinetic friction and L = BC. For an incline angle θ, the incline length is h/sin θ, the normal force is mg cos θ, and the friction work on the incline is μmg cos θ·(h/sin θ)=μmgh/tan θ=μmg·(horizontal projection CD). The remaining horizontal segment has length L−CD, giving friction work μmg(L−CD). Thus the total friction work is μmgL, independent of θ. By the work–energy theorem, ½mv²=mgh−μmgL, so v=√[2g(h−μL)], which is the same for both angles. Final answer: v1=v2.

The diagram shows two horizontal parallel plates separated by a distance d with a potential difference U between them, creating a uniform electric field in the region where oil droplets are sprayed. For an oil drop of mass m to remain suspended, the upward electric force must balance the downward gravitational force. The electric field between the plates is E = U/d, and the electric force on a charge q is F_e = qE. Setting this equal to the weight mg gives q(U/d) = mg, so the magnitude of the charge is q = mgd/U. Final answer: mgd/U.

The figure shows ions emitted from the origin \(O\) on the \(x\)-axis within a divergence angle \(\alpha\) that is bisected by the \(y\)-axis, so the boundary rays make angles \(\pm\alpha/2\) with the \(y\)-axis, and after deflection the ions land on the \(x\)-axis inside the segment \(MN\) of length \(L\), with \(M\) closer to \(O\) than \(N\). In a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to the plane, each ion moves in a circle of radius \(R = mv/(qB)\). For a ray emitted at angle \(\phi\) to the \(y\)-axis, the second crossing of the \(x\)-axis occurs at \(x = 2R\cos\phi\); hence the central ray (\(\phi=0\)) lands at \(N = 2R\), while the edge rays (\(\phi=\pm\alpha/2\)) land at \(M = 2R\cos(\alpha/2)\). The length of \(MN\) is therefore \(L = 2R - 2R\cos(\alpha/2) = 2R[1-\cos(\alpha/2)]\), which gives \(\cos(\alpha/2) = 1 - L/(2R) = 1 - qBL/(2mv)\). Final answer: \(\cos(\alpha/2) = 1 - \dfrac{qBL}{2mv}\).

The image shows two long straight parallel wires \(a\) and \(b\) carrying equal currents \(I\) in the same direction, indicated by the dots as out of the page, with \(O\) the midpoint of the line joining the wires and \(M\) and \(N\) located on the perpendicular bisector of that line at equal distances from \(O\). For a long straight wire, the magnetic field magnitude is \(B=\mu_0 I/(2\pi r)\), and its direction is given by the right-hand rule. Because the currents are in the same direction and \(M\) and \(N\) are symmetrically placed with respect to the two wires, the distances from each wire to \(M\) equal the corresponding distances to \(N\), so the total field magnitudes at \(M\) and \(N\) are equal. At \(M\), the fields from both wires add in the upward direction, while at \(N\) they add in the downward direction, so the two fields are opposite in direction. Final answer: the magnetic induction intensities at \(M\) and \(N\) are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.

The silicon photocell’s U–I curve \(a\) gives an open-circuit voltage of \(3.6\ \text{V}\) at \(I=0\), and the operating point with resistor \(b\) is the intersection at \(I=0.2\ \text{A}\), \(U=2.5\ \text{V}\). For a source with non-constant internal resistance, the internal resistance at the operating point is the ratio of the internal voltage drop to the current: \(r=\dfrac{E-U}{I}\). Substituting \(E=3.6\ \text{V}\), \(U=2.5\ \text{V}\), and \(I=0.2\ \text{A}\) gives \(r=\dfrac{3.6-2.5}{0.2}=\dfrac{1.1}{0.2}=5.5\ \Omega\). Final answer: \(5.5\ \Omega\)

In the x–t graph, curve 乙 represents car B; because car B is the front car and the cars move toward decreasing x, the front car has the smaller initial coordinate, x = 12 m. The velocity of car B is the slope of its x–t graph. The curve starts with a nearly horizontal tangent, so the initial velocity is small; as the curve becomes steeper, the magnitude of the velocity increases. The later part of curve 乙 is a straight line passing through about (10 s, 4 m) and (12 s, 0 m), whose slope is (0 − 4)/(12 − 10) = −2 m/s, so the velocity eventually becomes constant at about −2 m/s. Final answer: Car B’s velocity first increases in magnitude and then remains constant (negative direction, about −2 m/s).

The image shows ring A carrying a current I whose arrow, on the near side, points to the right, so as seen from above the current in A is clockwise; by the right-hand rule the magnetic moment and axial field of A point downward. As ring B falls coaxially from above, the downward magnetic flux through B increases while B is above the center plane of A, so Lenz's law requires an induced magnetic field upward, which corresponds to a counterclockwise current as seen from above—opposite to the clockwise current in A. After B passes below A, the downward flux through B decreases, so the induced field must be downward, corresponding to a clockwise current as seen from above—the same direction as the current in A. Final answer: When B is above A the induced current in B is opposite to the current in A; after B passes through A and is below it, the induced current in B is in the same direction as the current in A.

The battery’s left plate is the positive terminal and the coil is wound so that the visible front conductors slope downward to the right; by the right-hand grip rule the coil’s magnetic field inside points to the right. At the left end of the coil the field lines enter the coil, so the magnetic flux through the ring placed on the left is directed to the left and is increasing when switch S is closed. Lenz’s law requires the induced current to produce a magnetic field opposing this increase, i.e. directed to the right through the ring. Applying the right-hand rule to the ring, a magnetic field to the right corresponds to a current that is clockwise when viewed from the left. Final answer: clockwise (as viewed from the left).

The image shows a positively charged sphere with a uniform charge distribution, and points M, O, and N lie on the same straight diameter with O at the center, so M and N are symmetrically located inside the sphere at the same distance r = R/2 from O. For a uniformly charged insulating sphere, Gauss’s law gives the electric field inside at distance r from the center as E = kQr/R³, directed radially outward. Substituting r = R/2 yields E = kQ(R/2)/R³ = kQ/(2R²). Since M and N are at the same distance from the center, the field magnitudes are equal. Final answer: the electric field magnitude at both M and N is kQ/(2R²).

The image shows the Millikan oil-drop experiment apparatus, including a sprayer that produces oil droplets, two horizontal parallel plates with a potential difference U, and a microscope for observing the oil droplets. In this experiment, tiny oil droplets become electrically charged and are suspended between the plates; by balancing the downward gravitational force mg on a droplet with the upward electric force qE, where E = U/d is the electric field between the plates, the charge q on an individual droplet can be determined from qE = mg. Millikan observed that all measured droplet charges were integer multiples of a fundamental quantity, from which he deduced the charge carried by a single electron. Final answer: the charge of the electron (elementary charge).

The graph is a downward-opening parabola with its vertex at \((t_2,H_m)\) and roots at \(t_1\) and \(t_3\), so the particle’s position can be written as \(y(t)=-a(t-t_2)^2+H_m\) with \(a>0\), giving \(y(t_1)=y(t_3)=0\) and \(y(t_2)=H_m\). Since displacement relative to the origin \(O\) is just the position \(y(t)\), its rate of change is \(\frac{dy}{dt}=-2a(t-t_2)\), which is positive for \(t_1<t<t_2\), zero at \(t=t_2\), and negative for \(t_2<t<t_3\). Therefore, during the interval from \(t_1\) to \(t_3\), the displacement relative to \(O\) first increases from \(0\) to the maximum value \(H_m\), and then decreases back to \(0\). Final answer: It increases from 0 to \(H_m\) between \(t_1\) and \(t_2\), then decreases from \(H_m\) back to 0 between \(t_2\) and \(t_3\).

From Figure B, the alternating voltage is a sinusoid with maximum value \(U_m = 200\ \text{V}\) and period \(T = 2\times10^{-2}\ \text{s}\), so the angular frequency is \(\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{T} = \dfrac{2\pi}{2\times10^{-2}} = 100\pi\ \text{rad/s}\); since the waveform starts at the origin, its initial phase is zero, giving the instantaneous value \(u = U_m\sin(\omega t) = 200\sin(100\pi t)\ \text{V}\). The transformer turn ratio and the inductor coil in Figure A do not affect the expression for the primary voltage shown in Figure B. Final answer: \(u = 200\sin(100\pi t)\ \text{V}\).

The picture shows a high-speed maglev train, a car traveling at 100 km/h that brakes, a mortar shell being fired, and Liu Xiang finishing the 110 m hurdles in 13.07 s. A high-speed maglev train can move at constant velocity, so its acceleration may be zero, making option A correct. For the braking car, \(v_0=100\ \text{km/h}=\frac{250}{9}\ \text{m/s}\approx 27.78\ \text{m/s}\), and using \(0-v_0^2=2ax\) with \(x=31\ \text{m}\) gives \(a=-\frac{(27.78)^2}{2\times 31}\approx -12.4\ \text{m/s}^2\), not \(12.5\ \text{m/s}^2\), so B is incorrect. At the instant gunpowder ignites, the shell in the barrel is momentarily at rest but is acted upon by a large force, so its acceleration is not zero, making C incorrect. Liu Xiang’s average speed is \(\bar v=\frac{110}{13.07}\approx 8.42\ \text{m/s}\), so D is correct. Final answer: A, D.

The figure shows a cylindrical magnet A and a horizontal superconducting ring B levitating above it. When B is placed on A, the changing magnetic flux through B induces a current by Faraday’s law; because the ring is superconducting, its electrical resistance is zero, so the induced current does not decay through Joule heating. In the final stable levitation state, the upward magnetic force from this persistent current balances the weight of the ring, and the current must continue to flow to maintain the repulsive field and the flux through the loop. Therefore, the induced current still exists. Final answer: Yes, the induced current still exists.

When the switch S is closed toward a, the circuit containing source E1 and solenoid M is completed, so a current begins to flow through the coils of M and a magnetic field is established along the axis of the solenoid; because the switch was originally open, the magnetic flux through the nearby closed metal ring N increases suddenly from zero. According to Lenz’s law, the induced current in ring N must flow in the direction that opposes this increase in flux, so the magnetic field produced by the induced current points opposite to the solenoid’s field through the ring. This makes the face of the ring nearest the solenoid have the same magnetic pole as the facing end of the solenoid, producing a repulsive force between them. Therefore the ring is pushed away from the solenoid. Final answer: to the right.

The image shows a smooth inclined plane with angle θ, two blocks A and B of equal mass m connected by a light spring of stiffness k, and block B initially held against a fixed stop C while the system is at rest. Applying a constant force F up the incline to block A makes it move upward until B is just about to lose contact with C. For block A, the normal force does no work, gravity is conservative, and the spring force is also conservative, so the only non-conservative external force doing work is F. Using the work-energy relation W_F + W_g + W_spring = ΔK_A and noting that W_g = −ΔE_p,grav and W_spring = −ΔE_p,elastic, we get W_F = ΔK_A + ΔE_p,grav + ΔE_p,elastic, which is exactly the change in the mechanical energy of block A (including its kinetic, gravitational potential, and elastic potential energies). Final answer: the increase in the mechanical energy of block A.

The dots in the field region mean the uniform magnetic field points out of the page, and the rod ab is part of a circuit that includes the solenoid near the separate copper ring c. When ab moves leftward, the motional emf drives a current through the solenoid; for an induced current to exist in c, the solenoid current must change, because a constant current produces a constant magnetic flux and no induced current in c. A nearby conducting ring is attracted to the solenoid when the solenoid current is decreasing, since then the induced current in c is in the same direction as the solenoid current. The solenoid current is I = BLv/R, so decreasing current requires the rod’s leftward speed v to decrease. Final answer: the rod should move leftward while slowing down (decelerate to the left).

The image shows ring A constrained to move along a vertical rod and connected to hanging weight B by a light inextensible rope passing over a fixed pulley. At the instant considered, the rope segment between A and the pulley is horizontal, and A is rising with speed v1 along the vertical rod. Because the rope is inextensible, the speed of B equals the rate at which the length of the rope from A to the pulley changes, which is the component of A’s velocity along the rope. Since A’s velocity is vertical and the rope is horizontal at this instant, the angle between A’s velocity and the rope is 90°, so the component of A’s velocity along the rope is v1 cos 90° = 0. Therefore the speed of B is zero. Final answer: 0.

The figure shows two objects A and B of equal mass pressed against the vertical inner wall of a cylinder that rotates uniformly about its central vertical axis; both objects are at the same distance from the axis because they lie on the same cylindrical wall. For an object in uniform circular motion, the resultant (centripetal) force has magnitude \(F = m\omega^2 r\), where \(m\) is mass, \(\omega\) is angular speed, and \(r\) is the radius of the circular path. Since A and B have the same mass, share the same angular speed because they rotate with the cylinder, and have the same radius \(r\), their resultant forces magnitudes are equal. Final answer: \(F_A = F_B\) (the resultant forces are equal in magnitude).

The figure shows a rectangular coil with \(n\) turns rotating about axis \(OO'\) perpendicular to the uniform magnetic field \(B\), with the coil connected in series with resistor \(R\). The maximum induced emf is \(E_m = nBS\omega\). Substituting \(n=10\), \(B=\frac{2}{\pi}\,\text{T}\), \(S=0.2\,\text{m}^2\), and \(\omega=10\pi\,\text{rad/s}\) gives \(E_m = 10\cdot \frac{2}{\pi}\cdot 0.2\cdot 10\pi = 40\,\text{V}\). Since the coil starts from the neutral plane, the emf varies sinusoidally, so its rms value is \(E_{\text{rms}} = \frac{E_m}{\sqrt{2}} = 20\sqrt{2}\,\text{V}\). The total circuit resistance is \(R+r = 18+2 = 20\,\Omega\), giving rms current \(I_{\text{rms}} = \frac{E_{\text{rms}}}{R+r} = \frac{20\sqrt{2}}{20} = \sqrt{2}\,\text{A}\). The power consumed by resistor \(R\) is \(P_R = I_{\text{rms}}^2 R = (\sqrt{2})^2\cdot 18 = 36\,\text{W}\). Final answer: 36 W.

The image shows a monkey climbing upward along a vertical pole while the pole itself is carried horizontally by a person, with the monkey’s vertical rise along the pole labeled h and the horizontal ground displacement of the pole labeled x. Since the monkey’s motion relative to the ground is the vector sum of two perpendicular displacements—a vertical displacement h relative to the pole and a horizontal displacement x of the pole—its ground displacement magnitude is found using the Pythagorean theorem. The vertical motion is uniformly accelerated from rest, so h = ½ a t², and the horizontal motion is uniform, so x = v₀ t. Therefore the magnitude of the monkey’s displacement relative to the ground is √[x² + h²], which can also be written as √[(v₀t)² + (½ a t²)²] = √[v₀²t² + (a²t⁴)/4]. Final answer: sqrt(x^2 + h^2) (equivalently sqrt(v0^2 t^2 + a^2 t^4/4)).

The image shows two blocks, of masses m1 and m2 with m1 < m2, on a horizontal surface; force F1 on m1 is directed upward at an angle θ above the horizontal, and force F2 on m2 is directed downward at an angle θ below the horizontal, with |F1| = |F2| = F, and both blocks move the same horizontal distance d. The work done by a constant force is W = F d cos φ, where φ is the angle between the force and the displacement. For F1 the angle with the horizontal displacement is θ, giving W1 = F d cos θ; for F2 the angle with the horizontal displacement is also θ, giving W2 = F d cos θ. Therefore W1 and W2 are equal. Final answer: W1 = W2.

The image shows coil A connected in series with a switch and a sliding rheostat to an AC power supply M and N, while coil B is a closed multi-turn coil connected to a small bulb and placed near coil A. When the switch is closed, alternating current flows through coil A, producing a changing magnetic field; because coil B is adjacent to coil A, this changing magnetic field produces a changing magnetic flux through coil B, and by Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction an induced electromotive force is generated in coil B, driving an induced current through the bulb. Final answer: Yes, it is possible for the small bulb to light up.

The image shows the tall tower structure of the “Twin Heroes of Heaven and Earth” ride, which matches the scenario but supplies no numerical values, so the data come from the problem statement. During free fall from 76 m to 28 m, the cabin’s speed at 28 m satisfies \(v^2=2g(76-28)\). During braking over the remaining 28 m to a stop, \(0=v^2-2a(28)\), so \(a=\frac{76-28}{28}g=\frac{12}{7}g\). Since 15 m is within the braking zone, the hand must support the bottle against both gravity and the upward deceleration: \(N-mg=ma\), giving \(N=m(g+a)=1\cdot\left(g+\frac{12}{7}g\right)=\frac{19}{7}g=\frac{19}{7}(9.8)\,\text{N}=26.6\,\text{N}\). Final answer: 26.6 N.

The image shows the Sun, Earth, and Saturn with Saturn’s and Earth’s orbital paths around the Sun indicated by dashed ellipses. Using Kepler’s third law, which states that the square of a planet’s orbital period is proportional to the cube of its orbital radius (T² ∝ r³), the ratio of Saturn’s orbital period to Earth’s orbital period can be found if their orbital radii are known. Specifically, T_Saturn/T_Earth = (r_Saturn/r_Earth)^(3/2). Final answer: the ratio of their orbital (revolution) periods.

When S is closed toward a, battery E1 is connected to coil M; because the longer plate of E1 is on the right, that terminal is positive, so current enters the right end of M and leaves the left end. This makes the magnetic field in the iron core grow rapidly, so the magnetic flux through the closed metal ring N increases suddenly. By Lenz’s law, the induced current in N flows in a direction that creates a magnetic field opposing this increase, which makes the interaction between M and N repulsive. Therefore the ring is pushed away from the coil. Final answer: to the right (away from coil M).

The image shows a rectangular elevator cabin with a cable attached at the top center and a small shaded block resting on the cabin floor. For the elevator itself, the work done by the resultant force equals its change in kinetic energy by the work–energy theorem; since the elevator has mass M and its speed changes from v1 to v2, W_net = ΔK = ½M v2² − ½M v1² = ½M(v2² − v1²), which is also equal to M a H because v2² − v1² = 2aH for the constant upward acceleration a. Final answer: ½M(v2² − v1²).

The figure shows an ideal transformer with primary-to-secondary turns ratio 4:1; the primary is in series with a variable resistor and an AC source, while the secondary contains a fixed resistor \(R_0\) in series with a load resistor \(R\), and the voltmeter measures the voltage across \(R\). For an ideal transformer, \(U_1/U_2 = 4\) and \(I_1/I_2 = 1/4\). After the load is changed to \(R = 5R_0\), the voltmeter reads \(5.0\text{ V}\), so the secondary current is \(I_2' = 5.0/(5R_0)=1/R_0\). The total secondary resistance is then \(R_0+5R_0=6R_0\), giving secondary voltage \(U_2' = I_2'(6R_0)=6\text{ V}\), and primary current \(I_1 = I_2'/4 = 1/(4R_0)\). Since the input current is kept unchanged, the original secondary current is also \(I_2 = 4I_1 = 1/R_0\). Originally \(R=11R_0\), so total secondary resistance is \(12R_0\) and \(U_2 = I_2(12R_0)=12\text{ V}\). Therefore the original primary-coil voltage is \(U_1 = 4U_2 = 48\text{ V}\). Final answer: 48 V.

The figure shows a smooth horizontal rod on which block Q slides, a small smooth fixed ring at O, and a light rope passing over O: its left segment to Q makes angle θ with the horizontal, and its right vertical segment supports block P. Because the rod is smooth, the only horizontal force on Q is the tension component T cos θ directed toward O, so Q’s horizontal acceleration is a_Q = T cos θ / m_Q. The tension T remains positive while the rope stays taut, so for 0° ≤ θ < 90° we have cos θ > 0 and therefore a_Q > 0, meaning Q speeds up as it moves toward the vertical line through O. At θ = 90° the rope is vertical, cos θ = 0, and the horizontal force on Q vanishes, so a_Q = 0; for θ > 90° the horizontal component of tension reverses and Q begins to slow down. Hence Q’s speed is maximum when the left portion of the rope is vertical. Final answer: θ = 90° (π/2).

The figure shows a rectangular coil rotating about axis OO′, which is perpendicular to the uniform magnetic field B directed into the page, with the coil connected to an external resistor R. The maximum induced emf is \(E_{\mathrm m}=nBS\omega = 10\times \frac{2}{\pi}\times 0.2\times 10\pi\ \mathrm V = 40\ \mathrm V\), so the rms emf is \(E=\frac{E_{\mathrm m}}{\sqrt 2}=20\sqrt 2\ \mathrm V\). The total resistance of the circuit is \(R+r=18\ \Omega+2\ \Omega=20\ \Omega\), giving an rms current \(I=\frac{E}{R+r}=\frac{20\sqrt 2}{20}\ \mathrm A=\sqrt 2\ \mathrm A\). Therefore the electric power consumed on resistor R is \(P_R=I^2R=(\sqrt 2)^2\times 18\ \mathrm W=36\ \mathrm W\). Final answer: 36 W.

In the circuit, the two branches connected across the power supply are: an upper branch containing the self-inductance coil L and bulb L₁, and a lower branch containing resistor R and bulb L₂. When switch S is closed, the inductor opposes any sudden change in current through its branch according to the self-induced emf ε_L = -L ΔI/Δt, so at the instant the switch is closed the current through L₁ is essentially zero and L₁ is dark. Because the self-inductance coefficient L is very large, the current through L and L₁ rises only slowly; therefore the brightness of L₁ increases gradually from zero toward its steady-state value before the circuit becomes stable. Final answer: L₁ gradually becomes brighter (from dark to its normal steady brightness).

The frame is a right triangle with vertical side \(ab\) along the rotation axis, horizontal side \(bc\) of length \(l\), and hypotenuse \(ac\); the uniform magnetic field \(\mathbf B\) is directed upward parallel to \(ab\). Because \(\mathbf B\) is parallel to the rotation axis, the magnetic flux through the triangle is constant, so the total induced emf around the loop is zero, but side \(bc\) moves through the field. For a point on \(bc\) at distance \(r\) from the axis, the speed is \(v=\omega r\), and the motional electric field along \(bc\) is \((\mathbf v\times\mathbf B)\cdot d\mathbf r = B\omega r\,dr\); integrating from \(b\) to \(c\) gives \(\int_0^l B\omega r\,dr=\frac12 B\omega l^2\). This motional emf drives positive charge toward \(c\), so \(c\) is at the higher potential and \(U_b-U_c\) is negative. Final answer: \(U_{bc}=-\dfrac12 B\omega l^2\).

The image shows a right-triangular conducting frame abc with vertical side ab along the rotation axis, horizontal side bc, and hypotenuse ac; the uniform magnetic field B is directed upward, parallel to ab, and the frame rotates counterclockwise about ab with angular velocity ω. The magnetic flux through the frame is Φ = B·A = B A cos θ, where θ is the angle between B and the normal to the plane of the frame; because the rotation axis ab is parallel to B, rotating the frame about this axis does not change θ, so the flux remains constant. By Faraday’s law, the induced emf is ε = −dΦ/dt = 0, and therefore no current flows in the closed metal frame. Final answer: No, there is no current in the metal frame.

From Figure A the primary alternating voltage has a peak value of \(U_{1m}=22\sqrt{2}\ \text{V}\). For an ideal transformer the peak secondary voltage is \(U_{2m}=\dfrac{n_2}{n_1}U_{1m}\). With \(n_1=270\) turns and \(n_2=135\) turns, \(U_{2m}=\dfrac{135}{270}\times 22\sqrt{2}=11\sqrt{2}\ \text{V}\). The capacitor is connected in parallel with the secondary output, so the maximum voltage across it equals the peak secondary voltage, and the condition that the capacitor is just not broken down means this peak value is its breakdown voltage. Final answer: \(11\sqrt{2}\ \text{V}\) (about 15.6 V).

The v–t graph shows two particles starting from the same point and moving together from rest to 4 m/s during the first 3 s; after t = 3 s, particle A (甲) continues to speed up to 6 m/s at t = 5 s, while particle B (乙) stays at 4 m/s. Displacement equals the area under the v–t graph. From 0 to 3 s, both particles travel the same distance: \(s_0=\frac12\times3\times4=6\ \text{m}\). From 3 s to 5 s, particle A travels \(s_A'=\frac{(4+6)}{2}\times2=10\ \text{m}\), and particle B travels \(s_B'=4\times2=8\ \text{m}\). Thus the total displacements at t = 5 s are \(s_A=6+10=16\ \text{m}\) and \(s_B=6+8=14\ \text{m}\), so the separation is \(16-14=2\ \text{m}\). Final answer: 2 m.

The image shows Earth at the center and a satellite on a dashed circular orbit whose orbital radius is labeled \(R\), measured from Earth’s center, and the orbit is clearly outside Earth’s surface, so \(R\) is greater than Earth’s radius. For a satellite in a circular orbit, gravity supplies the centripetal force: \(\frac{GMm}{R^2}=\frac{mv^2}{R}\), giving orbital speed \(v=\sqrt{\frac{GM}{R}}\). The value \(7.9\ \text{km/s}\) is the first cosmic speed, which is the orbital speed at Earth’s surface radius \(R_{\text{Earth}}\): \(7.9\ \text{km/s}=\sqrt{\frac{GM}{R_{\text{Earth}}}}\). Because Luojia-1’s orbital radius \(R\) is larger than \(R_{\text{Earth}}\), its orbital speed must be smaller: \(v=\sqrt{\frac{GM}{R}}<\sqrt{\frac{GM}{R_{\text{Earth}}}}=7.9\ \text{km/s}\). Final answer: less than 7.9 km/s.

The image shows a satellite moving on a circular orbit of radius \(R\) centered on Earth. Its angular speed is \(\omega = \theta/t\). For circular motion, gravity supplies the centripetal force: \(G M m / R^2 = m \omega^2 R\). Canceling the satellite mass \(m\) and substituting \(\omega = \theta/t\) gives \(M = \omega^2 R^3 / G = (\theta/t)^2 R^3 / G = \theta^2 R^3 / (G t^2)\). Final answer: \(M = \dfrac{\theta^2 R^3}{G t^2}\).

The image shows the docked combination of Tianzhou-1 and Tiangong-2 orbiting Earth, which can be treated as a single object in uniform circular motion around Earth. For an object in circular orbit, the gravitational force provides the centripetal force: \( \frac{GMm}{r^2} = m\left(\frac{2\pi}{T}\right)^2 r \), where \(M\) is Earth’s mass and \(m\) is the mass of the orbiting combination. Solving for Earth’s mass gives \( M = \frac{4\pi^2 r^3}{G T^2} \). Earth’s average density is \( \rho = \frac{M}{V} \), with volume \( V = \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 \). Substituting \(M\) and simplifying yields \( \rho = \frac{3\pi r^3}{G T^2 R^3} \). Final answer: \( \rho = \dfrac{3\pi r^3}{G T^2 R^3} \).

The skater is leaning sharply into a turn on ice, with his body angled toward the inside of the curve and one hand near the ice, indicating he is following a curved path around a bend. If he is skating at constant speed along a circular arc, his speed does not change but the direction of his velocity continuously changes, so he undergoes uniform circular motion. This motion requires a centripetal acceleration \(a_c = v^2/r\) directed toward the center of the circular arc, produced by a net centripetal force \(F_c = m v^2/r\), which in this case comes from the horizontal component of the ice’s reaction force and friction as he leans into the turn. Final answer: uniform circular motion.

The image shows an electron gun emitting electrons inside a glass bulb, with front and back excitation coils producing a magnetic field that is perpendicular to the electron velocity, causing the electrons to follow a circular trajectory. The electrons are accelerated by a fixed voltage U, so their kinetic energy is eU = ½mv², giving a constant speed v = √(2eU/m). The magnetic Lorentz force provides the centripetal force, so evB = mv²/r and the orbit radius is r = mv/(eB). Because v and the electron charge/mass are unchanged, r is inversely proportional to the magnetic field B. Increasing the current in the excitation coils strengthens B, so the radius r must decrease. Final answer: the radius becomes smaller (decreases).

The diagram shows a central metal wire connected to terminal B and the surrounding metal pipe wall connected to terminal A. Air molecules are ionized, electrons attach to dust particles giving them a negative charge, and these negatively charged dust particles then move to and stick on the metal pipe wall. For negatively charged dust to be attracted to the wall, the wall must be positively charged, so terminal A must be the positive pole; consequently the central wire at terminal B must be the negative pole to supply electrons and produce the ionizing corona. Final answer: A is connected to the positive pole and B is connected to the negative pole.

The image shows electric power workers wearing metallic shielding suits while working on high-voltage overhead conductors. A conductive shielding suit encloses the body and, when bonded to the energized conductor, forms an equipotential surface similar to a Faraday cage. In electrostatic equilibrium, the electric field inside a conductor is zero, so the conductive suit redistributes charge on its outer surface and cancels the external electric field within the enclosed volume. Consequently, the electric field strength inside the human body becomes very small, essentially zero. Final answer: approximately zero.

The image shows two vertical capacitor plates connected to a battery, with a charged small ball suspended between them by a light insulating string and held stationary. Because the plates remain connected to the power supply, the potential difference \(U\) between them stays constant, and the uniform electric field between parallel plates is \(E = U/d\). Moving the left plate to the left increases the separation \(d\), so \(E\) decreases. The horizontal electric force on the ball is \(F = qE\), so its magnitude decreases. In equilibrium the tension \(T\) balances the vector sum of the downward gravitational force \(mg\) and the horizontal electric force, giving \(T = \sqrt{(mg)^2 + F^2}\). Since \(F\) becomes smaller while \(mg\) is unchanged, the tension \(T\) becomes smaller. Final answer: \(T\) decreases.

The image shows a right-triangular region ABC containing a uniform magnetic field (the × symbols), with the right angle at B, so sides AB and BC are perpendicular. A charged ion moving in a uniform magnetic field follows a circular arc of period T = 2πm/(qB), and the time spent in the field is t = (θ/2π)T = θm/(qB), where θ is the central angle of the arc from entry to exit. Because the picture only indicates that the ion leaves through boundary AB and does not show the entry point, entry direction, charge sign, or field magnitude, the exact θ cannot be determined from the image alone. If the ion entered from the adjacent side BC and turned through 90° before exiting through AB, then θ = π/2 and t = T/4 = πm/(2qB). Final answer: t = θm/(qB); a specific numerical time requires the missing entry conditions (for a 90° turn, t = πm/(2qB)).

The figure shows a right‑isosceles triangular magnetic‑field region ABC with the right angle at B, AB vertical, BC horizontal, AC as the hypotenuse, and the field directed into the page (× marks). For a charged ion in a uniform magnetic field the circular motion period is \(T=\frac{2\pi m}{qB}\), so the time on an arc of central angle \(\theta\) is \(t=\frac{m\theta}{qB}\). The longest arc that can still leave through AC occurs when the ion’s circular path is tangent to AC; because the angle between AB and AC is \(45^\circ\), this critical arc subtends \(\theta = 180^\circ-45^\circ = 135^\circ = \frac{3\pi}{4}\), giving a maximum time \(t_{\max}=\frac{m}{qB}\cdot\frac{3\pi}{4}=\frac{3\pi m}{4qB}\). Therefore, if the ion’s time in the field exceeds \(\frac{3\pi m}{4qB}\), its central angle is larger than the critical \(135^\circ\), so the trajectory turns back and strikes side AB before ever reaching AC. Final answer: No, it will not still exit from side AC; it will exit from side AB.

The point charge \(-q\) lies on the symmetry axis to the right of \(a\), with \(a\!-\!q=d\), \(O\!-\!q=2d\), and \(b\!-\!q=3d\); points \(b\) and \(a\) are symmetric about the geometric center \(O\) of the uniformly charged plate. At point \(a\), the field due to the point charge \(-q\) has magnitude \(k\frac{q}{d^{2}}\) and points to the right (toward \(-q\)). Since the total field at \(a\) is zero, the charged plate must produce a field at \(a\) of magnitude \(k\frac{q}{d^{2}}\) directed to the left. Because the uniformly charged plate is symmetric about \(O\), the field it produces at the symmetric point \(b\) has the same magnitude but opposite direction. Therefore the magnitude of the electric field produced by the charged thin plate at point \(b\) is \(k\frac{q}{d^{2}}\), or equivalently \(\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}d^{2}}\). Final answer: \(\frac{kq}{d^{2}}\) (or \(\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}d^{2}}\)).

The image shows two point charges, \(Q_1\) at point \(A\) and \(Q_2\) at point \(B\), located on a straight dashed line. For the whole three-charge system to be in equilibrium, \(Q_3\) must lie on the line \(AB\) outside the segment \(AB\), on the side of the smaller-magnitude charge \(A\). Let \(AB=d\) and place \(Q_3\) a distance \(x\) beyond \(A\) on the side opposite \(B\). Using Coulomb’s law, the force on \(A\) due to \(B\) has magnitude \(kQ_1|Q_2|/d^2=4kQ_1^2/d^2\), and for equilibrium this must equal the force on \(A\) due to \(Q_3\), so \(kQ_1|Q_3|/x^2=4kQ_1^2/d^2\). Similarly, balancing the force on \(B\) gives \(k|Q_2||Q_3|/(d+x)^2=4kQ_1^2/d^2\). Dividing the first equation by the second yields \((d+x)^2/x^2=|Q_2|/Q_1=4\), so \((d+x)/x=2\), giving \(x=d\). Final answer: on the straight line \(AB\), outside segment \(AB\) on the side of \(A\), at a distance equal to \(AB\) from \(A\) (on the extension of \(BA\) beyond \(A\)).

The image shows a small ball at point M launched horizontally to the right with speed v0 in a region where a uniform magnetic field B points into the page and a uniform electric field E points downward. The magnetic force on a moving charge is q v cross B; for a positively charged ball, the right-hand rule gives an upward magnetic force because v is to the right and B is into the page. This upward force opposes the downward gravitational force and the downward electric force qE, so the net downward acceleration with B is g plus qE/m minus q v_x B/m, which is smaller than the no-B value g plus qE/m. Therefore the ball falls more slowly and stays in the air longer when the magnetic field is present. If the ball were negatively charged the magnetic force would be downward and t1 would be less than t2, and if it were uncharged t1 would equal t2. Since the diagram does not indicate the charge sign, the relation is not unique; assuming the usual positive charge, Final answer: t1 > t2.

The image shows a 220 V water heater whose protective ground wire is broken, indicated by the X on the grounding conductor, so if the heater leaks electricity the leakage current must return through a person. The electricity-isolating resistance (the high-resistance path, such as the water resistance in an anti-electric wall) and the human body resistance are connected in series across the 220 V supply. Using the series voltage-divider relation \(U_{\text{body}} = U_{\text{supply}} \times \frac{R_{\text{body}}}{R_{\text{iso}} + R_{\text{body}}}\), because the isolating resistance is much larger than the human body resistance, only a small fraction of the 220 V appears across the body and the current through the body is small. Final answer: The electricity-isolating resistance is much greater than the human body resistance, and the two are connected in series.

The image shows the ball at the start of a straight oblique path, with a vertical reference line and the trajectory forming an angle θ; no lengths or field direction are labeled. For straight-line motion from rest the net force must lie along the trajectory. Gravity has a component mg sinθ perpendicular to the trajectory, so the electric force must supply an equal and opposite perpendicular component, but its component along the trajectory can be zero. Since the work done by a constant force is W = F∥s, the electric field force may therefore do no work. Final answer: 0 (zero work is possible).

The diagram shows the charged ball at its release point, a vertical line representing the direction of gravity, and a slanted line representing the straight-line trajectory that makes an angle θ with the vertical. Because the ball is released from rest and moves along this straight line, the net force must be directed along the trajectory; gravity has a component perpendicular to the trajectory, so the electric force must provide an equal and opposite perpendicular component. The component of the electric force along the trajectory, however, is not fixed by the given information: it can be in the direction of motion, opposite to the motion, or zero, subject only to the net force still pointing along the path. Since the change in electric potential energy is ΔU = −W_E = −qE·s, where s is the displacement along the trajectory, the work done by the electric force can be positive, negative, or zero. Therefore the electric potential energy can decrease, increase, or remain unchanged. Final answer: It may decrease, increase, or remain unchanged.

The figure shows four identical quarter-circular arc currents, one in each quadrant, all circulating in the same clockwise sense around the origin O, while the straight wire sections lie along the coordinate axes and are stated to produce no magnetic field at O. Because the arcs are symmetric and identical, each quadrant’s arc contributes the same magnetic-field magnitude B at O in the same perpendicular direction, so the total field at O has magnitude 4B; by the right-hand rule the clockwise arc currents give a total field directed into the plane. For the small wire P of length L carrying current I along the +x axis, the Ampere force is F = I L × B_total, giving magnitude F = I L(4B) = 4BIL, and since L is along +x while B_total is into the plane, the right-hand rule gives the force direction along the +y axis. Final answer: the Ampere force has magnitude 4BIL and is directed along the positive y-axis.

In the figure, coil A has a vertically upward magnetic field B that is increasing with time, and the two straight wires a and b are parallel and attract each other; plasma enters from the left with speed v0 between the upper plate P1 and lower plate P2. Because B inside A is increasing upward, Lenz’s law requires the induced current to produce an opposing downward magnetic field inside the coil; using the right-hand rule for the solenoid with the winding shown, the induced current in the external left loop flows from B down through wire a to A, so the current in a is downward. Parallel current-carrying wires attract only when their currents are in the same direction, so the current in b is also downward, which means the upper plate P1 is positive and the lower plate P2 is negative. For positive ions moving to the right to be deflected upward toward P1, the magnetic force F = q v × B must point upward; with v to the right and F upward, B must be directed into the page. Final answer: the uniform magnetic field between the plates is perpendicular to the paper and directed inward (into the page).

The image shows a large pendulum ride with disk A at the lower end of the arm, swinging in a vertical arc about the top pivot. At the lowest point of the swing the tourists move fastest, so they have a centripetal acceleration directed upward toward the pivot. For a pendulum released from an amplitude of 120°, energy conservation gives the centripetal acceleration at the bottom as a_c = v²/L = 2g(1 − cos 120°) = 2g(1 + ½) = 3g upward. The seat must therefore supply a normal force N satisfying N − mg = ma_c, so N = m(g + 3g) = 4mg, which is greater than the usual mg; the stated motor acceleration of 4.3g is consistent with this large upward apparent weight. Because the net acceleration is upward, the tourists experience an apparent weight larger than their normal weight. Final answer: overweight.

The image shows a parachutist hanging beneath an open parachute canopy, where any wind force would act mainly horizontally on the canopy and the person. Because the wind force is horizontal, it produces horizontal acceleration but does not change the vertical forces or vertical acceleration. The vertical fall from rest is governed by \(y=\frac12gt^2\), so the time to descend a height \(h\) is \(t=\sqrt{2h/g}\). Since this expression contains no horizontal-force term, the falling time is unaffected by a purely horizontal wind force. Final answer: The falling time is independent of the horizontal wind force (assuming the wind has no vertical component and does not alter vertical motion).

As shown in the image, a cup of water rests on a platform scale and a small wooden ball is tied to the bottom of the cup by a thin string. When the string breaks, the ball rises toward the surface; because wood is less dense than water, an equal volume of water must move downward to fill the space the ball leaves, and since that water has more mass than the ball, the center of mass of the water-ball system accelerates downward. For the whole cup-water-ball system, Newton’s second law gives \(N - (M+m)g = (M+m)a_{\text{cm}}\), where \(N\) is the scale’s normal force (its reading), \((M+m)g\) is the total weight, and \(a_{\text{cm}}\) is the center-of-mass acceleration; a downward \(a_{\text{cm}}\) means \(N < (M+m)g\). Therefore the scale reading decreases while the ball is accelerating upward, and it returns to the original total weight once the ball reaches the surface and stops. Final answer: the scale reading decreases during the ball’s ascent.

The figure shows an ideal transformer whose primary coil is connected to an AC source through ammeter A; the secondary circuit contains series resistor R1, and a parallel combination of resistor R2 (with ammeter A2), resistor R3 with switch S, and a sliding rheostat R with contact P; voltmeter V measures the voltage across this parallel combination. For an ideal transformer the total secondary voltage is fixed by the primary voltage and the turns ratio, so as the sliding contact P moves upward the resistance inserted by the rheostat in its branch increases, the equivalent resistance of the parallel load increases, the total secondary current therefore decreases, the voltage drop across R1 decreases, and consequently the voltage across the parallel combination measured by V increases. Final answer: increases.

In Figure A the bright white line is the path of a car lamp during the exposure, and the zebra-crossing length shown in the photograph is L = 3 m; by comparing this scale with the streak, the streak length is roughly twice the zebra-crossing length, so the car traveled about 2L = 6 m. Figure B lists the exposure time as 1/2 s. Using average speed = distance/time, v = s/t ≈ 6 m / 0.5 s = 12 m/s. Final answer: about 12 m/s (about 43 km/h).

The pump body is a rectangular solid of length \(L_1\) with a square cross section \(L_2\times L_2\); the upper and lower faces are connected to the power supply and ammeter, so the current \(I\) flows vertically through the liquid across the electrode separation \(L_2\), while the magnetic field \(B\) is directed outward perpendicular to the current, giving a magnetic (Ampere) force \(F=BI L_2\) along the channel. The liquid resistance between the electrodes is \(R=\rho L_2/(L_1 L_2)=\rho/L_1\), so \(I=U/R=U L_1/\rho\), but for the pump efficiency the useful mechanical work in time \(t\) is the gravitational potential energy gained, \(W_{\text{out}}=mgh\), and the electrical energy supplied is \(W_{\text{in}}=UIt\) because the supply and ammeter are ideal. Therefore the efficiency is \(\eta=W_{\text{out}}/W_{\text{in}}=mgh/(UIt)\). Final answer: \(mgh/(UIt)\).

The image shows two horizontal parallel plates separated by distance d; the upper plate has a small hole and is marked positive, the lower plate is negative, so the uniform electric field points downward with magnitude U/d, and droplets A and B lie on the same vertical line. Before the voltage is applied both droplets fall uniformly, so their speed is v0 = h1/t and the force balance m0 g = k (m0)^(1/3) v0 gives k = (m0)^(2/3) g t / h1. After the voltage is applied, A continues with the same velocity, which means the electric force on A is zero, so A is neutral (q_A = 0). B moves upward uniformly with speed h2/t; the upward electric force on B implies B carries negative charge, and force balance |q_B| U/d = m0 g + k (m0)^(1/3) (h2/t) yields |q_B| = m0 g d (h1 + h2)/(U h1), so q_B = - m0 g d (h1 + h2)/(U h1). The change in electric potential energy of B as it rises h2 is delta U_elec = q_B (U/d) h2 = - m0 g h2 (h1 + h2)/h1 (its gravitational potential energy increases by m0 g h2). After A and B merge the new droplet has mass 2 m0 and charge q_B; the non-drag net force has magnitude |2 m0 g - |q_B| U/d| = m0 g |1 - h2/h1|, and the drag coefficient is k (2 m0)^(1/3) = 2^(1/3) m0 g t / h1, giving a terminal speed of |h1 - h2| / (2^(1/3) t), directed downward if h2 < h1 and upward if h2 > h1. Final answer: (1) k = (m0)^(2/3) g t / h1; (2) q_A = 0, q_B = - m0 g d (h1 + h2)/(U h1) (B negative); (3) delta U_elec = - m0 g h2 (h1 + h2)/h1 (gravitational increase m0 g h2); (4) terminal speed |h1 - h2| / (2^(1/3) t), downward for h2 < h1, upward for h2 > h1.

The image shows the thread fixed at O with length L; at A the string makes angle θ with the vertical OC, B is at the same height as O, and C is vertically below O, so the path from B to C is a quarter circle of radius L. At equilibrium at A, resolving forces gives T cosθ = mg and T sinθ = qE, so tanθ = qE/(mg) and the electric field is E = (mg tanθ)/q directed horizontally to the right (since the positive charge is displaced toward B). With the stated θ = 30°, tan30° = 1/√3, hence E = mg/(√3 q); the supplied sin37° and cos37° values correspond to θ = 37° and are not needed for θ = 30°. From B to C, gravity does work mgL while the electric field does work −qEL, so the work–energy theorem gives mgL − qEL = ½mv_C²; substituting qE/mg = tanθ yields v_C = √[2gL(1 − tanθ)] = √[2gL(1 − 1/√3)]. At C the electric force is horizontal and therefore does not contribute to the radial (vertical) equation, so T − mg = mv_C²/L, giving T = mg + 2mg(1 − tanθ) = mg(3 − 2 tanθ) = mg(3 − 2/√3). Final answer: E = mg/(√3 q) horizontally to the right; v_C = √[2gL(1 − 1/√3)] and T = mg(3 − 2/√3).

The image shows square glass block ABCD with vertical face AB, and the laser rays make a 45° angle with face AB, so the angle of incidence with the normal to AB is 45°. The image shows a horizontal cylinder of total length \(2l\); the piston of mass \(M\) is at the left end, the opposite end is closed, and the two small opposing baffles \(A\) and \(B\) are at the midpoint, so the piston is initially a distance \(l\) above the baffles and encloses a gas column of length \(2l\). With the cylinder horizontal the gas pressure equals atmospheric pressure \(p_0\); after slow rotation to vertical with the opening upward, the piston is in equilibrium with the gas below supporting atmospheric pressure and the piston’s weight, so \(pS=p_0S+Mg\). Because the cylinder is thermally conductive and the rotation is slow, the gas temperature stays \(T_0\), and Boyle’s law gives \(p_0(2lS)=phS\), where \(h\) is the final gas-column length; thus \(h=2l p_0S/(p_0S+Mg)\) and the piston’s descent is \(2l-h=2lMg/(p_0S+Mg)\), which is less than \(l\) because \(p_0S>Mg\), so the piston does not reach the baffles. If the gas were cooled at the constant pressure \(p\), its length would become \(h/2<l\), so before the temperature reaches \(T_0/2\) the piston is stopped by the baffles at length \(l\); applying the ideal-gas law between the initial state and the final state of volume \(lS\) at temperature \(T_0/2\) gives \(p_0(2lS)/T_0=p'(lS)/(T_0/2)\), so \(p'=p_0\). Final answer: the piston descends by \(2lMg/(p_0S+Mg)\) and the final pressure is \(p_0\).

The figure shows a small block of mass \(m\) at the left end of a wooden board of mass \(M\) and length \(L\), resting on a rough horizontal surface. The maximum static friction between the board and the ground is \(\mu_1(M+m)g=0.1\times2\times10=2\,\mathrm{N}\), and the maximum static/kinetic friction between the block and board is \(\mu_2 mg=0.4\times1\times10=4\,\mathrm{N}\). For \(F=1\,\mathrm{N}\), this is less than the ground’s maximum static friction, so the whole system remains at rest; the board exerts a static friction on the block equal and opposite to the applied force, giving a frictional force of \(1\,\mathrm{N}\). For \(F=5\,\mathrm{N}\), the system moves, ground kinetic friction is \(2\,\mathrm{N}\), and if there were no slipping the common acceleration would be \(a=(F-2)/(M+m)=3/2=1.5\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\); the required static friction would be \(f=M a+2=1.5+2=3.5\,\mathrm{N}\), which is less than \(4\,\mathrm{N}\), so no slipping occurs and the frictional force on the block is \(3.5\,\mathrm{N}\). For \(F=8\,\mathrm{N}\), the no-slip required friction would be \(f=M a+2\) with \(a=(8-2)/2=3\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\), so \(f=5\,\mathrm{N}>4\,\mathrm{N}\), hence slipping occurs with kinetic friction \(4\,\mathrm{N}\); the block’s acceleration is \((8-4)/1=4\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\), the board’s acceleration is \((4-2)/1=2\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\), the relative acceleration is \(2\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\), and the time to travel the relative distance \(L=1\,\mathrm{m}\) is \(t=\sqrt{2L/a_{\text{rel}}}=\sqrt{2\times1/2}=1\,\mathrm{s}\). Final answer: (1) \(1\,\mathrm{N}\); (2) \(3.5\,\mathrm{N}\); (3) \(1\,\mathrm{s}\).

As shown, the ball is suspended from point \(O\) directly above \(O^{\prime}\), where block A rests on plate B; the region left of \(O^{\prime}\) is smooth and the region right of \(O^{\prime}\) is rough. After the collision B moves left at \(2\ \mathrm{m/s}\) while A moves right at \(2\ \mathrm{m/s}\); the horizontal forces decelerating B are the rightward kinetic friction from A, \(\mu_1 m_A g\), and the rightward ground friction, \(\mu_2(m_A+m_B)g\), giving B a deceleration \(a_B=\frac{[\mu_1 m_A+\mu_2(m_A+m_B)]g}{m_B}=\frac{[(0.4)(0.1)+(0.225)(0.4)]10}{0.3}=\frac{13}{3}\ \mathrm{m/s^2}\). B stops after traveling \(d=\frac{v_B^2}{2a_B}=\frac{4}{2(13/3)}=\frac{6}{13}\ \mathrm{m}\), and since the remaining driving force is less than the maximum static ground friction, B stays at rest, so the ground-friction heat is \(Q=\mu_2(m_A+m_B)gd=(0.225)(0.4)(10)\left(\frac{6}{13}\right)\approx0.42\ \mathrm{J}\). Meanwhile A decelerates on the rough right side with \(a_A=\mu_1 g=4\ \mathrm{m/s^2}\), reaching zero velocity in \(t=\frac{v_A}{a_A}=\frac{2}{4}=0.50\ \mathrm{s}\); this time equals one quarter of the pendulum period, \(t=\frac{T}{4}=\frac{\pi}{2}\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}\), so \(L=\frac{4gt^2}{\pi^2}=\frac{4(10)(0.50)^2}{10}=1.0\ \mathrm{m}\). Final answer: \(v_A=2\ \mathrm{m/s}\), \(Q\approx0.42\ \mathrm{J}\), \(L=1.0\ \mathrm{m}\).

In the left picture the piston handle is pulled upward so the cylinder hangs from it, while in the right picture the cylinder is inverted and the handle rests on the ground, so the enclosed gas must support the cylinder. When the cylinder is suspended, the excess atmospheric force balances its weight: \((p_0-p_1)S=Mg\), giving \(p_1=p_0-\dfrac{Mg}{S}\). After inversion, the gas pressure supports the cylinder weight plus atmospheric pressure: \((p_2-p_0)S=Mg\), so \(p_2=p_0+\dfrac{Mg}{S}\). Returning the piston to its initial position means the gas volume returns to its initial value; for a fixed amount of ideal gas at constant volume, \(p/T\) is constant, hence \(T_2=T_1\dfrac{p_2}{p_1}=T_1\dfrac{p_0+Mg/S}{p_0-Mg/S}\). Final answer: \(p_1=p_0-\dfrac{Mg}{S}\); heat the gas to \(T_2=T_1\dfrac{p_0+Mg/S}{p_0-Mg/S}\) (a temperature rise of \(\Delta T=\dfrac{2MgT_1}{Sp_0-Mg}\)).

The diagram shows an ideal transformer whose primary coil is connected to the AC source \(u=U\sin\omega t\) and whose secondary coil is connected to an AC ammeter and a motor that is lifting a mass \(m\) upward at constant speed \(v\). Taking the turns ratio \(n\) to mean \(n=N_1/N_2\), the RMS primary voltage is \(U/\sqrt2\), and for an ideal transformer the current ratio satisfies \(I_0/I=N_2/N_1=1/n\), so the primary current is \(I_0=I/n\). The secondary RMS voltage is \(U_2=U_1/n=U/(\sqrt2\,n)\), hence the electrical power supplied to the motor is \(P=U_2I=UI/(\sqrt2\,n)\). The motor’s coil resistance dissipates power \(I^2R\), and because the load rises at constant speed the mechanical output power is \(mgv\); energy conservation for the motor gives \(P=I^2R+mgv\), so \(v=(P-I^2R)/(mg)=[UI/(\sqrt2\,n)-I^2R]/(mg)\). Final answer: \(I_0=I/n\), \(P=UI/(\sqrt2\,n)\), \(v=\dfrac{UI}{\sqrt2\,n\,mg}-\dfrac{I^2R}{mg}\).

The figure shows a smooth vertical insulating circular track of radius \(R=2\ \mathrm{m}\) in a uniform electric field \(E=1\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{N/C}\) directed horizontally to the right, with a positively charged ball constrained to the inner side of the track. The ball moves under a constant effective force combining gravity \(mg=4\ \mathrm{N}\) downward and electric force \(qE=3\ \mathrm{N}\) to the right, whose magnitude is \(\sqrt{(qE)^2+(mg)^2}=5\ \mathrm{N}\). For the ball just to complete the circle, the normal force vanishes at the point where this effective force points toward the center, so the centripetal condition gives \(mv^2/R=\sqrt{(qE)^2+(mg)^2}\); thus the minimum kinetic energy is \(K_{\min}=\frac12mv^2=\frac12R\sqrt{(qE)^2+(mg)^2}=\frac12(2)(5)=5\ \mathrm{J}\). At that critical point the height above the bottom is \(h=R+R\frac{mg}{\sqrt{(qE)^2+(mg)^2}}=2+2\cdot\frac45=3.6\ \mathrm{m}\) and the horizontal displacement to the left is \(R\frac{qE}{\sqrt{(qE)^2+(mg)^2}}=2\cdot\frac35=1.2\ \mathrm{m}\), giving gravitational potential energy \(mgh=14.4\ \mathrm{J}\) and electric potential energy \(qE(1.2\ \mathrm{m})=3.6\ \mathrm{J}\); hence the total conserved energy is \(E_{\text{total}}=5+14.4+3.6=23\ \mathrm{J}\). The mechanical energy \(K+U_g=E_{\text{total}}-U_e=E_{\text{total}}+qEx\) is smallest at the leftmost point \(x=-R\), so \(E_{\text{mech,min}}=23-qER=23-6=17\ \mathrm{J}\). The sum \(U_g+U_e=mgR(1-\cos\theta)-qER\sin\theta\) is minimized where \(\tan\theta=qE/(mg)=3/4\); with \(\cos\theta=4/5\) and \(\sin\theta=3/5\), this minimum is \(8(1-\frac45)-6(\frac35)=-2\ \mathrm{J}\). Final answer: minimum kinetic energy \(5\ \mathrm{J}\), minimum mechanical energy \(17\ \mathrm{J}\), minimum sum of gravitational and electric potential energies \(-2\ \mathrm{J}\).

The image shows a conveyor belt inclined at angle θ to the horizontal and driven clockwise so that the belt moves up the incline with speed v, while a block is launched from the bottom up the belt with speed v0. Taking up the incline as positive, the normal force is N = mg cosθ and the kinetic-friction magnitude is f = μN = μmg cosθ. While the block moves faster up the belt than the belt itself, friction points down the incline, giving a deceleration a1 = g sinθ + μg cosθ = 10·(1/2) + (√3/5)·10·(√3/2) = 8 m/s²; the block slows from 6 m/s to the belt speed 2 m/s in t1 = (6−2)/8 = 0.5 s, traveling s1 = (6+2)/2·0.5 = 2 m while the belt travels 2·0.5 = 1 m, so the relative slide up the belt is 1 m. After that the block is slower than the belt, friction points up the incline, and the deceleration becomes a2 = g sinθ − μg cosθ = 10·(1/2) − (√3/5)·10·(√3/2) = 2 m/s²; it stops after t2 = 2/2 = 1 s, moving an additional s2 = (2+0)/2·1 = 1 m while the belt moves 2·1 = 2 m, a relative slide down the belt of 1 m. The maximum upward distance is therefore l0 = 2 m + 1 m = 3 m, so the minimum belt length is 3 m. For the return trip the block slides down from rest; relative to the upward-moving belt it moves down, so friction still points up the incline and the downward acceleration is a3 = g sinθ − μg cosθ = 2 m/s². Covering l0 = 3 m requires 3 = ½·2·t3², giving t3 = √3 s; the belt moves up 2√3 m in this time, so the relative sliding distance down the belt is 3 + 2√3 m. The total scratch length is the total relative sliding distance: 1 m + 1 m + (3 + 2√3) m = 5 + 2√3 m. Final answer: l0 = 3 m, s = (5 + 2√3) m.

The image shows two symmetrical rough inclined tracks at \(60^{\circ}\) to the horizontal, smoothly connected to a smooth circular arc of radius \(R=2\,\mathrm{m}\) and central angle \(120^{\circ}\); the block starts from rest at a vertical height \(h=3\,\mathrm{m}\) above the bottom of the arc. The figure shows a rectangular coil \(ABCD\) rotating between the poles of a magnet, connected through slip rings \(F\) and \(E\) to the primary of an ideal transformer, with an ideal voltmeter and ammeter on the primary side and a resistor \(R\) on the secondary side. The maximum induced emf is \(E_m=nBS\omega=200\times \sqrt{2}\times 0.01\times 100=200\sqrt{2}\,\text{V}\). Since timing starts from the neutral plane, the instantaneous emf is \(e=E_m\sin\omega t=200\sqrt{2}\sin(100t)\,\text{V}\). The voltmeter reads the rms value of the primary voltage, \(U_1=\dfrac{E_m}{\sqrt{2}}=\dfrac{200\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}}=200\,\text{V}\). For the ideal transformer with turns ratio \(N_1:N_2=2:1\), the secondary voltage is \(U_2=U_1\dfrac{N_2}{N_1}=200\times \dfrac{1}{2}=100\,\text{V}\), and the secondary current is \(I_2=I_1\dfrac{N_1}{N_2}=2\times 2=4\,\text{A}\), so the resistance is \(R=\dfrac{U_2}{I_2}=\dfrac{100}{4}=25\,\Omega\). Final answer: \(e=200\sqrt{2}\sin(100t)\,\text{V}\); voltmeter reads \(200\,\text{V}\); \(R=25\,\Omega\).

The photograph shows a heavy ramming block supported radially by four bamboo poles, corresponding to the four equal upward forces \(F\) described in the problem. The total work done by the four people while lifting the block through height \(h_1\) is \(W=4Fh_1\); since the block starts from rest on the ground and returns to ground level, this work becomes the kinetic energy just before impact, so \(\frac12mv^2=4Fh_1\). Substituting \(F=450\ \mathrm{N}\), \(h_1=0.20\ \mathrm{m}\), and \(m=80\ \mathrm{kg}\) gives \(v=\sqrt{8Fh_1/m}=\sqrt{8(450)(0.20)/80}=3.0\ \mathrm{m/s}\). For the penetration, the ground’s average upward force \(F_{\text{avg}}\) and gravity act over \(h_2\); using \((F_{\text{avg}}-mg)h_2=\frac12mv^2\) yields \(F_{\text{avg}}=mg+\frac{\frac12mv^2}{h_2}=(80)(9.8)+\frac{360}{0.03}\approx1.28\times10^4\ \mathrm{N}\), and by Newton’s third law the block exerts an equal downward average impact force of the same magnitude. Final answer: 1. \(3.0\ \mathrm{m/s}\); 2. \(1.28\times10^4\ \mathrm{N}\) downward.

The image shows a light spring hanging from a fixed support with ball A attached to the lower end of the spring and ball B hanging below A by a string, so at rest the spring supports the combined weight of A and B. With total mass \(m_A+m_B=0.100\,\text{kg}+0.500\,\text{kg}=0.600\,\text{kg}\) and stretch \(x=0.15\,\text{m}\), Hooke’s law at equilibrium gives \(k=(m_A+m_B)g/x=(0.600)(10)/0.15=40\,\text{N/m}\). After the string is cut, A alone is supported by the spring; its new equilibrium stretch is \(x_0=m_A g/k=(0.100)(10)/40=0.025\,\text{m}\). Since the spring is initially stretched by \(0.15\,\text{m}\), the amplitude is \(A=0.15-0.025=0.125\,\text{m}\), equivalently \(A=m_B g/k=(0.500)(10)/40=0.125\,\text{m}\). For the resulting simple harmonic motion, \(\omega^2=k/m_A=40/0.100=400\,\text{s}^{-2}\), so the maximum acceleration is \(a_{\max}=\omega^2 A=400(0.125)=50\,\text{m/s}^2\). Final answer: \(k=40\,\text{N/m}\), amplitude \(=0.125\,\text{m}\), maximum acceleration \(=50\,\text{m/s}^2\).

The image shows a generator with internal resistance 1 Ω connected to a step-up transformer with turns ratio 1:4, a transmission line of resistance R = 4 Ω, and a step-down transformer with turns ratio 4:1 supplying the lamps. The total number of lamps is 22 × 6 = 132, each rated 220 V, 40 W, so the useful load power is 132 × 40 = 5280 W and the step-down secondary current is 132 × (40/220) = 24 A. Because the step-down transformer ratio is 4:1, its primary current is I2 = 24/4 = 6 A and its primary voltage is U3 = 4 × 220 = 880 V. The transmission-line voltage drop is I2R = 6 × 4 = 24 V, so the step-up secondary voltage is U2 = 880 + 24 = 904 V. With the step-up ratio 1:4, the generator terminal voltage is U1 = 904/4 = 226 V and the generator current is I1 = 4 × 6 = 24 A. Therefore the generator output power is P = U1I1 = 226 × 24 = 5424 W. The generator emf is E = U1 + I1r = 226 + 24 × 1 = 250 V. The transmission efficiency is η = 5280/5424 ≈ 0.973, or about 97.3%. If the number of lamps is halved, the load power becomes 2640 W, the step-down secondary current becomes 12 A, I2 becomes 3 A, the line loss becomes 3² × 4 = 36 W, and the generator output becomes 2640 + 36 = 2676 W, which is not half of 5424 W (2712 W). Final answer: generator output power 5424 W, generator emf 250 V, transmission efficiency about 97.3%, and no, halving the lamps does not halve the generator output power; it becomes 2676 W.

From Figure A the crosswalk width is \(L_1=4\,\mathrm{m}\), each lane width is \(L_2=3.6\,\mathrm{m}\), the car and truck are \(L_3=40\,\mathrm{m}\) from the stop line, the car length is \(D_1=4\,\mathrm{m}\) and the truck length is \(D_2=6\,\mathrm{m}\), and the pedestrian speed is \(v=1.2\,\mathrm{m/s}\); Figure B shows the cargo with front clearance \(d_1\) and rear clearance \(d_2\). For the car to completely pass the crosswalk it must travel \(L_3+L_1+D_1=40+4+4=48\,\mathrm{m}\) in this time, so \(48=v_1t+\tfrac12a_1t^2=12\cdot3+\tfrac12a_1\cdot3^2\), yielding \(a_1=(48-36)/4.5=8/3\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\). For the truck to completely pass it must travel \(L_3+L_1+D_2=40+4+6=50\,\mathrm{m}\) in \(3\,\mathrm{s}\), so \(50=10\cdot3+\tfrac12a_t\cdot3^2\) and \(a_t=40/9\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\); the cargo accelerates at \(4\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\), so the backward relative acceleration is \(a_t-4=4/9\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\) and the minimum rear clearance is \(d_2=\tfrac12(a_t-4)t^2=\tfrac12\cdot(4/9)\cdot9=2\,\mathrm{m}\). For the ball to just pass the highest point on a rope, the tension there can be zero and gravity alone supplies the centripetal force, so mg = m v_top^2 / L, giving v_top = sqrt(gL) = sqrt(10 * 0.5) = sqrt(5) m/s, about 2.24 m/s. When the string breaks at the lowest point, the maximum-tension condition gives T_max - mg = m v^2 / L, so v = sqrt(L (T_max - mg) / m) = sqrt(0.5 (42 - 10)) = 4 m/s. The break point is at height h - L = 5.5 - 0.5 = 5 m above the ground, so the fall time is t = sqrt(2 (h - L) / g) = sqrt(2 * 5 / 10) = 1 s and the horizontal range is x = v t = 4 * 1 = 4 m. Final answer: the speed at the highest point is sqrt(5) m/s (about 2.24 m/s); at the moment the string breaks the speed is 4 m/s and the horizontal range is 4 m.

The diagram shows particle \(P\) moving leftward along rough plank \(AB\), whose left end \(B\) meets the smooth quarter-circular slider \(CD\) at the arc’s entry point \(D\), all on a smooth horizontal surface. Treating plank \(AB\) and slider \(CD\) as separate bodies that interact with \(P\) only after \(P\) reaches the arc, horizontal momentum is conserved for the \(P\!+\!AB\) system while \(P\) is on the plank: \(m v_0 = m\frac{v_0}{2}+m v_{AB}\), giving \(v_{AB}=\frac{v_0}{2}\) to the left. The work done by kinetic friction equals the mechanical energy lost: \(\mu m g L=\frac12 m v_0^2-\left[\frac12 m\left(\frac{v_0}{2}\right)^2+\frac12 m\left(\frac{v_0}{2}\right)^2\right]=\frac14 m v_0^2\), so \(L=\frac{v_0^2}{4\mu g}\). After \(P\) enters the smooth arc, horizontal momentum and mechanical energy for the \(P\!+\!CD\) system give \(m\frac{v_0}{2}=2mV\) at the highest point \(C\), hence \(V=\frac{v_0}{4}\), and \(\frac12 m\left(\frac{v_0}{2}\right)^2=\frac12(2m)V^2+mgR\), yielding \(R=\frac{v_0^2}{16g}\). Final answer: \(v_{AB}=\frac{v_0}{2}\) (leftward), \(L=\frac{v_0^2}{4\mu g}\), \(R=\frac{v_0^2}{16g}\).

For \(y>0.4\ \mathrm{m}\) the magnetic force alone produces circular motion with radius \(R=mv/(qB)=v/[(q/m)B]=(2\sqrt2)/(10\cdot0.5)=0.4\sqrt2\ \mathrm{m}\); the entry force is along \((1,-1)\), placing the center at \((0.8,0)\), so it follows a \(90^\circ\) clockwise arc from \((0.4,0.4)\) to \((1.2,0.4)\), taking \(t_2=R(\pi/2)/v=0.1\pi\ \mathrm{s}\).
