The image shows two long parallel rails on a 30° incline; region I has a uniform magnetic field B directed perpendicularly into the inclined plane, region II has a uniform field B directed perpendicularly out of the plane, rod ab (mass m, resistance R) is held by posts in region I, and rod cd (mass 2m, resistance R) starts from rest in region II and slides downward. The two rods and rails form a series circuit of total resistance 2R, and the motional emf produced by the moving cd rod is BLv, so the circuit current is I = BLv/(2R). For rod ab to just leave the posts, the upward magnetic force on it must balance its downhill gravitational component, giving I LB = mg sin 30°, so I = mg/(2BL); because the current increases monotonically with v before ab moves, this is the maximum current in ab. Using I = BLv_t/(2R) then gives v_t = 2R I/(BL) = 2R mg sin 30°/(B²L²) = mgR/(B²L²). For the energy, the motion of cd satisfies 2m dv/dt = 2mg sin 30° − B²L²v/(2R), whose terminal velocity is v_T = 2mgR/(B²L²) and time constant τ = 4mR/(B²L²); at time t, v_t = v_T/2, so e^(−t/τ) = 1/2 and the displacement is x = (v_T/τ)(ln 2 − 1/2). The electrical energy generated by cd equals the work done by gravity on cd minus its kinetic-energy gain: E_cd = 2mg sin 30° x − (1/2)(2m)v_t² = (8 ln 2 − 5)m³g²R²/(B⁴L⁴). Final answer: v_t = mgR/(B²L²), E_cd = (8 ln 2 − 5)m³g²R²/(B⁴L⁴), I_{ab,max} = mg/(2BL).

The figure shows a circular region of uniform magnetic field directed into the page, centered at \(O\) with radius \(1\,\mathrm{cm}\). Magnetic flux through a coil is \(\Phi = N B A_{\perp}\), where \(N\) is the number of turns and \(A_{\perp}\) is the coil area that actually lies in the field. For coil \(A\), radius \(r_A=1\,\mathrm{cm}=0.01\,\mathrm{m}\), \(N_A=10\), and the coil exactly matches the field region, so \(\Delta \Phi_A = N_A \pi r_A^2 \Delta B = 10\pi(0.01)^2(0.4-0.8) \approx -1.26\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{Wb}\). For coil \(B\), radius \(2\,\mathrm{cm}\) exceeds the field radius, so only the field-filled area \(\pi(0.01)^2\) contributes, giving \(\Delta \Phi_B = \pi(0.01)^2(0.4-0.8) \approx -1.26\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{Wb}\). For coil \(C\), radius \(r_C=0.5\,\mathrm{cm}=0.005\,\mathrm{m}\) lies entirely in the field; rotating the field through \(30^\circ\) from the normal changes the flux by \(\Delta \Phi_C = B\pi r_C^2(\cos30^\circ-1) = 0.8\pi(0.005)^2(\cos30^\circ-1) \approx -8.42\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{Wb}\). Final answer: \(\Delta\Phi_A\approx-1.26\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{Wb}\), \(\Delta\Phi_B\approx-1.26\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{Wb}\), \(\Delta\Phi_C\approx-8.42\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{Wb}\) (magnitudes \(1.26\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{Wb}\), \(1.26\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{Wb}\), and \(8.42\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{Wb}\), respectively).

The cylinder is open at the top with a fixed retaining ring, piston A has a small hole so the space above piston B is open to the atmosphere, piston B encloses the ideal gas below it, and the two pistons are connected by a light spring; initially A is 10 cm from the ring, B is 10 cm from the bottom, and the distance AB is 10 cm. For piston A the pressure forces cancel because of the hole, so vertical equilibrium requires the spring to push upward with force equal to the weight of A, \(F_s = mg = 10\,\mathrm{N}\). For piston B the upward gas force balances atmospheric pressure, the weight of B, and the downward spring force, so \(pS = p_0S + 2mg\), giving \(p = p_0 + 2mg/S = 1.0\times10^5\,\mathrm{Pa} + 2(10\,\mathrm{N})/(5\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m}^2) = 1.4\times10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}\). Near a flat boundary only the half-space contributes, so the mean potential is -a' N/V. The potential energy densities are therefore U_i = (N/V)(-2 a' N/V) = -2 a' N^2/V^2 and U_b = (N/V)(-a' N/V) = -a' N^2/V^2; with v=0 Bernoulli's law P_i+U_i=P_b+U_b and P_i=N k_B T/V give P_b = N k_B T/V - a' N^2/V^2. The total energy is kinetic plus pair potential, E = (3/2) N k_B T - a' N^2/V. Assuming the free expansion doubles the volume from V to 2V, energy conservation gives (3/2)N k_B T_f - a'N^2/(2V) = (3/2)N k_B T - a'N^2/V, so T_f = T - a'N/(3k_B V). Because the interaction correction to the free energy, -a'N^2/V, is independent of T, the entropy to first order is the ideal-gas entropy; hence ΔS = N k_B ln(2V/V) + (3/2)N k_B ln(T_f/T) ≈ N k_B ln 2 - a'N^2/(2VT). Final answer: interior potential = -2 a' N/V; boundary potential = -a' N/V; boundary pressure = N k_B T/V - a' N^2/V^2; total energy = (3/2) N k_B T - a' N^2/V; final temperature = T - a' N/(3 k_B V) for expansion to 2V; entropy increase = N k_B ln 2 - a' N^2/(2 V T) to first order in a' N/(V k_B T).

The image shows a block of mass \(m\) on a smooth incline of mass \(M\) and inclination angle \(\alpha\); the block is attached to a light spring of natural length \(L\) and stiffness \(k\) fixed at the top of the incline, and the incline rests on a rough horizontal surface. For the equilibrium position, forces along the incline give \(k(l_{\text{eq}}-L)=mg\sin\alpha\), so the spring length is \(l_{\text{eq}}=L+\frac{mg\sin\alpha}{k}\). The block is released from a compressed length \(\frac{3}{4}L\), an initial compression of \(\frac{L}{4}\); since the equilibrium extension is \(\frac{mg\sin\alpha}{k}\), the amplitude of the simple harmonic motion is \(A=\frac{L}{4}+\frac{mg\sin\alpha}{k}\), and the maximum elongation beyond the natural length is \(x_{\max}=\frac{mg\sin\alpha}{k}+A=\frac{L}{4}+\frac{2mg\sin\alpha}{k}\). For the incline to remain stationary, resolve forces on it: the ground friction must satisfy \(f=kx\cos\alpha-mg\cos\alpha\sin\alpha\) and the ground normal is \(N_g=Mg+mg\cos^2\alpha+kx\sin\alpha\), where \(x\) is the spring extension. Requiring \(|f|\le \mu N_g\) and \(N_g>0\) yields \(\mu\ge \frac{\cos\alpha\left(mg\sin\alpha+\frac{kL}{4}\right)}{Mg+mg\cos^2\alpha-\frac{kL}{4}\sin\alpha}\). Final answer: (1) \(L+\frac{mg\sin\alpha}{k}\); (2) \(\frac{L}{4}+\frac{2mg\sin\alpha}{k}\); (3) \(\mu\ge \frac{\cos\alpha\left(mg\sin\alpha+\frac{kL}{4}\right)}{Mg+mg\cos^2\alpha-\frac{kL}{4}\sin\alpha}\), with \(Mg+mg\cos^2\alpha>\frac{kL}{4}\sin\alpha\).

For the piston in the final state, p2 S + M g = p0 S + m g, so the required weight mass is M = m + p0 S/g - Mi. Using the isothermal relation p1 S h = p2 S h' gives the final piston height h' = p1 h / p2, and the rise is h' - h = h(p1/p2 - 1) = h[(p0 S + m g)/(Mi g) - 1] = h(p0 S + m g - Mi g)/(Mi g). Final answer: the mass of the weight is M = m + p0 S/g - Mi and the height the piston rises is h(p0 S + m g - Mi g)/(Mi g).

The image shows a small ball at the bottom of a vertical circle of radius \(R\), attached to a rope of length \(R\). At the lowest point the tension is \(T=7mg\), so the net upward force provides the centripetal force: \(T-mg=m v_0^2/R\), giving \(7mg-mg=m v_0^2/R\) and \(v_0^2=6gR\). The decrease in mechanical energy equals the work done against air resistance: \(W=E_0-E_1=3mgR-\frac52 mgR=\frac12 mgR\). Final answer: \(\frac12 mgR\).

Final answer: \(I_{\max}=\frac{\pi^2Ba^2n}{R+r}\), average emf \(=2\pi Ba^2n\), \(q=\frac{\pi Ba^2}{2(R+r)}\), \(W=\frac{\pi^4B^2a^4n}{2(R+r)}\).

The image shows a square table with a small disk at the center of its horizontal top; one edge of the tablecloth lies along side \(AB\) and the cloth is pulled horizontally with constant acceleration \(a\) perpendicular to \(AB\). Let \(d\) be half the table side, the distance from the disk to edge \(AB\). While still on the moving cloth, kinetic friction accelerates the disk at \(\mu_1 g\); the trailing edge of the cloth therefore closes the initial gap \(d\) with relative acceleration \(a-\mu_1 g\), so the disk leaves the cloth after a time given by \(t_1^2=2d/(a-\mu_1 g)\). Its speed then is \(v=\mu_1 g t_1\), its displacement on the cloth is \(x_1=\frac12\mu_1 g t_1^2=\mu_1 g d/(a-\mu_1 g)\), and on the bare table it slides an additional distance \(x_2=v^2/(2\mu_2 g)=\mu_1^2 g d/[\mu_2(a-\mu_1 g)]\) before stopping. To keep the disk on the table, \(x_1+x_2\le d\), which gives \(\frac{g}{a-\mu_1 g}\left(\mu_1+\frac{\mu_1^2}{\mu_2}\right)\le 1\), and solving yields \(a\ge 2\mu_1 g+\frac{\mu_1^2}{\mu_2}g\). Final answer: \(a\ge \mu_1 g\left(2+\frac{\mu_1}{\mu_2}\right)\).

The spring is attached to the wall and to ball C, making an angle of 60° with the vertical; the light rope passes over the smooth fixed pulley on B, makes 30° with the vertical at C, and runs horizontally to block A; the system is at rest. For ball C, horizontal equilibrium gives T sin30° = F_s sin60° and vertical equilibrium gives T cos30° + F_s cos60° = m_C g; from the horizontal equation T = F_s√3, and substituting into the vertical equation gives F_s(3/2 + 1/2) = (1)(10) = 10 N, so the spring force is F_s = 5 N. Using F_s = kΔx with Δx = 0.02 m gives k = 5/0.02 = 250 N/m. The rope tension is therefore T = 5√3 N. Block A is pulled to the right by the horizontal tension, so the static friction exerted by B on A must be f_{B→A} = 5√3 N to the left. For object B, the rope pulls the pulley to the left with horizontal components T from the horizontal segment and T sin30° from the inclined segment, while A pushes B to the right with the reaction friction T; the net horizontal force on B is T − (T + T sin30°) = −T/2, so the ground must exert friction T/2 to the right, giving f_{ground} = (5√3)/2 N. Final answer: (1) 250 N/m; (2) 5√3 N, directed to the left; (3) (5√3)/2 N, directed to the right.

No usable image is available, so the solution relies only on the stated quantities. At maximum speed the net force is zero, so the traction force equals the resistance force \(f\); using \(P = Fv\) gives \(f = P/v\). When the car moves at speed \(v/4\) with rated power, the traction force is \(P/(v/4)=4P/v\), so the net force is \(4P/v - P/v = 3P/v\), and the instantaneous acceleration is \(a = (3P/v)/m = 3P/(mv)\). For the constant-acceleration start, the traction force is \(2f = 2P/v\), giving a net force \(2P/v - P/v = P/v\) and acceleration \(a_0 = P/(mv)\). This constant traction can be maintained only until the engine power reaches \(P\), which occurs at speed \(u\) satisfying \(2f \cdot u = P\); since \(f = P/v\), this gives \(u = v/2\). The time for uniform acceleration is therefore \(t = u/a_0 = (v/2)/(P/(mv)) = mv^2/(2P)\). Final answer: (1) \(P/v\); (2) \(3P/(mv)\); (3) \(mv^2/(2P)\).

The diagram shows a generator connected to a step-up transformer with coils \(n_1\) and \(n_2\), a transmission-line resistor \(R\) between the two transformers, and a step-down transformer with primary \(n_3\) and secondary \(n_4\) supplying the user. For an ideal transformer, the voltage ratio equals the turns ratio. The generator output is \(400\ \text{V}\) and the step-up secondary is \(2\ \text{kV}=2000\ \text{V}\), so \(\frac{n_1}{n_2}=\frac{400}{2000}=\frac{1}{5}\), i.e. \(1:5\). The transmission current is \(I=\frac{P}{V_2}=\frac{10\,000}{2000}=5\ \text{A}\). The line power loss is \(10\ \text{kW}-9.5\ \text{kW}=0.5\ \text{kW}\), so \(R=\frac{P_{\text{loss}}}{I^2}=\frac{500}{25}=20\ \Omega\), giving a voltage drop \(IR=5\times20=100\ \text{V}\). Thus the voltage at the step-down primary is \(V_3=2000-100=1900\ \text{V}\). With the user voltage \(V_4=220\ \text{V}\), \(\frac{n_3}{n_4}=\frac{1900}{220}=\frac{95}{11}\), i.e. \(95:11\). Final answer: \(\frac{n_1}{n_2}=1:5\), \(\frac{n_3}{n_4}=95:11\).

The rails are parallel and inclined at \(30^\circ\) to the horizontal, the metal rod \(MN\) is perpendicular to the rails, and the uniform magnetic field \(B\) is directed vertically upward. Because the current in \(MN\) is perpendicular to \(B\), the Ampere force on \(MN\) is horizontal and lies along the rail direction. For the smooth-rail case, resolving forces along the incline gives \(F_A\cos30^\circ=mg\sin30^\circ\), so \(F_A=mg\tan30^\circ=(0.017)(10)(1/\sqrt3)\approx0.10\,\text{N}\approx0.1\,\text{N}\). The current is \(I=F_A/(BL)=0.10/(0.60\times0.15)\approx1.1\,\text{A}\), and from \(E=I(R_1+R_2+r)\) we get \(R_2=E/I-R_1-r=10/1.1-4-1\approx4\,\Omega\). For the rough-rail case with \(R_2=10\,\Omega\), \(I'=E/(R_1+R_2+r)=10/15\,\text{A}\) and \(F_A'=BI'L=0.60\times(10/15)\times0.15=0.060\,\text{N}\), still directed up the incline. The downward gravitational component along the rails is \(mg\sin30^\circ=0.085\,\text{N}\), while the upward Ampere component is \(F_A'\cos30^\circ=0.060\times0.85=0.051\,\text{N}\); since gravity is larger, static friction must act up the incline with magnitude \(f=mg\sin30^\circ-F_A'\cos30^\circ=0.085-0.051=0.034\,\text{N}\). Final answer: (1) Ampere force \(\approx0.1\,\text{N}\), \(R_2\approx4\,\Omega\); (2) friction \(\approx0.034\,\text{N}\) directed up the incline.

The image shows a horizontal metal rod PQ suspended by two identical vertical springs, with a uniform magnetic field represented by dots pointing horizontally outward (out of the page/screen), and a current I flowing from P to Q along the rod. For equilibrium with the current on, the total upward spring force from the two springs balances the rod’s weight plus the downward Ampere force: \(2kx = mg + F_{\text{Amp}}\). Substituting \(k=100\,\mathrm{N/m}\), \(x=0.02\,\mathrm{m}\), \(m=0.1\,\mathrm{kg}\), and \(g=10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\) gives \(F_{\text{Amp}} = 2(100)(0.02) - (0.1)(10) = 4 - 1 = 3\,\mathrm{N}\). Using the right-hand rule for current to the right and field outward, the Ampere force is directed vertically downward. Since \(F_{\text{Amp}} = BIL\), the magnetic induction is \(B = F_{\text{Amp}}/(IL) = 3/(3 \times 2) = 0.5\,\mathrm{T}\). Final answer: the Ampere force is 3 N downward, and the magnetic induction is 0.5 T directed horizontally outward.

In the circuit the DC source with emf \(E\) and internal resistance \(r\) is in series with \(R_1\) and \(R_2\), and the capacitor is connected across \(R_2\), so the steady current is \(I=\dfrac{E}{R_1+R_2+r}=\dfrac{60}{8+15+2}=2.4\ \text{A}\) and the voltage across the capacitor equals the voltage across \(R_2\): \(U=IR_2=2.4\times15=36\ \text{V}\). The capacitance is therefore \(C=\dfrac{Q}{U}=\dfrac{6\times10^{-8}}{36}\approx1.67\times10^{-9}\ \text{F}\). The electric field strength between the plates is \(E_{\text{field}}=\dfrac{U}{d}=\dfrac{36}{0.04}=900\ \text{V/m}\). Since plate A is grounded at \(0\ \text{V}\) and the field points from A toward B, plate B is at \(-36\ \text{V}\); point C is \(1\ \text{cm}\) from B, i.e. \(3\ \text{cm}\) from A, so its potential is \(V_C=-E_{\text{field}}\times0.03=-900\times0.03=-27\ \text{V}\). Final answer: \(C\approx1.67\times10^{-9}\ \text{F}\), \(E_{\text{field}}=900\ \text{V/m}\), \(V_C=-27\ \text{V}\).

The device in Figure 1 shows eight aligned metal drift tubes with odd- and even-numbered tubes connected to opposite poles of an AC supply, and Figure 2 shows a square-wave voltage of amplitude U and period T, positive for 0<t<T/2 and negative for T/2<t<T. At t=0 the electron is at plate 0, which is connected to the even-numbered tubes, and V_odd−V_even=+U, so the electron is accelerated from the even plate toward cylinder 1; energy conservation across the first gap gives ½mv1²=eU, hence v1=√(2eU/m). Inside any cylinder the field is zero, so the electron moves at constant speed, and it must remain in each cylinder for half a period so that the next gap is crossed during the favorable half-cycle; thus in cylinder n the electron has speed v_n=√(2neU/m) after n accelerations, and the required length is L_n=v_nT/2=(T/2)√(2neU/m). For finite gap width d, the transit time across the kth gap is t_k=2d/(v_k+v_{k+1})=d√(2m/(eU))(√(k+1)−√k), and the cumulative gap time after N gaps telescopes to Σt_k=d√(2m/(eU))√N. To remain synchronized this total gap time must not exceed T/2, so N≤eU T²/(8md²) and the maximum attainable speed is v_max=√(2N eU/m), which in the continuous limit gives v_max=eUT/(2md). Final answer: v1=√(2eU/m); the electron accelerates uniformly in each gap and moves uniformly inside each cylinder, reaching v2=√(4eU/m) before exiting cylinder 2; L_n=(T/2)√(2neU/m); v_max=eUT/(2md), or more precisely √[(2eU/m)⌊eUT²/(8md²)⌋].

The source S is on the y-axis a distance d above the origin O and the collector lies on the positive x-axis; the field is into the page, so a negative particle moves clockwise in a circle of radius R=mv/(qB). For all first-quadrant directions to reach the x-axis the limiting direction is straight up, whose circular path has bottom at y=d−R; requiring d−R≤0 gives R≥d and thus v1≥(q/m)Bd=(2×10^6)(5×10^−3)(1.2)=1.2×10^4 m/s. With v2=8×10^3 m/s the radius is R2=v2/((q/m)B)=0.80 m and the angular speed is ω=(q/m)B=1.0×10^4 rad/s; the fastest arrival is for horizontal emission, sweeping a central angle of 120°=2π/3, so t_min=(2π/3)/ω=2π/(3×10^4) s≈2.1×10^−4 s. For v2 the reachable directions satisfy R2(1+cosφ)≥d, i.e. 0≤φ≤60°; the landing coordinate is x(φ)=R2 sinφ+√[R2^2−(d−R2 cosφ)^2], which gives x_min=√[R2^2−(d−R2)^2]=2√3/5 m at both φ=0 and φ=60°, and a maximum where dx/dφ=0, namely d−R2 cosφ=R2 cosφ or cosφ=d/(2R2)=0.75, so x_max=2R2 sinφ=0.4√7 m. The length of the collection region where two different directions hit the same point is therefore L=x_max−x_min=0.4√7−2√3/5≈0.365 m. Final answer: minimum speed 1.2×10^4 m/s, minimum time ≈2.1×10^−4 s, overlap length ≈0.365 m.

The rectangular parallelepiped has thickness \(a\) along the \(y\)-direction, width \(b\) along the \(z\)-direction, and length \(c\) along the \(x\)-direction; the current flows in the \(+x\) direction, the magnetic field is in the \(+y\) direction, and the Hall electric field is in the \(-z\) direction. (1) A free electron moves opposite the conventional current, so its velocity is along \(-x\); with \(\mathbf B\) along \(+y\), the Lorentz force \(\mathbf F=-e\mathbf v\times\mathbf B\) is along \(+z\). (2) The electron current is \(I_n=n e v_n (ab)\), giving drift speed \(v_n=I_n/(n e a b)\); the magnetic force on one electron is \(e v_n B = B I_n/(n a b)\). Because the Hall field points in \(-z\), the electric force on an electron is also in \(+z\) and has magnitude \(eE\); hence the net \(z\)-force magnitude is \(F_{nz}=B I_n/(n a b)+eE\). (3) The top surface has area \(ac\), so in time \(\Delta t\) the number of electrons reaching it is \(N_n=n a c v_{nz}\Delta t\) and the number of holes is \(N_p=p a c v_{pz}\Delta t\). In the steady Hall state the total \(z\)-current is zero, so the electron and hole \(z\)-currents are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction: \(I_{nz}+I_{pz}=0\), which gives \(-e n a c v_{nz}+e p a c v_{pz}=0\), or \(n v_{nz}=p v_{pz}\). Final answer: (1) \(+z\); (2) \(F_{nz}=B I_n/(n a b)+eE\); (3) \(N_n=n a c v_{nz}\Delta t\), \(N_p=p a c v_{pz}\Delta t\), and the \(z\)-direction currents satisfy \(I_{nz}=-I_{pz}\) (equivalently \(n v_{nz}=p v_{pz}\)).

The figure shows a square conducting frame abcd with horizontal top side ab; the region above the dashed line is a uniform magnetic field directed into the page, and the frame is thrown upward so that ab enters the field at speed \(v_0\). While the frame is entering the field, the upward applied force \(F\), gravity \(mg\), and the downward magnetic force \(F_{\text{mag}}=B^2l^2v_0/R\) balance, giving \(F=mg+B^2l^2v_0/R\). With \(F=2\,\text{N}\), \(m=0.1\,\text{kg}\), \(l=0.2\,\text{m}\), \(v_0=2\,\text{m/s}\), and \(R=0.08\,\Omega\), this yields \(B=1\,\text{T}\). The entry time is \(t_1=l/v_0=0.2/2=0.1\,\text{s}\); after full entry the force is removed, so the frame rises as a projectile for \(t_2=v_0/g=2/10=0.2\,\text{s}\), making the total time to the highest point \(t=t_1+t_2=0.3\,\text{s}\). At the highest point the frame is \(h+l+v_0^2/(2g)=0.8+0.2+0.2=1.2\,\text{m}\) above the ground; on falling back to the fully-in-field position its speed is again \(2\,\text{m/s}\) downward. Since \(mg=B^2l^2v_0/R=1\,\text{N}\), the magnetic force exactly balances gravity during exit, so the frame leaves the field at constant speed \(2\,\text{m/s}\); it then falls freely through height \(h=0.8\,\text{m}\), giving landing speed \(v=\sqrt{v_0^2+2gh}=\sqrt{4+16}=\sqrt{20}=2\sqrt5\approx4.47\,\text{m/s}\). The Joule heat equals the work done against the magnetic force during entry and exit: each stage dissipates \((B^2l^2v_0/R)l=1\times0.2=0.2\,\text{J}\), so the total heat is \(Q=0.4\,\text{J}\). Final answer: \(B=1\,\text{T}\); time to highest point \(=0.3\,\text{s}\); landing speed \(=2\sqrt5\,\text{m/s}\approx4.47\,\text{m/s}\); total Joule heat \(=0.4\,\text{J}\).

The image shows a positive ion of mass \(m\) and charge \(+q\) accelerated from rest through the voltage \(U_0\) between plates \(P\,(+)\) and \(Q\,(-)\), then entering the square uniform-field region \(abcd\) of side \(L\) at point \(a\) with speed \(v_0\) along \(ab\), while the uniform electric field is directed along \(ad\) from \(a\) toward \(d\). (1) Energy conservation in the accelerator gives \(qU_0=\frac12mv_0^2\), so \(U_0=\frac{mv_0^2}{2q}\). (2) If the ion exits at \(c\), horizontal motion gives \(L=v_0t\) so \(t=L/v_0\), and vertical motion gives \(L=\frac12\frac{qE}{m}t^2=\frac12\frac{qE}{m}\left(\frac{L}{v_0}\right)^2\), yielding \(E=\frac{2mv_0^2}{qL}\); since the vertical separation between \(a\) and \(c\) is \(L\), the potential difference is \(U_{ac}=\varphi_a-\varphi_c=EL=\frac{2mv_0^2}{q}\), with \(a\) at the higher potential. (3) When the ion leaves the boundary with kinetic energy \(mv_0^2\), the work done by the field equals the kinetic-energy increase: \(qEy=mv_0^2-\frac12mv_0^2=\frac12mv_0^2\), where \(y\) is the upward displacement from \(a\); thus \(E=\frac{mv_0^2}{2qy}\). The trajectory \(y=\frac{qE}{2mv_0^2}x^2\) combined with this \(E\) gives \(y=\frac{x^2}{4y}\), so \(x=2y\). On the square boundary the only consistent point is \(x=L,\;y=L/2\) on side \(bc\), giving \(E=\frac{mv_0^2}{qL}\). Final answer: \(U_0=\frac{mv_0^2}{2q}\); \(U_{ac}=\frac{2mv_0^2}{q}\) (with \(a\) at higher potential); \(E=\frac{mv_0^2}{qL}\).

The graph shows car A moving at a constant velocity of 4 m/s, while car B starts at 10 m/s and decelerates uniformly to rest at t = 5 s, giving B an acceleration of a_B = (0 − 10)/5 = −2 m/s². Taking A’s initial position as zero and B initially 35 m ahead, the separation is s(t) = 35 + (v_B − v_A) averaged over time, which for 0 ≤ t ≤ 5 s becomes s(t) = 35 + 6t − t². The maximum separation occurs when the velocities are equal, 10 − 2t = 4, so t = 3 s; substituting gives s(3) = 35 + 18 − 9 = 44 m. For a collision, set the positions equal; by t = 5 s, B has traveled ½·10·5 = 25 m and is at 60 m, while A has traveled 4·5 = 20 m, leaving a 40 m gap. After t = 5 s, B is stationary and A closes this 40 m gap at 4 m/s, requiring 40/4 = 10 s, so the collision occurs at t = 5 + 10 = 15 s. Final answer: the maximum separation is 44 m and a rear-end collision may occur after 15 s.

The diagram shows a rectangular coil \(ABCD\) in a uniform magnetic field \(B\) directed horizontally to the right; the coil is symmetric about the vertical rotation axis \(OO'\), with sides \(AB\) and \(CD\) parallel to \(OO'\) and sides \(BC\) and \(AD\) perpendicular to it, and it rotates about \(OO'\) with angular velocity \(\omega\). For a coil of \(n\) turns and area \(S\) starting from the neutral plane, the instantaneous emf is \(e=nBS\omega\sin(\omega t)\). Here \(S=l_{AB}l_{BC}=(0.2\,\text{m})(0.5\,\text{m})=0.10\,\text{m}^2\), so the maximum emf is \(E_m=nBS\omega=100(0.1)(0.10)(100\pi)\,\text{V}=100\pi\,\text{V}\); therefore the magnitude of the induced emf is \(|e|=100\pi|\sin(100\pi t)|\,\text{V}\), with maximum value \(100\pi\,\text{V}\). For the average emf from \(t=0\) to \(t=T/4\), \(\bar e=\frac{1}{T/4}\int_0^{T/4}E_m\sin(\omega t)\,dt=\frac{2E_m}{\pi}=\frac{2(100\pi)}{\pi}\,\text{V}=200\,\text{V}\). Final answer: the induced emf has magnitude \(|e|=100\pi|\sin(100\pi t)|\,\text{V}\) (maximum \(100\pi\,\text{V}\)), and the average emf from \(t=0\) to \(t=T/4\) is \(200\,\text{V}\).

The image shows a uniform magnetic field directed into the page above the horizontal screen MN, with the particle source P located on MN and PC drawn perpendicular to MN; particles of charge -q are emitted from P at a common speed v, with their directions spread within an angle θ = 60° on either side of PC, and the left-hand boundary of this spread is shown reaching the movable collection plate EF near point B. Each particle moves in a circular path of radius R = mv/(qB). Taking P as the origin and PC as the y-axis, a particle emitted at angle φ from PC has its circular center at (R cosφ, -R sinφ), so the highest point of that trajectory is y_max = R(1 - sinφ). The greatest height occurs for the left-hand boundary φ = -θ, which means the plate first collects particles when d = R(1 + sinθ); therefore R = d/(1 + sinθ) and v = qBR/m = qBd/[m(1 + sinθ)]. The same trajectory meets the screen MN again at x = 2R cosφ, so as φ ranges from -θ to θ the landing points on MN range from 2R cosθ to 2R, giving a hit length L = 2R - 2R cosθ = 2R(1 - cosθ). Substituting θ = 60° (sinθ = √3/2, cosθ = 1/2) yields v = qBd/[m(1 + √3/2)] = 2qBd/[m(2 + √3)] = (4 - 2√3)qBd/m and L = 2d(1 - 1/2)/(1 + √3/2) = 2d/(2 + √3) = (4 - 2√3)d. Final answer: v = (4 - 2√3)qBd/m, L = (4 - 2√3)d.

Figure 2 shows two layers of identical cylindrical concrete pipes, with pipe A in the top layer and pipe B in the bottom layer; A rests in the groove formed by two bottom-layer pipes, so the line joining the centers of A and B makes a 60° angle with the horizontal. For part 1, the weight of A is supported equally by the two bottom contacts, giving \(2N\sin 60^\circ = mg\), hence \(N=\frac{mg}{\sqrt3}=\frac{1500\times10}{\sqrt3}=5000\sqrt3\,\text{N}\approx 8.66\times10^3\,\text{N}\). For part 2, the maximum friction deceleration of a top pipe is found from the two contact normal forces: \(F_f=2\mu N=2\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{3}\cdot\frac{mg}{\sqrt3}=\frac{2}{3}mg\), so \(a_f=\frac{F_f}{m}=\frac{2}{3}g=\frac{20}{3}\,\text{m/s}^2\). Since the truck brakes harder at \(8\,\text{m/s}^2\), the top layer slides forward with relative acceleration \(a_{\text{rel}}=8-\frac{20}{3}=\frac{4}{3}\,\text{m/s}^2\). The initial speed is \(43.2\,\text{km/h}=12\,\text{m/s}\), so the truck stops in \(t=\frac{12}{8}=1.5\,\text{s}\); during this time the top layer moves relative to the truck \(s_1=\frac12\cdot\frac43\cdot(1.5)^2=1.5\,\text{m}\) and reaches a relative speed \(v_{\text{rel}}=\frac43\cdot1.5=2\,\text{m/s}\). After the truck stops, the top layer slides an additional distance \(s_2=\frac{v_{\text{rel}}^2}{2a_f}=\frac{4}{2\cdot20/3}=0.3\,\text{m}\). The required minimum gap is therefore \(s_1+s_2=1.8\,\text{m}\). Final answer: (1) \(5000\sqrt3\,\text{N}\approx 8.66\times10^3\,\text{N}\); (2) \(1.8\,\text{m}\).

The image shows a 5 m wooden rod suspended from a fixed point, with its upper end at the suspension point and its lower end initially 5 m below it; the upper end A of the 5 m tall cylinder is 20 m below the suspension point, so the rod's lower end must fall 20 m − 5 m = 15 m to reach A, and the rod's upper end must fall 20 m + 5 m = 25 m to clear the lower end B of the cylinder. Using free-fall displacement s = ½gt² with g = 10 m/s², the time for the lower end to reach A satisfies 15 = ½(10)t₁², giving t₁ = √3 s; the time for the upper end to reach B satisfies 25 = ½(10)t², giving t = √5 s, so the time to pass through the cylinder is t₂ = √5 − √3 s. Final answer: t₁ = √3 s, t₂ = (√5 − √3) s.

The figure shows a uniform magnetic field directed vertically downward through a planar coil abcd whose plane makes an angle θ with the horizontal; because the angle θ is marked between side cd and the horizontal, cd is the line of greatest slope of the inclined plane. Magnetic flux is Φ = B·S = BS cos α, where α is the angle between the magnetic field and the normal to the coil; since a horizontal plane has its normal vertical, tilting the plane by θ from the horizontal tilts its normal by θ from the vertical field, so α = θ and the initial flux is Φ_initial = BS cos θ = (0.6 T)(0.4 m²) cos 60° = 0.12 Wb. Rotating the coil about cd by 120° rotates the normal in a plane perpendicular to cd; the component of B parallel to cd contributes no flux, while the perpendicular component B cos θ is projected onto the new normal with factor cos 120°, giving Φ_final = BS cos θ cos 120° = (0.6)(0.4)(0.5)(−0.5) = −0.06 Wb. Thus the change is ΔΦ = Φ_final − Φ_initial = −0.06 Wb − 0.12 Wb = −0.18 Wb. Final answer: the magnetic flux through the coil is 0.12 Wb and the change after the 120° rotation is −0.18 Wb.

The diagram in Figure B shows the basketball launched from the left with speed v1 at angle θ to the vertical, traveling horizontally a distance L to the vertical backboard, rebounding, and then traveling horizontally another distance L to the basket, which lies a vertical distance h below the impact point. Since the launch angle is measured from the vertical, the initial components are v1x = v1 sinθ = 5(0.8) = 4 m/s toward the backboard and v1y = v1 cosθ = 5(0.6) = 3 m/s upward. The work done by the student equals the kinetic energy imparted to the ball, so W = ½mv1² = ½(0.6)(5)² = 7.5 J. The time to reach the backboard is t1 = L/v1x = 0.6/4 = 0.15 s, and the vertical velocity just before impact is v2y = v1y − gt1 = 3 − 10(0.15) = 1.5 m/s, while the horizontal velocity remains 4 m/s; therefore v2 = √(4² + 1.5²) = √18.25 ≈ 4.27 m/s. Because the backboard is vertical, the collision exerts only a horizontal impulse, leaving the vertical velocity component unchanged at 1.5 m/s upward. For the rebound motion to the basket, the vertical displacement satisfies −h = v3y t2 − ½gt2², so −0.2 = 1.5t2 − 5t2², giving the positive root t2 = 0.4 s; the post-impact horizontal speed is then v3x = L/t2 = 0.6/0.4 = 1.5 m/s, and v3 = √(1.5² + 1.5²) = √4.5 ≈ 2.12 m/s. The average horizontal impact force is found from the impulse-momentum theorem: the horizontal momentum changes from +mv2x to −mv3x, so F = m(v2x + v3x)/Δt = 0.6(4 + 1.5)/0.01 = 330 N. Final answer: W = 7.5 J, v2 ≈ 4.27 m/s, v3 ≈ 2.12 m/s, F = 330 N.

The image shows two horizontal parallel plates with the upper plate A marked negative and the lower plate B marked positive and grounded; points C and D lie between the plates, with C closer to A and D closer to B. Since B is grounded, \(V_B=0\). The electric field is uniform, so the potential varies as \(\Delta V = E\, \Delta x\). The image shows horizontal conducting rails with metal rod ab resting across them, current I flowing along the rod from a to b, and a uniform magnetic field B making an angle θ with the rail plane. Resolve B into a component parallel to the rail plane, B cosθ, and a component perpendicular to the plane, B sinθ; the current along ab is perpendicular to the rail direction, so the perpendicular component produces a horizontal magnetic force F_x = I L B sinθ along the rails, while the parallel component produces a vertical magnetic force F_z = I L B cosθ. By the right-hand rule this vertical force is upward, so the normal force is N = mg − I L B cosθ, and because the rod is just in equilibrium the horizontal magnetic force equals the maximum friction f = μN. Thus μ = (I L B sinθ)/(mg − I L B cosθ) = (1×0.5×2×0.6)/(0.2×10 − 1×0.5×2×0.8) = 0.6/1.2 = 0.5. When B is reversed, both magnetic-force components reverse, so the vertical force is downward and N′ = mg + I L B′ cosθ, while the horizontal force is I L B′ sinθ; the rod just begins to move when I L B′ sinθ = μ(mg + I L B′ cosθ). Substituting μ = 0.5 gives 0.5 B′ × 0.6 = 0.5(2 + 0.5 B′ × 0.8), which simplifies to 0.3 B′ = 1 + 0.2 B′, so B′ = 10 T. Final answer: μ = 0.5, B = 10 T.

The image shows a person standing in front of a vertical wall that contains a cylindrical hole, with the hole’s center at half the person’s height. Relevant quantities are: person height \(1.6\,\text{m}\), so the top of the person is \(0.8\,\text{m}\) above the hole center; the person is \(0.6\,\text{m}\) in front of the wall; the hole has diameter \(d=1.0\,\text{cm}\) and depth \(L=1.4\,\text{cm}\). For part 1, the limiting ray comes from the top of the person and enters the opposite edge of the hole. Its angle \(\theta\) with the wall normal satisfies \(\sin\theta = \dfrac{0.8}{\sqrt{0.8^2+0.6^2}} = 0.8\). The steepest ray that can pass straight through the filled hole goes from one edge of the entrance to the opposite edge of the exit, giving an internal angle \(\varphi\) with \(\tan\varphi = d/L = 1.0/1.4\), so \(\sin\varphi = \dfrac{d}{\sqrt{d^2+L^2}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2.96}}\approx 0.581\). By Snell’s law, \(1\cdot\sin\theta = n\sin\varphi\), hence the minimum refractive index is \(n_{\min}=\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\sin\varphi}=0.8\sqrt{2.96}\approx 1.38\). For part 2, light entering at a grazing angle in air has incidence angle \(90^\circ\), so Snell’s law gives \(1 = n\sin\varphi\). To exit the hole, this internal angle cannot exceed the maximum geometric angle, so \(\sin\varphi \le d/\sqrt{d^2+L^2}\). Thus \(n_{\min}=\dfrac{\sqrt{d^2+L^2}}{d}=\sqrt{2.96}\approx 1.72\). Final answer: (1) about \(1.38\); (2) about \(1.72\).

The image shows a long block of mass \(M\) on a smooth horizontal surface moving to the right with initial velocity \(v\), with a small block of mass \(m\) placed gently on its right end with no initial velocity. Because the surface is smooth, the only horizontal force on each block is the kinetic friction between them, of magnitude \(f=\mu mg\). The relative sliding distance is \(L\), so the heat generated is \(Q=fL=\mu mgL\). The long block’s displacement relative to the ground is \(l\), so the work done by friction on it is negative and its kinetic energy loss is \(fl=\mu mgl\). The small block starts from rest and is dragged forward by friction; since it slides backward a distance \(L\) relative to \(M\), its ground displacement is \(l-L\), and by the work–energy theorem its kinetic energy increase is \(f(l-L)=\mu mg(l-L)\). The reduction in the system’s mechanical energy equals the energy dissipated as heat, so it is also \(\mu mgL\) (equivalently, \(\mu mgl-\mu mg(l-L)\)). Final answer: heat generated \(=\mu mgL\); increase in kinetic energy of \(m\) \(=\mu mg(l-L)\); kinetic energy lost by \(M\) \(=\mu mgl\); reduction in system mechanical energy \(=\mu mgL\).

The image shows a vertical slide bar (rod) standing on a horizontal table, with a slide block initially at rest at point A near the bottom and point B at the top of the rod a distance l above A. When the block is at rest, the table supports the combined weight of the rod and block, so the support force is N1 = (M + m)g = (0.6 + 0.2) × 10 = 8 N. During the upward slide, the frictional force on the block is downward, so by Newton’s third law the rod experiences an upward frictional force f = 1 N; vertical equilibrium of the stationary rod gives N2 + f − Mg = 0, hence N2 = Mg − f = 0.6 × 10 − 1 = 5 N. The perfectly inelastic collision conserves momentum, mv1 = (M + m)v′, so v′ = (0.2 × 8)/(0.8) = 2 m/s, and the subsequent rise under gravity gives h = v′²/(2g) = 2²/(2 × 10) = 0.2 m. Final answer: N1 = 8 N, N2 = 5 N, v1 = 8 m/s, h = 0.2 m.

Hence after returning, V_A = (sqrt(5) - 1)V and p_B = p0 V/(2V - x) = p0/(3 - sqrt(5)) = (3 + sqrt(5))p0/4. Final answer: p_B = 2 p0 when V_B = V/2; V_A = 0.4 V; after the piston returns, V_A = (sqrt(5) - 1)V and p_B = (3 + sqrt(5))p0/4.

The figure shows a vertical circle with center O, lowest point A, highest point B, a uniform electric field directed horizontally to the right, and point C on the lower-left side such that C, O, D are collinear and the line makes angle θ = 37° with the vertical. Because the ball can remain stationary at C, the resultant of gravity and the electric force must be directed along OC, giving tan θ = qE/(mg). The effective constant force is then F = √[(mg)²+(qE)²] = √(4²+3²) = 5 N. For the ball to just complete the circle, it must reach D with zero normal force, so this effective force provides the centripetal force: F = m v_D²/r. The increase in potential energy from C to D equals the work done against the effective force over the diameter, 2Fr. Since both gravitational and electric potential energies are zero at C, the conserved total mechanical energy is E_mech = ½ m v_D² + 2Fr = ½ F r + 2 F r = (5/2)Fr = (5/2)(5)(0.5) = 6.25 J. Final answer: (1) 1.0×10⁵ N/C; (2) 6.25 J.

The figure shows an inclined plane at 37° to the horizontal; the small block is thrown horizontally with speed \(v_0\), falls a vertical height \(h=0.8\ \text{m}\), and lands on the front end of the long board, which starts from rest on the slope with a baffle at its lower end. The fall time is \(t_1=\sqrt{2h/g}=\sqrt{1.6/10}=0.4\ \text{s}\), so the vertical speed just before impact is \(v_y=gt_1=4\ \text{m/s}\); with horizontal speed \(v_0=3\ \text{m/s}\), the impact speed is \(\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5\ \text{m/s}\) and the velocity is \(53^\circ\) below the horizontal. After the collision the block has no along-plane component, so it accelerates down the plane at \(a_m=g\sin37^\circ=6\ \text{m/s}^2\), while the board, now carrying the block, has acceleration \(a_b=[Mg\sin37^\circ-\mu(M+m)g\cos37^\circ]/M=[3\cdot10\cdot0.6-0.5\cdot4\cdot10\cdot0.8]/3=2/3\ \text{m/s}^2\). The relative acceleration is \(a_m-a_b=16/3\ \text{m/s}^2\) and the initial relative velocity is \(-0.8\ \text{m/s}\), so the relative displacement along the plane is \(x_{\text{rel}}=-0.8t+(8/3)t^2\). The block reaches its maximum rearward displacement when the relative velocity vanishes: \(-0.8+(16/3)t=0\), giving \(t=0.15\ \text{s}\); thus the minimum board length is \(L=-x_{\text{rel}}(0.15)=0.8(0.15)-(8/3)(0.15)^2=0.06\ \text{m}\). In this same \(0.15\ \text{s}\) the board travels \(s_2=v_{b0}t+\frac12a_bt^2=0.8(0.15)+\frac12(2/3)(0.15)^2=0.1275\ \text{m}\) to the baffle, so the initial front-end-to-baffle distance is \(d=s_0+s_2=0.16+0.1275=0.2875\ \text{m}\). Final answer: (1) \(5\ \text{m/s}\), perpendicular to the inclined plane and directed into it (equivalently \(53^\circ\) below the horizontal); (2) \(0.06\ \text{m}\); (3) \(0.2875\ \text{m}\) (about \(0.29\ \text{m}\)).

In Figure 2 the plates are separated by distance l, with the left plate positive and the right plate negative, so the current in the liquid between the plates flows from left to right along the +x direction. For the Ampere force on this current to be upward (+y), the uniform magnetic field must be perpendicular to the Oxy plane in the negative z-direction (into the page). Let the plate width (container width) be w and the liquid height between the plates be h; the resistance of the liquid column is R = ρ l/(h w), so the current is I = U/R = U h w/(ρ l) and the current density is J = I/(h w) = U/(ρ l). The upward electromagnetic body force per unit volume is therefore f = J B = U B/(ρ l). Let the initial liquid height be h0, so the outside level remains h0 while the inside level is 2h0 at stabilization. The pressure at the bottom of the inside column equals the hydrostatic pressure at the same depth outside, p_atm + ρ0 g h0, and the top is at atmospheric pressure. For a static column with upward body force f, the pressure drop over height h is (ρ0 g − f)h, so (ρ0 g − f)(2h0) = ρ0 g h0, giving f = ρ0 g/2. Substituting f = U0 B/(ρ l) yields U0 = ρ0 g ρ l/(2B). For continuous rise the equilibrium height h = ρ0 g h0/(ρ0 g − f) diverges, so the threshold is f ≥ ρ0 g, i.e. U B/(ρ l) ≥ ρ0 g, hence U ≥ ρ0 g ρ l/B. Final answer: (1) B is directed into the Oxy plane, along the negative z-axis; (2) U0 = ρ0 g ρ l/(2B); (3) U must satisfy U ≥ ρ0 g ρ l/B.

The two rails are inclined at 37° to the horizontal, the conductor rod ab is placed perpendicular to the rails, and the uniform magnetic field B is directed perpendicularly upward from the rail plane; a DC source of emf E and internal resistance r is connected across the upper ends of the rails, so the total circuit resistance is R+r. The current is therefore I = E/(R+r) = 3/(1.0+0.5) = 2 A, and the Ampere force on the rod is F = BIL = 0.5 × 2 × 0.4 = 0.4 N. With the current in the rod flowing from a to b as implied by the source polarity in the diagram and B out of the plane, the right-hand rule gives the Ampere force directed up the incline. The downhill component of gravity is mg sinθ = 0.04 × 10 × 0.6 = 0.24 N, the normal force is N = mg cosθ = 0.04 × 10 × 0.8 = 0.32 N, and because the rod is just about to slide up the incline the maximum friction force μN acts downward along the rails. Equilibrium along the rails gives BIL − mg sinθ = μ mg cosθ, so μ = (0.4 − 0.24)/0.32 = 0.5. Final answer: the Ampere force is 0.4 N directed up the incline, and the coefficient of friction is 0.5.

(2) The maximum exit speed occurs when the belt is fast enough that the box accelerates all the way across: \(v_{\max}=\sqrt{v_0^2+2aL}=\sqrt{25+23}=\sqrt{48}=4\sqrt{3}\ \mathrm{m/s}\approx 6.93\ \mathrm{m/s}\). The minimum exit speed occurs for a stationary belt (or any slow belt the box cannot reach before leaving); since the box does not stop within \(L\) because \(v_0^2/(2a)=12.5\ \mathrm{m}>L\), \(v_{\min}=\sqrt{v_0^2-2aL}=\sqrt{25-23}=\sqrt{2}\ \mathrm{m/s}\approx 1.41\ \mathrm{m/s}\). (3) For \(v=6.0\ \mathrm{m/s}\), the box reaches belt speed in \(t=(6-5)/1=1\ \mathrm{s}\) after traveling \(s=(6^2-5^2)/(2)=5.5\ \mathrm{m}\); in the next \(1/12\ \mathrm{s}\) it moves with the belt an additional \(0.5\ \mathrm{m}\), so at \(\Delta t=13/12\ \mathrm{s}\) it is \(6.0\ \mathrm{m}\) along the belt with speed \(6.0\ \mathrm{m/s}\). The image shows a small block of mass \(m_{2}\) on a wooden board of mass \(m_{1}\) on a smooth horizontal surface, with a light spring fixed to a vertical wall on the right at its natural length. Before the board touches the spring, the block-board system has no external horizontal force, so momentum is conserved: \(m_{2}v_{0}=(m_{1}+m_{2})v\), giving \(v=\frac{4\cdot 5/4}{5}=1\ \mathrm{m/s}\). The friction force on the board is \(\mu m_{2}g=4\ \mathrm{N}\); the board’s kinetic energy increases from \(0\) to \(\frac12 m_{1}v^{2}=0.5\ \mathrm{J}\), so the distance its right end travels to the spring is \(x_{1}=0.5/4=1/8\ \mathrm{m}\). After contact, while the block and board move together the spring provides the common acceleration; impending slip occurs when the required static friction equals \(\mu m_{2}g\), so \(m_{2}a=\mu m_{2}g\) and \(kx_{2}-\mu m_{2}g=m_{1}a\), yielding \(kx_{2}=\mu g(m_{1}+m_{2})\) and \(x_{2}=\frac{0.1\cdot10\cdot5}{20}=1/4\ \mathrm{m}\). Energy conservation before sliding gives \(\frac12(m_{1}+m_{2})v^{2}=\frac12(m_{1}+m_{2})v_{2}^{2}+\frac12kx_{2}^{2}\), so \(v_{2}^{2}=1-\frac{20(1/16)}{5}=3/4\) and \(v_{2}=\sqrt3/2\ \mathrm{m/s}\). Once sliding begins the board undergoes simple harmonic motion about \(x_{\mathrm{eq}}=\mu m_{2}g/k=1/5\ \mathrm{m}\) with \(\omega=\sqrt{k/m_{1}}=2\sqrt5\ \mathrm{rad/s}\); it reaches zero velocity at time \(t_{0}\) and returns to compression \(x_{2}\) at time \(2t_{0}\), which is the next instant when the board’s acceleration again equals the block’s constant acceleration \(-\mu g\). During \(2t_{0}\) the board’s net displacement is zero, while the block moves a distance \(v_{2}(2t_{0})-\frac12\mu g(2t_{0})^{2}=\sqrt3\,t_{0}-2t_{0}^{2}\) relative to the board, so the friction-generated internal energy is \(\Delta U=\mu m_{2}g(\sqrt3\,t_{0}-2t_{0}^{2})=4\sqrt3\,t_{0}-8t_{0}^{2}\ \mathrm{J}\). Final answer: (1) \(v=1\ \mathrm{m/s}\); (2) \(x_{1}=1/8\ \mathrm{m}\); (3) \(x_{2}=1/4\ \mathrm{m}\); (4) \(v_{2}=\sqrt3/2\ \mathrm{m/s}\); (5) \(\Delta U=(4\sqrt3\,t_{0}-8t_{0}^{2})\ \mathrm{J}\).

The diagram shows a trolley on an inclined plane with a cable running along the plane over pulleys to a hanging counterweight and a motor driving the cable, so the counterweight supplies a constant up-slope tension m0 g and the motor supplies an additional up-slope force. The motor input power is UI = 380*40 = 15200 W, the resistive loss is I^2 R = 40^2*0.25 = 400 W, so the mechanical power is 15200 - 400 = 14800 W; at v = 2 m/s the motor pulling force is 14800/2 = 7400 N. For the loaded trolley, M = m1 + m2 = 1300 kg, uniform uphill motion gives F_motor + m0 g = M g sin(theta) + k M g, while for the unloaded trolley uniform downhill motion gives m1 g sin(theta) = m0 g + k m1 g. Dividing by g yields sin(theta) + k = (7400 + 400)/(1300*10) = 0.6 and sin(theta) - k = 40/100 = 0.4, so k = 0.1 and sin(theta) = 0.5. After the motor is turned off, the loaded trolley and counterweight coast together; their initial kinetic energy is 1/2 (M + m0) v^2 = 1/2 (1300 + 40)(2^2) = 2680 J, and the net force opposing the motion up the slope is M g sin(theta) + k M g - m0 g = 1300*10*0.5 + 0.1*1300*10 - 40*10 = 7400 N, giving L = 2680/7400 ≈ 0.362 m. Final answer: k = 0.1, L ≈ 0.36 m.

On the line segment \(S_{1}S_{2}\), the path difference ranges from \(0\) at \(B\) to \(4\,\mathrm{m}\) at \(S_{1}\) and \(S_{2}\), so constructive interference occurs when \(\Delta r=0,2,4\,\mathrm{m}\), corresponding to \(n=0,1,2\). The case \(n=0\) gives the single midpoint \(B\); \(n=1\) gives two symmetric points between \(B\) and the sources; \(n=2\) gives the two endpoints \(S_{1}\) and \(S_{2}\), giving \(1+2+2=5\) points in total. The work required to overcome the electric field in moving a charge q from infinity to a point equals the change in electric potential energy, so the electric potential at A is V_A = W_{ext}/q = (2×10^{-6} J)/(2×10^{-8} C) = 100 V. For the move from B to infinity, the work done by the electric field is W_field = q(V_B - V_∞), and with V_∞ = 0 this gives V_B = W_field/q = (8×10^{-6} J)/(2×10^{-8} C) = 400 V. The image shows a coordinate system with a radioactive source at the origin O, a uniform upward electric field E in the region 0≤y≤d, a uniform magnetic field B directed into the page (indicated by ×) in the region d≤y≤2d, and a photosensitive plate ab at y=2d. (1) A particle moving from y=0 to y=d gains work W=qEd=q(3mv0²/(2qd))d=3mv0²/2 from the electric field. By the work-energy theorem, ½mv²=½mv0²+W=2mv0², so the speed at y=d is v=2v0. (2) In the magnetic field the speed stays 2v0 and the circular radius is r=mv/(qB)=2mv0/(qB). Because the electric field is vertical, the horizontal velocity component is unchanged; for a particle emitted along the +x direction the entry angle into the magnetic field satisfies tanφ=√3, so φ=60°. For entry angle φ, the top of the circular path is y_max=d+r(1+cosφ), which is largest at the smallest φ, namely 60°. Requiring no particle reach y=2d gives d+r(1+cos60°)=2d, so r(1+½)=d and r=2d/3. Therefore B=mv/(qr)=m(2v0)/(q·2d/3)=3mv0/(qd). Final answer: (1) 2v0; (2) B=3mv0/(qd).

The figure shows gas entering ionization chamber A, where it is ionized into positive ions; the ions then move into the uniform electric field between electrodes A and B, are accelerated by the potential difference U, and exit to the right as an ion beam. For an ion of mass m and charge Ze starting from rest, energy conservation gives ZeU = ½mv², so the exit speed is v = √(2ZeU/m) and the momentum per ion is mv = √(2mZeU). With N ions entering per unit time, the thrust is F₁ = Nmv = N√(2mZeU), which gives N = F₁/√(2mZeU). The power used to accelerate the beam is P = N·½mv² = NZeU, so F/P = [N√(2mZeU)]/(NZeU) = √(2m/(ZeU)). Because F/P = √(2m/(ZeU)), it can be increased by increasing the ion mass m, decreasing the ion charge Ze, or decreasing the accelerating voltage U. Final answer: N = F₁/√(2mZeU); F/P = √(2m/(ZeU)); increase m, decrease Ze, decrease U.

With \(\vec C(0)=0\) this yields \(\vec C=(qBd/(2m))(\hat n_0-\hat n)\), where \(\hat n_0\) is the initial \(\hat n\). The torque about the center gives \(I\,d\omega/dt=-q dB\,(\vec C\cdot\hat e)\), and with \(I=m d^2/2\) and \(\vec C\cdot\hat e=(qBd/(2m))\sin\theta\) one obtains \(d\omega/dt=-(qB/m)^2\sin\theta\). Integrating gives the first integral \(\omega^2=\omega_0^2-2(qB/m)^2(1-\cos\theta)\). For the dipole to reverse its orientation, \(\theta\) must reach \(\pi\), where \(1-\cos\theta=2\); hence the minimum initial angular speed satisfies \(\omega_0^2=4(qB/m)^2\), so \(\omega_{\min}=2qB/m\). At this threshold, \(\omega=2(qB/m)\cos(\theta/2)\), so \(dt=d\theta/[2(qB/m)\cos(\theta/2)]\); using \(d\vec R/dt=\vec C=(qBd/(2m))(\hat n_0-\hat n)=(qBd/(2m))(\sin\theta,1-\cos\theta)\), the \(x\)-component of the center-of-mass displacement is \(x(\theta)=d(1-\cos(\theta/2))\). As \(\theta\to\pi\), the velocity tends to a constant vertical vector and the trajectory approaches the line \(x=d\), so the distance from the origin to the asymptote is \(D=d\). Final answer: \(\omega_{\min}=2qB/m\) and \(D=d\).

Because the equilibrium displacement is to the right, the electric force must also act to the right, so the ball carries a positive charge. At equilibrium the horizontal and vertical force balances are \(T\sin\alpha=qE\) and \(T\cos\alpha=mg\); dividing gives \(\tan\alpha=qE/(mg)\), so the charge is \(q=mg\tan\alpha/E\). For the third part, assuming the ball is pulled to the horizontal position on the same side as the field (to the right), its horizontal coordinate changes from \(l\) to \(0\), a displacement of magnitude \(l\) opposite to the electric force; thus the work done by the electric field is \(W=\vec F_e\cdot\Delta\vec x=qE(-l)=-qEl=-(mg\tan\alpha/E)El=-mgl\tan\alpha\). Final answer: the ball is positively charged; \(q=mg\tan\alpha/E\); the work done by the electric field is \(-mgl\tan\alpha\) (magnitude \(mgl\tan\alpha\)).

The star radiates as a blackbody with total luminosity \(L=4\pi R_s^2\sigma T_s^4\), so the solar flux at the planet's orbit is \(F=L/(4\pi R_0^2)=\sigma T_s^4(R_s/R_0)^2\), and the planet intercepts power over its projected disk area \(\pi R^2\), giving \(P=\pi R^2\sigma T_s^4(R_s/R_0)^2\). Each hemisphere has area \(2\pi R^2\), so steady-state radiative balance gives \(P=2\pi R^2\sigma(T_1^4+T_2^4)\); the heat winds must transport from the bright side to the dark side equals the dark side's emission, \(Q=2\pi R^2\sigma T_2^4=P\,x^4/(1+x^4)\). Treating the atmospheric circulation as a reversible heat engine, the mechanical wind power is this heat current times the Carnot efficiency \((1-T_2/T_1)=(1-x)\), so \(P_w=Q(1-x)=P\,(1-x)x^4/(1+x^4)\). Maximizing \(f(x)=(1-x)x^4/(1+x^4)\) on \(0\le x\le 1\) (set the derivative to zero or evaluate numerically) gives a maximum near \(x\approx0.77\) and \(f\approx0.06\). Final answer: \(P=\pi R^2\sigma T_s^4(R_s/R_0)^2\); \(P_w=P\,(1-x)x^4/(1+x^4)\); the maximum possible wind power is about \(0.06P\), roughly \(6\%\) of \(P\).

The diagram shows the right-triangular cross-section \(ABC\) with \(\angle A=90^\circ\), \(\angle B=60^\circ\), so \(\angle C=30^\circ\); \(AC\) is horizontal, \(AB\) is vertical, and the ray enters side \(BC\) at \(D\), refracts to \(E\) on \(AC\), undergoes total internal reflection, and exits through \(F\) on \(AB\). Since \(EG\perp AC\), \(EG\) is vertical, and \(D\) is the midpoint of \(CG\), the refracted segment \(DE\) makes a \(30^\circ\) angle with \(AC\). At \(D\) the normal to \(BC\) makes \(60^\circ\) with \(AC\), so the angle of refraction is \(r=30^\circ\); Snell’s law gives \(\sin i=n\sin r=n/2\). At \(E\) the ray meets \(AC\) at \(30^\circ\) to \(AC\), i.e. \(60^\circ\) to the normal, so total internal reflection requires \(n\sin60^\circ>1\), hence \(n>2/\sqrt3\). The reflected ray makes \(30^\circ\) above \(AC\), strikes vertical side \(AB\) at \(30^\circ\) to its normal, and at \(F\) Snell’s law gives \(\sin e=n\sin30^\circ=n/2=\sin i\); thus the emergent ray makes angle \(i\) with the horizontal. The incident ray at \(D\) makes angle \(i\) with the normal to \(BC\), which is \(60^\circ\) below the horizontal direction of the emergent ray, so the outgoing ray is deflected by \(60^\circ\) relative to the incident ray. In the ring plane, for \(r\ll R\) the distance to a charge element is \(R[1+(r/R)^2-2(r/R)\cos\theta]^{1/2}\); applying the given Taylor expansion and integrating over \(\theta\) yields \(\Phi(r)\approx q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0 R)+qr^2/(16\pi\varepsilon_0 R^3)\), so writing \(\Phi=\Phi_0+\beta r^2\) gives \(\beta=q/(16\pi\varepsilon_0 R^3)\) and the electron force at point B is \(F_r=-e(-2\beta r)=2e\beta r=eqr/(8\pi\varepsilon_0 R^3)\). For transverse focusing the sign is \(q<0\) (so \(\beta<0\)); treating the active region as a short lens of effective length \(d\) with constant radial force gives focal length \(f=-mv^2/(2e\beta d)\). The capacitance of a thin toroid of major radius \(R\) and minor radius \(a\) is \(C\approx 4\pi^2\varepsilon_0 R/\ln(8R/a)\). When the switch is thrown to \(V_0\) the ring charges as \(q(t)=CV_0(1-e^{-t/R_0C})\); because \(f/v\gg R_0C\) while \(d/v\sim R_0C\), the electron crosses the active region while the charge is still changing, so the effective charge is the average \(q_{\text{eff}}=CV_0[1-(R_0Cv/d)(1-e^{-d/(vR_0C)})]\), and the focal length becomes \(f=8\pi\varepsilon_0 mv^2R^3/(eq_{\text{eff}}d)\). The image shows a block of mass \(m\) on the left end of a plank of mass \(M\), with a rightward arrow labeled \(v_0\) and a vertical barrier to the right on a smooth horizontal surface. Since the problem statement says the system is given velocity \(v_0\) to the right, I take the initial condition as the block and plank moving together to the right at speed \(v_0\), with no initial relative motion. Before hitting the barrier the plank moves right at \(v_0\); an elastic collision with the massive fixed barrier reverses the plank's velocity, so just after the collision the plank moves left at \(v_0\) while the block, whose velocity is unchanged during the instantaneous impact, still moves right at \(v_0\). After the collision no external horizontal force acts on the block-plank system, so horizontal momentum is conserved: \(m v_0 + M(-v_0) = (m+M)V\), giving the final common velocity \(V=\frac{m-M}{m+M}v_0\); for \(M>m\) this is directed to the left with magnitude \(\frac{M-m}{M+m}v_0\). The kinetic energy just after the collision is \(\frac12(m+M)v_0^2\) and the final kinetic energy is \(\frac12(m+M)V^2=\frac{(m-M)^2}{2(m+M)}v_0^2\), so the energy dissipated by friction is \(\frac{2mM}{m+M}v_0^2\); equating this to the work done by friction, \(\mu mg\,\Delta x\), gives the relative displacement \(\Delta x=\frac{2M}{(m+M)\mu g}v_0^2\), with the block sliding to the right relative to the plank. For \(M<m\) the block would slide off the right end unless the plank is at least this long, so the minimum required length is the same. Final answer: (1) \(V=\frac{m-M}{m+M}v_0\), i.e. to the left with magnitude \(\frac{M-m}{M+m}v_0\) for \(M>m\); (2) \(\Delta x=\frac{2M}{(m+M)\mu g}v_0^2\); (3) \(L_{\min}=\frac{2M}{(m+M)\mu g}v_0^2\).

For the two-object reversible Carnot process the total entropy change is zero, so C ln(Tf/100) + C ln(Tf/300) = 0, which gives ln(Tf^2/30000) = 0 and Tf = sqrt(100*300) = 100 sqrt(3), approximately 173.2 K. The heat leaving the 300 K object is C(300 - Tf) and the heat entering the 100 K object is C(Tf - 100), so the work done by the engine is W = C(300 - Tf) - C(Tf - 100) = C(400 - 2Tf) = C(400 - 200 sqrt(3)), approximately 53.6 C. For the three-object reversible process, energy conservation gives T1f + T2f + T3f = 100 + 300 + 300 = 700 K and entropy conservation gives T1f T2f T3f = 100*300*300 = 9.0e6 K^3. To maximize the temperature of the third object the other two final temperatures must be equal, so set T1f = T2f = T; then 2T + TH = 700 and T^2 TH = 9.0e6, yielding T = 150 K and TH = 400 K. Final answer: Tf ≈ 173.2 K and W ≈ 53.6 C; TL = 100 K; TH = 400 K.

For ball A to remain at rest on the smooth track, the tangential components of the electric and gravitational forces must cancel: \(qE\cos60^\circ = mg\sin60^\circ\), which gives \(qE/2 = mg\sqrt3/2\) and therefore \(E = \sqrt3\,mg/q\). For ball B placed at \(b\), the central angle between \(a\) and \(b\) is \(60^\circ\), so the line from \(a\) to \(b\) makes a \(30^\circ\) angle with the horizontal and the Coulomb force from A on B acts along this line. Because B is in equilibrium with no force from the track, the Coulomb force must balance both gravity and the electric force; the upward vertical component requires A and B to attract, so \(Q_B\) is negative. The image shows a single sculls rower in a red racing suit with both oars in the water, corresponding to the power phase in which the oars exert a forward driving force on the boat. Let the constant resistance be \(f\); then the driving force is \(F=2f\). During the power phase the net force is \(F-f=f\), so the acceleration is \(a_1=f/m\); during the recovery/glide phase the net force is \(-f\), so the acceleration is \(a_2=-f/m\). Hence the ratio of acceleration magnitudes is \(1:1\). Let \(a=f/m\). The boat enters each power phase at \(4\ \mathrm{m/s}\); after one second of power its speed is \(4+a\), and after one second of recovery it returns to \(4\ \mathrm{m/s}\). Each phase therefore has average speed \((4+4+a)/2=4+a/2\) and, lasting \(1\ \mathrm{s}\), covers \(4+a/2\) meters. Over two strokes there are four such phases, so \(4(4+a/2)=20\), giving \(a=2\ \mathrm{m/s^2}\). The resistance is \(f=ma=60\times2=120\ \mathrm{N}\), the driving force is \(F=240\ \mathrm{N}\), and the maximum speed occurs at the end of a power phase: \(v_{\max}=4+2=6\ \mathrm{m/s}\). The power generated by the oars at this maximum speed is \(P=Fv_{\max}=240\times6=1440\ \mathrm{W}\). Final answer: \(1:1\); \(6\ \mathrm{m/s}\); \(1440\ \mathrm{W}\).

The figure shows two parallel horizontal rails a distance \(l\) apart, with two identical conductor rods AB and CD of length \(l\) placed perpendicular to the rails so that they form a closed conducting loop; rod AB is pulled to the right, CD is initially stationary on the left, and the uniform magnetic field is directed vertically downward. At \(t=t_1\), \(v_{AB}=at_1\) and the current is \(i_1=Bl(v_{AB}-v_{CD})/(2R)\), so the speed of CD is \(v_{CD}=at_1-2Ri_1/(Bl)=2R\mu mgt_1/(B^2l^2t_0)-2Ri_1/(Bl)\). After the external force is removed, let \(u=v_{AB}-v_{CD}\); the equations of motion give \(du/dt=-(B^2l^2)/(mR)\,u\), so \(u(t)=u_1\exp[-(B^2l^2/(mR))(t-t_1)]\) with \(u_1=2Ri_1/(Bl)\). When CD comes to rest at \(t=t_2\), \(v_{AB}(t_2)=u(t_2)\) because \(v_{CD}=0\), giving \(v_{AB}(t_2)=[2Ri_1/(Bl)]\exp[-(B^2l^2/(mR))(t_2-t_1)]\). Final answer: the acceleration of AB is \(2R\mu mg/(B^2l^2t_0)\), the speed of CD when the force is removed is \(2R\mu mgt_1/(B^2l^2t_0)-2Ri_1/(Bl)\), and the speed of AB when CD stops is \([2Ri_1/(Bl)]\exp[-(B^2l^2/(mR))(t_2-t_1)]\).
